curriculum.siteTagline: See how databases actually work: interactive internals from bytes on disk to planet-scale consensus.

parts.title: Foundations: Machines, Data and the Shape of an Engine
parts.summary: The physics of storage and durability, the data models and SQL a beginner needs, and a map of a database engine including a WAL primer so every later module has its anchors.

modules.title: Start Here: Routes, Depth and How to Read a Mechanism
modules.why: Ninety-odd modules and several hundred subtopics presented as one front-to-back sequence serve nobody by default: an application engineer who needs index selection, EXPLAIN and isolation should not be told to read the FTL and epoch reclamation first, an SRE who arrives mid-incident needs a symptom-shaped entry point rather than chapter one, and the distributed track needs exactly one module from Part 5 rather than all thirteen. A short opener that states the routes, the depth legend and the predict-then-run method keeps the linear order as the default rather than the only option — and every route, count and time estimate on this page is generated from the curriculum's own module and prerequisite data, so no route it prints can contradict the dependency graph it draws.

subtopics.title: Three routes through the same modules
subtopics.covers: The three engineering routes, each stated as legs of the real prerequisite graph rather than written in prose — the application-engineer route (Part 1 → sql-to-logical-plan → physical-operators → cost-based-optimization → explain-and-query-tuning → index-selection-strategy → Part 4 → Part 5 → Part 10), the storage-internals route (Parts 1–4 plus the relational case studies) and the distributed-systems route (Part 1 anatomy → transactions-and-isolation → application-access → Part 4 → Parts 6–9) — with what each route may skip, where it can legitimately stop, and the subtopic count and rough time per leg computed from the curriculum data.
subtopics.visual: An interactive dependency graph of every module where picking a route — or a goal such as 'make this query fast' or 'design a sharded store' — lights the minimal path computed from the declared prerequisites, greys the rest and totals subtopics and estimated hours live, with a validator that flags any hand-written route step whose prerequisites are not already lit and a toggle showing which greyed modules become prerequisites if a later goal is added.

subtopics.title: Routes for operators, data engineers and platform engineers
subtopics.covers: The three routes the engineering opener omits — the SRE/DBA route (anatomy of an engine → WAL and recovery → replication and replication-operations → vacuum horizons → Part 10 operating, backups and incidents), the data-engineer route (data models → column stores → analytical engines and lakehouse formats → logs and CDC → warehouse pipelines and analytics delivery, skipping Parts 4 and 7 almost entirely), and the platform-engineer route (provisioning and fleet lifecycle → managed services and cost → security and tenancy → capacity, storage and upgrades) — each with what it may skip, where it can legitimately stop, the subtopics it shares with the application route, and the sideways entry points (a Part 12 playbook or decision guide) an on-call reader should use instead of the linear order.
subtopics.visual: The same module dependency graph gains role presets alongside the existing three, so selecting 'SRE on call', 'data engineer' or 'platform engineer' lights that route's minimal path with subtopic counts and hours computed from the curriculum data, greys the rest, and marks the playbook and decision-guide pages as alternative entry arrows into the middle of the route rather than at its start.

subtopics.title: Depth levels, prerequisites and stopping points
subtopics.covers: What foundations, core, advanced and expert mean on this site, how the per-subtopic basics/intermediate/deep marks differ from the module level, how prerequisites are stated and when skipping one is safe, and the explicit 'enough for most engineers' markers inside long modules.
subtopics.visual: A module card expands into its prerequisite chain read straight from each module's declared prerequisite list — so a route that contradicts the real graph shows up here as a broken edge — and the learner can simulate skipping a prerequisite, which greys out exactly the later subtopics whose explanation would then rest on an undefined term, listing the terms that would go undefined.

subtopics.title: How to use the simulations
subtopics.covers: The method every page assumes — change one input, predict the internal state before running, then compare against the state panel — plus what each simulator does and does not model (they show mechanism and relative cost, never absolute performance on your hardware) and how to read the shared visual conventions for pages, records, logs, nodes and messages.
subtopics.visual: A guided tour over one small buffer-pool simulator that asks the learner to predict the next eviction and the resulting hit rate before revealing them, scoring the prediction and teaching the predict-then-run loop used on every later page.

subtopics.title: Five questions to ask of any data system
subtopics.covers: The spine the whole curriculum returns to — what is the unit of durability, what is the unit of atomicity, what is the unit of replication and partitioning, what does a read see and how stale can it be, and what exactly happens on each failure — and why answering these five for a system tells you more than any feature list.
subtopics.visual: A five-slot card the learner fills in for PostgreSQL, DynamoDB and Kafka side by side, with each filled answer revealing the module that derives it and a mismatch detector that flags answers the learner guessed inconsistently (for example atomicity wider than the replication unit).

modules.title: Data Models and a Hands-On SQL Primer
modules.why: A true beginner needs the relational model, a way to turn a domain into tables, working SQL and a map of the non-relational models before relational algebra, query plans, isolation anomalies or per-store modeling can mean anything; this module gives every later module its vocabulary and a live sandbox to test claims against.

subtopics.title: Why a DBMS instead of files
subtopics.covers: The four problems a flat file cannot solve — interleaved concurrent writes, a crash mid-write leaving torn or duplicated records, lookups that cost a full scan, and integrity/physical data independence — and how every engine (PostgreSQL, SQLite, RocksDB) answers them by bundling a storage manager, an index, a transaction manager with a log, and a declarative query interface behind one API (Codd's data independence; Kleppmann's two-function append-and-grep database as the baseline).
subtopics.visual: A two-lane simulator where two clients append order rows to a shared CSV on the left and to a database table on the right; the learner toggles 'interleave writers', presses 'crash' mid-write, and grows the dataset to 100k rows, watching the file lane accumulate torn lines, duplicates and a linearly rising scan counter while the DB lane stays all-or-nothing and answers lookups in a handful of index steps.

subtopics.title: The relational model precisely: relations, keys, constraints and NULLs
subtopics.covers: Relations as sets of tuples over typed attribute domains (unordered, duplicate-free headings — and SQL's bag deviation), superkeys vs candidate vs primary vs foreign keys, referential integrity with ON DELETE RESTRICT/CASCADE/SET NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK constraints, three-valued logic (TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN) and its asymmetry — CHECK accepts UNKNOWN while WHERE rejects it, UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT (PostgreSQL 15) — plus natural vs surrogate keys and why uniqueness cannot be enforced by check-then-insert in application code.
subtopics.visual: A constraint enforcer over a customers/orders/items schema where the learner declares keys and foreign-key actions, then fires inserts, updates and deletes and watches each constraint check evaluate in order (PK, UNIQUE, FK, CHECK) with rows cascading, nulling or being rejected; flipping any value to NULL shows the predicate turn UNKNOWN and reveals which checks pass it and which do not.

subtopics.title: Entities, relationships and cardinality
subtopics.covers: The vocabulary of conceptual modeling — entities, attributes and relationships, weak entities and identifying vs non-identifying relationships, multi-valued and derived attributes, the attributes that are really entities (the repeated-column and comma-separated-list smells) — plus the three cardinalities (1:1, 1:N, M:N) crossed with participation/optionality (total vs partial) to give the six shapes a relationship edge can take, read in both Chen and crow's-foot notation.
subtopics.visual: A drag-and-drop ER canvas where the learner places entities and draws relationship edges, then sets each edge's cardinality and optionality with handles at both ends while the diagram re-renders in Chen and crow's-foot side by side and a sample population of rows below fills in live — every edit highlights its cell in the cardinality × participation matrix and shows one instance the new shape now permits and one it now forbids.

subtopics.title: Mapping an ER model to tables
subtopics.covers: The mapping rules that turn a drawn model into physical structure — 1:N as a FK on the many side (NOT NULL for total participation, nullable for partial, which is exactly where an outer join becomes necessary), M:N as a junction table with a composite PK plus an index in both directions, 1:1 as a merged table versus a split table with a UNIQUE FK, weak entities as composite keys, multi-valued attributes as child tables — which drawn cardinalities the DDL actually enforces and which survive only as a convention, a forward pointer that a faithful mapping usually lands near the normal forms checked in the next module, and the reverse skill of reading an unfamiliar schema's FK graph back into a diagram.
subtopics.visual: A generator that takes the drawn model and re-renders DDL, table diagram and a sample result set live — flipping an edge to M:N materializes a junction table with its two indexes, flipping to 1:1 offers merge-or-split with the row counts each produces, making participation partial turns the FK nullable and shows the outer join a query now needs, a 'violate it' button inserts a row the drawn cardinality forbids to reveal which declared constraint (or none at all) catches it, and a reverse mode hands the learner an unfamiliar FK graph to re-derive the cardinalities from.

subtopics.title: SQL primer: DDL, DML and single-table queries
subtopics.covers: CREATE TABLE with column types, defaults and constraints, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE with RETURNING, SELECT-WHERE-ORDER BY-LIMIT and the logical evaluation order FROM→WHERE→SELECT→DISTINCT→ORDER BY→LIMIT that differs from the textual order, explicit and implicit casts, IS NULL/COALESCE/NULLIF, and the mismatch between numeric, text, date and boolean types across PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite.
subtopics.visual: A sandbox backed by a small deterministic in-page SQL interpreter over a fixed customers/orders/items dataset (~40 rows, no engine download, no network) where the learner types statements and watches the table grid mutate; for every SELECT the clauses light up in logical evaluation order and a stepper walks the interpreter's own intermediate row set after each clause, so adding a NULL or changing LIMIT visibly alters exactly one stage.

subtopics.title: SQL primer: joins, GROUP BY, subqueries and set operations
subtopics.covers: Inner, left/right/full outer and cross joins as filtered row pairing with NULL padding, GROUP BY buckets and HAVING versus WHERE, aggregate semantics (COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col), SUM over empty groups), correlated subqueries, IN vs EXISTS, UNION/UNION ALL/INTERSECT/EXCEPT with set vs bag semantics, and the full evaluation order FROM→JOIN→WHERE→GROUP BY→HAVING→SELECT→DISTINCT→ORDER BY→LIMIT (window functions, recursive CTEs and LATERAL belong to the Advanced SQL module).
subtopics.visual: A join-and-group animator where two small tables sit as row strips, the learner picks a join type and drags the ON predicate, and every candidate row pair is drawn, kept or dropped, NULL-padded for outer joins, then swept into GROUP BY buckets that collapse into aggregate values; a toggle between UNION and UNION ALL shows duplicate rows being eliminated or retained.

subtopics.title: Document, key-value, wide-column and graph models
subtopics.covers: Each model's storage unit and query shape — opaque value by key (Redis, RocksDB, DynamoDB), nested document with one-to-many locality (MongoDB BSON, PostgreSQL jsonb), wide-column partition key + clustering columns + sparse timestamped cells (Bigtable, Cassandra, HBase), and property graphs with index-free adjacency vs triple stores (Neo4j, RDF) — schema-on-write vs schema-on-read, why 'NoSQL has no schema' is false, and the costs of leaving relational: joins move into application code or become write fan-out (detailed per-store modeling is in Part 5).
subtopics.visual: One blog dataset (users, posts, comments, tags) rendered simultaneously as relational tables, JSON documents, key-value pairs, wide-column partitions and a graph; the learner picks a query — fetch a post with its comments, all posts by tag, friends-of-friends who commented — and watches each model animate its lookups, joins, scatters or traversals with per-model counters of seeks and bytes touched.

subtopics.title: OLTP vs OLAP vs HTAP and the systems landscape
subtopics.covers: Workload shapes — many small indexed point transactions (PostgreSQL, InnoDB) vs scans of few columns over billions of rows (ClickHouse, DuckDB, Snowflake, BigQuery) — the row-vs-column intuition that drives them, the specialized families (time-series, search/inverted index, streaming logs, vector, caches, embedded engines), HTAP attempts (TiDB TiFlash replicas, SingleStore, Oracle dual format) versus the usual answer of CDC into a separate analytical store, and the canonical deployment of one system of record with derived stores (columnar internals in Part 2, logs and CDC in Part 8).
subtopics.visual: A workload builder where the learner dials read/write ratio, query shape (point, range, aggregate, full-text, similarity, append stream), row count, row width, columns touched and selectivity, and one small cost model per access shape computes rows scanned, bytes read, round trips and index entries written per row for each system family; the cards are ranked by the computed number with the arithmetic shown term by term, so nudging selectivity or columns-touched past a crossover inverts the ranking in front of the learner, and a composed-stack strip beneath places the winner inside a system-of-record-plus-derived-stores architecture.

modules.title: SQL Semantics, Types and Schema Design
modules.why: Once a beginner can write SQL and draw a schema, the next failures are silent rather than loud — NULL and fan-out traps that return plausible wrong numbers, type choices that lose money or shift timestamps across a DST boundary, and schemas whose redundancy makes a single update rewrite a cross product — and every later module on partitioning by time, ledgers, indexes and query plans assumes these are already right.

subtopics.title: SQL semantics engineers get wrong
subtopics.covers: NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, NOT IN returns nothing when the subquery contains a NULL (NOT EXISTS does not), aggregates skip NULLs but COUNT(*) does not, non-aggregated columns in GROUP BY (MySQL ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY vs PostgreSQL's primary-key functional-dependency rule), DISTINCT masking one-to-many join fan-out that double-counts SUM, ORDER BY without a unique tiebreaker and LIMIT without ORDER BY being nondeterministic, integer division, BETWEEN inclusivity, and implicit casts and collation mismatches that silently change results (and later defeat indexes).
subtopics.visual: A trap-query sandbox with a fixed set of deceptive queries over a small dataset where the learner drags NULLs and duplicate rows into the data, toggles NOT IN against NOT EXISTS, and attaches a one-to-many join, watching result sets and SUM/COUNT values diverge live with the offending rows and the UNKNOWN evaluations highlighted.

subtopics.title: Temporal types: instants, civil time and DST
subtopics.covers: timestamptz as a stored UTC instant versus timestamp without time zone as a wall-clock string (neither stores a zone) with the session TimeZone GUC deciding only rendering, AT TIME ZONE in both directions, DST gaps and overlaps that make some local times nonexistent or ambiguous, storing future events as civil time plus an IANA zone id rather than an instant, non-associative interval arithmetic and zone-aware date_trunc/generate_series bucketing, and precision limits — microsecond storage, epoch millis vs micros across APIs, MySQL DATETIME vs TIMESTAMP disagreeing about session zones.
subtopics.visual: A time lab where one moment written as timestamptz, as timestamp and as an epoch integer is re-rendered side by side under three session zones while the learner drags an event across a DST gap and then an overlap, watching a BETWEEN range query gain or lose the row and a date_trunc('day') bucket boundary slide against the UTC axis.

subtopics.title: Numeric types: exact money vs float drift
subtopics.covers: NUMERIC/DECIMAL exact decimal arithmetic and its storage and speed cost versus binary-float representation error, order-dependent float SUM that makes parallel or vectorized aggregation non-deterministic, integer minor units and explicit rounding rules for money, and integer widths with overflow behaviour that differs by engine (PostgreSQL raises where MySQL historically truncated).
subtopics.visual: A price column is summed as float8, as numeric and as integer cents in parallel columns with the drift accumulating cent by cent per row, while a reorder-rows shuffle and an enable-parallel-aggregation toggle make the float total itself change, and an overflow slider pushes a running counter past int4 to show the error or the wrap.

subtopics.title: Text, encoding and collation
subtopics.covers: text vs varchar(n) vs char padding semantics, utf8 vs utf8mb4 and what a length actually counts (bytes, code points, graphemes), C vs ICU collations and case- or accent-insensitive variants that change ORDER BY, equality and uniqueness, enums vs lookup tables vs CHECK, arrays and composite types, and UUID vs bytea vs text storage — each choice changing row bytes, index entry size, comparison semantics, and whether an implicit cast quietly disables an index; how a collation actually becomes index order, and the collation-version trap that silently corrupts indexes after an OS upgrade, are owned by Part 2 b-trees-and-variants ('Collation, Unicode and byte-comparable key encoding') and revisited operationally in Part 10.
subtopics.visual: A type/encoding/collation switchboard redraws the on-disk bytes per row and per index entry as the learner changes the column definition, while an emoji, an accented name and a trailing-space string expose that collation's ordering, equality and length answers side by side in one table — with a link out to the b-trees page that takes the same committed ordering fixture down a real tree.

subtopics.title: Normalization, functional dependencies and schema design
subtopics.covers: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms and attribute closure, the 1NF→2NF→3NF→BCNF ladder and the update/insert/delete anomalies each step removes, the lossless-join and dependency-preservation tests for a decomposition, when to stop normalizing (denormalization as a physical read-vs-write trade-off, not a modeling truth), key choice — identity/bigserial vs random UUIDv4 vs time-ordered UUIDv7/ULID vs natural composite keys — with its consequences for clustered storage (see B-Trees in Part 2), and the explicit stopping point: BCNF plus judgement is enough for almost every production schema, so the next page is an optional deep dive rather than the rest of this one.
subtopics.visual: A dependency decomposer where the learner drags functional-dependency arrows onto a wide denormalized table and watches it split step by step to BCNF, with the lossless-join check animated and any lost dependency flagged; then a single UPDATE is run against both the flat and the decomposed schema and the anomaly rows in the flat version are highlighted.

subtopics.title: Optional deep dive: multivalued dependencies, 4NF and the chase
subtopics.covers: An optional page for readers who want the theory behind the BCNF stopping point — skippable on a first pass, and its practical payoff lands again in Part 5 data-modeling-and-per-store-usage: multivalued dependencies as the source of row explosion BCNF cannot remove (one employee's independent skills and phone numbers forced into a cross product), the 4NF rule that every non-trivial MVD's determinant be a superkey, Fagin's theorem tying 4NF to lossless binary decomposition, join dependencies and 5NF/PJNF with the supplier-part-project example that no binary split fixes, the chase as the decision procedure for lossless join and dependency implication, and the engineer's translation that is the one thing to carry away — independent one-to-many facts belong in separate tables or separate arrays/subdocuments, and the symptom is an update that must rewrite a cross product of rows.
subtopics.visual: The learner drags MVD arrows onto a flat table and the tool materializes the cross-product rows those dependencies force, then decomposes into 4NF projections and runs the chase step by step to prove the natural join reconstructs exactly the original rows; issuing one update afterwards counts rows rewritten in the flat table against the decomposed schema.

modules.title: Hardware, the OS and What Durable Means
modules.why: Now that tables, rows and queries are on the table, this module supplies the machine-level facts the rest of the site keeps referring back to: every storage-engine decision is a response to latency ladders, NAND erase blocks, page-cache behavior and the exact promise fsync does or does not make.

subtopics.title: Memory hierarchy and latency numbers
subtopics.covers: The latency ladder from L1 (~1ns) through DRAM (~100ns), NVMe (~10-100us), HDD seek (~10ms) and cross-datacenter RTT (~100ms), why one seek costs ~10^5 DRAM accesses so engines move fixed pages (PG 8KB, InnoDB 16KB, SQLite 4KB) rather than bytes, latency vs bandwidth vs IOPS and why NVMe needs queue depth to deliver, the 64-byte cache line and TLB reach that shape in-memory layouts, Gray's five-minute rule as a $/GB-vs-$/IOPS breakeven for caching, and the working-set-exceeds-RAM cliff that the buffer-pool module builds on.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a device (DRAM, NVMe, SATA SSD, HDD, remote node) and drags sliders for access pattern (random 4KB to sequential 1MB), queue depth and working-set-size-vs-RAM while requests animate down the hierarchy; throughput and p99 counters update, a log-scale 'if L1 were one second' human-time column re-renders, and the five-minute-rule breakeven line moves as they change the $/GB and $/IOPS inputs.

subtopics.title: HDD and SSD internals: seeks, NAND and the FTL
subtopics.covers: HDD seek plus rotational latency and elevator scheduling making sequential I/O ~100x faster than random, versus NAND flash where pages (4-16KB) are written but only whole blocks (MBs) are erased, so the FTL maintains a logical-to-physical map, garbage collection copies live pages and produces device write amplification and latency spikes, mitigated by over-provisioning, TRIM/discard and wear leveling; why the same overwrite is cheap logically but expensive physically, why enterprise drives add power-loss-protected caches, and how ZNS exposes zones so log-structured engines place data themselves.
subtopics.visual: An FTL simulator: the learner issues writes and overwrites to logical addresses and watches flash blocks fill, invalid pages accumulate, GC trigger and copy live pages, with a write-amplification gauge and per-write latency trace; an over-provisioning slider and a TRIM toggle change how often GC fires, and a side-by-side HDD head animates seek distance for the same request stream.

subtopics.title: Storage abstractions: files, block devices and object stores
subtopics.covers: POSIX files as extent-backed byte arrays (fallocate, fragmentation, sparse files) versus raw block devices versus object stores like S3 with immutable whole-object PUT, expensive LIST, no byte-range overwrite and per-request pricing that pushes engines toward log-structured layouts; network block storage (EBS) adding ~ms latency and IOPS/bandwidth caps versus ephemeral local NVMe, and why RAID, EBS multi-AZ replication and cloud durability nines protect against different failures than a flushed write does, setting up the disaggregated designs in the architectures module.
subtopics.visual: The learner drops the same engine write path onto a chosen backend (local NVMe, EBS, S3) and watches each step get re-annotated: which operations are legal (in-place overwrite vs append-and-rename vs new object), per-step latency, and cumulative $ per GB and per operation, with a failure panel showing which of drive death, host death and AZ loss each backend survives.

subtopics.title: Encoding data: bytes, endianness and serialization
subtopics.covers: How a record becomes bytes: fixed-width vs LEB128/SQLite-style varints, IEEE-754 floats and why NaN and negative zero break naive comparison, length-prefixed vs delimited strings, alignment padding and its cost, and the split between formats that pin a byte order — SQLite's big-endian file header and page fields, Parquet, Protobuf and Avro fixing little-endian by spec — versus formats that simply write the host's native byte order and native alignment, PostgreSQL being the counterexample (pg_control and the whole data directory are native-endian and native-alignment, which is exactly why a data directory, a base backup or pg_upgrade cannot cross architectures and a dump/restore is required, the same trap that makes InnoDB tablespaces unsafe to copy between platforms); plus the difference between language-native serialization and portable schemas (Protobuf field tags, Avro writer/reader schemas) that DDIA chapter 4 draws, with schema-evolution compatibility rules owned by the data-modeling module and byte-comparable key encoding by the B-tree module.
subtopics.visual: A byte-level encoder where the learner edits a record's fields and types and watches the SQLite record format, Protobuf and JSON byte layouts re-render side by side with each byte color-coded by role (header, varint length, payload, padding), and toggles for varint-vs-fixed and alignment show total bytes; a host-architecture switch (little-endian vs big-endian host) then leaves the SQLite and Protobuf bytes identical while flipping a native-order PostgreSQL-style tuple, and a 'copy this file to the other host' button shows each format either parsing cleanly or decoding to garbage.

subtopics.title: The OS I/O path: syscalls, page cache and mmap
subtopics.covers: Pure kernel mechanics: how read()/write()/pread()/pwrite() copy through the kernel page cache, dirty pages waiting on writeback timers and dirty-ratio thresholds, readahead heuristics detecting sequential access and how random access defeats them, and mmap mapping file pages into the address space so that a plain load can fault to disk inside a critical section, with no eviction control, TLB shootdowns on unmap, SIGBUS on I/O error, msync as the only flush and no guaranteed ordering of dirty mapped pages; the engine-policy question of who should own the cache (Crotty et al. on mmap, double caching, O_DIRECT-vs-page-cache sizing) and the mechanics of bypassing and batching it (O_DIRECT alignment, io_uring submission and completion) both belong to the buffer-pool module and are only signposted here.
subtopics.visual: A page-cache step-through: the learner issues read(), write() and mmap accesses to file offsets and watches kernel pages populate, dirty bits set, readahead pull in neighbors and the writeback timer flush; a 'fault under latch' mode shows a thread stalled inside a critical section on an mmap page miss while others queue behind it.

subtopics.title: fsync, write barriers and the durability contract
subtopics.covers: What write() actually promises (page cache only) versus fsync/fdatasync (fdatasync skips metadata unless size changed) plus the device FLUSH/FUA that pushes a volatile drive write cache to media, why consumer drives without power-loss protection can acknowledge and lose data, the cost ladder (ms on HDD, tens of us on PLP NVMe) that motivates group commit, and fsyncgate (2018): Linux marked pages clean after a failed fsync so retries falsely succeeded, fixed in 2018 and back-patched to all then-supported PostgreSQL branches (9.4 onward) as PANIC-on-fsync-failure plus the data_sync_retry escape hatch, alongside Linux's per-file-descriptor error reporting (4.13+) and the still-live trap that a different process's fsync may never see the error at all.
subtopics.visual: A four-layer stack (user buffer, page cache, drive write cache, media) where the learner steps through write()/fdatasync()/fsync()/FUA and presses power-cut at any layer to see which bytes survive; toggles for volatile-vs-PLP cache and an inject-fsync-error button reproduce fsyncgate by showing the dirty bit cleared, the retried fsync returning success with the data gone, and a second process's fsync never learning of the error.

subtopics.title: Atomicity of writes and torn pages
subtopics.covers: Why the sector (512B or 4KB) is the only write the device guarantees atomic, so an 8KB or 16KB engine page can land half-old/half-new when power fails mid-write, why the WAL alone cannot fix a torn page because the log records assume an intact base image, how per-page checksums detect the tear but cannot repair it (PostgreSQL data_checksums is a 16-bit FNV-1a-derived page checksum with the block number mixed in, while CRC-32C in PostgreSQL covers WAL records rather than data pages; InnoDB uses a crc32c stored as a header/trailer pair), why detection strength matters — a fixed-width digest has a fixed collision probability, so a 16-bit checksum misses roughly 1 corruption in 65,536 versus about 1 in 4 billion for a 32-bit one — so bit rot and silent misdirected writes still need end-to-end checksums and scrubbing (ZFS, pg_checksums, innochecksum), and a preview of the defenses (full_page_writes, doublewrite, copy-on-write) whose internals belong to the WAL-and-recovery module, which also owns filesystem journaling and the safe-replace rename protocol.
subtopics.visual: A torn-write simulator: the learner writes a 16KB page as four sectors with a crash slider marking where power fails, sees the resulting page mixed old and new, then runs the checksum verifier to watch it flag the mismatch; a 'sector atomicity' toggle for 4Kn drives plus a page-size chooser show which page sizes can and cannot tear, and a detection-strength lab beside it scales the digest down to an observable 4-bit and 8-bit checksum over a small block, replays a few thousand random single- and multi-bit corruptions, and plots the measured miss rate against the analytic 2^-n curve with the extrapolation to real engine widths (PostgreSQL's 16-bit page checksum, InnoDB and PG WAL CRC-32C) printed as a labelled calculation rather than simulated.

subtopics.title: Filesystem crash consistency: journaling, rename and the safe-replace protocol
subtopics.covers: How journaling modes (ext4 data=ordered vs data=writeback, XFS metadata-only, btrfs/ZFS copy-on-write) decide which orderings survive a crash, why a newly created or renamed file needs fsync of the parent directory, why the safe-replace protocol is write-temp, fsync, rename, fsync-dir, the ext4 zero-length-file and delayed-allocation surprises, and how filesystems may reorder or coalesce writes so an engine must never infer ordering from issue order; ties to how SQLite's rollback journal and Postgres's pg_control updates depend on exactly these guarantees.
subtopics.visual: An ordering puzzle: the learner arranges write, fsync, rename and directory-fsync calls for a config-file replace under a chosen filesystem mode, then presses crash and the simulator enumerates every legal on-disk end state (old content, new content, zero-length, missing) the reordering rules allow, marking which orderings are safe and which lose data.

subtopics.title: Direct I/O and io_uring: alignment, submission and completion
subtopics.covers: The kernel contract of O_DIRECT - buffer address, file offset and length all aligned to the sector or logical block size, EINVAL when they are not, DMA straight into user memory, no readahead, and the fact that bypassing the page cache is still not durability (an fsync or O_DSYNC is required) - then how requests are actually submitted: a synchronous pread parking one thread per in-flight I/O versus io_uring's shared submission and completion ring buffers that batch many requests per syscall, and why a database that owns its buffer pool wants both (InnoDB's O_DIRECT plus AIO, PostgreSQL 18's io_method, RocksDB's use_direct_reads).
subtopics.visual: An alignment-and-queue lab: the learner dials a buffer address, file offset and length against a chosen logical block size and watches each O_DIRECT request either fail with EINVAL (with the offending field highlighted) or issue as a DMA transfer, then flips the submission path from sync pread to io_uring and watches submission/completion rings fill, syscalls-per-request drop and achieved IOPS climb as queue depth rises.

modules.title: Anatomy of a Database Engine
modules.why: A component map, a schema-to-files mapping, one traced read, a first look at transactions and versions, and a WAL primer give every later module a place to plug in; the module deliberately stops at 'enough to continue' after the WAL primer — the page-level write path belongs to Pages, Tuples and Heap Files and the concurrency primitives to The Buffer Pool, where the structures they touch are defined.

subtopics.title: Component map: parser, planner, executor, storage manager, log
subtopics.covers: The layered request loop every engine shares — wire protocol, parser, binder/analyzer, rewriter, optimizer, executor, access methods, buffer pool, storage manager — with the transaction, lock and log managers cutting across all layers (Hellerstein/Stonebraker's 'Architecture of a Database System'), the pluggable storage-engine seam (MySQL handler API for InnoDB/MyRocks, PostgreSQL table access methods, MongoDB over WiredTiger, CockroachDB/TiKV over RocksDB/Pebble), and a mapping from each layer to the later module that owns it and the knobs that size it (shared_buffers, work_mem, wal_buffers, innodb_buffer_pool_size).
subtopics.visual: A static, clickable index of the engine: the learner clicks any layer to open its knobs, its cross-cutting managers and its link to the owning module, and toggling the engine (PostgreSQL / MySQL+InnoDB / SQLite / RocksDB) adds, merges or removes layers in place (RocksDB has no parser or planner, SQLite has no network layer, MySQL exposes the handler-API seam); picking one of three statements annotates each layer with the rows in, rows out and bytes it handles for that statement rather than animating anything across them.

subtopics.title: Logical schema vs physical storage
subtopics.covers: Tables, indexes, views, sequences and constraints are catalog rows (pg_class, pg_attribute, pg_index; InnoDB's data dictionary; SQLite's sqlite_master) mapped onto physical objects — PostgreSQL relfilenodes with main/FSM/VM/TOAST forks, InnoDB .ibd tablespaces where the table is its clustered primary-key B+tree and secondary indexes store PK values, SQLite's single file of B-tree pages with rowid vs WITHOUT ROWID tables — which is what makes Codd's physical data independence real; DDL is then either a metadata edit (PG ADD COLUMN with no default or a non-volatile default, recorded in pg_attribute.attmissingval and materialized lazily; InnoDB instant ADD COLUMN) or a full rewrite under a new relfilenode (a volatile default, a non-binary-coercible type change, CLUSTER), and catalogs being tables creates a bootstrapping problem solved by hard-wired relations; placement adds one more level of indirection — a relation's file path resolves as tablespace → database → relfilenode — with tablespace provisioning, SET TABLESPACE locking, backup/PITR path coupling and per-tablespace planner cost hints left to Part 10, and page and tuple internals owned by Pages, Tuples and Heap Files.
subtopics.visual: A schema-to-files renderer: the learner writes a few CREATE TABLE/INDEX statements and sees the resulting on-disk objects for PostgreSQL, InnoDB and SQLite side by side (heap file plus forks and TOAST, index files; one .ibd with clustered and secondary trees; one .db file, each shown with its full tablespace → database → relfilenode path), then issues ALTERs and watches each classified as metadata-only (a catalog row flips, no file touched) or rewrite (a new relfilenode appears and the old file is streamed into it) while the catalog table rows update live.

subtopics.title: Row, column and key-value physical models
subtopics.covers: How one 'orders' table lays out under NSM row storage (PostgreSQL heap, InnoDB clustered), DSM column storage (ClickHouse MergeTree parts, Parquet row groups) and PAX hybrids, versus a sorted key-value engine where SQL rows become order-preserving byte keys (CockroachDB/TiKV /table/index/pk key encoding over RocksDB/Pebble, MyRocks) and where documents (MongoDB BSON on WiredTiger) and wide-column partitions (Cassandra partition key + clustering columns) are just prefixes in the same sorted key space; why an OLTP point lookup wants the whole row co-located while an OLAP aggregate over one of 100 columns reads ~1% of the bytes columnar and 100% row-wise, deferring encodings, compression and the full layout comparison to Column Stores, Compression and Columnar Formats.
subtopics.visual: A static side-by-side still opens the page — one query's bytes highlighted over a row layout and a column layout, to fix the intuition in one picture — and the interactivity is spent on the encoding Column Stores never covers: the learner edits a row and watches it become sorted byte keys, seeing the /table/index/pk key bytes and the value bytes form field by field, changing a value or column order reshuffle the key's sort position, and a document and a wide-column row land as prefixes in the same key space beside it.

subtopics.title: Life of a query: from SQL text to rows
subtopics.covers: Trace one SELECT with a WHERE and a JOIN from the wire-protocol message through parse (AST), bind/analyze (catalog lookups resolve names to OIDs and types), rewrite (views inlined), plan (cost-based choice of sequential scan vs index scan vs bitmap scan and nested loop vs hash join, driven by pg_statistic histograms and seq_page_cost/random_page_cost, i.e. storage physics from the previous module) and execute (Volcano next() calls pulling tuples through the operator tree, every page request going through the buffer pool and only misses reaching the OS and disk), with rows streamed back in the protocol's row format; each stage is deepened in Part 3.
subtopics.visual: A query stepper: the learner types a small SELECT over two toy tables, watches the AST and then the plan tree materialize, then single-steps execution as next() calls ripple down the operator tree while a buffer-pool panel counts hits, misses and disk reads per operator; flipping a 'has index' switch or dragging random_page_cost changes the chosen plan and the counters change with it.

subtopics.title: Transactions at 10,000 feet
subtopics.covers: ACID introduced informally as four distinct promises — atomicity (all-or-nothing, via undo or never-expose), consistency (application invariants the engine can only partly check through constraints), isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work), durability (survives a crash once COMMIT returns) — with BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT, autocommit as a per-statement transaction and the root of most lost-update bugs, the bank transfer separating atomicity from isolation, and a preview that single-node engines deliver these with the log, locks and versions while distributed ones need consensus; precise definitions, the anomaly catalog and isolation levels are owned by Part 4.
subtopics.visual: Two concurrent bank transfers on a shared timeline: the learner drags the interleaving of their read and write steps, toggles autocommit vs explicit BEGIN and isolation on/off, and injects a crash before or after COMMIT, while a meter shows sum(balances) holding or breaking, which writes the other transaction can see, and which writes survive the crash.

subtopics.title: Versions, snapshots and the garbage horizon
subtopics.covers: The one idea Part 2 keeps assuming and this page owns as its anchor: an UPDATE does not overwrite in place but writes a new version of the row while the old one stays reachable, a reader takes a snapshot at a point in time and sees exactly the versions that were current then, a version becomes garbage only once no live or future snapshot can see it — the garbage horizon set by the oldest running transaction — and someone must then reclaim it, which is why a long-running reader keeps dead rows alive; the same shape appears as PostgreSQL heap tuples with xmin/xmax awaiting vacuum, InnoDB undo records reached by rollback pointers and purged later, and LSM versions of a key that compaction may only drop when no snapshot falls between them, and it is the reason online index builds must wait for older transactions — version chains, visibility rules and the per-engine storage layouts are deepened by MVCC: Semantics, Version Storage and Snapshots, while reclamation, bloat, freezing and the cost the horizon imposes belong to Garbage Collection: Vacuum, Freezing and Horizons.
subtopics.visual: The shared VersionTimeline primitive (declared in the visual-system spec and reused by MVCC: Semantics, Version Storage and Snapshots in its 'Multiversion fundamentals' preset) in its horizon-only preset: the learner issues updates and deletes to build a chain of versions along a time axis, opens and closes reader transactions whose snapshots appear as vertical lines, and each version is shaded live as visible-to-this-reader, superseded-but-still-needed or collectable — dragging the oldest open reader forward moves the garbage horizon and the backlog of uncollectable versions grows or drains in front of the learner, with a 'reclaim' button showing what the collector can and cannot take (the per-version visibility decision trace and write-write conflict lane stay switched off here and belong to the Part 4 preset).

subtopics.title: WAL primer: log records, LSNs and log-before-page
subtopics.covers: The module's 'enough to continue' boundary and the last page a Part 1 reader needs: why the log is written first — each change becomes a log record (physical page image, logical operation, or physiological — PostgreSQL's block-referenced records with full-page images after a checkpoint, InnoDB mtr redo records, SQLite journaling whole pages) with a monotonically increasing LSN that is also its byte position, every page carries the pageLSN of the last record applied to it, the write-ahead rule (a dirty page may not reach disk until the log through its pageLSN is durable) and the commit rule (commit means the log is flushed through the commit record, which is where synchronous_commit=off and innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=0/2 buy latency by moving the client's acknowledgment ahead of the fsync), plus a replay sketch: redo from the last checkpoint applying a record only if its LSN exceeds the page's pageLSN, which makes replay idempotent; the per-engine write call chain is traced in Pages, Tuples and Heap Files, and ARIES undo with CLRs, checkpoints, group commit and torn-page defenses are owned by Write-Ahead Logging and Crash Recovery.
subtopics.visual: A log-and-pages animation: the learner applies updates to a few pages and watches records append to the WAL strip with LSNs while the pages are stamped with their pageLSN; a 'flushed LSN' cursor advances on fsync (and a durability switch moves the 'ack sent to client' marker to before or after that fsync), an attempt to evict a dirty page whose pageLSN lies beyond the cursor is blocked, and a 'crash' button then steps replay from the checkpoint, comparing each record's LSN against the on-disk pageLSN and either applying or skipping it.

parts.title: Storage Engines: Pages, Trees, Logs and Columns
parts.summary: The single-node storage substrate in depth: page layout, buffer management, B-trees and LSM trees, the full family of access methods, practical index selection, and columnar analytical storage.

modules.title: Pages, Tuples and Heap Files
modules.why: The slotted page and heap file are the unit of everything above them; the byte layout of a tuple decides what every page, index and log record above it has to move around.

subtopics.title: Page anatomy and the slotted page
subtopics.covers: The fixed-size page (8KB PostgreSQL, 16KB InnoDB, 4KB SQLite) as the unit of I/O and latching, with a header (LSN, checksum, flags, pd_lower/pd_upper free-space bounds), a slot/line-pointer array growing forward and tuple bytes growing backward so a (page, slot) address stays stable while tuples move during in-page compaction; PostgreSQL's ItemIdData states (LP_NORMAL/LP_REDIRECT/LP_DEAD/LP_UNUSED — redirect and dead pointers being produced by the HOT-update and pruning machinery covered later in this module) versus InnoDB's FIL header, infimum/supremum sentinel records, singly linked record list and page directory of owner slots, versus SQLite's cell-pointer array and fragmented-bytes counter.
subtopics.visual: The shared PageView primitive in slot-map mode as a page editor: the learner inserts, updates and deletes variable-length tuples into one 8KB page and watches the line-pointer array, pd_lower/pd_upper gap, tuple bytes and fragmented holes update live, a 'compact' button slides tuples down while slot numbers stay fixed, and the site-wide engine selector (persisted across every page that offers the comparison) re-renders the same records as an InnoDB page (infimum→records→supremum list plus page directory) or a SQLite cell-pointer page.

subtopics.title: Tuple layout: headers, null bitmaps, alignment and varlena
subtopics.covers: The bytes of one row: PostgreSQL's 23-byte HeapTupleHeader (t_xmin, t_xmax, t_cid/t_xvac, t_ctid, t_infomask hint bits, t_hoff) followed by an optional null bitmap and typalign-padded attributes, so column order changes row size (int4 before int8 wastes 4 bytes) and NULLs cost bits not bytes; varlena values with 1-byte short headers versus 4-byte headers, fixed-width columns enabling cached offset arithmetic (attcacheoff) while any preceding variable-width or nullable column forces a walk; InnoDB's COMPACT/DYNAMIC record (variable-length-lengths list, null flags, 5-byte record header, hidden DB_ROW_ID/DB_TRX_ID/DB_ROLL_PTR) and SQLite's varint-typed record header; dropped columns surviving as attisdropped placeholders.
subtopics.visual: The PageView primitive in byte-grid mode as a column-order byte-map: the learner drags columns of different types (bool, int4, int8, text, numeric, timestamptz) into an order and toggles NULLs, and the tool renders the header, null bitmap, each attribute's bytes and highlighted padding bytes with a bytes-per-row and rows-per-page counter, while the site-wide engine selector re-renders the same row as an InnoDB compact record or SQLite record so the learner sees where each engine spends its header bytes.

subtopics.title: Heap file organization and free space management
subtopics.covers: How a relation becomes files: PostgreSQL relfilenode segments of 1GB with side forks — the Free Space Map (one byte per page at 1/256 granularity in a binary-tree of pages, lazily updated and repaired by VACUUM) and the Visibility Map (all-visible and all-frozen bits per page that gate index-only scans and freezing) — the FSM search that decides where an insert lands, the relation extension lock and bulk extension under contention, and why only trailing empty pages can be truncated so interior dead space is bloat; InnoDB's tablespace geometry with 1MB extents, file segments, XDES descriptors and FSP_FREE/FSP_FREE_FRAG lists.
subtopics.visual: A heap-growth simulator over a strip of PageView tiles in fill/heat mode: the learner runs insert/update/delete mixes (sequential, random, delete-a-prefix, delete-a-suffix) and watches each page's fill, its FSM byte and VM bits update, the FSM lookup that places the next tuple, extension at the tail, and a VACUUM step that resets FSM values and truncates trailing empty pages but leaves interior holes, with the site-wide engine selector swapping to an InnoDB extent/segment view of the same workload.

subtopics.title: HOT updates, redirect line pointers and opportunistic page pruning
subtopics.covers: The update path that decides whether one UPDATE writes one heap tuple or N index entries: a HOT update is taken only when no indexed column changed and the new version fits on the same page (the entire reason fillfactor exists), storing the new version as a heap-only tuple (HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE) linked from the old version's t_ctid with HEAP_HOT_UPDATED set, so no index entry is written and an index scan still lands on the root line pointer — converted to LP_REDIRECT once the chain's head is dead — and walks the chain to the visible version; opportunistic pruning (heap_page_prune_opt) fires on ordinary page access under a cleanup lock, collapsing dead chain members into redirects and reclaiming their tuple bytes so a plain SELECT recovers space without VACUUM, while only VACUUM's two passes can free the line pointers themselves because that requires removing index entries, with index scans marking entries LP_DEAD (kill_prior_tuple) as the cheap counterpart, the n_tup_hot_upd / n_tup_newpage_upd counters that say whether a workload is actually getting HOT, and the contrast with InnoDB, which updates the record in place and pushes prior column values into an undo record reachable via DB_ROLL_PTR so only indexes whose keys changed are maintained.
subtopics.visual: The reusable update-stream component (PageView in slot-map mode, the same one embedded by index-selection-strategy's write-cost meter and the PostgreSQL case study): the learner sets fillfactor, picks which columns an UPDATE touches and whether any of them is indexed, then streams updates and watches each new version either chain inside the page behind an LP_REDIRECT root — with the index-entry counter staying flat while an index scan animates its hop through the redirect and down the t_ctid chain — or spill to a new page and fan out one entry per index, while a 'read this page' button fires opportunistic pruning that collapses dead chain members and frees their bytes, a VACUUM step shows the two passes that finally release line pointers, live n_tup_hot_upd / n_tup_newpage_upd counters track the HOT ratio, and the engine selector replays the same stream as an InnoDB in-place update plus undo record.

subtopics.title: Large values: TOAST and overflow pages
subtopics.covers: Keeping wide values from blowing the page: PostgreSQL TOAST fires when a tuple exceeds TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD (~2KB), first compressing (pglz or LZ4) then moving attributes out of line per strategy (PLAIN/MAIN/EXTENDED/EXTERNAL) into ~2000-byte chunks in a pg_toast relation keyed by (chunk_id, chunk_seq) with its own B-tree, leaving an 18-byte pointer that an UPDATE of other columns shares without recopying, at the cost of detoasting on every read, a 1GB per-value ceiling and the 4-byte-OID chunk_id space; InnoDB DYNAMIC rows storing a 20-byte off-page pointer versus the older 768-byte prefix of COMPACT/REDUNDANT, SQLite overflow-page chains, and the read amplification that motivates blob separation in LSM engines (see the LSM module).
subtopics.visual: A value-growth lab: the learner drags a text column's length from 100 bytes to 10MB and watches the row shrink to a TOAST pointer, chunks land in the toast relation and toast index, and a read follow the chain with an I/O counter; strategy and compression pickers (EXTENDED/EXTERNAL/MAIN, pglz/LZ4) change what happens at each threshold, an unrelated-column UPDATE shows the pointer being shared, and the site-wide engine selector replays it as InnoDB off-page storage or a SQLite overflow chain.

subtopics.title: Checksums, corruption detection and on-disk format evolution
subtopics.covers: How a page proves it is intact and which version it is, taking the torn write and sector-atomicity story from Part 1 as given and leaving repair to the WAL module: PostgreSQL's 16-bit FNV-derived pd_checksum (data_checksums, verified on every read and recomputed on write, with the page LSN in the header tying the page to its WAL position) and pd_pagesize_version, InnoDB's CRC32C in the FIL header plus a checksum and LSN low bits in the FIL trailer so a head/tail mismatch is exactly how a torn write is detected, and SQLite's absence of page checksums (WAL frame checksums only, checksum VFS as an extension); why checksums catch bit rot and misdirected writes but not stale-but-valid pages, and how format versioning constrains upgrades — pg_upgrade requires an unchanged page layout, InnoDB row-format and tablespace-format flags, SQLite's file format frozen since 2004 as a compatibility promise.
subtopics.visual: The PageView primitive in hex+field-decode mode as a page inspector: the learner hovers over bytes of a realistic 8KB page and sees each field decoded (header, LSN, checksum, line pointers, tuple headers), then flips any bit and clicks 'read' to watch verification fail with the engine's actual error, turning data_checksums off to see the same corruption pass silently, switching engines to watch InnoDB's header/trailer pair flag a half-written page, and dragging a format-version slider to reveal which header fields exist in each layout version.

subtopics.title: Catalog storage, the bootstrap problem and cache invalidation
subtopics.covers: How the engine's self-description is itself stored and read, once you know how tuples and pages work (the logical↔physical map and the metadata-vs-rewrite classification of DDL belong to the anatomy module, and interpreting statistics belongs to cost-based optimization): pg_class, pg_attribute, pg_index and pg_type are ordinary heap tables read with ordinary MVCC rules, which raises the bootstrap problem of finding a catalog's file before you can read a catalog — solved by nailed catalogs and the pg_filenode.map file that maps shared and nailed relations outside the catalogs themselves — plus the relcache and syscache every backend builds over those rows, the shared invalidation queue that DDL broadcasts so other backends discard stale entries at their next lock acquisition, and why a backend can briefly hold a stale definition; InnoDB's data-dictionary tables inside mysql.ibd since 8.0 with its own dictionary cache, and SQLite's sqlite_schema plus the schema cookie that forces a reparse.
subtopics.visual: A catalog-as-tables inspector with two backends side by side: the learner runs DDL in backend A and watches the actual pg_class/pg_attribute/pg_index rows being inserted or flipped (attisdropped) row by row, then follows the invalidation message travelling to backend B — reading it once before the message lands to see a stale relcache answer, and again after — with a 'cold start' button that replays the bootstrap by resolving pg_class through pg_filenode.map before any catalog read, and an ANALYZE step that materialises a pg_statistic row as the hand-off to cost-based optimization.

modules.title: The Buffer Pool
modules.why: The buffer pool decides which pages hit disk, when dirty pages may leave memory, and how long a restarted or failed-over system runs cold.

subtopics.title: Buffer pool structure: frames, page table and pins
subtopics.covers: A fixed array of page-sized frames indexed by a page table (PostgreSQL's partitioned hash on BufferTag = relation/fork/block, InnoDB's page hash) whose per-frame descriptor holds a pin/refcount, dirty bit, usage count, valid and I/O-in-progress flags, and the miss path that picks a victim, writes it back if dirty, swaps the tag, takes the I/O lock so concurrent misses on the same page wait rather than double-read, and only then marks the frame valid — with the pin contract (a pinned frame is never evicted) and the hit/read counters behind EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and pg_stat_io.
subtopics.visual: An 8-frame pool where the learner clicks page ids to request them and steps through the hash-bucket lookup, victim choice, dirty write-back, I/O-in-progress wait and pin/unpin transitions on each descriptor, with a second 'thread' requesting the same missing page to show it blocking on the I/O lock, a live hit/miss counter, and a slider that resizes the pool mid-run.

subtopics.title: Cache warm-up: cold pools, dump/load and prewarming
subtopics.covers: Why a restart, failover, replica promotion or pool resize leaves an empty pool in which every read is a miss and latency rides the device until the working set is re-read, and the machinery for shortening that window — InnoDB's innodb_buffer_pool_dump_at_shutdown / innodb_buffer_pool_load_at_startup persisting only the page identifier list (space id, page number) under innodb_buffer_pool_dump_pct with the load running in the background, PostgreSQL's pg_prewarm in prefetch/read/buffer modes and the autoprewarm worker dumping block ids every autoprewarm_interval, a standby kept warm by replay versus one promoted cold, and Aurora's page cache surviving a database-process restart because it lives outside the process — plus the arithmetic that makes warm-up a first-class RTO term (working set ÷ device throughput, or ÷ random-read IOPS when the prewarm is not sequential) and the reason a resized pool is also a cold pool; the failover, cloud-native and disaster-recovery modules assume this mechanism.
subtopics.visual: A warm pool serving a steady point-read workload that the learner restarts, fails over or resizes and watches the hit rate collapse and p99 latency jump onto the device curve, then races three recovery strategies on the same bandwidth-limited device — no prewarm, dump-and-load of the page id list, sequential prewarm of the hot relation — with a stopwatch measuring when the hit rate rejoins its pre-restart line and that number dropping into an RTO budget bar beside failover detection and promotion time.

subtopics.title: Replacement policies: LRU, CLOCK, LRU-K, 2Q and ARC
subtopics.covers: Why exact LRU costs a list move and a lock on every hit, how CLOCK's second-chance reference bit approximates it (PostgreSQL's clock-sweep with usage_count capped at 5 and decremented per pass), how LRU-K's backward K-distance, 2Q's A1in/A1out/Am queues and ARC's adaptive T1/T2 lists with B1/B2 ghost entries distinguish one-touch pages from re-referenced ones, plus LIRS and Belady's OPT as the unreachable bound and the cliff when a looping working set slightly exceeds the pool.
subtopics.visual: A policy playground where the learner picks LRU, CLOCK, LRU-K, 2Q or ARC, composes an access trace from hot-set, loop and random segments, and steps through it watching reference bits and the clock hand, K-history, queue membership or ghost lists inside each frame while a hit-rate curve for the chosen policy is drawn against OPT for the same trace.

subtopics.title: How good can a cache policy be? OPT, competitive ratios and the stack property
subtopics.covers: Belady's MIN as the offline optimum plus the result that no deterministic online policy beats k-competitive (LRU and CLOCK achieve it, randomized marking reaches O(log k)), so the headroom from a cleverer policy is bounded and usually smaller than the headroom from more memory, the stack/inclusion property that makes one pass over a trace yield an entire miss-ratio curve by reuse distance (Mattson) and which policies have it (LRU, LFU) versus which do not (CLOCK, ARC, 2Q, TinyLFU) so their MRCs must be simulated per size, and the working-set model behind the cliff when a looping scan just exceeds the pool — the framing for sizing shared_buffers, innodb_buffer_pool_size or a Redis tier from a captured trace instead of a rule of thumb.
subtopics.visual: The learner replays a trace through OPT, LRU, CLOCK and ARC with a live competitive-ratio readout against OPT, then computes an MRC in one reuse-distance pass and overlays it on measured hit rates per size, watching the prediction match LRU exactly while visibly diverging from the non-stack policies, and grows a loop-scan working set past the pool to produce the cliff the curve predicted.

subtopics.title: Scan resistance: sequential flooding, ring buffers and midpoint insertion
subtopics.covers: How a single table scan evicts the entire hot set under LRU (sequential flooding) and the engine-level defenses: PostgreSQL's 256KB BAS_BULKREAD ring for scans of tables larger than a quarter of shared_buffers, the 16MB bulk-write ring for COPY/CTAS, the VACUUM ring and synchronized scans that let concurrent scans share the ring; InnoDB's old/young LRU sublists with the 3/8 midpoint (innodb_old_blocks_pct) and the innodb_old_blocks_time window before promotion; RocksDB's fill_cache=false and high-priority cache pool; and the trade-off that a bypassed scan cannot warm the pool.
subtopics.visual: A pool holding a hot working set served by point reads while the learner launches a full scan and toggles between naive insertion, a PostgreSQL-style ring buffer and InnoDB-style midpoint insertion, watching the hot frames get flooded out or survive, the scan recycle its own small ring of frames, and the point-read hit rate dip or hold during and after the scan.

subtopics.title: Dirty pages, write-back and the WAL-before-data rule
subtopics.covers: The dirty bit and pageLSN, the invariant that a frame may be written only after the WAL is flushed through its pageLSN (PostgreSQL's XLogFlush inside FlushBuffer, which is what makes a steal policy safe), InnoDB's flush list ordered by oldest-modification LSN so the checkpoint LSN is its head and recovery starts there, the division of labour between PostgreSQL's background writer, checkpointer with checkpoint_completion_target and sorted writes, and backends evicting dirty pages themselves, InnoDB's page cleaner with adaptive flushing driven by innodb_io_capacity and innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct, and the sync-flush stall when checkpoint age approaches redo log capacity.
subtopics.visual: A dirty-page dashboard where the learner drives a write workload and watches frames turn dirty with their pageLSNs, the flush list order itself by LSN and the WAL flush pointer advance, then tries to evict a dirty frame and sees the WAL flush forced first, and tunes checkpoint interval, redo log size and I/O capacity to see spread-out flushing versus checkpoint-age stalls on an I/O timeline.

subtopics.title: Prefetching and asynchronous reads
subtopics.covers: OS readahead heuristics versus engine-issued prefetch (posix_fadvise WILLNEED, PostgreSQL effective_io_concurrency for bitmap heap scans, the PostgreSQL 17 streaming-read API and the 18 AIO subsystem with worker and io_uring methods), InnoDB linear and random read-ahead keyed on innodb_read_ahead_threshold, RocksDB compaction and iterator auto-readahead, index prefetch along leaf sibling pointers, and the depth trade-off where deeper queues overlap more I/O with CPU (Little's law) but waste bandwidth and pollute the cache when access turns random.
subtopics.visual: A scan timeline with a prefetch-depth slider and a sequential/random access toggle where the learner watches I/O requests on parallel device lanes overlap with CPU processing, the total elapsed time shrink until the device queue saturates, and wasted reads and evicted useful pages appear when the access pattern stops being sequential.

modules.title: Buffer Pool Memory, mmap and Contention
modules.why: Past the caching policy, the pool becomes a memory-budgeting, kernel-interface and scalability problem: where the rest of the server's RAM goes, why mmap cannot replace a buffer pool, what engines that delete the page table gain, and the hot page no amount of partitioning fixes.

subtopics.title: Memory beyond the pool: shared, per-backend and context allocation
subtopics.covers: The static allocation map of a database process — shared allocations (shared_buffers, WAL buffers, lock and predicate lock tables, SLRU caches, InnoDB's buffer pool and log buffer) versus backend-local budgets (work_mem, hash_mem_multiplier, maintenance_work_mem, temp_buffers) and the work_mem × connections × plan nodes × workers arithmetic that makes the map an upper bound rather than a reservation — plus memory contexts and arenas (PostgreSQL AllocSet, generation and slab contexts, jemalloc arenas in MySQL and RocksDB) that make bulk free cheap, huge pages and TLB reach over a large pool, and effective_cache_size as a planner hint that allocates nothing; per-operator grants and spill policy belong to Execution Engines, host and cgroup overcommit and the OOM killer to Operating.
subtopics.visual: A treemap of one server's memory where the learner sizes shared_buffers, WAL buffers and lock tables and sets connections and per-backend budgets, watching the shared block and the per-backend stack re-partition against physical RAM and the OS cache remainder, while a side panel animates a memory context allocating many small chunks and releasing them all in one reset and a huge-pages toggle shows the TLB entries needed to cover the pool collapse.

subtopics.title: Buffer pool vs OS page cache vs mmap
subtopics.covers: Double caching when a buffer pool sits atop a buffered file (PostgreSQL's historically small shared_buffers plus OS cache and the extra memcpy per read) versus O_DIRECT ownership of I/O (InnoDB innodb_flush_method=O_DIRECT, RocksDB use_direct_reads, PostgreSQL's debug_io_direct and AIO trajectory), and the case against mmap from Crotty et al.: the kernel may write a dirty mapped page before its WAL is flushed, page faults stall under latches with no async I/O, eviction triggers TLB shootdowns, I/O errors surface as SIGBUS, and page-cache eviction is single-threaded — with LMDB accepting these via read-only mappings and copy-on-write, SQLite offering mmap optionally and MongoDB abandoning MMAPv1.
subtopics.visual: A three-mode page-flow diagram (buffer pool over page cache, O_DIRECT, mmap) with a slider dividing RAM between pool and page cache where the learner reads and dirties pages and watches duplicate copies and memcpys appear or vanish, then in mmap mode triggers kernel writeback of a dirty page before the WAL flush and crashes to see the write-ahead rule violated.

subtopics.title: Beyond the page table: pointer swizzling, in-memory engines and anti-caching
subtopics.covers: Designs that take the page table off the hot path or remove it entirely — engines with no buffer pool at all (Hekaton, VoltDB, Redis) versus larger-than-memory designs that keep memory-speed access while still spilling: LeanStore's swizzled versus unswizzled references where a resident child is reached by a raw pointer with no hash probe and validated optimistically, its cooling stage with randomly sampled epoch-based eviction and the unswizzle-from-parent step that eviction must perform, Umbra's variable-size buffer frames backed by a large virtual-memory reservation, H-Store/VoltDB anti-caching that evicts cold tuples to disk and aborts-and-restarts transactions that touch them before merging the block back, Redis-on-flash tiering, and the working-set economics and trade-off (no lookup per access versus references that must be found and invalidated) that decide when each pays.
subtopics.visual: The same skewed access trace raced through three engines side by side — pure in-memory hitting an OOM wall as the learner shrinks RAM below the working set, a classic hash-table pool paying a probe per page access, and a swizzling pool whose hot references render as direct pointers — with per-access lookup and instruction counters, hit rates and abort counts, and a step-through of one eviction that cools a page, walks to its parent to unswizzle the pointer and writes it out, plus an anti-caching mode where a transaction touching an evicted tuple aborts and restarts after the block merge.

subtopics.title: Latching the buffer pool and hot-page contention
subtopics.covers: The hot-page pathologies no amount of partitioning fixes — the rightmost B-tree leaf under monotonic inserts, upper index levels, sequence and counter pages — and the synchronization layers underneath them: PostgreSQL's per-buffer header state word updated by CAS (pin count and flags), the content LWLock in shared or exclusive mode, the 128 BufMappingLock partitions over the page table, the atomic clock hand and the I/O-in-progress lock; InnoDB's multiple buffer pool instances each with their own mutex, LRU and flush list, and its rw-locked page hash; and how the buffer_content versus BufferMapping wait events tell a genuinely hot page apart from mere table contention, the former answered by optimistic version-based latching rather than more partitions.
subtopics.visual: The shared thread-contention animator from Part 1, opened already in the pathology: every thread pinned to one hot frame, where the learner's knobs are the page-table partition count and the number of pool instances and turning them up visibly changes nothing (header CAS retries and the shared/exclusive content-latch queue stay saturated, throughput flat), until the same threads are spread across many pages and the mapping-lock contention those knobs were built for finally disappears — each configuration labelled with the wait event it produces.

modules.title: B-Trees: Structure, Maintenance and Key Encoding
modules.why: The B+tree is the default index of every OLTP engine, and its shape, split behaviour, key encoding and the external-memory bounds behind them decide real lookup and range-scan cost.

subtopics.title: B+tree structure, invariants and search
subtopics.covers: A balanced multiway tree whose fanout in the hundreds keeps height at 3–4 for billions of keys, with the invariants every engine maintains (all leaves at one depth, half-full occupancy except the root, ordered separator keys in internal nodes that need not be real keys, records only in leaves, a sibling-linked leaf chain) and their cost consequences: point lookup = height page reads with binary search inside each node, range scan = one descent plus a leaf-chain walk, B-tree vs B+tree fanout loss, and what a leaf entry actually holds in PostgreSQL nbtree (TID), InnoDB (PK values in secondaries, rows in the clustered tree) and SQLite (rowid) as covered in the pages module.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets fanout (4–128) and page size, types a point key or a range, and watches the descent highlight each separator comparison node by node, tally page reads, then walk the leaf chain, while a readout shows height, keys addressable and the effect of switching values into internal nodes (B-tree mode).

subtopics.title: Insert, split, delete and merge
subtopics.covers: Leaf insert, overflow split at the midpoint promoting a separator (copy-up from leaves, push-up from internals), cascading splits that grow a new root, delete with underflow handled by redistribution from a sibling or a merge that pulls the separator down and can collapse the root, plus how real engines diverge from the textbook: PostgreSQL never merges and instead marks empty pages half-dead for later recycling by VACUUM, InnoDB merges only below MERGE_THRESHOLD, SQLite's balance routine rebalances across three siblings, and a split costs two or three page writes plus WAL — WAL that is not an ordinary transactional undo record, as the next subtopic explains.
subtopics.visual: A small-fanout tree with an insert/delete console and a 'textbook' vs 'real engine (lazy delete)' toggle where each step animates separator promotion, split cascades to the root, redistribution vs merge vs a half-dead page, with a per-operation pages-written counter.

subtopics.title: Crash safety of structure modifications: atomic splits and incomplete-split repair
subtopics.covers: Why a split cannot simply be undone when its transaction aborts — the tree is shared physical structure, not that transaction's data, and a concurrent reader or writer may already have descended into the new page — so engines make the structure-modification operation atomic with respect to recovery instead: PostgreSQL nbtree logs the split of both pages as one multi-page WAL record and leaves the parent's downlink insertion pending behind an INCOMPLETE_SPLIT flag that the next descent (or VACUUM) is obliged to finish, InnoDB wraps the whole SMO in a mini-transaction whose redo records are written and replayed as an indivisible group with no undo at all, and ARIES generalizes this as a nested top action that commits independently of the enclosing transaction with a dummy CLR skipping past it and any compensation done logically (delete the key, merge later) rather than by byte-level page restore — and the half-finished right-linked state a crash leaves behind is exactly the state the Lehman-Yao reader of b-tree-concurrency-and-write-optimized-variants tolerates by following the right link, so the recovery rule and the concurrency rule are the same rule seen from two sides.
subtopics.visual: A split runs as a WAL record sequence the learner scrubs through with a draggable crash point, and at any position the simulator kills the engine and restarts it: the learner sees which pages made it to disk, whether redo replays the split as one record or leaves an INCOMPLETE_SPLIT downlink missing, then issues a search that either follows the right link to find the key anyway or (with the flag repair path disabled) descends into a dead end, with a 'roll back the inserting transaction' button showing the key vanishing while the split stays.

subtopics.title: Fill factor, fragmentation and splits under load
subtopics.covers: How fillfactor (PostgreSQL 90% leaves, InnoDB 15/16 and innodb_fill_factor) reserves in-page room, why monotonic keys with the rightmost-split optimization (split at the insertion point, PostgreSQL's fastpath insert) yield nearly full pages while UUIDv4 keys yield 50–70% fill and splits everywhere, how splits let logical and physical leaf order diverge so range scans turn into random I/O (pgstatindex leaf_fragmentation), the hot rightmost-leaf contention of sequential keys, UUIDv7/ULID as the fix, and repair via REINDEX or OPTIMIZE TABLE.
subtopics.visual: An insert-stream selector (monotonic int, UUIDv4, UUIDv7, timestamp-plus-random) and a fillfactor slider drive a live leaf-occupancy histogram, split counter, and a physical page map whose logical-to-physical arrows scramble as splits land, with pages-touched for a range scan updating alongside.

subtopics.title: Bulk loading and index construction
subtopics.covers: Bottom-up build from sorted input (external sort, write leaves left to right at the target fillfactor, build each parent level from the last key of each child page) versus repeated top-down inserts, as done by PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX (tuplesort with parallel workers bounded by maintenance_work_mem, then _bt_load) and InnoDB's sorted index build for ALTER, with the cost model (N log N sort plus N/F sequential page writes vs N descents with random splits), why the result is exactly full and physically ordered, and pointers to external sort in physical-operators and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in indexes-beyond-the-b-tree.
subtopics.visual: The same key set builds side by side: a repeated-insert tree animating splits versus a bottom-up builder that sorts into runs, merges them, lays leaves in order and stacks parent levels, with page writes, fill percentage, physical order and I/O time compared, and a work_mem slider changing the number of sort runs.

subtopics.title: Key layout, prefix compression and suffix truncation
subtopics.covers: How keys are laid out in variable-length cells with a slot directory, suffix truncation of separators (PostgreSQL 12) so an internal key holds only enough bytes to separate its children and fanout rises, prefix compression of shared leading bytes (WiredTiger, MyISAM), PostgreSQL 13 deduplication folding duplicate keys into posting lists of TIDs, the Lehman-Yao high key stored on every PostgreSQL page, why wide InnoDB primary keys shrink every secondary index's fanout, and normalized keys as the bridge to byte-comparable encoding.
subtopics.visual: An index over long composite string keys rendered at the byte level per page, with toggles for suffix truncation, prefix compression and deduplication that visibly shrink cells and change internal fanout, tree height and total page count.

subtopics.title: Collation, Unicode and byte-comparable key encoding
subtopics.covers: Why a B-tree's order is only as stable as its comparator: memcomparable encoding used by MyRocks, TiKV, CockroachDB and FoundationDB's tuple layer (sign-flipped integers, big-endian floats, NULL-first bytes, 0x00 escaping in strings, descending order via complement) so keys compare by memcmp, versus locale collation through glibc strcoll or ICU where the glibc 2.28 collation change reordered existing PostgreSQL indexes into silent corruption, ICU collversion tracking and pg_collation warnings, C/C.UTF-8 vs linguistic collations, MySQL utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci case-insensitive equality and pad attributes, and the symptoms (missed lookups, duplicate uniques) that require REINDEX as discussed in the upgrades subtopic of the operating module, which reuses this page's committed ordering fixture for its own collation-trap visual.
subtopics.visual: Keys come from a shipped fixture — about 24 hand-chosen strings (punctuation, spaces, case pairs, accents, an emoji) whose orderings under C/memcmp, glibc 2.27, glibc 2.28 and a pinned ICU version were generated offline and committed as a JSON table with provenance, since a browser has only its own unversioned ICU — and the learner picks a comparator to see the encoded bytes and the table-lookup order, builds the B-tree live from that order, then presses 'upgrade libc' so the leaves keep their old physical layout while a real binary search descends the tree, misses a key that is present, and a unique insert lands as an accepted duplicate.

subtopics.title: Why fanout B: the external-memory model, optimality bounds and cache-oblivious layouts
