subtopics.covers: The DAM/external-memory model (memory M, block size B, cost counted in block transfers) in which a scan costs N/B, B-tree search is Θ(log_B N) and provably optimal, external sorting is Θ((N/B)·log_{M/B}(N/B)) and the permutation lower bound explains why the sort-then-build of the bulk-loading subtopic provably beats N random inserts, the insert-versus-query optimality curve on which B-trees, Bε-trees (B^{1-ε} amortized inserts) and leveled LSMs all sit as points and which the RUM conjecture projects onto a third axis, cache-oblivious structures that hit the same bounds with no knowledge of B (van Emde Boas layout, funnel sort, cache-oblivious lookahead arrays), and why production engines still hard-code page sizes anyway — latching, checksums, prefetch, TLB reach and the buffer pool all need a named unit.
subtopics.visual: Sliders for B and M drive block-transfer counters as the same key workload runs over a linear array, a B-tree of tunable fanout, a van Emde Boas-laid-out tree and an LSM, with measured I/Os plotted against the analytic curves; changing B leaves the cache-oblivious layout's curve untouched while the fixed-fanout tree's optimum visibly shifts, and a bulk-load-versus-insert race shows the permutation bound as a gap that never closes.

modules.title: B-Tree Concurrency and Write-Optimized Variants
modules.why: Once many cores hit the same index, correctness and throughput come from latch protocols, the memory model beneath them and safe reclamation — and the same pressure produced the latch-free, write-optimized and copy-on-write descendants of the B+tree, which only make sense once you have seen both a B+tree and an LSM and can price one against the other; this module is the first 'enough for most engineers, stop here' boundary in Part 2, so a reader who stops after it still has the complete core storage spine, while everything here is what you need before reading engine source or designing an index yourself.

subtopics.title: B-tree concurrency: latch crabbing and Lehman-Yao
subtopics.covers: Latch coupling (crabbing) that holds a parent latch until the child is proven safe (not full for inserts, above half for deletes), optimistic descent with read latches and restart, optimistic lock coupling with per-node version counters (LeanStore, Umbra), and Lehman-Yao B-link trees where a right-link plus high key on every page lets readers detect a concurrent split and move right without parent latches, as PostgreSQL nbtree does with lazily completed splits and half-dead page deletion gated on btpo_xact/safexid, contrasted with InnoDB's index-level rw-lock with SX mode plus page latches and the top-down/left-to-right ordering that avoids latch deadlock.
subtopics.visual: Two threads (an inserter that triggers a split and a reader) descend the same tree while the learner picks crabbing, optimistic coupling or B-link mode and steps each thread, watching latch badges and blocked states on nodes, version-check restarts, and in B-link mode the reader comparing against a high key and following the right link to find the moved key.

subtopics.title: Memory models, atomics and what makes optimistic latching correct
subtopics.covers: Why lock-free engine code needs more than a CAS — x86-TSO's store buffering versus the weaker reordering of ARM and POWER, C++ acquire/release/seq_cst and the compiler barriers that stop reordering, the seqlock validation pattern that makes the optimistic lock coupling of the previous subtopic correct (acquire-load the version, read the payload, fence, re-check and restart) as used by LeanStore, Umbra and Silo's TID validation, the ABA problem and the tagged pointers or epochs that close it, false sharing and cache-line ping-pong that make a 'lock-free' counter slower than a mutex, and Herlihy's wait-free hierarchy showing that atomic registers (consensus number 1) cannot implement consensus while compare-and-swap (∞) can — the reason the hardware primitive every engine leans on is CAS.
subtopics.visual: Two threads run a seqlock-style optimistic read against a concurrent writer on a simulated weak-memory machine where the learner can delete individual fences and watch the reader observe a torn record that the identical schedule on TSO would have hidden, with counters for failed re-checks and restarts, a false-sharing toggle that co-locates two counters on one cache line and collapses throughput, and an ABA replay where a tagged pointer rejects the swap that the plain pointer accepted.

subtopics.title: Bw-tree: delta chains and the mapping table
subtopics.covers: The Bw-tree's mapping table of page IDs to pointers as the single indirection that makes updates latch-free: delta records prepended by a compare-and-swap on the mapping slot, consolidation when chains grow past a threshold, two-phase latch-free splits (split delta then index-entry delta) and multi-step merges, the read-path cost of chasing delta chains, LLAMA's log-structured page store, deployment in Hekaton (SQL Server In-Memory OLTP) and Azure DocumentDB, and the CMU OpenBw-Tree evaluation showing that a well-built B+tree with optimistic lock coupling usually wins.
subtopics.visual: The learner applies inserts and updates that appear as delta records chained onto a page through the mapping table, triggers consolidation, initiates a split and steps through both CAS phases while a second concurrent writer's CAS fails and retries, with a pointer-chase count for each read shown live.

subtopics.title: Memory reclamation for latch-free structures: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
subtopics.covers: The safe-freeing problem once nodes are unlinked without latches (use-after-free and ABA under concurrent readers) and its answers: epoch-based reclamation with per-thread enter/exit and per-epoch retire lists freed only when every thread has advanced, hazard pointers that publish the exact pointers in use and scan them before freeing, RCU grace periods and quiescent-state reclamation, how the Bw-tree and Hekaton use epochs, RocksDB's SuperVersion reference counts with thread-local caching, PostgreSQL's transaction-id-based page recycling as an epoch analog, and the failure mode where one stalled thread pins memory growth.
subtopics.visual: Several reader threads traverse a linked structure while a writer unlinks nodes; the learner chooses epochs, hazard pointers or RCU and can pause any reader, watching retire lists drain only when the slowest reader exits (memory climbing under epochs) versus a hazard-pointer scan that frees everything except the one node still published.

subtopics.title: Bε-trees, fractal trees and copy-on-write B-trees
subtopics.covers: Write-optimized and snapshot-friendly variants: Bε-trees whose internal nodes carry message buffers so inserts, deletes and upserts land at the root and flush downward in batches, cutting per-insert cost by roughly B^(1-ε) at the price of scanning buffers on every lookup (TokuDB/PerconaFT, BetrFS), and copy-on-write B-trees that path-copy from leaf to root and swap a root or meta page per commit to get atomic commit and free reader snapshots without a WAL (LMDB's alternating meta pages, BoltDB, Btrfs, ZFS, CouchDB's append-only tree), with their costs of path-copy write amplification, a single writer, and free pages pinned by the oldest open reader, cross-referenced to shadow paging in the recovery module.
subtopics.visual: A mode switch between a Bε-tree, where the learner watches root and internal buffers fill and cascade flushes with a disk-writes counter racing a plain B+tree on the same inserts, and a COW tree where each commit copies the modified path, flips the meta page, can be crashed mid-commit and reopened from the last valid meta, and a draggable 'oldest reader' handle shows which old pages cannot yet be freed.

subtopics.title: Persistence by path copying: fat nodes, versions and why snapshots are cheap
subtopics.covers: The general result behind the previous subtopic's COW trees — Driscoll–Sarnak–Sleator–Tarjan persistence: partial versus full persistence, path copying with its O(depth) write amplification and O(1) version switch, and fat nodes with per-field version stamps plus the node-splitting trick that bounds their growth, mapped onto the shipping structures that are all the same idea (LMDB and BoltDB swapping a root page, ZFS and Btrfs clones, CouchDB's append-only tree, Datomic's structurally shared index, Git's object model, and MVCC version chains as coarse partial persistence), together with the one cost model they share — bytes written proportional to path length, old versions pinned by the oldest live root, branches and time travel priced only at the diverged nodes — and why Iceberg snapshot expiry, Neon branch retention and filesystem clone billing all fall out of it.
subtopics.visual: The learner updates one leaf of a shared tree and watches the copied path form while untouched subtrees stay shared, with per-version root pointers listed beside bytes-written and pages-pinned meters, then holds an old reader open to see reclamation blocked for exactly the nodes its root still reaches, and switches to a fat-node representation where the same history is stored as per-field version stamps with a visibly different read cost.

modules.title: Log-Structured Merge Trees
modules.why: LSM trees power RocksDB, Cassandra, and most distributed stores; the write path, the sorted-run file format and the filtered read path explain both their speed and where that speed quietly disappears.

subtopics.title: Append-only logs and Bitcask hash indexes
subtopics.covers: Append-only segment files with an in-memory hash directory mapping key to (file_id, offset, size) as in Bitcask/Riak: CRC+timestamp+key+value record framing, overwrite-by-append, tombstone records, merge that rewrites closed segments keeping only the newest live record per key and emits hint files so restart rebuilds the index without scanning values, and the two hard limits (every key must fit in RAM, no range scans) that motivate sorted runs and SSTables.
subtopics.visual: The learner puts, overwrites and deletes keys and watches records append to the active segment while hash-index arrows re-point to the newest offset; a Merge button rewrites closed segments dropping dead records and emits hint files, and a Crash/Restart button replays hint files versus full segment scans with a rebuild-time and RAM counter.

subtopics.title: Write path: WAL, memtable, flush and write stalls
subtopics.covers: A write appends to the WAL (sync policy sets the durability window), then inserts into a sorted memtable (RocksDB arena skiplist, Cassandra's 5.0 trie memtable, Pebble batchskl) stamped with a monotonic sequence number, with WriteBatch atomicity and write-group leader batching; at write_buffer_size the memtable becomes immutable and a background flush writes an L0 SSTable, and too many immutables or L0 files trip RocksDB's slowdown/stop write stalls (max_write_buffer_number, level0_slowdown/stop_writes_trigger, pending_compaction_bytes).
subtopics.visual: Keys stream into an animated skiplist while the WAL bar grows; memtable-size and flush-speed sliders let the learner watch the memtable freeze, a fresh one open, L0 files stack up, and the write-rate gauge throttle then halt as each stall trigger is crossed, with the sequence-number counter ticking per write.

subtopics.title: Skip lists: probabilistic balance without rebalancing
subtopics.covers: The geometric level distribution (p=1/4 in RocksDB, 1/2 classic) giving O(log n) expected search with no rotations or rebalancing, search as a staircase of forward pointers, why insert is a per-level compare-and-swap so a memtable needs no structural latch (RocksDB's InlineSkipList with arena allocation and its concurrent variant, Pebble's batchskl), the ~1.33-pointers-per-node space overhead and cache-unfriendly pointer chasing, the tail-latency variance probabilistic balance implies, the cache-conscious alternatives engines have moved to (Cassandra 4.1's pluggable memtable API and the trie memtables it enabled in 5.0, ScyllaDB, Masstree, ART), and the other shipping uses — Redis sorted sets paired with a hash, LevelDB, HBase's concurrent skip-list map.
subtopics.visual: The learner inserts keys and watches each one coin-flip its height into the level lanes, then runs a search that walks the top lane and drops down level by level with a comparison counter, adjusts p and n to see expected height and comparisons track the analytic curve, and steps two concurrent inserters doing per-level CAS so one visibly retries when a forward pointer moves beneath it.

subtopics.title: Writes that must read first: constraints, secondary indexes and Merge
subtopics.covers: Blind append is only true for pure key-value writes: a unique constraint or a secondary index forces a Get/GetForUpdate through the memtable, the immutables and every level (paying exactly the filter and read-amplification cost of the read path) before the Put, giving the MyRocks/TiKV/CockroachDB per-row cost model of one clustered write plus N index writes plus M merged reads and collapsing the LSM's headline write advantage; RocksDB's Merge operator removes read-modify-write for commutative updates by appending merge operands that reads and compaction collapse through an associative merge function, and SingleDelete deletes a key in one cheap step only under its contract that the key was Put exactly once — violate it and an older value reappears.
subtopics.visual: Toggles for 'unique index' and a k-secondary-indexes dial sit on the write-path animation: each write sprouts read probes fanning down the level tree with filter checks, block reads, latency and write-amp meters climbing, then switching a counter column from read-modify-write to a Merge operator makes the probes vanish as operands stack and collapse at read or compaction time, and a SingleDelete issued against a twice-written key visibly resurrects the old value.

subtopics.title: SSTable format: blocks, restart points, index, filters, footer
subtopics.covers: The LevelDB/RocksDB block-based table: prefix-compressed data blocks with restart points every 16 keys enabling binary search, per-block compression and checksum trailer, index block of shortest-separator keys (suffix truncation), Bloom/ribbon filter block, metaindex, properties block and the fixed footer with magic number; partitioned index and filters for huge files, and Cassandra's Data/Index/Summary/Filter/CompressionInfo components.
subtopics.visual: SSTable explorer: the learner types keys, builds the file and sees data blocks, restart-point arrays, index, filter and footer laid out byte-by-byte with hover decoding; running Get(key) animates footer to index block to binary search over restart points to linear decode within the interval, and a restart-interval slider shows the file-size versus search-steps trade.

subtopics.title: Read path, Bloom filters and the block cache
subtopics.covers: Point lookup consults memtable, immutables, every L0 file (they overlap), then one file per level found by binary search over version key ranges, checking the Bloom filter (FP ≈ (1−e^(−kn/m))^k, 10 bits/key ≈ 1%) and the sharded LRU/Clock block cache (compressed vs uncompressed tiers, pinned index/filter blocks) before touching disk; range scans use a merging iterator over all sources and cannot use Bloom filters except prefix Bloom, so read amplification grows with L0 count and run count.
subtopics.visual: Bloom sandbox plus multi-level probe: the learner sets bits/key and k, inserts keys and watches bits set and the empirical false-positive rate converge on the formula; then issues Gets for present and absent keys across a level tree and counts filters checked, block-cache hits/misses and disk block reads, with an L0 file-count slider showing read amplification climb.

subtopics.title: Deletes, tombstones, TTL and snapshots
subtopics.covers: Deletes are writes: point tombstones, SingleDelete and range tombstones (RocksDB DeleteRange fragmented ranges) shadow older versions until a compaction reaches a level where no lower file overlaps the key (bottommost in general); Cassandra gc_grace_seconds retains tombstones for anti-entropy so a replica offline longer resurrects zombies; snapshots pin sequence numbers so compaction must keep the newest version at or below each live snapshot; TTL and compaction filters drop expired rows; tombstone-heavy scans (the queue anti-pattern) read thousands of dead entries per live row (snapshot-aware GC continues in the MVCC module).
subtopics.visual: Insert then delete keys while holding snapshots: the learner steps compactions and sees which versions and tombstones each one may drop given the live-snapshot list and overlap with lower levels, runs a range scan whose counter shows tombstones skipped per live row returned, and moves a gc_grace slider against a replica-down timer to trigger zombie resurrection.

subtopics.title: Beyond Bloom: cuckoo, quotient, xor and ribbon filters
subtopics.covers: The ~log2(1/ε) bits-per-key lower bound and how far each design sits above it, Bloom's k scattered probes and its inability to delete, blocked/split-block Bloom trading a little false-positive rate for one cache line (Impala, Parquet), cuckoo filters storing fingerprints under partial-key cuckoo hashing to gain deletion and locality at high load factors, quotient filters' quotient/remainder plus metadata bits enabling merge and resize, xor filters' static construction at ~1.23x the information-theoretic bound with three lookups and binary fuse filters' at ~1.08x, and ribbon filters' banded linear-system solve giving tunable space-versus-build-time (RocksDB's choice for bottom levels) — each judged by the operational questions that decide it: can it be built during compaction, merged, deleted from, and does it fit the block cache.
subtopics.visual: The prior page's Bloom sandbox sits embedded read-only at the learner's last-used bits/key as a fixed baseline row, and all interaction goes to the alternatives: the learner builds blocked Bloom, cuckoo, quotient, xor and ribbon over the same key set, watching a cuckoo eviction chain, an xor three-hash construction and a ribbon band being solved, then attempts a delete, a merge and a mid-compaction build on each so it visibly succeeds or is refused, while one shared chart plots every design's measured false-positive rate and cache-line footprint against the log2(1/ε) floor so the gap above the bound is the common axis.

modules.title: LSM Compaction, Amplification and Crash Safety
modules.why: Everything an LSM costs in practice — write amplification, space bloat, stalls, recovery time and bulk-load behavior — is decided by the compaction policy and the version/manifest machinery that installs its output.

subtopics.title: Why compaction exists: the three amplifications and the RUM trade-off
subtopics.covers: The problem compaction solves — every flush adds another sorted run, so run count drives read amplification (runs probed per lookup, worst in L0 where files overlap and a point read may touch every file), obsolete versions and tombstones drive space amplification (total bytes over live bytes), and merging them away costs write amplification (bytes written to disk over bytes from the user, visible as RocksDB's W-Amp column and as SSD endurance burn); the RUM conjecture that read, update and memory overheads cannot all be minimized at once, why filter bits are the memory knob that buys read amp back (Monkey's insight that small levels deserve more bits per key), how a B+tree (page-per-update write amp, fragmentation space amp, stable tail latency) sits at a different corner of the same triangle than an LSM, and the fourth cost the triangle hides — cache invalidation, since a compaction rewrites the very files whose data, index and filter blocks the block cache holds, so every cached block for the rewritten range dies at once and reads degrade until the cache re-warms, mitigated by cache_index_and_filter_blocks with pinned top-level and partition filters (or by keeping filters out of the LRU entirely).
subtopics.visual: Amplification triangle: the learner drags a point among read, write and space, sees the matching configuration (run count per level, size ratio, per-level filter bits), and runs the same insert/read workload against an animated B+tree and an LSM with live W-amp/R-amp/S-amp meters, an L0-overlap probe count, a block-cache occupancy bar whose blocks for a rewritten range go dark the moment a compaction commits, and latency histograms that diverge as the read/write-ratio, value-size and filter-pinning controls move.

subtopics.title: Compaction strategies: leveled, tiered, TWCS and lazy leveling
subtopics.covers: Leveled (LevelDB/RocksDB default, Cassandra LCS): one sorted run per level with 10x size ratio, picking by level score and kMinOverlappingRatio, overlap-bounded merges giving about 1.1x space amp but roughly 10x write amp per level; size-tiered/universal (Cassandra STCS, RocksDB universal, ScyllaDB ICS): merge similar-sized runs for low write amp at 2x space and higher read amp; TWCS and FIFO for TTL time-series so whole windows expire by file drop; Dostoevsky lazy leveling and Fluid LSM hybrids that tier the small levels and level the largest; subcompactions, rate limiting and trivial moves for monotonic keys; and the two operational signatures of running compaction — the p99 read sawtooth each time a big compaction invalidates the block cache for the range it rewrote (routinely misattributed to the compaction's I/O), and the block whose checksum fails mid-compaction, which aborts the job and lets it retry forever so a single bad block surfaces as permanently growing compaction debt, L0 buildup and write stalls rather than as a read error.
subtopics.visual: Compaction simulator: choose leveled, tiered, TWCS or lazy leveling, set size ratio and L0 trigger, stream a random, monotonic or TTL time-series workload, and watch files merge across levels with the selected input set, overlap range and output files highlighted step by step, with per-compaction bytes read/written, a compaction-debt timeline, a block-cache bar and p99 trace that sawtooth after each commit, and a 'corrupt a block' button that makes the chosen compaction abort and retry while debt, L0 count and stall risk climb until the learner quarantines the file.

subtopics.title: Key-value separation and blob storage
subtopics.covers: WiscKey's split of keys plus pointers in the LSM and values in an append-only value log (RocksDB BlobDB with min_blob_size, TiKV Titan, Badger) cuts compaction write amp for large values but loses range-scan locality (random value fetches, WiscKey's parallel prefetch), requires value-log GC that rewrites live blobs and reinserts pointers or tracks blob-file liveness through compaction, and adds space amp from dead blobs until GC runs.
subtopics.visual: Toggle KV separation with value-size and min_blob_size sliders: the same workload shows compaction bytes shrinking as values move to the blob log, a range scan fanning out into random blob reads with an I/O counter, and dead-blob space growing until the learner triggers GC and watches live blobs rewritten and LSM pointers updated.

subtopics.title: Manifest, versions and crash safety
subtopics.covers: A Version is the immutable set of live files per level with key ranges and seqno bounds; every flush, compaction and ingest commits a VersionEdit (files added/deleted, next file number, last sequence, log number) appended to the MANIFEST, with CURRENT swapped atomically on manifest rollover; obsolete files are deleted only when the versions referencing them (iterators, snapshots) drop to zero refcount; recovery reads CURRENT to MANIFEST, replays WALs numbered at or above log_number into a memtable under a WAL recovery mode (kTolerateCorruptedTailRecords vs kAbsoluteConsistency), and column families share one WAL with per-CF log numbers and atomic flush.
subtopics.visual: Crash-and-recover step-through: the learner picks a crash point (mid-flush, SSTable written but VersionEdit not yet logged, mid-manifest rollover, torn WAL tail) and then steps recovery through CURRENT, each MANIFEST edit and WAL replay, watching the live file set rebuild, orphan files get garbage-collected and the memtable reconstructed.

subtopics.title: Bulk loading and external SSTable ingestion
subtopics.covers: Building SSTables offline (RocksDB SstFileWriter, Cassandra sstableloader/CQLSSTableWriter, CockroachDB AddSSTable in IMPORT and rebalancing) and installing them via IngestExternalFile as a VersionEdit that bypasses WAL and memtable: flushing the memtable if it overlaps, picking the lowest level with no key overlap, stamping a global sequence number (rewritten in the file or placed beneath everything with ingest_behind) so newer writes win and existing snapshots do not see the data, and the consequences of files landing in L0 as sudden compaction debt and read amp.
subtopics.visual: The learner builds a sorted external file, chooses ingest options (allow_blocking_flush, ingest_behind) and drops it into a populated tree: the animation checks overlap against memtable and each level, picks the target level, stamps the global seqno, appends the VersionEdit, and then compares compaction work and write-amp meters against streaming the same rows through the write path.

modules.title: Indexes Beyond the B-Tree
modules.why: Hash, bitmap, spatial, inverted and range-summary access methods each serve predicates a B-tree cannot, the hash function underneath them decides whether buckets stay short or collapse into skew, and building any of them online is its own mechanism.

subtopics.title: Hash indexes: extendible and linear hashing
subtopics.covers: Static hashing with overflow chains, extendible hashing (global/local depth, directory doubling only when the overflowing bucket's local depth equals global depth, else a local split), linear hashing (round-robin split pointer, the h_i / h_{i+1} hash family, overflow pages tolerated between splits), and the Postgres hash AM (bucket/overflow/bitmap pages, stores 32-bit hash codes not keys so it wins for wide keys, WAL-logged only since PG 10, equality-only with no ORDER BY, uniqueness or multi-column), plus InnoDB's adaptive hash index as a self-tuning shortcut over hot B-tree pages; in-memory hash tables for joins belong to the physical-operators module.
subtopics.visual: An extendible-hashing sandbox: the learner inserts keys and sees each key's hash bits, the directory with its global depth and buckets with their local depths; an overflow triggers either a local bucket split or a full directory doubling, and a tab switches to linear hashing where the split pointer advances round-robin and overflow chains grow and drain, with directory size and average chain length counters updating live.

subtopics.title: Hash functions inside the engine: universality, avalanche and adversarial keys
subtopics.covers: What engines need from a hash (uniformity and avalanche, bytes per cycle, seedability, and explicitly not cryptographic strength) and where each is used — murmur3 for Cassandra's token ring, xxHash and CRC32C in RocksDB and page checksums, SipHash as the keyed defence after the 2011 HashDoS collision attacks, PostgreSQL's hash_any family feeding hash joins, hash aggregation, hash partitioning and the hash AM — the universal and pairwise-independent families that make linear-probe and bucket-chain lengths provably short, why reusing the same hash and seed for partitioning and then for the join's hash table collapses every row into one bucket and needs a second seed, the birthday bound that sizes 64-bit versus 128-bit fingerprints and content hashes, and the practical failure signature of one partition or bucket holding everything under structured or adversarial keys.
subtopics.visual: The learner feeds key sets (sequential integers, hostnames, adversarially chosen collisions, UUIDs) through a selectable hash and sees an avalanche bit-flip matrix, a bucket-occupancy histogram and a probe-length distribution drawn against the theoretical curve, then deliberately reuses one hash and seed for partitioning and for the join hash table to watch every row pile into a single bucket until a second seed is applied.

subtopics.title: Bitmap indexes and bitmap heap scans
subtopics.covers: Stored bitmap indexes (Oracle, Druid, warehouses) keeping one bitmap per distinct value with WAH/Roaring compression and word-level AND/OR/NOT for low-cardinality star-schema predicates but suffering lock contention under concurrent DML, versus Postgres's run-time TID bitmaps: any index feeds a Bitmap Index Scan, BitmapAnd/BitmapOr combine them, the heap is visited in physical page order for sequential I/O, and when work_mem overflows the bitmap degrades from exact TIDs to lossy page-granular bits so every tuple on those pages must pass a Recheck Cond.
subtopics.visual: Two predicate sliders over a page grid: the learner watches each index produce a bitmap over the pages, ANDs them into one, then walks the heap in ascending page order; shrinking a work_mem slider flips chunks of the bitmap from exact to lossy, and a counter shows rows rechecked and discarded climbing while pages read stays flat.

subtopics.title: BRIN, zone maps and min/max data skipping
subtopics.covers: Block Range INdexes summarizing each pages_per_range (default 128) with min/max (plus minmax_multi, inclusion for ranges/boxes and bloom opclasses in PG 14), scans that union all ranges whose summary may match into a lossy page bitmap with recheck, the pruning arithmetic that makes BRIN a few KB yet useless unless pg_stats.correlation is near ±1, summaries that only widen on updates and unsummarized tails after inserts (autosummarize, brin_summarize_new_values), and the same mechanism reappearing as Parquet row-group statistics, ClickHouse minmax skip indexes and Snowflake micro-partition pruning (the column-stores module covers choosing sort keys to make it work).
subtopics.visual: A correlation slider shuffles values across a strip of heap pages; the learner runs a range predicate and sees each block range's [min,max] summary, the ranges pruned versus scanned, and index size vs pages read, then appends out-of-order rows to watch a summary widen and a fresh tail range appear unsummarized until 'summarize' is pressed, and adjusts pages_per_range to trade index size against pruning precision.

subtopics.title: GiST and R-trees for spatial and range data
subtopics.covers: R-trees keeping minimum bounding rectangles whose overlap forces search down multiple subtrees, insertion by least-enlargement ChooseSubtree and splits by linear, quadratic or R*-tree (minimize overlap and margin, forced reinsert) heuristics that decide query cost, and the GiST generalization via consistent/union/penalty/picksplit/compress callbacks powering PostGIS geometry, range types, exclusion constraints and lossy tsvector signatures, KNN via a best-first distance priority queue, Postgres's NSN/right-link concurrency and buffered builds, and the alternative of mapping space onto a B-tree or KV key with Z-order, geohash, S2 or H3 cells (DynamoDB, Cassandra, MongoDB 2dsphere).
subtopics.visual: The learner draws rectangles on a canvas and watches the R-tree's bounding boxes grow and split, toggling quadratic vs R*-tree split with a live total-overlap metric; dragging a query window highlights every node whose MBR intersects it (showing the multi-path descent), and dropping a point runs a KNN search whose priority queue expands nodes in distance order.

subtopics.title: GIN inverted indexes and posting lists
subtopics.covers: Generalized Inverted Index extracting many keys per item (array elements, tsvector lexemes, JSONB keys/values under jsonb_ops vs hashed paths under jsonb_path_ops) into an entry B-tree whose small posting lists are inline varbyte-delta-compressed TIDs and large ones become posting trees, multi-key queries answered by intersecting or unioning posting lists via consistent/triConsistent with heap recheck when lossy, the fastupdate pending list that batches inserts unsorted until gin_pending_list_limit or VACUUM flushes it (fast writes, tail-latency spikes, slower reads while it fills), no ordering support, and why each row costs many index entries on write.
subtopics.visual: The learner adds documents with tag arrays or JSONB and watches the entry tree and posting lists form, then sees new inserts land in the pending list and flush into the main structure on a threshold; running a @> or && query animates the pointer walk that intersects posting lists, and a jsonb_ops/jsonb_path_ops toggle shows the key count per document change.

subtopics.title: Full-text indexes: term dictionaries, postings and skip lists
subtopics.covers: Querying a prebuilt full-text index rather than constructing one: term dictionary lookup by binary search over dictionary blocks or an FST/trie walk, postings stored as delta-gap varbyte or Elias-Fano runs with skip pointers, boolean queries executed as leapfrog intersection/union with the lowest document-frequency term driving evaluation order, phrase queries verified by positional adjacency in position lists, prefix and wildcard queries as dictionary range scans expanded into a disjunction, Lucene's immutable per-segment term dictionaries and doc values with merging, why Postgres GIN stores no positions so phrase matching and ranking must recheck the heap, and pg_trgm trigram indexes turning LIKE '%x%' into a postings intersection; the analyzer pipeline and BM25 ranking parameters belong to the advanced-sql module.
subtopics.visual: Starting from a prebuilt index, the learner issues a query and watches the term dictionary lookup resolve each term (binary search over blocks, or an FST walk), then two posting lists advance side by side with skip-pointer jumps highlighted as the cursors leapfrog, a phrase check compares position lists for adjacency and a prefix query opens a dictionary range, while counters track postings visited versus documents matched and a toggle reverses the evaluation order so starting from the common term visibly inflates postings visited.

subtopics.title: Top-k without scanning everything: the threshold algorithm, WAND and block-max
subtopics.covers: Fagin's threshold algorithm and NRA as the formal solution to top-k over several sorted lists under a monotone scoring function together with their instance-optimality result, and the shipping descendants that implement it — WAND and block-max WAND in Lucene and PISA, MaxScore, per-block maximum contributions stored alongside postings so whole blocks are skipped once they cannot beat the heap's threshold — the monotonicity requirement that makes BM25 eligible and an arbitrary scoring UDF ineligible, the ways production breaks the bounds (a personalized boost, a post-filter, a freshness multiplier, deleted-document masks) so early termination silently degrades to a full scan, and the same pattern outside search in LSM top-k merges, ORDER BY ... LIMIT over an ordered index, and the per-shard over-fetch a scatter-gather must do before the coordinator merge.
subtopics.visual: The learner issues a multi-term query and steps a scorer that maintains a top-k heap and a live threshold while postings advance and whole blocks are skipped as their stored maximum contribution falls below it, with counters for postings visited against postings available, then adds a non-monotone boost or a selective filter and watches the stored upper bounds go stale so the identical query degenerates into scanning every posting.

subtopics.title: Building indexes online: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY internals
subtopics.covers: Plain CREATE INDEX holding a ShareLock that blocks writes, versus CONCURRENTLY's three phases: register an invalid catalog entry and wait out conflicting transactions, build from a first snapshot while indisready lets concurrent writers maintain the new index, then a second snapshot scan validates by merging every TID the first pass missed and waits for transactions older than the reference snapshot before flipping indisvalid, leaving an INVALID index (needing DROP or REINDEX CONCURRENTLY) if anything fails, with the HOT-chain and indcheckxmin caveats; InnoDB online DDL builds the index in place while a row log (innodb_online_alter_log_max_size) captures concurrent DML replayed under a brief exclusive metadata lock; the schema-evolution module covers operating these safely.
subtopics.visual: A timeline with concurrent transactions and arriving writes: the learner steps through each CONCURRENTLY phase and sees which writes were captured by the build snapshot, which the index maintains itself once indisready is set, and which the validation scan back-fills, while the wait points block on the transactions still open; a 'fail' button leaves the index INVALID, and an InnoDB tab shows the row log filling and being applied at the final lock.

modules.title: Tries, Learned and Vector Indexes
modules.why: Trie- and radix-shaped structures, succinct encodings, learned models and approximate-nearest-neighbour graphs are where access-method design has moved, and each one's real cost shows up after the first build — in updates, drift and rebuilds.

subtopics.title: SP-GiST, tries and adaptive radix trees
subtopics.covers: Space-partitioning trees with non-overlapping regions (quadtrees, k-d trees, radix tries for text and inet) exposed through SP-GiST's config/choose/picksplit/inner_consistent/leaf_consistent callbacks and their unbalanced, data-dependent depth, and the Adaptive Radix Tree of HyPer and DuckDB: byte-indexed nodes of type 4/16/48/256 that grow and shrink, path compression by lazy expansion and pessimistic/optimistic prefixes, binary-comparable key transformation, O(key length) lookups without comparisons, optimistic lock coupling for concurrency, and Masstree as a trie of B+trees; skip lists and other memtable structures belong to the lsm-trees module.
subtopics.visual: The learner inserts strings into an ART and watches nodes upgrade 4→16→48→256 as children are added, prefix chains collapse under path compression, and per-node memory tally in a side panel against an equivalent B+tree; a second tab drops points into a quadtree and shows the non-overlapping partitions splitting and a range query visiting only touching cells.

subtopics.title: Succinct and learned indexes: rank/select, Elias-Fano and RMI
subtopics.covers: Succinct structures that stay queryable near the information-theoretic minimum — bit vectors with O(1) rank/select via block and superblock counters, Elias-Fano monotone sequences behind postings and offset arrays, wavelet trees and the FM-index/BWT for substring search, and their shipping cousins Roaring bitmaps, Lucene's FST term dictionary and RocksDB ribbon filters — alongside learned indexes that replace traversal with a prediction: the RMI's staged models plus a bounded max-error window closed by local binary search, PGM-index's piecewise-linear segments with provable bounds, ALEX's gapped arrays and node splits and LIPP for updates, learned Bloom filters and Bourbon's learned lookups inside an LSM's SSTables, the cost model that makes them win (read-mostly, sortable, smoothly distributed numeric keys, cache-resident models) and the limits that keep the B-tree the default (build cost, inserts, string keys, distribution shift, concurrency and safe reclamation, no worst-case guarantee), which is why engines ship learned components rather than learned indexes.
subtopics.visual: The learner shapes a key distribution (uniform, Zipf, clustered timestamps, sequential ids) and sees a B+tree, an Elias-Fano encoded array answering rank/select probes, and an RMI built side by side with bytes-per-key and probes-per-lookup meters; a lookup animates the model predicting a position, its error bound drawing a search window and a local binary search finishing inside it, and appending skewed or out-of-distribution keys makes the prediction drift and the window widen until it costs more than the tree descent and a retrain is triggered.

subtopics.title: Why high dimensions break indexes: distance concentration and intrinsic dimension
subtopics.covers: The concentration of measure that drives the ratio of farthest to nearest distance toward one as dimension grows (Beyer et al.'s 'when is nearest neighbour meaningful'), why every space-partitioning index — kd-tree, R-tree, M-tree, quadtree — degenerates to a full scan above roughly ten to twenty dimensions because a query ball intersects nearly every cell, intrinsic versus ambient dimension as the reason real embedding manifolds stay searchable at 768 dimensions while uniform random vectors do not, the LSH framework of (r, cr, p1, p2)-sensitive families with banding and amplification and its sublinear query bound, why graph indexes beat it on real data while LSH still wins for dedup, streaming similarity and shingled near-duplicate detection, and the measurement a senior should run first — the distance histogram and an intrinsic-dimension estimate over their own corpus — to predict recall before choosing an index.
subtopics.visual: The learner raises the ambient dimension of a generated dataset and watches the query-to-point distance histogram collapse toward a single spike while a kd-tree's visited-cell count climbs to the whole tree, then swaps in data on a low-intrinsic-dimension manifold embedded at the same ambient dimension so the histogram spreads and pruning resumes, with LSH bands and an HNSW graph answering the same queries under the shared RecallSweep component plotted against dimension on the x-axis.

subtopics.title: Vector indexes: IVF, HNSW and quantization
subtopics.covers: Exact kNN as O(n·d) versus approximate nearest neighbor, IVF with k-means centroids (nlist) and nprobe Voronoi cells visited, HNSW's layered navigable small-world graph (M, efConstruction, efSearch) searched by greedy descent from the top layer with a bounded candidate heap, recall versus distance computations, scalar and product quantization (subspaces, codebooks, asymmetric distance) and binary quantization for memory, DiskANN/Vamana keeping the graph on SSD with PQ codes in RAM, the filtered-search problem (pre-, post- and in-graph filtering, pgvector iterative scans), and build cost and maintenance_work_mem for pgvector HNSW versus per-segment HNSW in Lucene.
subtopics.visual: A 2D point cloud where the learner builds an HNSW graph and sees its layers, then places a query and watches the greedy descent and candidate heap layer by layer while the shared RecallSweep component plots recall@k against distance computations per query — this page's one x-axis — as efSearch and M are dragged; an IVF tab shows Voronoi cells and the nprobe lists searched, and a PQ toggle distorts the displayed distances to show quantization error.

subtopics.title: How churn degrades a vector index: tombstones, merges and centroid drift
subtopics.covers: The index-internal mechanics of change — why an HNSW delete can only be a tombstone whose node stays linked as a routing hop so the graph remains navigable, and how accumulated tombstones inflate the candidate heap and cut reachability until the structure is rebuilt, why an update is a delete plus an insert that leaves the old neighbourhood behind, how Lucene/Elasticsearch build one immutable graph per segment so background merges must re-link the graph from scratch and that merge work dominates ingest cost, pgvector's per-insert graph-repair cost and the index bloat that only a full rebuild reclaims, DiskANN/Vamana-style in-place delete consolidation that splices a deleted node's neighbours together instead of tombstoning, IVF centroid drift as a structural fact — the partition boundaries were fitted to the old distribution, so new points land in the wrong cells and nprobe must rise to hold recall until reclustering — and immutable-segment designs over object storage that never mutate a graph at all and treat rebuild as the only maintenance operation; the operational side of this (recall SLOs, shadow indexes, alias cutover, re-embedding runs and their cost) belongs to Part 5's search-and-vector-retrieval module.
subtopics.visual: The learner streams inserts, updates and deletes into a rendered HNSW graph and watches tombstoned nodes stay linked as routing hops while reachable-but-dead fraction, heap size and graph diameter climb and the shared RecallSweep component plots recall@10 against deletions applied — this page's one x-axis — then triggers a segment merge or an in-place delete consolidation and sees the graph re-link with CPU time and index size charged; an IVF tab drifts the data distribution and shows points landing outside their fitted cells until reclustering refits the centroids.

modules.title: Index Selection and Query-Aware Indexing
modules.why: Choosing composite, covering and partial indexes against real predicates, sort orders and write costs is the most common daily database decision, and getting it wrong is the leading cause of both slow queries and write-amplified, bloated tables; it sits at the end of Part 3, after the planner modules, because every judgement call here is read straight off the cost model and cardinality estimates taught in cost-based-optimization and off the real plans, buffer counts and workload inventories the learner has just learned to collect and read in explain-and-query-tuning.

subtopics.title: Selectivity, correlation and the decision to build an index
subtopics.covers: Deciding whether a usable index is worth building: estimated selectivity from n_distinct, MCVs and histograms, pg_stats.correlation deciding how many distinct heap pages a range touches, random_page_cost vs seq_page_cost and effective_cache_size setting the roughly 2–10% crossover from index scan to bitmap heap scan to sequential scan, why an index on a boolean or status column is useless unless partial, MySQL's ~30% rule of thumb and FORCE INDEX as the manual override, when clustering the table beats indexing it, and the reads you never wrote — referential integrity is enforced by system triggers that issue a child-side `SELECT 1 FROM ONLY child WHERE fk = $1 FOR KEY SHARE` on every parent DELETE or key UPDATE, so an unindexed child FK column means a sequential scan per parent row (multiplied down the graph by ON DELETE CASCADE, and escalated to a share lock on the whole child table in Oracle): index the child side of every foreign key you delete or re-key through, even when no query in the inventory names it — the estimation machinery itself lives in cost-based-optimization and the catalogue of predicates that hide a sargable column (casts, functions, OR, NOT IN, ORDER BY … LIMIT flips) was already catalogued in explain-and-query-tuning.
subtopics.visual: ScanLab is reused read-only but the learner must commit first — set selectivity and correlation, then choose 'create this index', 'leave it' or 'cluster the table' before the crossover is revealed, after which a scoreboard scores the bet in pages read, index bytes added and writes amplified, dragging random_page_cost slides the crossover line across the choice just made, and a second tab replays advanced-sql's cascade tracer with a child-side scan-and-lock counter that collapses from rows-scanned-per-parent-row to one seek the moment the FK index exists.

subtopics.title: Composite indexes and the leftmost-prefix rule
subtopics.covers: An index on (a,b,c) serves equality on a, a+b, a+b+c and a range on the last used column; the ESR ordering (equality columns, then the sort column, then the range column) keeps the scan one contiguous leaf range and satisfies ORDER BY without a sort, a leading range or a gap turns later columns into in-index filters (InnoDB index condition pushdown, PostgreSQL index filter rows), one composite usually beats several single-column indexes combined by BitmapAnd, skip scans (Oracle INDEX_SKIP_SCAN, MySQL 8.0 loose index scan, PostgreSQL 18) relax the rule only for low-cardinality leading columns, and direction is part of the key: nbtree stores a per-column ASC/DESC and NULLS FIRST/LAST in pg_index.indoption and a scan can only reverse the whole key, never one column, so an index serves ORDER BY forward or backward only when every column's declared direction matches or every one is inverted — `ORDER BY a DESC, b ASC` needs `CREATE INDEX … (a DESC, b ASC)`, and adding NULLS LAST to an ASC column (or NULLS FIRST to a DESC one, against the defaults ASC ⇒ NULLS LAST and DESC ⇒ NULLS FIRST) silently disqualifies the index and reintroduces a full sort under LIMIT.
subtopics.visual: The learner drags table columns into index order, toggles ASC/DESC and NULLS FIRST/LAST per column, and types WHERE/ORDER BY clauses; a rendered B+tree highlights the contiguous leaf range that will be seeked versus entries merely filtered after the seek, counts leaf entries read and heap rows returned, and a 'sort needed' badge appears the instant the declared directions or NULL placements stop matching the query's.

subtopics.title: Covering indexes and index-only scans
subtopics.covers: Index-only scans answer a query without touching the heap when every referenced column is in the index (INCLUDE payload columns in PostgreSQL 11+ and SQL Server; InnoDB secondary indexes implicitly carry the primary key, so covering means PK plus columns and skips the second clustered-index descent — see row identifiers in pages-tuples-heap-files), but in PostgreSQL each heap page must be all-visible in the visibility map or the scan falls back to a heap fetch, so index-only scans are exactly as good as VACUUM keeps the VM and SELECT * silently defeats them.
subtopics.visual: The learner adds columns to a covering index and runs a query; the animation walks the index leaf, checks a visibility-map bit per heap page (which the learner can dirty by simulating updates without vacuum), counts 'Heap Fetches' versus pure index reads, and shows index size growing as INCLUDE columns are added.

subtopics.title: Partial and expression indexes
subtopics.covers: Partial indexes (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, WHERE status = 'pending') shrink hot-subset indexes by orders of magnitude and enforce conditional uniqueness, but are used only when the planner can prove the query predicate implies the index predicate (PostgreSQL predtest.c does constant and operator-family implication, not arbitrary logic); expression indexes on lower(email) or (data->>'sku') require a textually matching expression and an IMMUTABLE function (timezone-dependent casts and collation-dependent functions are the classic traps), with generated columns (PostgreSQL 12, MySQL 5.7) and MySQL 8.0.13 functional indexes as alternatives.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes an index predicate or expression and a query predicate; the simulator runs a step-by-step implication check showing whether the index qualifies and why not when it fails, then contrasts index size and lookup pages for partial versus full index on a soft-deleted table where the learner tunes the live-row fraction.

subtopics.title: Pagination done right: keyset vs OFFSET
subtopics.covers: OFFSET n LIMIT m walks and discards n index entries or heap rows (O(n) per page) and skips or repeats rows when concurrent inserts shift positions; keyset pagination with WHERE (created_at, id) > (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT m turns every page into one index range seek using a unique tiebreaker column, encodes the last key in an opaque signed cursor token, needs the row-value comparison expanded by hand for mixed sort directions and NULL-sorting columns, and pushes total-count display toward statistics-based estimates rather than COUNT(*).
subtopics.visual: The learner pages through a 1M-row index with OFFSET versus keyset while a slider streams concurrent inserts; per request the animation shows entries scanned and discarded, highlights rows skipped or duplicated between consecutive pages, and plots latency against page number for both strategies.

subtopics.title: Write cost, HOT and the indexes-per-update meter
subtopics.covers: Every secondary index is another B-tree written on INSERT, DELETE and any UPDATE that changes an indexed column or fails HOT eligibility because the page lacks fillfactor room, multiplying dirtied pages and WAL bytes; InnoDB buffers non-unique secondary index changes in the change buffer, PostgreSQL 13 deduplication and 14 bottom-up index deletion slow bloat, random-key inserts cause page splits and half-empty leaves, and the operational discipline is finding dead and redundant-prefix indexes via pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan or sys.schema_unused_indexes, measuring bloat with pgstattuple, and rebuilding with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (the HOT/t_ctid mechanism itself lives in pages-tuples-heap-files and online build internals in indexes-beyond-the-b-tree).
subtopics.visual: The update-stream component from pages-tuples-heap-files is embedded read-only to drive the heap (its fillfactor and touched-column controls already set the HOT ratio), and the learner's only action here is toggling the index set on the table while a selection scoreboard shows per-index pages written, WAL bytes per row and bloat percentage climbing over simulated time, a throughput gauge falling as indexes are added, and a detector flagging indexes with zero scans or a redundant prefix of another.

subtopics.title: Choosing the index for JSONB, arrays and text search
subtopics.covers: Picking among real candidates for semi-structured predicates: GIN jsonb_ops (every key and value; serves ?, ?|, ?& and @>) versus jsonb_path_ops (hashed full paths, containment only, far smaller and faster), neither of which serves equality or range on a single key — that needs an expression B-tree on (data->>'sku') or a generated column; GIN array_ops for @> and &&, pg_trgm GIN/GiST for LIKE '%x%', ILIKE and similarity, tsvector GIN for @@ with recheck, the GIN fastupdate pending list (gin_pending_list_limit) trading insert latency for merge spikes, and MySQL 8.0.17 multi-valued and MongoDB multikey indexes as equivalents — the posting-list internals themselves are in indexes-beyond-the-b-tree.
subtopics.visual: Given a document shape and a set of predicates, a candidate table lists GIN jsonb_ops, GIN jsonb_path_ops, expression B-tree, generated column, pg_trgm and 'none', each row marked servable or not with the reason plus measured index size, entries written per insert and lookup cost, and the learner wins by covering all four predicates at the smallest total write cost.

subtopics.title: Indexing for hybrid search: which indexes the pipeline needs
subtopics.covers: Reading a hybrid query shape (a full-text branch, an approximate-nearest-neighbour branch and a metadata filter over one corpus) purely as an indexing problem: which index each branch needs in order to seek rather than scan — a tsvector GIN for the text branch, an HNSW or IVFFlat index with its build parameters and build-time cost for the vector branch, and a B-tree the filter is sargable against — what each costs in bytes, entries written per insert and rebuild time, and how the chosen index set decides where filtering can happen, since pre-filtering needs an index the filter is sargable against, post-filtering needs overfetch, and filtering inside the index needs engine support (pgvector iterative index scans, filtered HNSW, Elasticsearch filtered kNN), which is why a selective filter over an ANN branch built without one leaves qualifying rows unreturned — rows the branch should have found but did not, the quantity called recall; how the branches' results are combined, reranked and measured is a retrieval-quality question owned by search-and-vector-retrieval.
subtopics.visual: The same candidate-table-plus-scoreboard format as the JSONB page — tsvector GIN, HNSW, IVFFlat, metadata B-tree, partial index per tenant and 'none', each marked servable or not per branch with build time, bytes and entries written per insert — plus a filter-selectivity slider that tightens the metadata predicate and counts, against a known ground-truth set, how many qualifying rows the ANN branch fails to return until the learner adds the index that makes pre-filtering possible.

subtopics.title: The list endpoint: optional filters, sort options and one index set
subtopics.covers: Why k optional predicates crossed with m sort orders implies far more query shapes than a table can carry indexes for, how the mandatory filters (tenant_id, status, not-deleted) become the leading columns under the ESR rule while the optional ones become in-index filters or partial-index conditions, why the convenient (col = $1 OR $1 IS NULL) idiom makes every shape unsargable and what replaces it (dynamic SQL per shape, per-shape partial indexes, generated columns), cursors that must encode the entire sort tuple plus a unique tiebreaker so switching sort invalidates the cursor and mixed directions must match the index's declared per-column direction, total counts degraded to estimates or maintained separately, and the point at which arbitrary filter and sort combinations stop being an indexing problem and belong in a search engine or a columnar replica.
subtopics.visual: A filter-and-sort builder emits the real query while the learner edits a candidate index set, and a scoreboard grades all twenty filter/sort combinations as index-served, filtered-after-seek or sequential scan with buffers per combination — flipping one predicate to the OR-null form turns a seek into a scan in front of them, adding a fourth index shows the write-cost meter climb, and changing the sort order breaks an in-flight cursor.

subtopics.title: Designing the index set for a workload
subtopics.covers: Indexing a whole workload rather than one query: taking a query-and-frequency inventory as input (collected from pg_stat_statements and the slow log exactly as in explain-and-query-tuning), merging single-column indexes into composites with shared prefixes, scoring each candidate by reads saved times frequency against writes added times update rate plus buffer-pool footprint plus a constraint-maintenance term for the child-side lookups foreign keys, unique constraints and cascades issue on their own, validating a candidate without building it via hypothetical indexes (HypoPG, SQL Server Database Engine Tuning Advisor, Oracle SQL Access Advisor), and the constraints that bound the answer — an index-count budget per table, replicas that share the same indexes, and distributed stores where global secondary indexes cost cross-partition writes (see partitioning-and-sharding).
subtopics.visual: A workload panel lists ten queries with frequencies, a write rate and the FK/cascade graph; the learner adds, merges and drops indexes while a scoreboard recomputes total read cost, constraint-maintenance cost, total write cost and storage in real time, highlighting which queries each index serves, flagging candidates that are redundant prefixes of another, and reddening any FK child column left unindexed.

modules.title: Column Stores, Compression and Columnar Formats
modules.why: Analytical storage wins not by clever execution but by what it refuses to read: columnar layout touches only projected columns, lightweight encodings shrink them enough to scan in cache and evaluate predicates without decoding, entropy sets the floor those encoders are chasing and explains why ordering beats codec tuning, block compressors and open formats like Parquet/ORC/Arrow — plus the post-2022 successors aimed at random access, wide schemas and fast decode — decide what a reader must fetch over a network, semi-structured JSON either shreds into typed sub-columns or costs 10-100x to scan, and sort keys plus min/max metadata skip most blocks outright — these are the primitives every analytical engine and table format in the next module is built out of.

subtopics.title: Columnar layouts: NSM, DSM, PAX and row groups
subtopics.covers: NSM row pages vs DSM column files vs Ailamaki's PAX minipages (columnar inside one page so a scan touches only the needed cache lines) vs the row-group/column-chunk/page hierarchy of Parquet and stripes of ORC, with tuple reconstruction by position (virtual IDs, no join index) and early vs late materialization deciding how much of the other columns a selective filter must fetch, as in C-Store projections, DuckDB row groups and ClickHouse parts.
subtopics.visual: A 20-column table rendered as NSM pages, PAX pages and DSM column chunks with a row-group-size slider; the learner picks which columns a query projects and a filter selectivity, then toggles early/late materialization and watches bytes read, cache lines touched, seeks issued and position-based reconstruction lookups counted per layout.

subtopics.title: Lightweight encodings: RLE, dictionary, delta, bit-packing, FOR and friends
subtopics.covers: Per-column-chunk encodings chosen by cardinality, sortedness and type — dictionary (sorted dictionaries let range predicates run on codes), RLE and Parquet's RLE/bit-packing hybrid, delta and delta-of-delta for timestamps, frame-of-reference and PFOR with exception patching, Gorilla XOR and ALP for floats, FSST for strings, cascaded encodings as in BtrBlocks — plus why engines evaluate predicates and aggregates directly on encoded data and SIMD-unpack only the survivors.
subtopics.visual: An encoding lab: the learner pastes or generates a column (sorted ids, random ints, low-cardinality strings, monotonic timestamps, sensor floats), stacks an encoding chain, and sees the exact bit layout, bits-per-value and a compression-ratio bar; running a predicate then shows whether it executes on the codes without decoding and how many values had to be unpacked.

subtopics.title: Entropy and the limits of compression: what ratio should you expect?
subtopics.covers: Zero-order versus higher-order conditional entropy as the floor no encoder can beat, why dictionary plus RLE plus bit-packing already sit near that floor for low-cardinality and sorted columns while ZSTD's entropy stage only collects the remainder, why sorting or clustering a column lowers its conditional entropy and is therefore a bigger lever than any codec swap (the theory under ClickHouse ORDER BY, Redshift compound sort keys and Parquet row-group ordering), why random UUIDs, encrypted blobs and already-compressed payloads cannot compress at all, arithmetic coding's optimality versus Huffman's per-symbol rounding loss, and using measured compressed size as an estimate of how much information a column actually carries when sizing storage and scan bandwidth.
subtopics.visual: The learner shapes a column's value distribution and its physical ordering and sees measured bits-per-value for each encoding chain plotted against the computed zero-order and order-k entropy floors, so sorting the column drags the floor down and the encoders follow it while a high-entropy random column's bars refuse to move no matter which codec or level is chosen.

subtopics.title: Block compression: LZ4, ZSTD, trained dictionaries and hole punching
subtopics.covers: General-purpose LZ77-family compressors (LZ4, Snappy, ZSTD with FSE/Huffman entropy stages) applied per block on top of lightweight encodings, the CPU-cycles-vs-ratio-vs-random-access trade-off that sets block size, RocksDB's LZ4-upper/ZSTD-bottom levels with trained ZSTD dictionaries, ClickHouse codec chains (Delta+ZSTD, T64, DoubleDelta), Postgres TOAST pglz vs lz4, and the two InnoDB designs — ROW_FORMAT=COMPRESSED with zlib and an in-page modification log versus transparent page compression via fallocate PUNCH_HOLE that leaves sparse files at filesystem-block granularity.
subtopics.visual: A 16KB page compression bench where LZ4 is implemented in-page so its ratio and match/literal breakdown update live as the learner edits block content, while ZSTD levels and trained-dictionary results are served from a clearly labelled precomputed fixture over three fixed sample blocks (encoded column chunk, JSON rows, random bytes) and an explicitly parameterised cost model with editable, on-screen compress and decompress throughput constants turns those sizes into estimated point-read times; switching the storage mode between compressed-page format and hole punching then animates the on-disk sector map filling with holes and shows whether a small update fits the modification log or forces recompression.

subtopics.title: Open formats: Parquet, ORC, Arrow and nested data (Dremel)
subtopics.covers: Parquet's file anatomy — row groups, column chunks, dictionary and data pages, the Thrift footer with per-chunk min/max statistics, the page index and optional bloom filters read via footer-first range requests on object stores — ORC's stripes with index/data/footer streams and 10k-row indexes, Dremel repetition and definition levels that shred repeated and optional nested fields into flat columns and reassemble them with a finite-state machine, and Arrow's in-memory layout (validity bitmaps, offset buffers, 64-byte alignment, dictionary arrays) enabling zero-copy IPC and Flight.
subtopics.visual: A record shredder: the learner edits a nested JSON document with optional and repeated fields, watches each leaf column's values with repetition and definition levels recompute live, then selects a subset of columns and steps the assembly FSM that rebuilds records; a side panel shows the resulting Parquet column chunk as pages with statistics and the footer offsets a reader would fetch first.

subtopics.title: After Parquet: Lance, Vortex and Nimble
subtopics.covers: What Parquet's row-group-plus-footer design costs for post-2022 workloads and how the successors answer it — Lance's per-row offsets, versioned datasets and embedded vector indexes making random point fetches and re-embedding cheap, Meta's Nimble/Alpha attacking footer metadata that dominates wide and deeply nested schemas, Vortex's cascading compressed arrays with zero-copy-to-Arrow decode and predicate pushdown into encodings, multimodal blob storage alongside columns, and the small-file and footer-parse costs that bound real jobs — against the compatibility gravity (engine support, catalogs, tooling) that keeps Parquet the default anyway.
subtopics.visual: One dataset written in Parquet, Lance and Vortex-style layouts where the learner switches access pattern — full scan, narrow projection, a point fetch of 100 random row ids, a 2000-column schema — and watches metadata bytes parsed, requests issued and decode time per format, the random-access case collapsing Parquet's whole-row-group read into a per-row offset lookup on Lance.

subtopics.title: Shredding JSON into columns: VARIANT, dynamic columns and variant Parquet
subtopics.covers: Schema-less counterpart to Dremel shredding: Snowflake VARIANT sub-columnarization with a fallback blob, ClickHouse JSON/Dynamic columns with per-path subcolumns and max_dynamic_paths overflow, the Parquet variant/shredding spec and BigQuery JSON, schema inference and drift with path explosion and per-file metadata cost, predicate and projection pushdown on shredded paths versus full-document parsing, and when to promote a hot path to a first-class typed column.
subtopics.visual: The learner pastes documents whose shape drifts over time and watches the engine infer per-path sub-columns with inferred types while a path-count meter climbs to the limit and the remainder spills into a generic blob column, then filters on a shredded path and on an overflowed one, comparing bytes read and rows per second.

subtopics.title: Sort keys, clustering and multi-dimensional data skipping
subtopics.covers: Why min/max zone maps only prune when physical order correlates with the predicate, single-dimension sort keys and the leftmost-prefix rule of ClickHouse ORDER BY tuples and Redshift compound keys, interleaved keys and space-filling curves (Z-order/Morton and Hilbert in Delta OPTIMIZE ZORDER, Iceberg rewrites and Databricks liquid clustering) that spread pruning power across dimensions, Snowflake's clustering depth and overlap metrics driving automatic reclustering, ClickHouse skip indexes (minmax, set, bloom_filter, ngrambf) and how inserts and merges degrade clustering over time — BRIN basics are in Indexes Beyond the B-Tree.
subtopics.visual: A two-dimensional block map of a table: the learner chooses the physical order (sort by A, sort by B, compound A,B, Z-order, Hilbert), sets block size, drags a rectangular range predicate over the (A,B) plane and sees which blocks survive pruning and the pruned fraction; streaming new inserts then raises a clustering-depth histogram until a recluster button restores it.

modules.title: Analytical Storage Engines
modules.why: Columnar layout and encodings are inert until an engine organizes them into a live table: MergeTree parts and granules, real-time segments handed to deep storage, delta-plus-main stores that keep a columnar table fresh under OLTP writes, the newer move of putting a second execution engine and columnar format inside the OLTP server itself, and the mirror-image move the cloud vendors shipped after 2022 — a transactional row store stitched in under a columnar platform — the concrete answers to "how do rows arrive, become queryable and get reorganized" that separate ClickHouse from Pinot from an HTAP engine from a Postgres with an embedded analytical engine bolted on from a warehouse selling itself as your operational database (the lakehouse file-and-catalog answer comes later, in Lakehouse Table Formats, Catalogs and Change Feeds, once object-store semantics and optimistic concurrency are established).

subtopics.title: ClickHouse MergeTree internals: parts, granules, marks and merges
subtopics.covers: Immutable parts written per INSERT (compact vs wide, level-encoded part names), per-column .bin files of compressed blocks with .mrk marks storing (compressed offset, decompressed offset) per granule, the sparse primary.idx holding one key per 8192-row (or adaptive index_granularity_bytes) granule and its binary-search-plus-generic-exclusion selection of mark ranges, PRIMARY KEY as a prefix of ORDER BY, partition keys with MinMax partition pruning, background merges that also implement Replacing/Summing/Aggregating/Collapsing semantics, heavy mutations rewriting parts versus lightweight deletes via a _row_exists mask, projections and TTL moves — replication and sharding live in the ClickHouse case study.
subtopics.visual: A MergeTree sandbox: the learner fires insert batches and watches named parts appear and background merges combine them by level; issuing a query with a predicate on the ORDER BY prefix steps through primary.idx binary search selecting granule ranges, the marks file resolving those granules to compressed-block offsets, and a bytes-read counter, with toggles for a skip index, a mutation rewriting parts, and a lightweight delete masking rows.

subtopics.title: Segment-based real-time OLAP: Druid, Pinot and upsert tables
subtopics.covers: The user-facing-analytics tier with second-level freshness and thousands of concurrent queries — real-time ingestion tasks making rows queryable within seconds and then handing sealed segments to deep storage, a controller assigning segments to historical/server nodes with replication, brokers doing scatter-gather with segment pruning over time and partition metadata, Pinot's star-tree, inverted, range and sorted indexes plus upsert tables keyed by a primary key with partition-local key maps, StarRocks and ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree as the same idea in other engines, and the freshness-versus-concurrency-versus-cost profile that distinguishes this tier from a warehouse.
subtopics.visual: Events stream into a real-time segment that the learner can query immediately, then watch hand off to deep storage, be assigned and replicated to historical servers and be pruned or scanned by a broker fan-out for a given filter, with an upsert toggle showing a primary-key map redirecting reads to the newest record and a star-tree toggle collapsing an aggregation into a precomputed node.

subtopics.title: Hybrid row/column and HTAP storage: delta store plus columnar main
subtopics.covers: The write-optimized delta plus read-optimized main pattern in its real forms — SQL Server clustered columnstore with ~1M-row rowgroups, a delta rowstore B-tree closed at 1,048,576 rows, the tuple mover, delete bitmaps and segment elimination; SAP HANA's dictionary-encoded delta merged into main; Oracle Database In-Memory dual format with a transaction journal; TiDB TiFlash columnar replicas kept current from the same replication log that feeds the row store (the Raft learner mechanism itself in Consensus Protocols); SingleStore rowstore-to-columnstore and Citus columnar stripes — and the resulting costs: every scan must union main, delta and delete bitmap, merges compete with writes, and freshness trades against analytical throughput, with query-side HTAP replicas and materialized views covered in Analytical Query Platforms.
subtopics.visual: A dual-store simulator: OLTP writes stream into a delta row store while the learner sets the rowgroup close threshold, merge trigger and read/write mix, watching the delta B-tree fill, the tuple mover compress a closed rowgroup into encoded segments, the delete bitmap grow under updates, and each analytical query's cost split into columnar segment scan, delta scan and bitmap filtering alongside a freshness gauge.

subtopics.title: Analytics inside Postgres: embedded engines, columnar mirrors and Iceberg-backed tables
subtopics.covers: The wave that puts a second execution engine and storage format inside one Postgres server — pg_duckdb and pg_mooncake/pg_lake routing scans into DuckDB over Parquet and Iceberg via custom scan nodes and foreign or table access methods, ParadeDB's pg_search exposing a Tantivy BM25 index as an index AM, Citus columnar, Hydra and Timescale hypercore as columnar TAMs, AlloyDB's columnar engine as an in-memory mirror — plus the seams that decide whether it works: which predicates, projections and aggregates cross the boundary, how a mirror is refreshed and which snapshot it answers from, transaction and visibility scope across the two engines, memory and thread contention with OLTP backends, and the managed-service allowlist that decides whether you may install any of it.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs one analytical query against the same table stored as a heap, as a columnar TAM mirror and as an Iceberg-backed foreign table and watches the plan split at the custom-scan boundary — which filters and aggregates cross into the embedded engine and which rows come back — while bytes scanned, mirror freshness lag and a concurrent OLTP workload's p99 move as the analytical query runs beside it.

subtopics.title: OLTP inside the warehouse: hybrid tables and lakebases
subtopics.covers: Bolting a row store under a columnar platform rather than the reverse — Snowflake Unistore hybrid tables as a separate transactional key-value-backed store with its own indexes and point-write latency, asynchronously mirrored into columnar storage and joinable with standard tables in one statement; Databricks Lakebase attaching a managed Postgres to the lakehouse with automated sync in both directions; Oracle HeatWave and AlloyDB's columnar pairings as the same idea from the OLTP side — and the contract each one actually offers: transaction scope and isolation across the two stores, mirror lag and whether a cross-store join is snapshot-consistent, per-row write cost and concurrency ceilings, and the OLTP features (foreign keys, long transactions, connection scale, sub-millisecond point reads) the platform quietly does not provide.
subtopics.visual: One order workflow writes through a hybrid table and reads back from both sides while the learner watches the row-store write path, the asynchronous mirror into columnar storage with a freshness clock, and a join across hybrid and standard tables resolving from two engines at two timestamps — then raises point-write rate, transaction length and connection count until the platform's limits reject the workload, with the identical run replayed against a plain OLTP database beside it.

modules.title: Lakehouse Table Formats, Catalogs and Change Feeds
modules.why: A pile of immutable Parquet files in an object store becomes a table only when a metadata tree, a conditional pointer write and a catalog that arbitrates writers turn it into something with snapshots, deletes, schema evolution and concurrent commits — so this module belongs in Part 8 immediately after cloud-native-disaggregated-storage, whose object-store semantics (put-if-absent, compare-and-set, listing costs) it builds on directly, and after serializability-without-blocking, whose read-validate-write discipline is literally the commit protocol, and it runs before distributed-and-analytical-query so that distributed execution can assume table formats exist; from there it answers the five questions a lakehouse actually raises: how a commit is made atomic, what changes when the table is continuously upserted rather than appended to, who performs and guards the commit, whether the metadata belongs in files or in a database, and how a downstream consumer reads the table as a stream of changes instead of a snapshot.

subtopics.title: Lakehouse table formats: Iceberg, Delta and Hudi
subtopics.covers: How ACID lands on immutable Parquet files in an object store — Iceberg's metadata tree (table metadata JSON to snapshot to manifest list to manifests with per-file column stats to data files) committed by claiming the next table version with a conditional write (the put-if-absent / compare-and-set pointer swap that is the object store's only atomic primitive, from Cloud-Native and Disaggregated Architectures) and then validating a loser's writes against the winner and retrying — exactly the read-validate-write discipline of optimistic concurrency control from Serializability Without Blocking — plus Delta's _delta_log JSON actions and checkpoints serialized by put-if-absent writes, Hudi's timeline with copy-on-write vs merge-on-read, Iceberg v2 position/equality delete files and deletion vectors, hidden partitioning via partition transforms, schema evolution by column ID, time travel, snapshot expiry, orphan files and the small-files problem that compaction jobs exist to fix.
subtopics.visual: An Iceberg write-path step-through where the learner issues inserts, row deletes and a compaction and watches each data file, delete file, manifest, manifest list and new versioned metadata JSON get written in order before a conditional pointer write claims the next version, then walks an older snapshot's tree for a time-travel query and expires snapshots to see which files become unreachable — closing with a single short beat where a second writer loses the pointer swap, revalidates and retries (the mechanism the catalogs page then replays read-only).

subtopics.title: Mutable tables on object storage: LSM formats and primary-key tables
