subtopics.covers: What changes when a lake table is updated continuously rather than appended to — Apache Paimon's LSM-organized primary-key buckets with merge engines and changelog producers, Hudi merge-on-read with record-level indexes and its copy-on-write alternative, Iceberg equality deletes and deletion vectors and the compaction debt they accrue, and ClickHouse/StarRocks primary-key tables as the non-lake comparison — plus the cost model that picks among them: read amplification from unmerged deletes, compaction as a standing bill that must keep pace with ingest, commit frequency against small-file and metadata growth, and the freshness-versus-query-latency curve that decides whether the upsert belongs on the lake or in a serving store fed by CDC.
subtopics.visual: The learner streams an update-heavy CDC feed into a copy-on-write table, a merge-on-read table with deletion vectors and an LSM primary-key table, watching files written per commit, delete files accumulating, per-query merge work and compaction backlog climb on each, then tunes commit interval and compaction concurrency until freshness, query latency and total bytes rewritten visibly trade against one another and one design falls behind ingest entirely.

subtopics.title: Catalogs: the Iceberg REST protocol, Polaris, Unity, Glue and Nessie
subtopics.covers: The catalog as the thing that actually performs the commit and guards the table — the Iceberg REST protocol's table-pointer swap, commit conflict responses and client-side manifest revalidation and retry, the implementations and what each adds (Polaris, Databricks Unity, AWS Glue, Nessie's git-like branches and tags, Hive Metastore as the legacy baseline), credential vending that hands an engine a scoped expiring token for only the files in a snapshot instead of raw bucket grants, multi-engine concurrent writes from Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake and DuckDB and the conflict classes they hit, catalog-driven maintenance (compaction, snapshot expiry, orphan-file cleanup) and cross-format interop via Delta UniForm and Apache XTable.
subtopics.visual: A commit race plays read-only as a short recap strip while the learner's actual controls sit on the catalog's own jobs: request credential vending for a snapshot and watch a scoped expiring token be minted, read a file inside the snapshot successfully and a file outside it get a 403, then pick pairs of engines (Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake, DuckDB) and pairs of operations to see which conflict class the catalog returns for each and which client-side revalidation clears it, and run a maintenance job that rewrites small files and expires snapshots so older pointers become unreadable.

subtopics.title: Branches, tags and write-audit-publish on the lake
subtopics.covers: Using snapshot pointers as a workflow primitive — Iceberg branches and tags with per-reference retention, Nessie's multi-table git-like commits and merges, Delta shallow clones — to implement write-audit-publish (write to an audit branch, run quality checks against it, fast-forward the main pointer only on pass), per-pull-request data environments and zero-copy experiment forks, plus the mechanics that decide whether it works in your stack: which commits fast-forward versus need a real merge, how a branch pins data files against snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup, whether each engine and catalog resolves branch and tag references at read time, and how forgotten branches become silent storage cost.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes a batch to an audit branch and watches the metadata tree grow a second pointer sharing every existing file, runs a quality check that fails and then passes, fast-forwards main so readers see the whole batch atomically, then expires snapshots and runs orphan cleanup to see the branch pin exactly the files retention would otherwise have removed — and a forgotten branch keep paying for them.

subtopics.title: Where table metadata lives: manifest trees versus a catalog database
subtopics.covers: Why file-based table metadata becomes the bottleneck — an Iceberg commit rewriting metadata JSON, a manifest list and manifests per snapshot, planning that fetches and parses many manifests over high-latency object storage, retained snapshots inflating the tree, and every writer racing the same pointer at high commit rates — versus keeping snapshots, file lists and statistics as rows in a transactional database (DuckLake's SQL catalog, Snowflake's FoundationDB metadata layer, Delta's checkpoint-plus-log compromise, REST catalogs that already hold the pointer), traded off on commit latency, planning cost, multi-engine openness, and the new single point of failure the catalog database becomes.
subtopics.visual: A pure commit-rate sweep with no race animation: the learner streams commits at a chosen rate, snapshot-retention setting and compaction cadence into a file-based table and a catalog-database table side by side and reads the resulting curves — commit latency percentiles, metadata bytes parsed per plan, catalog round trips per query and retry-and-backoff rate — watching the file-tree design's planning cost climb with retained snapshots while the database design's cost concentrates in one server.

subtopics.title: Reading changes out of a lakehouse table: CDF, incremental scans and row lineage
subtopics.covers: Consuming a table as a stream rather than a snapshot — Delta Change Data Feed with its _change_data files and insert/update/delete rows, Iceberg incremental scans diffing snapshot ranges by appended data files plus delete files with v3 row lineage making row-level updates traceable, Hudi incremental queries over its timeline, and Flink or Spark Structured Streaming reading a table as a source with checkpointed snapshot offsets — plus the traps: compaction and snapshot expiry destroying a range a consumer still needs, merge-on-read deletes making a change ambiguous, replays that are not idempotent, and rewrite-only OPTIMIZE output surfacing as spurious changes.
subtopics.visual: The learner performs inserts, merges, deletes and a compaction on a table while a downstream consumer reads incrementally from a chosen snapshot, watching which files each snapshot range contributes and which rows are emitted as insert, update or delete, then expires a snapshot or runs OPTIMIZE mid-stream to see the consumer either break with a missing-range error or be flooded with rewritten rows.

parts.title: Query Processing: From SQL Text to Executed Plan
parts.summary: Parsing, rewriting, physical operators, cost-based optimization, execution engines with resource control, and the EXPLAIN literacy that ties them together.

modules.title: From SQL Text to Logical Plan
modules.why: Every rewrite that matters happens before a single cost is computed; a senior engineer must know what the front end resolves (and silently casts), which transformations the engine applies blindly, which genuinely need statistics, and which fences (views, CTEs, outer joins, volatile functions) stop them cold.

subtopics.title: Parsing and the AST
subtopics.covers: How a lexer turns SQL text into tokens and an LALR(1) grammar (PostgreSQL's bison gram.y, MySQL's sql_yacc, SQLite's Lemon parser) shift-reduces them into a raw parse tree that knows only syntax — so a misspelled keyword fails here while a nonexistent column passes — with operator precedence, reserved vs non-reserved keywords, dialect divergence (LIMIT/TOP/FETCH FIRST, quoting rules, ON CONFLICT vs MERGE) and $1/? parameter placeholders all living in this layer, the placeholders being what lets a statement be parsed once and bound many times (plan caching itself belongs to execution-engines-and-resource-control).
subtopics.visual: The learner picks one of six queries from a palette and edits only its marked fragments (predicate, join type, column list) so unsupported syntax is unreachable, then steps the site-wide toy-SQL parser and watches its recursive-descent call stack push and pop — parseSelect → parseFromItem → parseExpr — with each return snapping one AST node into place, a side note showing the equivalent reduce sequence a generated LALR(1) table would have produced; a deliberately malformed fragment halts at the offending token naming the production that expected something else, while swapping in a nonexistent column lets the tree finish untouched, foreshadowing the binder.

subtopics.title: Binding, name resolution and semantic analysis
subtopics.covers: The analyzer resolves every identifier against the catalog (pg_class/pg_attribute OIDs via search_path, MySQL's data dictionary) using scoping rules for aliases, USING/NATURAL columns and outer references from correlated subqueries, infers types and injects implicit casts (a varchar column compared to an int literal gets the cast on the column side, silently blocking index use, whereas an unknown-typed literal is coerced to the column's type), resolves function overloads, validates GROUP BY/aggregate usage and privileges, and injects row-level-security policies as extra predicates, emitting a query tree whose nodes carry resolved OIDs and types.
subtopics.visual: On the AST the toy parser just produced, the learner steps the binder identifier by identifier while a catalog panel highlights the matched table/column and each node acquires a type badge; choosing the `code = 42` predicate fragment on a varchar column shows the cast land on the column with an 'index unusable' flag lighting up, and switching the fragment to `code = '42'` moves the cast onto the literal and clears the flag.

subtopics.title: Relational algebra operators and the logical evaluation order
subtopics.covers: The core operators (σ, π, ⋈, ×, ∪, −, ρ) plus SQL's extensions (γ grouping/aggregation, τ sort, δ duplicate elimination, outer/semi/anti joins and the apply/dependent join that represents a correlated subquery), how SELECT-FROM-WHERE-GROUP BY-HAVING-ORDER BY-LIMIT maps to a tree evaluated in a different order than it is written, how bag semantics (projection keeps duplicates, UNION ALL vs UNION) and NULL's UNKNOWN in WHERE diverge from set algebra, and why every node carries cardinality, ordering and uniqueness properties that later phases exploit.
subtopics.visual: The learner selects a palette query over small sample tables and its clauses light up in logical evaluation order while the toy planner's logical tree grows node by node, each node displaying the intermediate relation the instrumented pull executor actually produced; a bag/set toggle changes duplicate handling live, and inserting a NULL into the sample data shows WHERE dropping the row while COUNT(*) and COUNT(col) diverge.

subtopics.title: Relational calculus, Codd's theorem and the limits of first-order queries
subtopics.covers: Tuple and domain relational calculus as the declarative twin of the algebra, Codd's theorem that safe calculus expressions and algebra expressions have identical expressive power (the formal licence for an optimizer to pick any equivalent plan), domain-dependent/unsafe expressions like {t | ¬R(t)} and the range restrictions SQL enforces through FROM, the correspondence SELECT↔π, WHERE↔σ, EXISTS↔∃ and NOT EXISTS↔∀ by double negation (relational division as 'students who took every course'), and the locality argument that transitive closure is not first-order expressible — which is exactly why WITH RECURSIVE had to be added to the language rather than written as a clever join.
subtopics.visual: The learner assembles a calculus expression from quantifier, atom and negation blocks (no free text) and watches it translate term by term into an algebra tree and into the matching toy-SQL query, with an 'unsafe' toggle that drops the range restriction and shows the result set blow up over the whole domain; a division exercise then builds 'took every course' by nesting two NOT EXISTS while the quantifier structure is highlighted, and a reachability query shows the algebra tree failing to close the loop until a fixpoint node is added.

subtopics.title: Algebraic equivalences and rewrite rules
subtopics.covers: The always-safe transformations applied before any cost is computed — selection pushdown and pull-up, projection pruning, join commutativity/associativity, constant folding and predicate simplification, transitive-equality closure via PostgreSQL's equivalence classes (a=b AND b=5 ⇒ a=5), IN-list and OR-to-UNION rewrites, MySQL's const-table and impossible-WHERE detection — and their legality limits: outer joins block reordering unless the predicate is null-rejecting (the Galindo-Legaria/Rosenthal simplification that turns LEFT JOIN ... WHERE t.x IS NOT NULL into an inner join), while volatile functions, LIMIT and window functions stop pushdown, as encoded in Calcite's rule framework and PostgreSQL's preprocess phases.
subtopics.visual: On a palette query's plan tree the learner clicks rewrite rules one at a time and watches predicates slide down, unused columns drop off projections and per-edge row counts from the instrumented executor shrink; flipping the join-type fragment to LEFT JOIN greys out the reorderings now refused, and adding an IS NOT NULL predicate on the nullable side collapses the outer join to inner and re-enables them.

subtopics.title: Views, CTEs and materialization fences
subtopics.covers: How the rewriter inlines views into the query tree (PostgreSQL's rewrite system, MySQL's MERGE vs TEMPTABLE view algorithm) so their predicates and joins participate in optimization, why security_barrier views and non-leakproof functions deliberately block pushdown, the CTE fence history — PostgreSQL <12 always materialized WITH queries, 12+ inlines single-reference, non-recursive, side-effect-free CTEs unless MATERIALIZED/NOT MATERIALIZED overrides, recursive and data-modifying CTEs always materialize, MySQL 8 merges CTEs like derived tables — and how DISTINCT ON, window functions and LIMIT inside a subquery act as barriers; materialized views and incremental maintenance are covered in distributed-and-analytical-query.
subtopics.visual: The learner toggles MATERIALIZED/NOT MATERIALIZED on a CTE in a palette query and changes how many times it is referenced, watching the toy planner flip between an inlined tree and a materialized node with a fence line that an outer WHERE predicate stops at while edge row counts update; a security_barrier switch on a view shows a leaky function's predicate pinned above the view boundary.

subtopics.title: Rule pipelines: where heuristics end and cost begins
subtopics.covers: How real engines sequence rewrites — PostgreSQL's fixed pipeline (rewriter, then pull_up_sublinks, pull_up_subqueries, reduce_outer_joins, remove_useless_joins before join search), MySQL's prepare/optimize phases, Calcite's HepPlanner (fixed-order heuristic) vs VolcanoPlanner (cost-driven exploration), SQLite's NGQP as a cost-guided greedy search — why rule ordering matters when rules are not confluent, which decisions genuinely need statistics (join order, access path, OR-to-UNION, subquery materialization) versus which are always-good, and why the logical plan's properties (columns, keys, orderings, equivalence classes) are the interface handed to cost-based-optimization.
subtopics.visual: The same four-table palette query is planned twice side by side by the toy package's rule-only pipeline and its cost-aware one; the learner drags rules into a different order in the heuristic pipeline and watches the output plan shape change, then moves a data-skew slider and sees the fixed plan's executor-measured cost diverge while the cost-aware planner re-picks its join order.

modules.title: Rewrite Legality, Decorrelation and Recursive Evaluation
modules.why: Whether a correlated subquery becomes one free semi join or a per-row re-execution, and whether an aggressive rewrite still returns the same answer, is decided in this layer; a senior engineer needs the actual decision procedure for legality (containment, the chase, and the bag-, NULL- and incomplete-information traps that void textbook equivalences), the unnesting machinery that removes dependent joins, and the fixpoint theory behind recursion, magic sets and incremental maintenance. It is positioned fifth in Part 3, after physical-operators, join-algorithms-at-the-limit and cost-based-optimization, because the rewrites here are only meaningful once hash/semi/anti joins, Bloom-filter semi-join reduction and the planner's search space are already familiar — and it opens with the data-vs-combined-complexity frame that explains every blow-up in the module, so the application-engineer route in start-here-routes-and-method can skip it entirely and lose nothing it needs downstream.

subtopics.title: Data complexity vs combined complexity: cheap in the rows, expensive in the query
subtopics.covers: Vardi's distinction between data complexity (a fixed conjunctive query evaluates in AC0/LOGSPACE, so per-row work is polynomial and parallelizable), query complexity and combined complexity (NP-complete for conjunctive queries, which is why planning, containment testing and view matching blow up with query size, driving PostgreSQL's join_collapse_limit/from_collapse_limit and GEQO, MySQL's optimizer_search_depth and SQLite's beam search), plus the outliers — recursive Datalog's PTIME-completeness explaining why fixpoints are inherently sequential, and the practical rule that the fix for a slow plan is usually fewer relations in the query, not fewer rows in the table.
subtopics.visual: A two-axis lab where raising the number of joined relations makes the planner's explored-plan counter and planning-time bar explode while executor rows-per-second stays flat, and raising row count does the reverse, with the GEQO/collapse-limit thresholds drawn as vertical lines the learner crosses and watches the planner switch from exhaustive DP to heuristic search mid-run.

subtopics.title: Query equivalence, containment and the chase: when is a rewrite legal?
subtopics.covers: Conjunctive-query containment decided by homomorphism on the canonical database (and its NP-completeness), equivalence as mutual containment, the chase as the procedure for containment and lossless decomposition under functional and inclusion dependencies, why bag semantics breaks set-based equivalences (projection duplicates, UNION vs UNION ALL, count-preserving rewrites), why three-valued logic invalidates NOT IN ↔ NOT EXISTS and OR-to-UNION on nullable columns, and how real engines approximate these decision procedures — Calcite's rule framework and materialized-view matcher, Oracle and Snowflake MV rewrite, and PostgreSQL's predtest.c operator-family implication test that decides whether a partial index qualifies.
subtopics.visual: Two palette queries (with editable predicate fragments) sit side by side while the tool builds each one's canonical database and searches for a homomorphism, animating the mapping it finds or highlighting the witness tuple that proves non-containment; flipping the semantics from set to bag, or inserting a single NULL into the sample data, flips a previously green equivalence to red and names the rule that just became unsound.

subtopics.title: Incomplete information: certain answers and what a NULL actually means
subtopics.covers: Codd tables, v-tables and c-tables as the formal models of unknown values, certain versus possible answers and the demonstration that SQL's three-valued evaluation is neither (it returns rows that are not certain and drops rows that are), the consequences a senior meets in production — an outer join that manufactures NULLs then feeds a WHERE or a SUM, NOT IN over a nullable subquery, COUNT and AVG silently skipping unknowns so a metric answers a different question, and the sentinel values ('', 0, 1970-01-01) that hide the unknown from the engine entirely — plus the disciplines that restore certainty (NOT NULL with an explicit unknown member, is-known companion columns, COALESCE at one documented boundary, per-source closed-world declarations in an integration or semantic layer) and the connection to federation and data exchange, where an unshippable predicate turns every answer into a merely possible one.
subtopics.visual: The learner fills a small table with unknowns and the tool computes three result sets for each query side by side — the certain answers (true in every completion), the possible answers, and what SQL actually returns — so a left join plus a filter visibly drops a certain row and an aggregate reports a value no completion produces, while a sentinel-value toggle replaces the NULLs and shows the same query returning a confidently wrong number with nothing marked unknown at all.

subtopics.title: Subquery unnesting and decorrelation
subtopics.covers: Why a correlated subquery evaluated naively is an apply operator re-running the inner query per outer row, how EXISTS/IN become semi joins, NOT EXISTS an anti join, and NOT IN over a nullable column needs a null-aware anti join (or yields no rows), how scalar subqueries become outer joins guarded by a single-row check and the Kim/Dayal 'count bug' where COUNT must yield 0 not NULL, Neumann and Kemper's general unnesting that pushes a dependent join down through operators using the DISTINCT domain of outer columns until it becomes an ordinary join (Hyper, Umbra, DuckDB), versus PostgreSQL's narrower pull_up_sublinks and MySQL's semijoin strategies (FirstMatch, LooseScan, DuplicateWeedout, Materialize), and why scalar subqueries in SELECT lists remain a common trap.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs a correlated palette query through the instrumented pull executor and watches its per-outer-row re-execution counter and total row-visit meter climb, then presses 'unnest' to see the dependent join pushed down step by step, the DISTINCT domain materialize, and the tree settle into a single hash semi join with the counters collapsing; switching the predicate fragment to a NOT IN variant with one NULL inserted shows the null-aware branch that a plain anti join would get wrong.

subtopics.title: Advanced rewrites: join elimination, aggregate pushdown, CSE and magic sets
subtopics.covers: Rewrites that need schema knowledge or cross-tree information — join elimination when the joined side is unique and unreferenced (PostgreSQL's remove_useless_joins for LEFT JOINs) or guaranteed by a trusted NOT NULL foreign key (SQL Server, Oracle, and why NOT VALID or nullable FKs disable it), eager/lazy aggregation that pushes GROUP BY below a join to shrink the join input (Yan and Larson; Oracle group-by placement), DISTINCT and ORDER BY elimination from keys and functional dependencies, common-subexpression elimination and shared scans (DuckDB, Oracle, Snowflake), and sideways information passing / magic sets from Datalog that feed one side's key set into the other side's scan, the ancestor of the bloom-filter runtime filters in Spark, ClickHouse and Oracle.
subtopics.visual: The learner toggles the toy catalog's constraints (FK, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, VALID) and watches a join vanish from or reappear in the plan tree with a label naming the invariant that licensed it, then drags a GROUP BY below a join while a fan-out slider shows the executor's intermediate row count shrink or explode, and finally flips a magic-set/runtime-filter toggle to animate a key set flowing sideways from one scan to prune the other.

subtopics.title: Row-level provenance: why is this row in my answer?
subtopics.covers: Why-, how- and where-provenance and the provenance-semiring framework in which annotations combine with multiplication across joins and addition across unions so bag semantics, trust levels, probabilities and delta counts are all the same computation under different semirings, implementations a senior can actually reach for (ProvSQL, Trio, Spark and dbt lineage at coarser grain), the three uses that justify it — explaining a wrong aggregate by tracing contributing rows, exposing a join fan-out because one source row appears twice in the annotation, and propagating a deletion or erasure request into every derived row — and the storage cost that pushes production systems to column-level lineage plus targeted row-level tracing rather than always-on annotation.
subtopics.visual: A small pipeline where clicking any output row or aggregate value highlights exactly the source rows and renders the semiring expression that produced it, then deleting one source row shows which outputs change, shrink or vanish, and a seeded fan-out bug is caught because the annotation for one output contains the same source row twice while the rendered SUM silently double-counts it.

subtopics.title: Datalog and fixpoint evaluation: recursion the engine can reason about
subtopics.covers: Rules and least-fixpoint semantics, naive versus semi-naive evaluation where only facts derived in the previous round drive the next (the formal justification for SQL's working-table rule), stratified negation and why unstratified programs have no unique model, monotone recursive aggregation, magic-set rewriting as the bridge from a top-down query to bottom-up evaluation (the ancestor of sideways information passing), DRed's over-delete-then-rederive algorithm for incremental maintenance, and the engines that ship it — Soufflé, LogicBlox, DDlog, Datomic, RelationalAI — against SQL's restrictions (linear recursion, no mutual recursion, no aggregation inside the recursive term in most engines).
subtopics.visual: A block-based rule editor over a small graph (atoms and negations dragged in, no free text) lets the learner step rounds under naive and semi-naive evaluation side by side, watching newly derived facts appear while the naive side re-derives the same facts repeatedly with a wasted-derivation counter; adding a negated body atom makes the stratification checker either assign strata or light a cycle red, and deleting one base fact runs DRed's over-delete and re-derive passes in front of the learner.

modules.title: Physical Operators: Scans, Joins, Sorting and Aggregation
modules.why: Every plan node is one of a dozen algorithms whose I/O and memory behavior you must be able to predict.

subtopics.title: Access paths: sequential, index, index-only and bitmap scans
subtopics.covers: Heap page fetch counts for each path as a function of selectivity and physical correlation (pg_stats.correlation), why a poorly clustered index scan re-fetches the same heap page many times, index-only scans gated by the visibility map (the 'Heap Fetches' counter and why a freshly written table gets none), PostgreSQL's bitmap index scan building a TID bitmap that is sorted into physical page order before the bitmap heap scan and degrades to lossy page-level chunks when work_mem overflows (with BitmapAnd/BitmapOr combining indexes), MySQL's MRR and index condition pushdown as the equivalent trick, plus seq-scan ring buffers, synchronized scans and effective_io_concurrency prefetch (bitmap index structure itself belongs to indexes-beyond-the-b-tree, prefetch mechanics to buffer-pool).
subtopics.visual: This page is the declared OWNER of the shared ScanLab primitive (consumers, per the visual-system reuse ledger: index-selection-strategy, indexes-beyond-the-b-tree, cost-based-optimization and explain-and-query-tuning, each carrying only its own payload over the identical heap-page grid, index leaf strip and selectivity/correlation sliders), and its own payload is the mechanism layer: the learner picks seq, index, index-only or bitmap scan and watches the fetch-order arrows, the page counter, the visibility-map bits, and (for bitmap) the TID sort step and the exact-to-lossy collapse as they drag the bitmap memory slider down.

subtopics.title: Nested loop and index nested loop join
subtopics.covers: Tuple-at-a-time nested loop at |R|·|S| comparisons, block nested loop costing B(R)+⌈B(R)/(M−2)⌉·B(S) pages, index nested loop turning the inner side into |R| B-tree probes so cost is B(R)+|R|·(depth + matches), why it is the only choice for non-equi and cross joins and the winner for small outer sets, correlated subqueries and LIMIT (near-zero startup cost), PostgreSQL's Memoize node (14) caching inner results keyed by the outer parameter, MySQL's join buffer BNL and Batched Key Access, inner-side rescan vs Materialize, and the catastrophe when the outer cardinality estimate is off by 1000× (explain-and-query-tuning covers diagnosing it).
subtopics.visual: Two row strips joined by a step button: each outer row sweeps the inner side, then the learner toggles an inner index to see scans become probes, drags a buffer-page slider to see block nested loop amortize inner passes, turns on Memoize to watch repeated keys hit a cache, and spins a 'true outer rows vs estimate' dial to watch the I/O counter explode.

subtopics.title: External sort and sort-merge join
subtopics.covers: Run generation by quicksort (runs of M pages) or replacement selection (runs averaging 2M), heap-based k-way merge with passes = 1+⌈log_(B−1)(runs)⌉ and I/O ≈ 2N·passes, PostgreSQL tuplesort's state machine (in-memory quicksort, bounded top-N heapsort under ORDER BY LIMIT, external merge with abbreviated keys and multiple temp tapes), incremental sort exploiting an index prefix, then merge join on two sorted streams with mark/restore to rewind the inner side on duplicate keys, why merge join is free when an index or previous merge already supplies the order (interesting orders), and how its ordered output feeds ORDER BY and GroupAggregate without a further sort.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets N data pages and M buffer pages and steps through run generation and merge passes with a pass counter and I/O tally (doubling M visibly removes a pass), flips on LIMIT to watch a bounded heap replace the runs, then feeds two sorted streams with duplicate keys into a merge join and watches the inner cursor mark and restore.

subtopics.title: Hash join: build, probe, partitioning and spilling
subtopics.covers: Building a hash table on the smaller (inner) input and probing with the larger, classic in-memory vs Grace hash join (partition both inputs to disk, cost ≈ 3·(B(R)+B(S))) vs hybrid hash keeping partition 0 resident, PostgreSQL's nbatch doubling mid-build with tuples re-partitioned to per-batch temp files and the probe side written out for later batches, the skew optimization that keeps MCV probe keys in memory, recursive partitioning and the batch explosion when one key dominates, match bits for outer/full hash joins, the equi-join requirement and unordered output, SQL Server memory grants, and runtime Bloom/bitmap filters pushed from the build side into the probe scan (Oracle, SQL Server, ClickHouse, DuckDB) as semi-join reduction.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets work_mem and both input sizes; the build hash table fills, batches spawn and spill to labeled temp files, the probe side streams through and re-reads each batch, and a key-skew slider makes one bucket overflow so the learner watches nbatch double repeatedly while the disk-bytes counter climbs.

subtopics.title: Aggregation, DISTINCT and grouping strategies
subtopics.covers: HashAggregate keeping one transition state per group vs sort-based GroupAggregate streaming groups in memory-bounded fashion, the planner's choice driven by estimated ndistinct × state size against work_mem (and the OOM that ndistinct misestimates caused before PostgreSQL 13 learned to spill by partitioning overflow groups to disk and re-aggregating), DISTINCT as aggregation with no aggregates or Unique over sorted input, DISTINCT inside aggregates and ordered-set aggregates forcing per-group sorts, partial/final aggregation with combine functions for parallel and distributed plans (execution-engines-and-resource-control, distributed-and-analytical-query), and GROUPING SETS via multiple sort passes or MixedAggregate hash sets.
subtopics.visual: Rows stream into a hash table whose group entries grow with transition states; the learner toggles to sort mode to see groups emitted as key boundaries pass, lowers the memory limit to watch overflow groups partition to disk and re-aggregate, and drags an ndistinct slider to see the planner flip between hash and sort strategies.

subtopics.title: Window function execution
subtopics.covers: The WindowAgg operator: partition by sort (or hash) then sort within the partition on ORDER BY, buffering the current partition in a tuplestore that spills past work_mem, frame evaluation for ROWS vs RANGE vs GROUPS (peer rows, exclusion), incremental running aggregates using moving-aggregate inverse transition functions instead of O(n²) recomputation, ranking functions that need only the current row and peer boundaries, stacking one WindowAgg per distinct window definition sharing sorts, PostgreSQL 15's run condition that stops a partition early for WHERE rank ≤ k, and DuckDB's segment-tree evaluation for arbitrary frames (SQL semantics live in advanced-sql).
subtopics.visual: A sorted partition strip with sliding frame brackets: the learner switches ROWS/RANGE/GROUPS to see which peers enter the frame, toggles incremental vs recompute evaluation and watches the operation counter diverge, and adds a rank ≤ k predicate to see the run condition cut the partition short.

subtopics.title: Aggregates as algebra: monoids, inverses and the cost of a window
subtopics.covers: Classifying every aggregate by the structure it actually has — a commutative monoid, which is what makes partial aggregation, parallel and distributed merging and reusable rollups legal; a group with an inverse, which is what lets a sliding window subtract the departing row and is exactly PostgreSQL's moving-aggregate inverse transition function (SUM and COUNT have one, MIN, MAX and string_agg do not); and holistic aggregates with no bounded summary (exact median, COUNT DISTINCT) that force full state or a sketch that restores mergeability — plus the sliding-window algorithms that recover amortized O(1) with no inverse (two-stacks, FlatFAT, DABA, and the segment tree DuckDB's window operator builds), and the consequences that follow mechanically: why AVG must be stored as SUM and COUNT, why a percentile rollup must store a t-digest or KLL state rather than a number, and why stream state size is a property of the aggregate's class rather than of the event rate (sketch algorithms themselves belong to analytical-query-platforms, streaming state to stream-processing-and-derived-state).
subtopics.visual: The learner picks an aggregate and slides a window across a stream while three implementations run side by side — recompute per window, inverse-subtract, and a segment tree or two-stacks — with operations per emitted row and retained state plotted, so switching SUM to MIN collapses the inverse lane into recomputation until the tree restores it, and a second panel re-rolls hourly rollups into daily ones showing which aggregates survive the second pass and which silently produce a wrong number.

subtopics.title: Semi, anti joins and set operations
subtopics.covers: EXISTS and IN becoming hash or merge semi joins that stop at the first inner match (no duplicate fan-out), NOT EXISTS becoming an anti join, why NOT IN over a nullable inner cannot be an anti join under three-valued logic (a single NULL empties the result and PostgreSQL falls back to a hashed SubPlan or nested loop with NULL checks), outer-join-plus-IS-NULL rewritten to anti join, the build-side flexibility that arrived in stages (right anti join plan shapes in PostgreSQL 16, right semi join in 17), UNION as HashAggregate or Sort+Unique vs UNION ALL as a plain Append, INTERSECT/EXCEPT via HashSetOp with per-input flag counts, and Bloom-filter semi-join reduction in analytic engines (Trino, ClickHouse).
subtopics.visual: An inner set with a NULL toggle: the learner runs IN, EXISTS, NOT IN and NOT EXISTS and watches the plan node chosen and the result rows highlight or vanish when the NULL is inserted, then switches to UNION vs UNION ALL vs INTERSECT to watch the dedup structure and flag counters at work.

subtopics.title: Write operators: ModifyTable, junk TIDs and Halloween protection
subtopics.covers: The ModifyTable/ExecModifyTable node pulling rows from an ordinary source plan and applying INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE, the junk ctid and tableoid columns carried up from the scan so the write can address the physical tuple its scan produced (and the EvalPlanQual re-check when that tuple moved under READ COMMITTED), the Halloween problem stated with UPDATE emp SET salary = salary * 1.1 WHERE salary < 50000 driven by an index on salary re-finding and re-raising the same row forever, and the three defences — a per-statement command id so the scan's snapshot excludes rows written by the same command (PostgreSQL's t_cid / cmin-cmax rules, see mvcc-storage-vacuum-gc), a blocking eager spool that fully separates read from write (the unexplained Table Spool SQL Server inserts for 'Halloween protection'), or choosing a read path the write cannot perturb — plus RETURNING projecting the post-modification tuple, ON CONFLICT's speculative-insertion token and abort path, and BEFORE/AFTER row trigger interleaving with the modify node (heap-level tuple writes belong to pages-tuples-heap-files).
subtopics.visual: An index-ordered UPDATE stepping through an index on salary: with the per-statement command-id rule toggled off the learner watches each raised row re-enter the index to its right and get re-raised pass after pass until it exits the predicate range, then switches the rule back on or inserts an eager spool to see read and write phases separate, with side toggles for RETURNING rows flowing out and an ON CONFLICT speculative insert aborting on a conflicting key.

subtopics.title: Choosing among operators: cost intuition
subtopics.covers: Side-by-side page and CPU cost formulas for nested loop, index nested loop, hash and merge join and for hash vs sort aggregation, the crossover boundaries set by outer cardinality, inner index presence, input sortedness and interesting orders, build size vs memory, equi vs non-equi predicates, and LIMIT (startup cost vs total cost), the output-order property each operator provides or destroys — including MergeAppend, the ordered append that binary-heap-merges one sorted child stream per partition or UNION ALL branch, requires every child to deliver the required pathkeys (an index on each partition, or an explicit per-child sort), answers ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT n over a range-partitioned table by pulling only n rows from the heap, and demotes to Append plus a full Sort of every partition when the sort key is incompatible with the child orderings or one partition lacks the index (with enable_partitionwise_* and ordered-append costing as the knobs; pruning itself belongs to execution-engines-and-resource-control), PostgreSQL's seq_page_cost=1/random_page_cost=4/cpu_tuple_cost=0.01 defaults and how an SSD-tuned random_page_cost shifts every crossover, and what SQLite (nested loop only), MySQL (nested loop plus hash) and PostgreSQL (all three) can pick from (calibration and statistics belong to cost-based-optimization).
subtopics.visual: Sliders for |R|, |S|, memory, inner index, sortedness, LIMIT and random_page_cost drive four live cost curves that cross over on a log-scale chart while the chosen join node in a small plan tree changes color, and a second panel runs ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT n over a strip of partitions where the learner drops one partition's index or changes the sort key and watches the binary-heap MergeAppend — which stops after n rows — collapse into Append plus a full Sort with every partition's rows counted.

modules.title: Join Algorithms at the Limit: Worst-Case-Optimal, Cache-Aware and Distributed
modules.why: Binary hash and merge joins run into three separate ceilings — a provable complexity bound on output size, the memory hierarchy, and the network between shards — and the algorithms that break each one are where modern join execution is headed.

subtopics.title: Join complexity: the AGM bound and worst-case-optimal joins
subtopics.covers: The AGM fractional-edge-cover bound on maximum join output (the triangle query's N^1.5) and the proof sketch that any binary plan must materialize an intermediate larger than the final answer on cyclic queries, the worst-case-optimal algorithms that instead join attribute-by-attribute over sorted tries (NPRR, Leapfrog Triejoin, Generic Join) as implemented in LogicBlox, RelationalAI, Kùzu, Umbra and DuckDB's graph patterns, and the variable orders, trie-building cost and index requirements that decide whether a WCOJ actually beats a binary plan on a real workload.
subtopics.visual: The learner draws a query graph from presets (chain, star, triangle, clique) and sets relation sizes, and the tool prints the AGM bound, then races a binary hash-join plan whose intermediate result visibly exceeds the final output against a leapfrog triejoin advancing sorted iterators attribute by attribute, with per-step tuple counters and a running intermediate-size meter against the bound.

subtopics.title: Acyclic queries: GYO, semi-join reduction and Yannakakis's algorithm
subtopics.covers: GYO ear removal as the test for acyclicity with treewidth as the dial saying which regime a query is in, full semi-join reduction and Yannakakis's algorithm making acyclic joins linear in input plus output, the approximations real engines ship instead — Bloom-filter and sideways-information-passing reducers met in physical-operators' hash-join and set-operation pages, LIP, and runtime filter pushdown — and hybrid plans that run Yannakakis over the acyclic part of a query and a worst-case-optimal join over the cyclic core.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks an acyclic preset and watches GYO strip ears one at a time to prove acyclicity, then runs the bottom-up and top-down semi-join passes with dangling tuples visibly vanishing from each relation before any join work starts, with per-relation counters and a toggle that adds one edge to make the query cyclic so the reduction visibly stalls with tuples still dangling.

subtopics.title: In-memory parallel joins: radix partitioning and cache-aware hashing
subtopics.covers: No-partition hash join (one shared table built concurrently with CAS or latched buckets, as in PostgreSQL Parallel Hash) vs radix-partitioned join that uses multi-pass radix partitioning with software write-combining buffers to keep each partition inside L2 and each pass's fan-out under the TLB entry count, the Blanas-vs-Balkesen/Teubner sort-vs-hash debate, SIMD sort-merge join with bitonic merge networks and MPSM, hash table layouts (bucket chaining vs linear probing, 16-bit tag filters in HyPer/Umbra unchained tables), group prefetching and AMAC to hide cache misses, Bloom filters ahead of the probe, and skew- and NUMA-aware scheduling of partitions.
subtopics.visual: An explicit, editable cache model — L1/L2 capacity, TLB entries, cache-line size and a named cycle penalty per cache and TLB miss, all shown as parameters rather than measurements — drives the simulation: the learner picks no-partition, one-pass or two-pass radix and sets the radix bits per pass, then watches partitions fan out while the tool derives per-phase miss counts and cycle estimates from the simulated fan-out and working-set sizes (each number labeled as a model output), so a pass whose fan-out exceeds the TLB entry count makes the derived TLB-miss term jump.

subtopics.title: Distributed join strategies: co-located, broadcast, shuffle and semi-join reduction
subtopics.covers: How the same join algorithms choose a data-movement strategy across shards — co-located join when both sides share a partition key, broadcasting the small side, shuffling both sides by the join key, and semi-join or Bloom-filter reduction that ships a filter instead of rows — with the per-strategy cost model in bytes on the wire and peak memory per node, the partition-key and replicated-dimension-table design choices that make co-location possible, and the cutover points where one strategy overtakes another; exchange-operator plumbing, skew and salting, and fragment-level fault tolerance are covered in distributed-and-analytical-query.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets node count, per-shard table sizes, join selectivity and which column each table is partitioned on, then picks a strategy and watches rows or filter bitmaps travel along the node-to-node edges with per-phase byte counters and a peak-memory bar per node, so repartitioning one table onto the join key collapses the shuffle edges to zero and enabling the semi-join reducer shrinks the shipped payload before the join runs.

modules.title: Cost-Based Optimization
modules.why: Cardinality estimation and join-order search are where plans go wrong, and knowing why is the difference between guessing and fixing.

subtopics.title: Cost models: I/O, CPU and their calibration
subtopics.covers: PostgreSQL's cost = seq_page_cost*pages + random_page_cost*random fetches + cpu_tuple_cost/cpu_index_tuple_cost/cpu_operator_cost, with effective_cache_size feeding the Mackert-Lohman index_pages_fetched curve and pg_stats.correlation scaling index-scan heap fetches; startup vs total cost under LIMIT and EXISTS; MySQL's mysql.server_cost/engine_cost tables with memory vs disk block costs and SQLite NGQP's fixed heuristic costs; why cost is a unitless ranking rather than seconds and how random_page_cost=4.0 on NVMe systematically penalizes index scans.
subtopics.visual: Sliders for random_page_cost, seq_page_cost, effective_cache_size, table size and index correlation redraw cost-vs-selectivity curves for seq scan, index scan and bitmap heap scan, with the crossover selectivities sliding as knobs move; a LIMIT toggle swaps the comparison to startup cost and shows the index scan winning where it lost on total cost.

subtopics.title: Statistics: histograms, MCVs, ndistinct and sketches
subtopics.covers: ANALYZE's two-stage block-and-row reservoir sample of 300*default_statistics_target rows producing pg_statistic's null_frac, avg_width, MCV list with frequencies, equi-depth histogram over the non-MCV remainder, Haas-Stokes/Duj1 n_distinct (negative values as a ratio of rows) and physical correlation; InnoDB persistent stats from innodb_stats_persistent_sample_pages index dives and MySQL 8 singleton/equi-height histograms; HyperLogLog and count-min sketches for distinct counts and heavy hitters in ClickHouse, Snowflake and BigQuery; autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor and why stale stats after a bulk load are the leading cause of sudden plan changes.
subtopics.visual: The learner sculpts a column's distribution (uniform, Zipf, bimodal), sets the sample size and stats target, and watches sampled rows land, the MCV list fill with frequencies and equi-depth bucket boundaries snap into place beside the true distribution; a side panel shows HyperLogLog registers updating and its ndistinct error converging, and a 'bulk load 10x rows' button shows every statistic frozen until the autoanalyze threshold is crossed.

subtopics.title: Single-column cardinality estimation
subtopics.covers: PostgreSQL's eqsel (MCV hit, else (1 - sum of MCV freqs)/(ndistinct - n_mcv)), scalarltsel/scalargtsel via MCV partial sums plus linear interpolation inside a histogram bucket, BETWEEN as a range conjunction, LIKE 'abc%' converted to a range plus patternsel for the remainder, IS NULL from null_frac, and the clamp to at least one row; out-of-histogram-range predicates as the situation that fires that clamp constantly — after any append-heavy load `WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 hour'` or `WHERE id > $last_seen_max` falls past the last bucket boundary, estimates one row over the hottest slice of the table and invites a nested loop — with the ascending-key problem and its per-engine mitigations (Oracle's linear decay outside the sampled range, SQL Server trace flag 2371 and ascending-key handling, PostgreSQL's dependence on autoanalyze frequency plus partitioning so the hot partition carries its own statistics); the default constants when nothing is known (DEFAULT_EQ_SEL 0.005, DEFAULT_INEQ_SEL 0.333, DEFAULT_RANGE_INEQ_SEL 0.005, DEFAULT_MATCH_SEL) that fire on expressions, functions and parameters; MySQL's index dives (eq_range_index_dive_limit) versus histogram-based estimates.
subtopics.visual: Using the statistics built in the previous subtopic, the learner types a predicate (=, <, BETWEEN, LIKE 'ab%', IS NULL, or f(x) = c) and the selectivity formula assembles term by term, lighting up the MCV entries and histogram buckets it consumes with the interpolated fraction inside a partial bucket, while an estimate-vs-actual bar pair updates; dragging the constant past the last bucket boundary into rows appended since ANALYZE collapses the estimate to the one-row clamp as the actual bar spikes, and wrapping the column in a function collapses the whole derivation to the default constant.

subtopics.title: Plan stability, hints and regressions
subtopics.covers: Plan flips when growing or drifting data crosses a cost crossover, after a stale-then-refreshed ANALYZE, or when an upgrade changes costing (PG 12 CTE inlining, JIT thresholds, MySQL 8 hash join); pinning mechanisms compared: pg_hint_plan (Leading, HashJoin, Rows, Set), MySQL optimizer hints (JOIN_ORDER, NO_INDEX_MERGE), Oracle SQL Plan Baselines and SQL Server Query Store forced plans, plus enable_* GUCs as diagnostics rather than fixes; parameter sniffing and generic-vs-custom plans are covered in execution-engines-and-resource-control; why a pinned plan silently rots as data changes and how to run plan-regression checks around upgrades.
subtopics.visual: A timeline slider grows and skews a table while two plans' cost curves and measured latency are plotted; at the crossover the optimizer flips plans and latency jumps, the learner pins a hint or baseline and watches the pinned plan hold steady, then keeps dragging the timeline until the pinned plan is the slow one and the unpinned optimizer would have done better.

subtopics.title: Correlation, multi-column statistics and join estimation
subtopics.covers: The attribute-value-independence assumption multiplying per-predicate selectivities and its collapse on correlated columns (city/zip, make/model); fixes in PostgreSQL CREATE STATISTICS (ndistinct, dependencies, mcv), Oracle column groups, SQL Server multi-column density and the 2014 cardinality estimator's exponential backoff; the equi-join estimate |R|*|S|/max(ndv(R.a), ndv(S.b)) under the containment assumption and eqjoinsel's MCV-on-MCV matching; foreign-key-based join selectivity in PostgreSQL 9.6+, which recognizes a matching validated FK constraint and estimates the equi-join at |child| rows instead of the ndistinct formula — and why a NOT VALID or otherwise untrusted constraint silently drops back to the worse estimate; Leis et al. 'How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really?' showing q-error growing exponentially with join count, underestimates dominating, and nested-loop disasters that follow.
subtopics.visual: The learner drags a correlation slider on a two-column scatter plot and issues a conjunctive predicate, watching the independence estimate and the true count separate and snap back when extended statistics are enabled; a second panel chains 2 to 5 joins and plots the q-error at each level on a log scale, growing exponentially under independence and flattening under extended statistics, a validated FK on the join key, or exponential backoff, with a toggle that feeds the previous page's out-of-range one-row estimate in as the leaf and shows that single error propagating undiminished to the top of the join tree.

subtopics.title: Bounding instead of guessing: q-error and pessimistic cardinality estimation
subtopics.covers: Moerkotte's q-error as the multiplicative error metric plus the result that bounds a plan's suboptimality by a power of it (so a factor-2 estimator costs a factor-4 plan while a 1000x underestimate is unbounded), the asymmetry that an underestimate picks nested loops and unspills hash tables while an overestimate only over-provisions, and the upper-bound estimators built to exploit it — AGM and degree-sequence bounds over join keys, Cai et al.'s pessimistic cardinality estimation with bound sketches, Hertzschuch's simplicity-done-right bounds, Umbra-style bounded estimates — contrasted with sampling estimators (InnoDB index dives, join-key sketches) that can still underestimate, closing with the practitioner's versions of the same idea: a rows= hint, enable_nestloop=off as a blunt upper bound, and why a plan chosen under bounded error is the robustness goal rather than an accurate estimate.
subtopics.visual: A three-join query where the learner shapes skew and correlation while an independence-assumption estimator, a sampling estimator and an AGM-style upper bound run side by side with per-node q-error on a log scale and the plan each one picks, so the underestimating lane produces a nested-loop blowup whose measured cost exceeds the bound's predicted factor while the pessimistic lane's conservative hash join lands inside it.

subtopics.title: Selinger bottom-up dynamic programming
subtopics.covers: System R's algorithm: enumerate access paths per relation, then the cheapest plan per subset of relations level by level, keeping extra entries for interesting orders (sort orders useful to a later merge join, GROUP BY or ORDER BY), avoiding cross products, restricting to left-deep trees and choosing the join method per pair; PostgreSQL's standard_join_search with pathkeys as interesting orders, parameterized paths carrying required outer relids so an inner index scan can take the outer row's value as an index key — the machinery that makes index nested loops and LATERAL references reachable inside bottom-up enumeration at all — add_path's dominance test on cost, pathkeys, rows, parallel safety and required outer relids, join_is_legal constraints from outer joins, and join_collapse_limit; complexity O(3^n) for bushy versus O(n*2^n) left-deep, and DB2's equivalent bottom-up planner.
subtopics.visual: A 4-table join is planned level by level: each DP cell shows candidate paths with cost and sort order, dominated paths grey out as add_path prunes them, a merge-join path surviving purely because of its pathkeys is highlighted, a parameterized index path survives beside a cheaper unparameterized one because its required outer relids make the two incomparable and is then consumed by the nested loop above, and the winning tree assembles from the top cell; toggling 'allow bushy' adds the extra cells and reveals the cost of the wider search.

subtopics.title: Cascades and Volcano top-down optimization
subtopics.covers: A memo of groups holding logically equivalent expressions with hash-consed deduplication; transformation rules (join commutativity/associativity, predicate pushdown) versus implementation rules (logical join to hash, merge or nested loop); required physical properties (ordering, distribution, partitioning) satisfied by enforcers such as Sort and Exchange; top-down search with cost upper bounds and branch-and-bound pruning, rule promise ordering and exploration on demand; used by SQL Server, Greenplum Orca, CockroachDB (Optgen), Apache Calcite and Doris, and why distributed engines favor it over Selinger for property-driven pruning and extensibility.
subtopics.visual: The learner fires rules on memo groups and watches deduplicated expressions appear, then demands a physical property (sorted by x, or hash-distributed on k) at the root and steps the top-down search: the cost bound descends, branches exceeding it are cut, an enforcer Sort or Exchange is inserted where a child cannot deliver the property, and each group records its winner per required property.

subtopics.title: Join ordering search space and heuristics
subtopics.covers: n! left-deep and (2n-2)!/(n-1)! bushy orders versus connected-subgraph enumeration in DPccp/DPhyp (Moerkotte and Neumann) whose cost depends on query graph shape (chain, star, clique) rather than table count; PostgreSQL's GEQO genetic search past geqo_threshold=12 with edge-recombination crossover and from_collapse_limit/join_collapse_limit=8 splitting, MySQL's greedy search with optimizer_search_depth and optimizer_prune_level, SQLite's NGQP N-nearest-neighbor beam search, greedy operator ordering and IKKBZ for linear cost functions, and DuckDB's DPhyp-then-greedy fallback.
subtopics.visual: The learner builds a query graph from chain, star and clique presets, and live counters compare the left-deep, bushy and connected-subgraph plan-space sizes; running DPccp, GEQO, MySQL greedy and NGQP beam search side by side animates which subsets each visits and plots the cost it settles on against the exhaustive optimum.

subtopics.title: Adaptive and learned optimization
subtopics.covers: Runtime adaptation: SQL Server adaptive joins with a row threshold that switches hash to nested loop, Oracle adaptive plans with statistics collectors and cardinality feedback, DB2 LEO's learned corrections, Spark AQE coalescing shuffle partitions and switching to broadcast at stage boundaries, and Kabra-DeWitt mid-query re-optimization; robust plan selection favoring flat cost curves under estimation error and plan bouquets; learned cardinality estimators (MSCN, Naru, DeepDB) and learned steering (Bao, Neo) with their failure under data and workload drift; why pipelined OLTP engines rarely re-plan mid-query.
subtopics.visual: A plan executes and reveals actual row counts at a probe point where an adaptive join's threshold decides hash versus nested loop live, with a cost and latency meter comparing the adaptive and static plans; a second panel fits a deterministic fixed-seed lookup-table estimator over a sampled training set in milliseconds, then a drift slider scrubs precomputed distributions and plots the memorized model's error crossing above the histogram's as the data it memorized disappears.

modules.title: Execution Engines, Vectorization and Parallelism
modules.why: Operator models, per-tuple CPU cost, vectorization, parallelism, pruning, spill behaviour and plan caching decide throughput and tail latency, and they are the layer where a plan that looked cheap turns into hours of CPU and temp files.

subtopics.title: Volcano iterator model
subtopics.covers: The open/next/close pull interface (Graefe) where every operator returns one tuple per virtual call, pipelining vs pipeline breakers (Sort, hash build, HashAggregate must drain their whole input before emitting), the per-tuple cost of virtual dispatch, branch misprediction and per-node qual/projection evaluation in PostgreSQL's ExecProcNode and MySQL 8.0's iterator executor, and the materialization-model contrast (VoltDB/H-Store emit whole results) that explains why tuple-at-a-time is fine for OLTP row counts and disastrous for scans.
subtopics.visual: The learner clicks next() on the root of a Filter→HashJoin→Scan tree and watches the call descend and a single tuple bubble up, with per-node call and row counters, pipeline breakers glowing while they swallow their entire input before releasing a first row, and a 'run 10k rows' button that reports function calls per output row.

subtopics.title: Expression evaluation, tuple deforming and the per-tuple CPU budget
subtopics.covers: The two largest line items in a real executor CPU profile: PostgreSQL 10's compiled expression-step machine (ExecInterpExpr walking a flattened step array) as the thing JIT later replaces, the split between qual evaluation on each node and final projection, fmgr function-call overhead and why operators on pass-by-reference and NULLable types cost more, and the tuple-deforming curve as a function of the highest column ordinal touched and of any preceding variable-width or NULLable column ahead of it (why the attcacheoff shortcut from pages-tuples-heap-files matters, why physical column order changes CPU and not just bytes, and why SELECT * is measurably expensive even at a 100% buffer-hit rate) — the per-tuple work that batching and code generation exist to amortize.
subtopics.visual: A scan→filter→project pipeline runs under a live CPU profile split into deform, qual-eval, projection and dispatch bars while the learner moves column count, the highest referenced ordinal, the position of the first variable-width or NULLable column and predicate complexity, then flips SELECT * versus two columns and toggles vectorized or JIT mode to watch those same bars, not the others, collapse.

subtopics.title: Vectorized execution
subtopics.covers: Vector-at-a-time processing of ~1024–2048 values per column in the MonetDB/X100 lineage (DuckDB, ClickHouse, Velox, Photon, CockroachDB's vectorized engine), selection vectors vs bitmasks, branch-free SIMD predicate evaluation, interpretation overhead amortized over a batch, intermediates sized to stay L1/L2-resident, late materialization, the simple analytic cost model engineers reason with (cycles ≈ rows × (per-tuple dispatch + branch-miss rate × penalty + cache-miss rate × latency), with dispatch divided by batch size and miss rate rising once a batch's working set leaves L1/L2), and why PostgreSQL gets column batches only through extensions while its core stays tuple-at-a-time.
subtopics.visual: A few hundred rows animate the mechanism honestly — the selection vector filling slot by slot, batch boundaries, late materialization of the payload columns — beside an explicitly labelled cost model whose parameters (dispatch cycles, branch-miss rate and penalty, L1/L2/DRAM latencies and working-set size) the learner edits, so the modelled 1M-row tuple-at-a-time vs vectorized figures and the batch-size vs cycles-per-row curve with its L1/L2 knee are derived from those numbers rather than presented as measurements.

subtopics.title: Parallel query execution
subtopics.covers: PostgreSQL's Gather/Gather Merge over parallel-aware Seq Scan (block-range handoff through shared memory), Parallel Hash Join with a shared hash table built cooperatively, Partial/Finalize aggregates, parallel safe/restricted/unsafe function labels and what makes a plan node parallel-aware, max_parallel_workers_per_gather and max_parallel_workers as the pools, worker launch and shared-memory setup cost that makes small queries slower in parallel, per-worker memory multiplying work_mem, and the Amdahl ceiling imposed by a serial Sort, Finalize or Gather tuple-queue bottleneck; exchange-based MPP parallelism is in distributed-and-analytical-query, morsel scheduling in compiled-execution-and-user-code.
subtopics.visual: A scan-heavy aggregate plan with a worker slider: the learner watches block ranges handed out to workers through shared memory, partial aggregates accumulating per worker and merging at Gather, a per-worker timeline showing launch overhead and the serial tail, and a speedup-vs-workers curve that flattens then declines as the tuple queue and worker startup dominate.

subtopics.title: Partition pruning and partition-wise execution
subtopics.covers: What the planner and executor do with a declaratively partitioned table: plan-time pruning from constants, execution-time pruning from bound parameters and why runtime pruning only fires for parameterised (and generic) plans, join-derived pruning, Append vs MergeAppend ordered scans over partitions, partition-wise joins and aggregates and why enable_partitionwise_join/aggregate default off (planning cost and per-partition memory multiplication), planning time growing with partition count because the planner still considers every partition, and the statistics trap that makes a correctly partitioned table plan worse than the table it replaced — autovacuum never processes the partitioned parent, so the parent's pg_statistic stays empty (or frozen at whatever a manual ANALYZE last produced) and every estimate that spans partitions, including partition-wise join costing and any predicate on a non-partition-key column, falls back to defaults, with per-partition statistics collected normally, the same trap in the legacy inheritance case, and MySQL and Oracle's global vs partition-level and incremental statistics as the contrast; partitioning is not sharding (one process, one buffer pool — the wins are pruning, DROP PARTITION and vacuum locality), with ATTACH/DETACH protocol, the partition-key-in-unique-key rule, lock budgets and cross-partition row movement in schema-evolution-and-migrations, real sharding in partitioning-and-sharding and retention patterns in application-data-patterns.
subtopics.visual: A monthly range-partitioned table the learner drives three ways: typing a predicate as a constant, a bound parameter or a join-derived condition greys out partitions at plan time vs execution time; a partition-count slider drives a planning-time meter and flips MergeAppend to a sort; and a 'parent statistics empty' badge — cleared by running a manual ANALYZE on the parent and re-armed by a simulated autovacuum pass that skips it — visibly flips the chosen plan between a partition-wise join and a single default-estimated hash join, with estimated-vs-actual row counts shown side by side.

subtopics.title: Spill shapes: what each operator writes to disk
subtopics.covers: The distinct on-disk artifact each spilling operator produces once its budget is exceeded — Sort's initial sorted runs and their k-way merge passes (PostgreSQL's logical tape set packing all tapes into one temp file, merge order limited by the per-tape buffer), Hash Join's per-batch files where both build and probe sides are partitioned, written and re-read exactly once per batch (plus batch explosion and slicing when a batch still will not fit), and HashAggregate's overflow partitions (PG13+) re-read and re-aggregated, recursively when a partition is still too big — with bytes written, re-read counts, temp_file_limit and temp tablespaces, compressed or buffer-managed spill blocks in ClickHouse and DuckDB, and double-buffering through the OS page cache that makes a 'disk' spill sometimes never touch a platter; budgets and the RAM ceiling live in buffer-pool, plan symptoms in explain-and-query-tuning, spill algorithms in physical-operators, grant queueing in query-scheduling-and-admission-control.
subtopics.visual: Three temp-file canvases side by side for the same spilled input: Sort's runs appear then merge pass by pass into fewer, longer runs; Hash Join's build and probe partitions fill and are then re-read batch by batch; HashAgg's overflow partitions spill and recurse — each with live bytes-written, bytes-re-read and pass-count meters and a page-cache layer showing which reads never reached the device, so the learner sees the three do not degrade alike.

subtopics.title: Prepared statements and plan caching
subtopics.covers: Server-side prepared statement lifecycle (parse once, plan per execute), PostgreSQL's custom-vs-generic rule (five custom plans, then generic if average custom cost plus planning overhead is no cheaper) with plan_cache_mode overrides and generic plans' fallback to default selectivities, plan invalidation through relcache/catalog invalidation on DDL and ANALYZE, SQL Server's plan cache with parameter sniffing and OPTION(RECOMPILE), Oracle bind peeking and adaptive cursor sharing, MySQL's absence of a shared plan cache, and the PgBouncer transaction-mode prepared-statement problem (protocol-level tracking in 1.21); the wire protocol is in application-access, plan regressions in cost-based-optimization.
subtopics.visual: The learner executes a prepared statement against a skewed status column, picking each parameter value; an execution strip shows custom vs generic choice, PG's running average custom cost against the generic cost, the flip at execution six and per-execution time, and issuing ALTER TABLE or ANALYZE or flipping plan_cache_mode shows the cache entry invalidate and re-plan.

modules.title: Morsel Parallelism, JIT Compilation and User Code
modules.why: Push-based morsel scheduling and data-centric code generation are how modern engines spend CPU on your data instead of on dispatch, and user code — inlined, interpreted, sandboxed or across a network hop — is the one thing the optimizer cannot see inside, so it silently sets the plan, the parallelism and the per-row cost.

subtopics.title: Push-based and morsel-driven parallelism
subtopics.covers: Cutting a plan into pipelines at breakers, producers pushing into consumers (Umbra, DuckDB, Velox drivers), HyPer's ~100k-tuple morsels dispatched to a fixed thread pool with NUMA-local placement and work stealing, elastic parallelism where threads join or leave between morsels, the pipeline-dependency DAG the scheduler walks, skew tolerance through dynamic morsel assignment vs static exchange partitioning, and the contrast with exchange-operator parallelism (Postgres Gather, MPP exchanges in distributed-and-analytical-query).
subtopics.visual: A plan colored into pipelines above a thread-count slider and a data-skew slider: worker threads grab morsels from two NUMA sockets, steal from the other socket once local work is exhausted, and per-thread timelines fill, then a 'static exchange partitioning' toggle shows stragglers appear on the skewed partition while other threads idle.

subtopics.title: JIT compilation of queries
subtopics.covers: Data-centric code generation (HyPer, Neumann 2011) that fuses a whole pipeline into one loop keeping tuples in registers, LLVM as the backend, PostgreSQL's JIT for expressions and tuple deforming gated by jit_above_cost/jit_inline_above_cost/jit_optimize_above_cost and its compile-latency trap on short queries and per-worker compilation, Umbra's adaptive tiers (bytecode interpreter → fast codegen → optimized LLVM), Hekaton and SingleStore compiled procedures, and the compiled-vs-vectorized findings (Kersten et al. 2018): compilation wins on computation-heavy pipelines, vectorization on memory-bound scans and profilability.
subtopics.visual: The learner builds a small Scan→Filter→Agg plan and toggles JIT to see the generated fused-loop pseudo-code beside the interpreted operator tree, scrubs the row count and optimization tier to watch a compile-time vs per-row-savings break-even chart, then enables Umbra-style adaptive mode and watches the tier upgrade mid-query as rows accumulate.

subtopics.title: UDFs, stored procedures and server-side logic
subtopics.covers: PL/pgSQL as an interpreter over SPI with per-statement plan caching and per-call fmgr overhead, SQL-language functions inlined only when single-SELECT and non-VOLATILE, how volatility, STRICT, COST/ROWS and parallel-safety labels gate index use, predicate pushdown, parallelism and CTE-fence behavior, the per-row scalar UDF as a hidden nested loop, SQL Server's Froid inlining (2019) rewriting scalar UDFs into relational expressions, Hekaton natively compiled procedures, Oracle PRAGMA UDF, and PL/Python, PL/v8 and extension languages that the planner can never see into.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes a small scalar function body, picks its language and volatility label, and the plan of a query calling it re-renders to show whether it inlines, blocks the index, forces serial execution or runs as a per-row SPI call with a call-count meter, then a Froid-style inlining toggle shows the function body dissolve into a relational subtree.

subtopics.title: Running user code in a sandbox: WASM, Arrow-batched and remote UDFs
subtopics.covers: How user logic executes when it cannot run as a trusted in-process function — WebAssembly UDFs and stream transforms (ScyllaDB WASM UDFs, Redpanda Data Transforms, Proxy-Wasm, the WASM-in-managed-Postgres proposals) with their per-invocation memory and time limits and absent syscalls, sandboxed language runtimes (Snowflake's Java and Python UDF sandbox and Snowpark containers, BigQuery's isolated JavaScript), vectorized UDFs that take and return Arrow batches rather than rows (pandas UDFs, Snowflake vectorized Python, DuckDB and Polars extensions) and the order-of-magnitude the batch size buys, and remote or external functions that turn a per-row call into a batched HTTP round trip with its own retry, concurrency and cost semantics — plus what the optimizer loses in every case: no inlining, opaque cost and selectivity, no predicate pushdown, and determinism it must take on faith.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs one transformation as an in-process scalar function, a WASM-sandboxed function, an Arrow-batched vectorized function and a remote function over the same rows, watching invocation count, batch size, wall-clock split between engine and sandbox, memory-limit kills and HTTP round trips, then moves the call into a WHERE clause to see which forms the planner can push into the scan and which force a full scan with a post-filter.

modules.title: Query Scheduling, Admission Control and Cancellation
modules.why: Once queries outnumber cores and memory grants, the queue discipline and the abort path decide whose latency suffers and whether one runaway query takes down the server.

subtopics.title: Scheduling policy: FIFO, shortest-job-first, fair sharing and head-of-line blocking
subtopics.covers: Why FIFO is variance-minimizing but suffers head-of-line blocking when a long query sits in front of short ones, why SJF/SRPT minimizes mean response time yet starves large jobs (and needs a size estimate the optimizer's cost supplies, badly), processor sharing and least-attained-service as the estimate-free approximations behind multi-level feedback queues, priority aging as the anti-starvation patch, multi-resource fairness (max-min, dominant resource fairness) as the notion multi-tenant pools need, and priority inversion as the characteristic failure of every priority or class scheme layered on a database — a low-priority transaction holding a row lock, a buffer pin or an advisory lock (or parked in a throttled pool) makes the high-priority class slower, with the partial remedies being never throttling or descheduling a lock holder, admitting at transaction rather than statement granularity, priority-aware deadlock victim selection and wound-wait, and priority inheritance where the lock manager supports it (the lock-manager machinery itself is in lock-based-concurrency-control and distributed-transactions) — with Redshift WLM queues and short-query acceleration as the shipped example and PostgreSQL's single undifferentiated queue as the baseline the pooler has to fix; the mechanisms that enforce a policy (grants, slots, tokens) are the next subtopic, queueing arithmetic is in performance-literacy-and-tradeoffs.
subtopics.visual: On a shared queue substrate a mixed arrival stream of short and long queries feeds one server and the learner changes only the ordering discipline — FIFO, split short/long queues, SJF fed by cost-model size estimates, priority classes with aging, fair-share pools — watching per-class latency distributions, a starvation clock ticking on the oldest long query, a size-estimate-error slider that routes a huge query into the short queue and reintroduces head-of-line blocking, and a lock toggle that gives the head-of-queue low-priority job a row lock the high-priority job needs so raising priority visibly makes the important class slower.

subtopics.title: Query scheduling and admission control
subtopics.covers: Why PostgreSQL has none (process-per-connection, max_connections as the only gate, poolers as the de facto throttle), SQL Server Resource Governor workload groups with CPU and memory caps and grant queues with RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits, Oracle Resource Manager, ClickHouse max_concurrent_queries and workload scheduling, Snowflake warehouse queuing, and CockroachDB's token-based admission control with CPU and IO slot pools, elastic vs regular work and LSM store-overload signals, all grounded in the queueing argument for bounding concurrency (running everything thrashes; queueing preserves throughput and p99) and in the admission-side face of priority inversion — a gate that holds back a lock-holding transaction blocks the class it was meant to protect; retry storms are in backups-incidents-disaster-recovery, noisy neighbors in security-and-tenant-isolation.
subtopics.visual: The same queue substrate now exposes the two things ordering cannot express — a bounded running set and a shared memory-grant pool — so the learner compares no admission against slot-based and grant-based admission with priorities, the signature artifact being the no-admission run where in-flight work keeps climbing while goodput collapses into the thrash curve, then layers per-tenant tokens on top and adds a bursting tenant to watch the tokens hold the line.

subtopics.title: Feedback control in databases: setpoints, gain and oscillation
subtopics.covers: Reading each self-tuning loop as a controller with a measured variable, a setpoint and an actuator — InnoDB adaptive flushing driven by checkpoint age and dirty ratio, RocksDB's rate limiter and write stalls keyed on pending compaction bytes, checkpoint_completion_target, autovacuum cost delay, AIMD and gradient-based adaptive concurrency limits (Netflix concurrency-limits, Envoy adaptive concurrency), and queue-depth or CPU-driven autoscalers — together with the control facts that decide whether they help: proportional gain against overshoot, integral windup once the actuator saturates, dead time from a lagging measurement (a five-minute average driving a one-minute actuator guarantees a limit cycle), hysteresis and cooldowns as the standard damping, and the coupled-loop pathology where an autoscaler and an admission controller drive the same variable in opposite directions.
subtopics.visual: A plant-and-controller sandbox where the learner sets setpoint, gain, measurement delay and actuator limits against a simulated database whose load they perturb, watching the controlled variable settle, overshoot or lock into an oscillation, then adding a second controller on the same actuator to reproduce the fighting-loops collapse and damping it back with hysteresis and a cooldown.

subtopics.title: Query cancellation and timeouts inside the engine
subtopics.covers: Cooperative cancellation via PostgreSQL's SIGINT→ProcessInterrupts at CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS points, the family statement_timeout vs lock_timeout vs idle_in_transaction_session_timeout vs transaction_timeout (17) and where each fires, pg_cancel_backend vs pg_terminate_backend, the cancel key sent on a separate connection, uncancellable phases (blocked in read() or fsync, inside a critical section or LWLock, extension code without interrupt checks), parallel worker cancellation, MySQL KILL QUERY and max_execution_time, and cleanup after abort (temp files, locks, the transaction left in error state); cross-fragment cancellation is in distributed-and-analytical-query, client-side timeouts in application-access.
subtopics.visual: The learner starts a long query and drops a cancel or timeout at a chosen moment on its timeline; the executor's phase strip highlights the next CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS point and shows the request-to-abort latency depending on whether the query is in a tight loop, inside fsync, waiting on a lock or in an extension without checks, with the timeout knob that would have fired lit up.

modules.title: EXPLAIN Literacy and Query Tuning
modules.why: Plan reading turns every earlier mechanism — statistics, operators, access paths and memory budgets — into a diagnosable symptom in the plan output, and a repeatable tuning workflow turns those symptoms into fixes that survive the next stats refresh or upgrade.

subtopics.title: Reading the plan tree: costs, rows, loops, buffers and time
