subtopics.covers: How to read PostgreSQL EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, WAL, SETTINGS, FORMAT JSON) output as a tree evaluated bottom-up: startup vs total cost in seq_page_cost units, estimated rows vs actual rows per loop (total = rows × loops), inclusive node time that must have child time subtracted to find the dominant node, planning vs execution vs trigger vs JIT time, shared hit/read/dirtied/written and temp read/written buffers, track_io_timing I/O timings that separate CPU-bound from I/O-bound nodes, per-worker stats under Gather, the observer effect of instrumentation itself — two clock readings per tuple per node can double or triple measured runtime on a high-row nested loop and move where the time appears, so EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, BUFFERS) and the timing-independent buffer counters are the stable comparison and pg_test_timing measures the host's clock cost — and the standing caveat that elapsed time no node accounts for is usually a lock wait rather than a plan problem — diagnosis of which belongs to lock-based-concurrency-control — with pev2/explain.dalibo.com as the reading aid.
subtopics.visual: An interactive plan tree for a fixed 4-node query where clicking any node opens its estimated/actual/loops/buffers panel; a toggle switches the time bars from inclusive to exclusive (children subtracted) so the true hot node lights up, a loops slider on a nested-loop inner side shows how per-iteration rows and time multiply into the totals the parent reports, a TIMING ON/OFF switch adds or removes the per-tuple clock cost so the hot node visibly changes while the buffer bars stay fixed, and a final toggle injects unaccounted elapsed time so the sum of node times visibly falls short of the total.

subtopics.title: Scan-level diagnostics: Index Cond vs Filter, Heap Fetches and lossy bitmaps
subtopics.covers: The scan-node lines that reveal wasted work: Index Cond (used for the index search) vs Filter (evaluated after fetching, reported as Rows Removed by Filter), Index Only Scan Heap Fetches caused by an unset visibility map after writes without VACUUM, Bitmap Heap Scan Recheck Cond — printed unconditionally on every bitmap heap scan but actually evaluated only for lossy pages or lossy index AMs, so it is the 'Heap Blocks: exact=/lossy=' line and not the presence of the recheck line that tells you whether it cost anything — Heap Blocks exact vs lossy when the bitmap exceeds work_mem, Seq Scan chosen on purpose once selectivity passes the random_page_cost break-even, Parallel Seq Scan rows split per worker, and the MySQL equivalents Using index / Using index condition / Using where in Extra.
subtopics.visual: A plan-text reading drill: only the EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) scan-node lines are shown, and from 'Index Cond' vs 'Filter', 'Rows Removed by Filter', 'Heap Fetches' and 'Heap Blocks: exact=/lossy=' the learner predicts how many pages were touched, how many fetched rows were thrown away and whether the printed Recheck Cond ever ran, then hits Reveal to unfold the same heap-page grid used elsewhere in the curriculum as the answer key with mispredicted pages flagged — including one scored case where the ANALYZE wall clock and the buffer counts disagree because instrumentation, not I/O, dominated.

subtopics.title: Spotting misestimates and their causes
subtopics.covers: Reading the estimated/actual ratio at each node and tracing it to its leaf origin: stale statistics after bulk loads (autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor, default_statistics_target), the independence assumption across correlated predicates fixed by CREATE STATISTICS (ndistinct, dependencies, mcv), default selectivities for expressions, functions, JSONB/array operators and LIKE that have no stats until an expression index or expression stats exist, join estimates |R||S|/max(ndv) that compound exponentially with join count (Leis et al.), the rows=1 trap that steers the planner into nested loops, and the parameterized-statement case where a generic plan estimates against default selectivities instead of your parameters — inspected with EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN) (PG16) on a statement containing $1 placeholders, recognized in auto_explain output by the $1 parameters and the flat default-looking estimates that mark a captured plan as generic rather than custom, and forced either way with plan_cache_mode=force_generic_plan/force_custom_plan so a session that 'looks fine with literals but is slow from the app' stops being called intermittent — with the estimation theory itself owned by cost-based-optimization and the generic/custom decision mechanism by execution-engines-and-resource-control.
subtopics.visual: A three-join plan tree with a root-cause selector (stale stats, correlated city/zip columns, function on a column, JSONB containment, generic plan for a parameterized query); choosing one makes the leaf estimate diverge and the error bars grow up the tree and flip the join method, then applying the matching fix (ANALYZE, CREATE STATISTICS, expression index, plan_cache_mode=force_custom_plan) shrinks the ratio bars back toward 1 node by node — and the generic case adds a side-by-side EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN) vs EXPLAIN-with-literals pane plus an auto_explain capture the learner must label generic or custom before revealing.

subtopics.title: Spills, batches and memory symptoms in plans
subtopics.covers: The plan lines that mean an operator exceeded its budget: Sort Method quicksort vs top-N heapsort vs external merge Disk: N kB, Hash Buckets/Batches with original vs actual batch counts that reveal a misestimated build side, HashAggregate Batches and Disk Usage since PostgreSQL 13 (hash_mem_multiplier), Incremental Sort presorted-key groups, temp read/written buffers and log_temp_files/temp_file_limit, work_mem being per operator per parallel worker rather than per query, and MySQL Using filesort / Using temporary with sort_buffer_size and tmp_table_size — reading as symptoms the spill algorithms from physical-operators and the allocation model from buffer-pool's 'Memory beyond the pool'.
subtopics.visual: A fixed plan containing a Sort, a Hash Join and a HashAggregate, each with a memory bar; the learner drags a single work_mem slider and watches every node's label flip at its own threshold (quicksort→external merge, Batches 1→4→16, HashAggregate spills), with temp bytes written and elapsed time accumulating in a footer that shows the operators do not fail gracefully at the same point.

subtopics.title: Join order and join method problems
subtopics.covers: Diagnosing the classic join pathologies from the plan: a Nested Loop whose inner side is a Seq Scan or a Materialize repeated loops=N times, a nested loop chosen because the outer side was estimated at 1 row, a Hash node built on the larger input with batch explosion, a Merge Join forced to add explicit Sorts instead of using index order, Memoize (PG14) caching inner lookups by key, semi/anti join nodes from EXISTS/NOT EXISTS, outer joins that restrict reordering, join_collapse_limit/from_collapse_limit and GEQO past geqo_threshold, enable_nestloop=off as a diagnostic rather than a fix, and MySQL's Batched Key Access, Block Nested Loop and hash join with STRAIGHT_JOIN.
subtopics.visual: A four-table join where each table has a slider for its true size and a second slider for what the planner believes; the plan tree re-renders its join order and methods as beliefs change, an estimated-vs-actual cost gauge shows the gap, and enable_* toggles and a Memoize switch let the learner see which alternative the planner should have picked.

subtopics.title: Common anti-patterns and rewrites
subtopics.covers: Query shapes that produce recognizable bad plan nodes and their rewrites: SELECT * defeating index-only scans, functions or implicit casts and collation mismatches on indexed columns, OR across columns rewritten as UNION ALL or served by BitmapOr, NOT IN on nullable columns that cannot become an anti join versus NOT EXISTS, correlated scalar subqueries in the SELECT list appearing as SubPlan executed per row versus a hashed SubPlan or LATERAL join, DISTINCT hiding join fan-out, CTE materialization fences before PG12 and the MATERIALIZED keyword, volatile functions blocking predicate pushdown, ORDER BY with LIMIT on a non-matching index, and row-level security policies appearing as hidden Filters — with pagination owned by index-selection-strategy and decorrelation theory by sql-to-logical-plan.
subtopics.visual: A before/after sandbox: the learner picks an anti-pattern from a list, the offending plan node (SubPlan, Filter, Seq Scan, Unique) is highlighted in the left tree, and toggling the rewrite morphs the tree on the right with a diff strip showing buffers, rows removed and time before and after.

subtopics.title: Plans in other engines: MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB, ClickHouse
subtopics.covers: The same concepts in other dialects: MySQL's tabular EXPLAIN (type=ALL/range/ref/eq_ref, key, rows, filtered, Extra) versus EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE and EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+) with actual time/rows/loops and optimizer_trace; SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN lines (SCAN vs SEARCH USING INDEX, COVERING INDEX, AUTOMATIC INDEX, USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY) versus raw VDBE bytecode from EXPLAIN; DuckDB's EXPLAIN ANALYZE pipeline tree with per-operator timing, vector counts and filter/projection pushdown into Parquet; ClickHouse's EXPLAIN PLAN, PIPELINE, ESTIMATE and indexes=1 showing parts and granules selected by the primary key and skip indexes; and SQL Server actual plans with warnings and Query Store as the reference point.
subtopics.visual: A four-pane comparison driven by pre-authored plan text, not a live planner: twelve captured states (3 queries × index present/absent × 2 table sizes) stored as tagged JSON, so flipping a control swaps in the real recorded output for all four engines and hovering a tagged concept in any pane (index range search, sort, hash join, granules skipped) lights its equivalent lines in the other three — making visible which engines change their choice at the same point and which do not.

subtopics.title: The tuning workflow: find, reproduce, hypothesize, verify, guard
subtopics.covers: The repeatable loop: find candidates in pg_stat_statements ranked by total_exec_time versus mean_exec_time versus calls versus shared_blks_read (and the MySQL slow query log with long_query_time), capture real plans with auto_explain sampling and log_min_duration_statement, reproduce on realistic data volume and statistics rather than a tiny dev database, test hypotheses with hypopg hypothetical indexes, rewrites, extended statistics or configuration, verify by buffers and plan shape rather than wall-clock alone, and guard against regressions with statement_timeout, plan-snapshot tests in CI, plan_cache_mode, and forced plans (pg_hint_plan, SQL Server Query Store, Oracle SQL Plan Baselines) as a last resort — since stats refreshes and major-version upgrades flip plans without any code change.
subtopics.visual: A guided lab: a sortable pg_stat_statements top list where re-sorting by total, mean or calls surfaces different culprits; picking one opens its plan, the learner chooses a hypothesis (hypothetical index, rewrite, CREATE STATISTICS, work_mem) and a before/after scorecard updates buffers, time and plan shape; a final 'time passes' button injects a stats refresh or upgrade that flips the plan and shows whether the chosen guard catches it.

parts.title: Transactions, Concurrency Control and Recovery
parts.summary: Serializability and isolation levels precisely, locking, MVCC from semantics through vacuum, non-blocking serializability, and write-ahead logging with ARIES recovery.

modules.title: Transactions, Serializability and Isolation Levels
modules.why: The anomaly catalog and the engine isolation matrix are the vocabulary for every concurrency and distributed-consistency discussion that follows.

subtopics.title: ACID precisely
subtopics.covers: Atomicity is abortability (InnoDB rolls back through the undo log; Postgres never undoes, an aborted xid's tuples are simply invisible), Consistency is the application's invariants plus declared constraints the engine merely checks (deferred constraints at COMMIT), Isolation is a spectrum whose ideal is serializability, and Durability means the WAL is fsynced or quorum-replicated before COMMIT returns (synchronous_commit levels, innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit) — so 'ACID-compliant' means nothing without naming the isolation level and durability setting, and BASE is marketing rather than a model.
subtopics.visual: A two-account transfer stepped statement by statement with a failure injector — crash before COMMIT, concurrent writer, power loss after COMMIT returned, constraint violation on the last row — where for each injection the learner watches which mechanism (undo or invisibility, locks or versions, WAL replay, constraint check) restores which letter, and a durability knob that flips synchronous_commit=off exposes the acknowledged-but-lost window.

subtopics.title: Schedules, conflicts and serializability
subtopics.covers: Two operations conflict when they touch the same item and at least one writes (rw, wr, ww); a schedule is conflict-serializable iff its precedence graph is acyclic, view serializability is broader but NP-complete to test so real engines target conflict serializability; recoverable, cascadeless and strict schedules constrain commit order for recovery (strict 2PL delivers strict), and serializable says nothing about real-time order — that stronger property is strict serializability, owned by consistency-models.
subtopics.visual: The shared TimelineEditor primitive holds the reads, writes and commits of three transactions as one ordered operation list the learner reorders with keyboard or move-up/move-down buttons (drag is an optional enhancement) and advances with a 'step next operation' control, while the shared graph builder — here in precedence-graph mode, the same component the Adya page later switches into dependency mode — redraws rw/wr/ww edges on every change, reddens a cycle, prints the topological serial order when acyclic, and re-grades the schedule as recoverable, cascadeless or strict as commit points move.

subtopics.title: The anomaly catalog
subtopics.covers: The eight named anomalies — dirty write, dirty read, non-repeatable (fuzzy) read, phantom, lost update, read skew, write skew and Fekete's read-only transaction anomaly — each replayed as a concrete two- or three-transaction history (bank transfer, on-call doctors, counter increment, meeting-room booking) together with the application code pattern that produces it (read-modify-write, check-then-insert, range check then update) and the invariant it breaks, since lost update and write skew are the two that bite real applications most — with the caveat that the dirty-read scenario is unreachable on PostgreSQL, which accepts SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED and silently runs READ COMMITTED, so it must be replayed in InnoDB or SQL Server mode before anyone concludes they have proven something about dirty reads.
subtopics.visual: Pick an anomaly and step its scripted interleaving in the shared stepper: each transaction's private view of the rows sits beside the committed table so the learner sees exactly which stale or uncommitted value every read returned, the violated invariant lights up at commit (both doctors off call, negative balance, sum mismatch), a 'what code wrote this' pane shows the ORM or SQL pattern responsible, and an engine-mode selector drives the same history under different rules records so that choosing Postgres for the dirty-read scenario greys the run out with an 'accepted but upgraded to READ COMMITTED' badge and offers the InnoDB or SQL Server mode that actually exhibits it.

subtopics.title: Isolation levels: ANSI, the Berenson critique and Adya's graphs
subtopics.covers: ANSI SQL-92 defines READ UNCOMMITTED/READ COMMITTED/REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE by prohibited phenomena P1–P3; Berenson et al. (1995) showed the definitions are ambiguous (strict vs loose readings), omit dirty write, lost update and write skew, and cannot place snapshot isolation or cursor stability; the four levels are also not four everywhere, since an MVCC engine has no cheap way to expose uncommitted data and Postgres therefore implements only three, mapping READ UNCOMMITTED onto READ COMMITTED; and Adya's thesis replaces phenomena with dependency graphs of ww, wr and rw edges, defining each level by the cycles it forbids (G0, G1a/G1b/G1c, G2-item, G2, G-single), the vocabulary Jepsen's Elle checker uses (see verification-jepsen-simulation).
subtopics.visual: The same TimelineEditor and graph builder as the previous page, now switched to Adya mode so the extension is visible: the learner edits a history (item reads, predicate reads, writes, commits, aborts) through the ordered list, the graph gains ww/wr/rw dependency edges over the earlier precedence edges, any cycle is classified as G0, G1c, G2-item, G2 or G-single and named, and the ANSI-vs-Adya level matrix lights the column showing which levels permit that history — with the READ UNCOMMITTED column flagged as unimplemented-and-upgraded on MVCC engines so a G1a history has nowhere to run there.

subtopics.title: Snapshot isolation semantics
subtopics.covers: A transaction reads from a snapshot fixed at its first statement (Postgres: xmin, xmax and in-progress xid list; InnoDB: read view) and never blocks on readers or writers; concurrent writers to the same row are resolved by first-committer-wins (Oracle, SQL Server SNAPSHOT error 3960) or first-updater-wins block-then-abort (Postgres 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update'), which prevents every ANSI phenomenon and the lost update yet leaves predicate reads unprotected, so write skew and the read-only anomaly commit — fixable with SELECT FOR UPDATE, a materialized conflict row or a constraint, or by SSI (serializability-without-blocking).
subtopics.visual: A commit timeline on which the learner drags each transaction's start and commit markers and watches the snapshot it captures (the visible version of every row highlighted), then issues overlapping updates to compare first-committer-wins abort with Postgres first-updater block-then-abort; the on-call doctors scenario runs through to a committed write skew, and toggling SELECT FOR UPDATE or a shared on-call-count row turns the second transaction into a block or a serialization failure.

subtopics.title: Read Committed up close: statement snapshots and re-checks
subtopics.covers: READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot per statement (Postgres) or per consistent read (InnoDB), so one transaction sees different committed states across its statements; an UPDATE, DELETE or SELECT FOR UPDATE that hits a row modified by an in-flight transaction waits, then re-evaluates its WHERE clause against the new version (Postgres EvalPlanQual, InnoDB semi-consistent reads), which stops the lost update inside a single UPDATE SET x = x + 1 but not the SELECT-then-UPDATE pattern, lets a single statement observe a mix of states, and is why SQL Server's locking READ COMMITTED and RCSI behave differently under concurrent writers.
subtopics.visual: Step a Read Committed transaction while a concurrent writer commits between its statements: each statement's snapshot is drawn as a fresh frame over the row version chain, an UPDATE that hits a locked row shows the wait, the re-check against the new version and the resulting row count, and switching the code between UPDATE SET x = x + 1 and SELECT-then-UPDATE shows one increment surviving and the other silently lost.

subtopics.title: Transaction boundaries in practice
subtopics.covers: Autocommit wraps every statement in its own transaction; BEGIN opens one whose snapshot is taken at the first query, not at BEGIN (so SET TRANSACTION and pg_export_snapshot ordering matters); SAVEPOINT creates subtransactions (Postgres assigns subxids that overflow the 64-entry per-backend cache into the SLRU and slow every snapshot — see mvcc-storage-vacuum-gc); an error in Postgres aborts the whole transaction (25P02) until ROLLBACK whereas MySQL rolls back only the statement; and idle-in-transaction sessions hold locks and pin the xmin horizon, governed by idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout, lock_timeout and READ ONLY / DEFERRABLE modes.
subtopics.visual: A session console where the learner types BEGIN, statements, SAVEPOINT, ROLLBACK TO, a failing statement and COMMIT against a Postgres-mode or MySQL-mode state machine and watches the session state (idle / in transaction / aborted), the snapshot-taken marker, the subtransaction stack with its 64-entry cache overflowing, and the locks and xmin horizon held while the session idles in transaction until a timeout fires.

subtopics.title: Multiversion serializability and one-copy serializability
subtopics.covers: Why the single-version theory of 'Schedules, conflicts and serializability' does not carry over unchanged — a multiversion schedule is correct when its multiversion serialization graph is acyclic (MVSR), snapshot isolation produces schedules that can be MVSR-admissible yet not conflict-serializable, and 'serializable' under MVCC means equivalent to some serial order of the same transactions rather than to a single-version history — plus one-copy serializability as the criterion for replicated data (an execution over many replicas must be equivalent to a serial execution on one logical copy), its strict/real-time variant, why an async read replica yields a locally serializable but not 1SR system, and where PostgreSQL SSI, InnoDB REPEATABLE READ, Spanner's external consistency and CockroachDB's serializable each land on that map.
subtopics.visual: The same TimelineEditor and graph builder in multiversion mode: the learner composes a history whose reads carry explicit version arrows, and the multiversion serialization graph is drawn beside the plain conflict graph so MVSR-acyclic-but-conflict-cyclic histories are obvious; enabling a replica lane that answers one read from a stale version inserts the edge that breaks 1SR while each individual copy's local schedule still checks out as serializable.

subtopics.title: What real engines actually give
subtopics.covers: The engine × level matrix: Postgres READ COMMITTED (per-statement snapshot), REPEATABLE READ = SI with first-updater-wins, SERIALIZABLE = SSI, and READ UNCOMMITTED accepted-but-upgraded to READ COMMITTED so no dirty read is observable; InnoDB REPEATABLE READ = SI for consistent reads but next-key locking for locking reads and writes (so write skew still commits and mixing the two read kinds surprises), SERIALIZABLE turns every SELECT into a shared-lock read, and its READ UNCOMMITTED is real; SQL Server/Sybase implement READ UNCOMMITTED and NOLOCK for real, where the hazard is not only P1 — an allocation-order scan racing page splits and row movement can return the same committed row twice or skip it entirely, a corruption of the result set that appears in none of the eight named anomalies; Oracle's 'SERIALIZABLE' is SI (ORA-08177); SQL Server also offers locking REPEATABLE READ, SNAPSHOT and RCSI; SQLite is serializable through the database lock (WAL mode: one writer, many readers); CockroachDB and Spanner default to serializable / strict serializable; MongoDB separates level from default like the rows above — its default read concern is local, evaluated per operation with no multi-document isolation at all, snapshot semantics arrive only inside a multi-document transaction or under readConcern snapshot, and a plain find() routed to a secondary returns stale and non-monotonic results unless a causally consistent session or majority read concern is used; Cassandra and DynamoDB give no multi-row isolation outside LWT or TransactWriteItems — and the defaults (PG RC, MySQL RR, Oracle RC, SQL Server RC) are weaker than developers assume.
subtopics.visual: An engine-and-level explorer with no hand-authored cells: each engine/level is a declarative rules record (snapshot policy per-statement or per-transaction, read-lock policy, write-conflict rule first-committer-wins / first-updater-wins / blocking, predicate protection none / next-key / SIREAD, a level-accepted-but-upgraded flag that visibly rewrites the requested level to the one actually run, and the error code it raises) that the anomaly-catalog stepper is replayed under, so every cell resolves to allowed / blocked / aborted / unreachable-here with the mechanism animated from the rules — an InnoDB next-key wait, a Postgres RR snapshot read, an SSI abort, an ORA-08177, a Postgres READ UNCOMMITTED request silently promoted to READ COMMITTED, a MongoDB run where switching read concern from the local default to snapshot (and routing the read to a secondary with and without a causal session) changes which values the same history returns, and in the NOLOCK cell an allocation-order scan stepping across a page that splits mid-scan so the learner watches one row returned twice and another skipped — with the rules record shown beside the run, which is why selecting 'REPEATABLE READ' on Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server side by side yields three different result rows.

modules.title: Lock-Based Concurrency Control
modules.why: Strict 2PL, intention locks, gap locks and deadlock detection are what InnoDB, SQL Server and (for writes) PostgreSQL actually run; a senior engineer must be able to predict which rows and ranges a statement locks, why a queued ALTER TABLE freezes an entire service, and how to read a blocking chain at 3 a.m., because lock pile-ups are the single most common database production incident — note that PostgreSQL's habit of recording row locks inside the tuple header is only previewed here and is fully defined, together with version chains and MultiXacts, in mvcc-storage-vacuum-gc.

subtopics.title: Two-phase locking and strict 2PL
subtopics.covers: The growing/shrinking phases and the lock point, the proof sketch that ordering transactions by lock point yields a conflict-equivalent serial schedule, why plain 2PL still permits cascading aborts and unrecoverable schedules, strict 2PL (hold X locks to commit) and rigorous 2PL (hold all locks) as the fix, conservative 2PL as deadlock-free but impractical, and the fact that InnoDB, SQL Server and DB2 run strict 2PL for writes while PostgreSQL combines strict 2PL on writers with MVCC reads.
subtopics.visual: A multi-lane timeline of three transactions with draggable lock-acquire and lock-release markers: the learner drags a release earlier than a later acquire and watches the growing/shrinking phase bands break, the precedence graph gain a cycle and the equivalent-serial-order label vanish, then drags an X-release before commit and aborts the other transaction to watch the cascading abort propagate.

subtopics.title: Lock modes and compatibility matrices
subtopics.covers: Shared and exclusive modes, the update (U) lock of SQL Server and DB2 that prevents the classic S-to-X conversion deadlock, PostgreSQL's four tuple lock strengths (FOR KEY SHARE, FOR SHARE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR UPDATE) and their 4x4 matrix, lock conversion and upgrade rules, and how a request is checked against both the granted group and earlier waiters so that a queued X blocks later S requests (PostgreSQL) versus InnoDB's FIFO-with-CATS (Contention-Aware Transaction Scheduling) ordering.
subtopics.visual: Several transactions fire lock requests of chosen modes at one row and each request marks the exact compatibility-matrix cell it is tested against — every cell and badge dual-encoded with a glyph plus short label (✓ compatible, ✗ conflict, ⏳ queued, mode letters S/X/U) over theme-defined colors so no verdict rests on color alone — first against the granted group and then against each waiter in the queue, and the learner switches two concurrent readers from S-then-upgrade-to-X to U locks to watch the conversion deadlock disappear.

subtopics.title: Granularity and intention locks
subtopics.covers: The database-table-page-row hierarchy, the IS/IX/SIX/S/X 5x5 matrix and the protocol that every ancestor must carry an intention lock so a table-level request is decidable without scanning rows, SQL Server and DB2 lock escalation (roughly 5,000 locks per statement, LOCK_ESCALATION AUTO/TABLE/DISABLE, LOCKLIST overflow) and its blocking side effects, PostgreSQL's eight relation lock modes from ACCESS SHARE to ACCESS EXCLUSIVE as the intention-lock instantiation with row locks that never escalate because they are recorded in the row itself, and MySQL metadata locks as the table-level analogue.
subtopics.visual: A tree of table, pages and rows with every node labelled by its held mode (IS/IX/SIX/S/X) and status glyph rather than color alone: the learner takes a row X lock and watches IX propagate up to page and table, requests a table S or SHARE lock from another transaction and sees the conflict detected at the intention level with no row scan, then raises a lock-count slider until escalation collapses thousands of row locks into one table X lock and previously unrelated rows flip to a 'blocked' badge.

subtopics.title: Row-level locking on real engines: FOR UPDATE, SKIP LOCKED, NOWAIT
subtopics.covers: PostgreSQL recording the row lock in the tuple header itself, which is why row locks never escalate and consume no shared memory (the header fields and the several-lockers-share-one-row case are defined in mvcc-storage-vacuum-gc), foreign-key checks taking KEY SHARE on the parent so FOR NO KEY UPDATE does not block child inserts, InnoDB locking index records so that an UPDATE with no usable index locks every scanned record (semi-consistent read relaxes this only under READ COMMITTED) and secondary-index locks propagating to the clustered record, SELECT FOR UPDATE as the standard cure for lost updates and write skew, and the wait semantics of NOWAIT (immediate error), SKIP LOCKED (unfair skip, no queue) and lock_timeout / innodb_lock_wait_timeout; queue-table design patterns are owned by application-data-patterns.
subtopics.visual: A two-session statement stepper over a table with a primary key and one secondary index, toggled between PostgreSQL and InnoDB: the learner runs an UPDATE or SELECT FOR UPDATE with or without a usable index and sees exactly which tuples (lock mark written into the row) or index records (lock structs) get locked, each tagged with its mode letters, then issues the second session's FOR UPDATE with plain wait, NOWAIT or SKIP LOCKED and watches it block, error or skip past the locked rows.

subtopics.title: Deadlocks: detection, prevention and victims
subtopics.covers: Waits-for graph cycle detection and its engine variants (PostgreSQL runs the check only after deadlock_timeout and aborts the process that detected it, InnoDB checks on every wait with a search depth limit and picks the transaction with least undo, SQL Server's lock monitor runs every 5 seconds honoring DEADLOCK_PRIORITY), innodb_deadlock_detect=OFF plus timeouts for hot workloads, timestamp-based prevention with wait-die and wound-wait (used by Spanner's lock manager), the common real-world triggers (opposite update order, foreign-key checks, gap-lock inserts, S-to-X conversion) and the application cure of consistent lock ordering, short transactions and retry on 40P01 / error 1213.
subtopics.visual: The learner schedules lock requests from several transactions and the waits-for graph draws itself edge by edge; when a cycle forms it is flagged with a ⟳ glyph and a 'deadlock' label as well as a theme-safe highlight, and the learner picks a policy (PostgreSQL timeout detection, InnoDB immediate detection, wait-die, wound-wait) to see which transaction is marked 'victim: aborted' and how long the others waited, then replays the schedule with acquisitions sorted by key and watches the cycle never form.

subtopics.title: Lock queues, DDL locks and blocking chains in production
subtopics.covers: The FIFO lock queue rule that makes a waiting ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (or MySQL MDL exclusive) request conflict with every later ACCESS SHARE, so an ALTER TABLE stuck behind one idle-in-transaction session freezes all reads on that table, head-blocker versus chain diagnosis with pg_locks, pg_blocking_pids(), wait_event=Lock, performance_schema.data_lock_waits / sys.innodb_lock_waits and sys.dm_tran_locks blocking_session_id, and the safety rails lock_timeout with retry on migrations, statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and pg_terminate_backend; which DDL statements take which lock and rewrite is owned by schema-evolution-and-migrations.
subtopics.visual: An incident replay: a long transaction holds ACCESS SHARE, an ALTER TABLE queues behind it, and live traffic piles up into a growing queue whose entries carry explicit 'granted'/'waiting on' labels while a blocking-tree panel (what pg_blocking_pids would return) draws the chain; the learner intervenes by setting lock_timeout on the DDL, terminating the head blocker or cancelling the ALTER and watches the queue drain or the outage lengthen.

subtopics.title: Phantoms, predicate locks, gap and next-key locks
subtopics.covers: Why row locks cannot lock rows that do not yet exist, predicate locking as the exact-but-costly answer and index-range locking as the practical approximation, InnoDB under REPEATABLE READ with record, gap, next-key (record plus preceding gap) and insert-intention locks including the supremum pseudo-record, unique-equality lookups degrading to a pure record lock, gap locks disabled under READ COMMITTED except for foreign-key and duplicate-key checks, the gap-lock deadlock produced by two inserts into one gap, SQL Server SERIALIZABLE key-range locks (RangeS-S, RangeX-X), unique-index insert conflicts waiting on the in-progress inserter's transaction id in both engines, and the contrast with PostgreSQL, which prevents phantoms not by blocking but with SIREAD locks under SSI (serializability-without-blocking).
subtopics.visual: A sorted index drawn as keys with visible gaps: the learner runs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE with an equality or range predicate under InnoDB RR, InnoDB RC or SQL Server SERIALIZABLE and watches record, gap, next-key or key-range locks paint the index with each span tagged by its lock-type label (REC, GAP, NEXT-KEY, INS-INTENT, RangeS-S) rather than color alone, then attempts inserts at chosen positions from a second session to see which acquire insert-intention locks and block, and finally fires two concurrent inserts into the same gap to produce and diagnose a gap-lock deadlock.

subtopics.title: Commutativity as a lock mode: abstract locks, open nesting and logical undo
subtopics.covers: Generalizing the shared/exclusive matrix of 'Lock modes and compatibility matrices' to Weihl's commutativity-based concurrency control, where compatibility is defined over operations (two increments commute, increment and read do not) so the conflict matrix can be far wider than S/X, plus the multi-level and open-nested transactions whose inner actions commit early and are undone by compensation rather than physical undo (ARIES nested top actions and the CLR machinery built in write-ahead-logging-and-recovery, InnoDB index structure modifications whose B-tree split commits inside an uncommitted transaction), Herlihy-Koskinen transactional boosting as the STM formulation, the shipping descendants previewed here and owned elsewhere — escrow and reservation locks and increment-only aggregate rows (write-side-data-patterns), Cassandra counter columns and PN-counter CRDTs (leaderless-quorums-crdts) — and the price: every abstract operation needs a hand-written inverse, an aborted transaction can no longer be undone by restoring bytes, and one read of the hot value collapses the whole scheme back to exclusive.
subtopics.visual: Two transactions issue increments, decrements and reads at one hot row while the learner toggles between a read/write matrix and a commutativity matrix and watches the conflict cells flip their ✓/✗ glyph-and-label badges, the lock queue drain and the throughput meter rise, then aborts one transaction and steps its rollback as a compensating increment (labelled CLR) rather than a page restore, and finally adds a read into the transaction to watch commutativity collapse back to exclusive and the queue re-form.

subtopics.title: Lock manager internals
subtopics.covers: The shared lock table hashed by lock tag with per-lock granted masks and wait queues, per-transaction lock lists for release-at-commit, PostgreSQL's 16 lock partitions each under an LWLock, fast-path relation locks (a per-backend slot array for weak modes that falls back to the shared table when a strong lock exists) and max_locks_per_transaction sizing the shared-memory table, the fact that PostgreSQL row locks occupy no shared-table entry at all — the lock lives in the row, so only a waiter creates a transient tuple lock and then sleeps in XactLockTableWait on the holder's xid — InnoDB's lock_sys hashed by (space, page_no) with per-page lock structs holding a heap_no bitmap and implicit locks materialized from the row's trx_id only on conflict, its sharded lock_sys latches since 8.0.21, and SQL Server's lock hash with lock owner blocks.
subtopics.visual: A live view of the partitioned lock hash table filling as a workload runs — per-backend fast-path slots versus shared-table entries, partition contention counters labelled with numbers rather than heat color alone — and a click on any locked row that shows either PostgreSQL's picture (no shared-table entry; a transient tuple lock and a wait on the holder's xid) or the InnoDB per-page lock bitmap; the learner then opens enough locks to exhaust max_locks_per_transaction and watches the out-of-shared-memory error fire.

modules.title: MVCC: Semantics, Version Storage and Snapshots
modules.why: Multiversioning is how modern engines read without blocking, and the version-storage design an engine picks decides read cost, write amplification, index bloat and whether it needs a vacuum at all.

subtopics.title: Multiversion fundamentals: version chains, visibility and snapshots
subtopics.covers: Every write creates a version stamped with a creator and (later) a deleter transaction id or commit timestamp; a snapshot is a fixed set of 'committed before me' transactions and the visibility predicate selects the newest version whose creator is in that set and whose deleter is not, so readers never block writers, while write-write conflicts still need first-committer-wins (abort, Oracle/PG REPEATABLE READ) or first-updater-wins (block on the row lock then re-check the new version, PG READ COMMITTED's EvalPlanQual, InnoDB's current-read) and every engine's garbage horizon is simply the oldest live snapshot (isolation semantics themselves live in transactions-and-isolation, the collection of garbage in vacuum-freezing-and-horizons).
subtopics.visual: A per-key version timeline where the learner opens transactions, writes and commits, then drags a snapshot cursor and watches each version's visibility test evaluate creator-committed? / deleter-committed? step by step, and where two concurrent writers on one key collide and a toggle shows first-committer-wins (abort) vs first-updater-wins (block, then re-read the new version).

subtopics.title: Version storage: append-only heap, undo deltas, version stores and timestamped keys
subtopics.covers: The four layouts and who pays: append-only in-heap with old-to-new t_ctid chains where the newest version costs a chain walk and every non-HOT update writes a new entry into every index (PostgreSQL); in-place newest with new-to-old undo deltas reachable via a rollback pointer so old snapshots pay chain reconstruction and secondary indexes carry no version info (InnoDB, Oracle rollback segments); a separate version store (SQL Server tempdb, Hekaton) ; and timestamp-suffixed keys in an LSM where versions are just adjacent sorted entries (RocksDB sequence numbers, CockroachDB MVCC keys), with the read/write/space tradeoffs quantified by Wu et al. VLDB 2017.
subtopics.visual: The same UPDATE sequence applied side by side to a heap, an undo-delta store, a version store and an LSM key space; the learner switches between a fresh reader and an old-snapshot reader and watches the chain each one must traverse light up, the bytes consumed by each design grow, and the per-index write counter tick only on the append-only side.

subtopics.title: Swapping Postgres's heap: table access methods, zheap and OrioleDB
subtopics.covers: The table access method API and the constraint that index AMs address rows by TID, zheap's in-place updates with undo records so aborts roll back instead of leaving dead tuples, OrioleDB's undo-log MVCC with row-level WAL, index-organized tables, its own page cache bypassing double buffering and optional S3 offload, Citus columnar and TimescaleDB hypercore as other TAM instances, and the trade: no bloat, no vacuum and lower write amplification against extension compatibility, pg_upgrade paths and ecosystem maturity.
subtopics.visual: The same update-and-abort workload runs side by side on a heap, a zheap-style in-place engine and an OrioleDB-style engine with live counters for tuple versions created, index entries written, WAL bytes, table size and vacuum work, while a rollback on each lane shows dead tuples accumulating on the heap versus an undo chain being walked and discarded on the others.

subtopics.title: PostgreSQL MVCC: xmin/xmax, snapshots, virtual xids and pg_xact
subtopics.covers: HeapTupleHeader t_xmin/t_xmax/t_cid/t_ctid plus infomask flags (HEAP_XMAX_LOCK_ONLY, HEAP_XMAX_IS_MULTI, HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN); a snapshot is (xmin, xmax, xip[], subxip[], suboverflowed, curcid) so any xid < xmin is settled, >= xmax is invisible and in-between consults xip; HeapTupleSatisfiesMVCC's decision tree including own-transaction cmin/cmax rules, xmax used as a row-lock marker rather than a delete, aborted deleters, and the 2-bit pg_xact lookup (in progress / committed / aborted / subcommitted) that every unresolved xid costs; and the lazy-xid rule underneath it all, where a transaction starts with only a virtual xid (backendID, localXID) and is assigned a real xid at its first write (or when a subtransaction or an explicit assignment forces it), so a read-only transaction never appears in pg_xact, never advances the xid counter toward wraparound and takes a `virtualxid` rather than a `transactionid` lock — which is why pg_locks shows virtualxid rows with no row behind them, why XactLockTableWait only works on a holder that has already written, and why a long read-only transaction is cheap in xids yet still pins the xmin horizon through its snapshot.
subtopics.visual: A heap page whose tuples display their header fields; the learner starts, commits and aborts transactions, takes a snapshot (its xmin/xmax/xip drawn as a number line), and clicks any tuple to step through the visibility decision tree branch by branch, with each session's xid slot showing a virtual (backendID, localXID) until its first write flips it to a real xid that joins xip and the wraparound counter, and the pg_xact page lookup animated whenever a status is not yet known.

subtopics.title: Hint bits and reads that write
subtopics.covers: The first reader to resolve a tuple's xmin/xmax through pg_xact caches the result as HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED/INVALID and HEAP_XMAX_COMMITTED/INVALID infomask bits, dirtying the page without a WAL record (unless wal_log_hints or data_checksums force a full-page image after the first post-checkpoint modification), which is why a SELECT after a bulk COPY becomes a write storm, why unhinted pages thrash the small pg_xact SLRU, why pg_rewind requires wal_log_hints, and why VACUUM and freezing are the other hint setters; InnoDB avoids this by consulting the in-memory transaction system with its trx id instead.
subtopics.visual: The learner bulk-loads rows, commits, then runs a SELECT and watches pages flip to dirty as hint bits get set and a pg_xact-lookup counter drops on the second scan; toggling wal_log_hints/checksums makes WAL bytes appear from a pure read, and a checkpoint button shows the resulting write-back I/O.

subtopics.title: InnoDB MVCC: undo logs, read views and purge
subtopics.covers: The clustered record carries DB_TRX_ID and DB_ROLL_PTR into undo log records living in rollback segments inside undo tablespaces (insert undo dropped at commit, update undo kept for MVCC); a ReadView {low_limit_id, up_limit_id, m_ids, creator_trx_id} decides visibility and old versions are rebuilt by walking the undo chain; secondary indexes are only delete-marked and use PAGE_MAX_TRX_ID to decide whether a clustered-index lookup is needed; purge threads truncate history only past the oldest read view, so history list length (SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS) is the lag metric and one long transaction bloats undo tablespaces and slows every reader of hot rows.
subtopics.visual: The learner updates one row repeatedly and watches the undo chain grow behind DB_ROLL_PTR; opening read views at different points and stepping a read shows the chain walk and version reconstruction, a secondary-index probe shows the PAGE_MAX_TRX_ID shortcut vs clustered lookup, and closing views lets purge advance with history list length falling in real time.

subtopics.title: Snapshot acquisition scalability: ProcArray, CSN and epochs
subtopics.covers: PostgreSQL builds each snapshot by scanning the ProcArray under a shared lock, O(connections) per statement, which PG14 mitigated with dense xid arrays and cached horizons but which still makes snapshot cost scale with connection count; commit-sequence-number designs (Oracle SCN, Greenplum, PostgresPro, CSN-in-pg_xact proposals) make a snapshot a single number so visibility is commitCSN <= snapshotCSN at the price of a commit-time CSN store; InnoDB's trx_sys mutex on commit and ReadView creation is the analogous hotspot; Silo/Cicada replace a global counter with decentralized epochs so commit ids are (epoch, local) and only epoch advance is shared (their validation protocols are covered in serializability-without-blocking).
subtopics.visual: A connection-count slider drives a ProcArray; each snapshot animates the scan and its latency bar grows with connections, then switching to CSN mode collapses the snapshot to one counter read while a commit-path view shows how many transactions contend on the single counter versus per-thread epoch slots.

modules.title: Garbage Collection: Vacuum, Freezing and Horizons
modules.why: Every multiversion engine must reclaim old versions, and the horizon that pins them, the freezing race against a 32-bit counter and the tiny SLRUs behind both cause the bloat, stalls and write-refusal outages seniors must recognize on sight.

subtopics.title: Vacuum, dead tuples and bloat
subtopics.covers: VACUUM's phases (heap scan collecting dead TIDs bounded by maintenance_work_mem / PG17's TidStore, index bulkdelete, a second heap pass setting LP_UNUSED, FSM and visibility-map all-visible updates, tail truncation under a brief exclusive lock), autovacuum triggering by threshold + scale_factor with PG13 insert-based triggers and cost-based delay throttling (vacuum_cost_limit/delay, autovacuum_max_workers), the five things that let vacuum run without reclaiming anything — long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions, replication slots, orphaned prepared transactions, hot_standby_feedback (replication module) and orphaned temp schemas left by crashed backends whose temp tables autovacuum can never touch (diagnosed by joining pg_class to the pg_temp_N namespaces, then dropping the orphan schema) alongside the pg_class/pg_attribute catalog bloat that heavy CREATE TEMP TABLE churn leaves behind — the opposite design choice of bounding snapshot age so the old reader breaks instead of the table (Oracle overwriting undo and raising ORA-01555 'snapshot too old'; PostgreSQL's old_snapshot_threshold, which did the same until it was removed in 17 for missing cases and occasionally returning wrong answers), and measuring and reclaiming the result with pg_stat_user_tables, pgstattuple, VACUUM FULL's full rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE versus pg_repack's online swap.
subtopics.visual: An autovacuum simulator where a workload slider generates updates while the learner tunes threshold, scale factor, cost delay and worker count and watches dead tuples, visibility-map bits, free space and bloat percentage move; opening a long transaction, a stale replication slot or an orphaned pg_temp schema drags the horizon line backwards so each vacuum pass reports 'dead but not yet removable', a 'bound snapshot age' toggle instead kills the old reader with a snapshot-too-old error and lets reclamation proceed, and a reclaim button contrasts VACUUM FULL blocking all readers against pg_repack swapping in a rebuilt copy.

subtopics.title: Freezing and transaction-id wraparound
subtopics.covers: Why a 32-bit xid space is circular with only 2^31 of visible past, so every live tuple must eventually be frozen: xmin replaced by the HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN infomask (FrozenTransactionId before 9.4), per-relation relfrozenxid and per-database datfrozenxid advancing only as far as the oldest unfrozen tuple, vacuum_freeze_min_age and vacuum_freeze_table_age turning a normal vacuum into an aggressive one that ignores the all-visible skip, autovacuum_freeze_max_age forcing a non-cancellable anti-wraparound vacuum, the all-frozen VM bit that lets later passes skip whole ranges, and the ladder when freezing loses — age(relfrozenxid) climbing, warning at xidWarnLimit, writes refused at xidStopLimit and recovery via single-user mode — plus the failsafe (vacuum_failsafe_age) that drops throttling and index cleanup, and the 64-bit-xid proposals that would retire the whole problem.
subtopics.visual: A circular xid clock where the learner runs a workload that advances the counter and watches age(relfrozenxid) sweep toward the limits; triggering an aggressive vacuum animates tuple xmins flipping to FROZEN and drags the relfrozenxid hand forward, while pinning the horizon with a long transaction, a stuck slot or an orphaned temp schema lets the hand cross the warn line into the stop line, refusing writes until single-user mode clears it.

subtopics.title: Postgres SLRUs: subtransactions, multixacts and their wraparound
subtopics.covers: SLRUs are tiny fixed buffer pools over 8KB page files (pg_xact, pg_subtrans, pg_multixact/offsets and members, pg_commit_ts, pg_serial; PG17 makes sizes configurable and banks the locks); each PGPROC caches only 64 subxids so a transaction with more SAVEPOINTs, PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION blocks or ORM nested transactions sets suboverflowed on every concurrent snapshot and forces visibility checks through pg_subtrans page lookups (the SubtransSLRU lock-contention outage pattern, worse on hot standbys); multixacts are created when several lockers share a row (FOR KEY SHARE, FK checks) with a 32-bit offsets space plus a 2^32 members space that need their own freezing (vacuum_multixact_freeze_*), and members exhaustion halts writes.
subtopics.visual: The learner opens a transaction with a savepoint-count slider; crossing 64 flips every snapshot to overflowed and each concurrent visibility check animates a pg_subtrans page fetch through a small SLRU ring showing hits, misses and lock waits; a second mode adds concurrent FOR KEY SHARE lockers and shows multixact offsets/members files grow toward their wraparound limits.

subtopics.title: MVCC and indexes: dead entries, bottom-up deletion and page recycling
subtopics.covers: PostgreSQL index entries carry no visibility info, so dead heap tuples leave dead index entries removed only by VACUUM's bulkdelete or opportunistically by scans marking LP_DEAD (kill_prior_tuple) and by PG14 bottom-up deletion that targets version churn from non-HOT updates on unrelated indexes; deleted leaf pages are stamped with the xid that deleted them (btpo_xact, full 64-bit in PG14) and recycled only once no in-flight scan can still follow a link past the horizon; index-only scans fall back to heap fetches wherever the VM is not all-visible; InnoDB instead delete-marks secondary entries and defers to PAGE_MAX_TRX_ID checks; REINDEX CONCURRENTLY is the cure for bloat neither path fixes.
subtopics.visual: A B-tree leaf whose entries point at heap versions; the learner issues non-HOT updates and watches dead entries pile up, runs an index scan that flags LP_DEAD, toggles bottom-up deletion to see churn absorbed before a split, and watches a fully deleted page sit in the 'awaiting horizon' state until the last old scan finishes and it is recycled.

subtopics.title: Garbage collection in LSM and in-memory engines
subtopics.covers: One oldest-reader horizon produces a different pathology in every engine: RocksDB versions are sequence-numbered keys and compaction may only drop a version if no live snapshot falls between it and the next newer one, so each pinned snapshot preserves one version per key across every level (plus compaction filters and TTL); PostgreSQL pins dead tuples the vacuum report calls 'dead but not yet removable' while InnoDB instead lets history-list length climb as purge stalls (mechanics in mvcc-storage-vacuum-gc); Cassandra keeps tombstones for gc_grace_seconds to avoid zombie resurrection; CockroachDB's gc.ttlseconds and protected timestamps are the distributed form (cluster-wide horizon in distributed-transactions); Hekaton uses cooperative GC where transactions unlink dead versions they encounter plus parallel GC threads keyed on the oldest active transaction, and Silo/Bw-tree-style engines rely on epoch-based reclamation (mechanics in b-trees-and-variants); in every design one idle transaction freezes cleanup globally.
subtopics.visual: A single draggable oldest-reader/horizon handle drives four engine lanes side by side — Postgres heap tuples going 'dead but not yet removable', InnoDB history-list length climbing as purge stalls, RocksDB per-key versions retained per pinned snapshot (the lsm-trees compaction component embedded read-only), and a Hekaton version chain whose cooperative unlink can no longer detach anything — each with its own 'uncollectable bytes' meter, so dragging the one handle backwards produces four different pathologies at once and releasing it drains the meters at four different speeds.

modules.title: Serializability Without Blocking: TO, OCC and SSI
modules.why: Timestamp ordering, optimistic validation and serializable snapshot isolation are how PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE, in-memory engines like Hekaton and Silo, FoundationDB and application code with version columns get serializable results without holding 2PL locks; the price is aborts instead of waits, so the SQLSTATE 40001 retry loop, its false positives and the contention regime where optimism thrashes follow directly from these protocols.

subtopics.title: Optimistic locking in application code: version columns and compare-and-set
subtopics.covers: The lost-update hazard in read-modify-write code and its optimistic fix — UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ? followed by a rows-affected check — generalized to HTTP ETag/If-Match, DynamoDB ConditionExpression and TransactWriteItems, etcd compare-and-swap on mod_revision and Redis WATCH/MULTI, why a monotonic counter beats a timestamp or content hash (the ABA problem), why Hibernate @Version and Rails lock_version raise a stale-object error instead of merging, and the contention point at which SELECT FOR UPDATE's waiting becomes cheaper than repeated retries.
subtopics.visual: Two editors load the same row (version 7) into side-by-side forms and the learner submits them in any order: with the version check the second UPDATE matches zero rows and turns red with a 'stale, reload' prompt, a 'no version column' toggle shows the same submit silently overwriting the first editor's change, and a contention slider adds more editors so the retry counter and wasted-work meter climb until a FOR UPDATE toggle trades the retries for a visible wait queue.

subtopics.title: Timestamp ordering: read/write timestamps, the Thomas write rule and MVTO
subtopics.covers: Basic T/O assigns each transaction a start timestamp and keeps per-item read-TS and write-TS, aborting a read of an item whose write-TS lies in the reader's future and a write to an item already read by a later transaction, with the Thomas write rule silently dropping a blind write outrun by a newer write-TS (view- but not conflict-serializable), the recoverability problem that forces commit dependencies or delayed reads, deadlock-freedom paid for with starvation of long transactions that keep restarting with fresh timestamps, and multiversion T/O (MVTO) where reads never abort because they select the version with the largest write-TS below their own timestamp — the lineage behind CockroachDB's timestamp cache and read-refresh, covered in distributed-transactions.
subtopics.visual: A timeline where the learner drags read and write operations from three timestamped transactions onto items A, B and C; each item displays its live rts/wts pair, every operation is checked against them with the rule that fires printed inline, a late operation aborts its transaction which restarts with a new timestamp, a Thomas-write-rule toggle turns the late blind write into a skipped write, and an MVTO toggle grows a version list per item so the reads that previously aborted now succeed against an older version.

subtopics.title: Optimistic concurrency control: read, validate, write
subtopics.covers: Kung and Robinson's three phases — reads into a private workspace with buffered writes, validation, then write-out — with backward validation (my read set against the write sets of transactions that committed during my lifetime) versus forward validation (my write set against the read sets of still-active transactions), the serial validation critical section and its parallel-validation relaxation, the transaction number assigned at validation that becomes the serialization order, the thrash regime where every abort discards an entire read phase so throughput collapses past a conflict threshold, and FoundationDB's resolvers as a production instance checking read conflict ranges against writes newer than the read version inside a 5-second window.
subtopics.visual: A three-lane simulator (read, validate, write) where N transactions with learner-set read-set and write-set sizes flow through; the validation lane intersects each transaction's read set with recently committed write sets (backward) or its write set with active read sets (forward, via a toggle), overlaps flash and send the transaction back to the start, and a contention slider drives live committed-per-second and wasted-work curves that expose the thrash cliff.

subtopics.title: Serializable snapshot isolation: rw-antidependencies and dangerous structures
subtopics.covers: Fekete, Cahill and Röhm's theorem that every non-serializable SI execution contains a pivot transaction with an incoming and an outgoing rw-antidependency (T1 reads what T2 later writes, T2 reads what T3 later writes) where T3 commits first, which turns write skew (the on-call doctors) and Fekete's read-only transaction anomaly into a detectable graph shape rather than an outcome to reason about, why ww edges are already handled by first-committer-wins and wr edges by the snapshot, the abort choice (kill whichever transaction closes the structure, since the pivot may already be committed), and the corollary that reads and writes never block — only conflict edges are recorded, unlike 2PL's blocking predicate locks.
subtopics.visual: This page reuses the shared TimelineEditor and dependency-graph builder declared in transactions-and-isolation, running in Adya mode with a thin SSI overlay: the learner steps the on-call doctors history — published here as the named preset `write-skew-oncall` so the anomaly catalog deep-links into this page with the identical history already loaded — in any interleaving while wr, ww and rw-antidependency edges grow beside the timeline, the pivot lights up the instant two consecutive rw edges close through it, and an SI/SSI toggle either lets the schedule commit with the invariant visibly broken or aborts the pivot or the last committer according to the commit order the learner produced.

subtopics.title: SSI in PostgreSQL: SIREAD locks, promotion and false positives
subtopics.covers: PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE (9.1, Ports and Grittner) implements SSI with non-blocking SIREAD locks on tuples, pages and relations stored in a shared predicate-lock table bounded by max_pred_locks_per_transaction/_per_relation/_per_page, promotion to coarser granularity as counts grow, btree index-page locks covering the ranges a scan touched versus relation-level locks for seq scans and non-btree indexes, conflict records that outlive a committed transaction until every concurrent transaction finishes (summarized into an SLRU when memory runs short), and the consequences: false-positive 40001s from page or relation granularity, contention on the predicate-lock partitions for hot pages, SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE waiting for a safe snapshot to skip the protocol entirely, and the roughly 10-20% overhead over REPEATABLE READ.
subtopics.visual: A heap-page grid plus a btree index for one table where the learner runs three concurrent SERIALIZABLE transactions with adjustable WHERE clauses: each read paints SIREAD locks on the exact tuples, index pages or the whole relation depending on the plan chosen, a lock-count dial triggers promotion from tuple to page to relation in front of the learner, and widening one predicate or lowering the promotion threshold turns a non-conflicting write into a false-positive rw edge and a 40001 that the learner traces back to the coarse lock.

subtopics.title: MVOCC in Hekaton, Silo and in-memory OLTP
subtopics.covers: In-memory engines validate rather than lock: Hekaton keeps begin/end timestamps in latch-free version chains, assigns a begin timestamp at start and an end timestamp at commit, re-reads its read set and re-scans its scan set at validation to catch phantoms, and handles reads of not-yet-committed versions with commit dependencies that can cascade; Silo removes the global counter with epoch-based group commit (a 40 ms epoch plus per-thread TIDs ordered only across epochs), locks its write set in address order, re-validates read-set TIDs and btree node versions for phantoms and persists whole epochs for durability; TicToc and Cicada derive the commit timestamp from per-record read/write timestamps so serial order is discovered instead of assigned; and H-Store/VoltDB sidestep the question with single-threaded partitions.
subtopics.visual: A Silo commit timeline with a ticking epoch counter across four worker threads: the learner starts transactions that record read-set TIDs and btree-node versions, then at commit watches phase 1 lock the write set in sorted order, phase 2 re-check every read-set TID and node version (a concurrent insert into a scanned node flips its version and fails validation with a phantom label), and phase 3 stamp new TIDs into the current epoch, while a durability lane persists closed epochs so commits are acknowledged only when their epoch ends.

subtopics.title: Retry loops and serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001)
subtopics.covers: SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure) and 40P01 (deadlock_detected) are the errors OCC/SSI push onto the application — raised at any statement or at COMMIT, and in Postgres even for a transaction that only read — so correct handling restarts the whole transaction from BEGIN with fresh reads rather than re-issuing one statement, keeps side effects (emails, HTTP calls, queue publishes) outside the transaction or idempotent via keys, bounds attempts with exponential backoff plus jitter to break the livelock of the same transactions colliding again, treats a retry as unsafe once a COMMIT's outcome is unknown (connection dropped mid-commit) or a partial result has been externalized, and knows the engine specifics: CockroachDB's SAVEPOINT cockroach_restart and server-side automatic retry only when the whole transaction arrives in one batch, PgBouncer transaction-pooling constraints, and ORMs that bubble the error up by default.
subtopics.visual: A client-side retry loop drawn as a state machine (BEGIN → statements → COMMIT → success, or 40001 → backoff → restart) driven by a contention slider that makes the server inject 40001 at a random point including COMMIT; the learner chooses statement-level versus transaction-level restart and sees stale reads leak through the former, toggles a non-idempotent side effect inside the loop and watches duplicate emails pile up, adjusts backoff and jitter until a livelock of repeatedly colliding transactions dissolves, and sets max attempts to read p99 latency and give-up rate on the meters.

subtopics.title: Transaction chopping: splitting long transactions without losing serializability
subtopics.covers: Shasha, Llirbat, Simon and Zhu's result that a transaction may be cut into pieces run as separate transactions while preserving serializability exactly when the chopping graph — S-edges between sibling pieces, C-edges between conflicting pieces of different transactions — contains no SC-cycle, the practical corollary that the first piece must contain every decision-making read while later pieces are conflict-free appends, the consequences when the rule is broken (intermediate states become visible and earlier pieces cannot be rolled back, so compensation is required — the single-node cousin of the sagas in logs-streams-derived-data), and the real applications: chunked backfills and migrations, shortening lock hold time on hot rows, and the chopping-based parallelism in Calvin, IC3 and Lynx — with 'this transaction cannot be chopped' as the signal to keep it whole and short instead.
subtopics.visual: The learner drags scissors between the statements of two long transactions and the tool draws the chopping graph with S- and C-edges, lighting any SC-cycle red, then runs the chopped and uncut versions side by side with lock-hold-time and throughput meters while a concurrent reader observes an intermediate state precisely in the runs where a cycle existed.

subtopics.title: Robustness: proving a workload is safe at a weaker isolation level
subtopics.covers: Fekete's static test over transaction programs rather than histories (a cycle with two consecutive rw-antidependency edges through a pivot means this program set is not serializable under SI) and the promotions that make a non-robust mix robust without moving everything to SERIALIZABLE — materializing the conflict in a shared row, promoting exactly one read to SELECT FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE, or chopping the transaction — plus the later robustness results against READ COMMITTED and MVRC (Vandevoort, Ketsman, Neven) and Bernardi–Gotsman's criteria for parallel snapshot isolation and causal consistency, the practical procedure of recovering each program's read and write sets from the ORM or the statement log, and the limits that make this a re-run rather than a proof: dynamic predicates, per-connection mixed levels, and the new transaction program another team ships next quarter.
subtopics.visual: The learner declares transaction programs as read and write sets rather than histories and the shared Adya graph builder runs over programs instead of a single history, marking the vulnerable rw edges and pivots and reporting robust-at-RC, robust-at-SI or not-robust, then applying one promotion (a FOR UPDATE, a materialized conflict row, a chop) visibly removes the edge while a run panel executes the real transaction mix at that level and counts anomalies to confirm or refute the verdict.

subtopics.title: Choosing a concurrency control protocol
subtopics.covers: Yu et al.'s 1000-core evaluation and Wu et al.'s MVCC study show that conflict rate, read/write mix, transaction length and core count — not ideology — pick the winner: 2PL (no-wait or wait-die) for short high-contention writes, OCC/MVOCC for low-conflict and read-mostly loads where aborts are cheap, MVCC with snapshot reads plus first-committer-wins for read-heavy mixed workloads, SSI when write-skew correctness justifies the overhead and retry cost, centralized timestamp allocation as the scalability ceiling that drove epochs and decentralized TIDs, and deterministic execution (Calvin, VoltDB) as the zero-abort alternative that demands read/write sets up front — condensed into a decision matrix for the practical choices of REPEATABLE READ plus SELECT FOR UPDATE, SERIALIZABLE with a retry loop, or application-level compare-and-set.
subtopics.visual: A workload panel with sliders for contention (Zipf theta), read/write ratio, transaction length and core count feeding a live model that plots throughput and abort rate for 2PL-no-wait, 2PL-wait-die, OCC, MVTO and SSI side by side, highlights the crossover points where the leading protocol changes, and prints the decision-matrix cell the learner's workload lands in with its Postgres-level recommendation.

modules.title: Write-Ahead Logging, Checkpoints and the Commit Path
modules.why: The log is the contract behind every commit acknowledgement: what a COMMIT returns means exactly "these bytes were durable", and the record format, the two WAL rules, the commit pipeline, the checkpoint cadence and the torn-page defenses together decide which bytes those are and how much I/O and latency the guarantee costs.

subtopics.title: Log records, LSNs and the two rules of write-ahead logging
subtopics.covers: Physical (before/after byte images), logical (operation-level), physiological (page-oriented redo, logical undo) and command (transaction-input) record types as instantiated by PostgreSQL XLogRecords with block references and full-page images, InnoDB mini-transaction (mtr) redo records, SQLite whole-page frames, and the VoltDB/H-Store, Hekaton and Redis-AOF style log that records the invocation rather than its effect — a tiny log whose price is a CPU-bound re-execution at recovery and a hard determinism requirement (no NOW(), no unordered scans, single-threaded or deterministically scheduled execution, the same discipline Calvin imposes in the distributed-transactions module); the LSN as a monotonic byte offset, pageLSN stamped on every page, per-transaction prevLSN backchains, the insert-LSN vs flushed-LSN pointers of the log buffer (PG wal_buffers and wal_insert_locks, InnoDB log writer/flusher threads); and the two invariants that make it all work: the WAL rule (flush the log through pageLSN before the buffer pool may write the page, see the buffer-pool module) and the commit rule (all of a transaction's records durable before COMMIT is acknowledged).
subtopics.visual: The learner applies updates to a few pages in a tiny buffer pool and watches records append with LSNs and prevLSN arrows, pages get their pageLSN stamped, and the insert/flush pointers advance; a record-type switch (physical/logical/physiological/command) changes the bytes written per update and shows why replaying a physical record twice is safe, a logical one is not, and a command record shrinks the log to a single line that can only be replayed by re-executing it against identical state, with a non-deterministic call injected to break it; dragging a dirty page toward disk ahead of the flushed-LSN is blocked with the violated precondition highlighted.

subtopics.title: Steal/no-steal and force/no-force: why ARIES needs both undo and redo
subtopics.covers: The buffer-policy quadrant: steal (uncommitted dirty pages may be written, so undo information is mandatory) and no-force (committed pages need not be written at commit, so redo information is mandatory), why no-steal/force recovers trivially but pins the buffer pool and turns every commit into random page I/O, and why ARIES chose steal/no-force; how PostgreSQL is steal/no-force yet has no undo pass because MVCC makes uncommitted versions merely invisible (commit status lives in clog), how InnoDB pairs a circular redo log with undo tablespaces, how LSM engines are effectively no-steal because only committed WriteBatches enter the memtable, and how shadow paging is the no-steal/force corner.
subtopics.visual: A quadrant selector drives a simulation of interleaved transactions against a small buffer pool: the learner watches which evictions are refused (no-steal), which commits stall on page writes (force), then crashes at a random instant and sees the required recovery actions (undo, redo, both, neither) light up and replay for that quadrant, with the transaction outcomes verified against a committed/aborted ledger.

subtopics.title: Group commit and the log I/O pipeline
subtopics.covers: fsync latency as the ceiling on single-threaded commit rate and group commit as the fix: PostgreSQL's XLogFlush flushing through the latest inserted LSN plus commit_delay/commit_siblings and wal_sync_method (fdatasync vs open_datasync vs O_DIRECT), InnoDB's log writer/flusher thread split and binlog group commit with the LOGICAL_CLOCK dependency tracking, the internal two-phase commit between InnoDB redo (XA prepare) and the binlog (binlog write is the commit point, sync_binlog), RocksDB's write-group leader election and pipelined writes, and Silo/TigerBeetle-style epoch commit where acknowledgement waits for the batch's durability.
subtopics.visual: The learner raises concurrent-committer count and disk fsync latency while toggling group commit on and off, and watches a timeline where individual commit records coalesce into shared fsync calls, each transaction's latency bar and the fsyncs-per-second counter update, and a throughput-vs-latency chart fills in; an InnoDB mode overlays the redo-prepare/binlog-write/commit handshake so the learner sees which step is the real commit point.

subtopics.title: Checkpoints: fuzzy checkpoints and the recovery-time vs I/O trade-off
subtopics.covers: Sharp vs fuzzy checkpoints, begin/end checkpoint records that snapshot the dirty page table and transaction table without quiescing, and the redo start point as min(recLSN); PostgreSQL's checkpoint_timeout/max_wal_size triggers, the redo pointer in pg_control, checkpoint_completion_target spreading flushes across the interval, the full-page-write storm after each checkpoint and wal_compression; InnoDB's flush list ordered by oldest-modification LSN, the checkpoint LSN advancing as pages flush, adaptive flushing and the synchronous flush stall when checkpoint age nears innodb_redo_log_capacity; the LSM analogue where a memtable flush plus MANIFEST update lets the WAL be deleted; and the in-memory analogue where there are no dirty pages at all — Hekaton's paired checkpoint data and delta files, VoltDB snapshots and Redis RDB/BGSAVE — so snapshot frequency is the sole RTO knob against a CPU-bound replay (which process performs the writes — backend, bgwriter, checkpointer, page cleaner — belongs to the buffer-pool module, the knob-to-metric transfer function to the operating module, and the conversion of a checkpoint distance into an actual recovery-time estimate to 'How long recovery takes' in the crash-recovery module, which is where this knob's real cost is read off).
subtopics.visual: Sliders for checkpoint interval and completion target sit above a running write workload; the learner watches the dirty-page count, the flush-I/O curve (spiky vs spread), the post-checkpoint FPI surge in WAL bytes and total WAL size respond, then hits crash at any moment to see the redo span from the last checkpoint's redo pointer and an estimated recovery time, making the RTO-vs-runtime-I/O trade explicit; a mode switch replaces pages with an in-memory snapshot plus command log so the same crash shows recovery time growing with snapshot age instead of with dirty pages.

subtopics.title: Defenses against torn pages: full-page writes, doublewrite and checksums
subtopics.covers: Taking the torn 16 KB page from the hardware module as given and spending the page on the repair protocols: PostgreSQL full_page_writes logging a whole page image on first modification after each checkpoint so redo restores the image before applying later records, InnoDB's doublewrite buffer (write to the doublewrite area, fsync, then in place; recovery checks checksums and restores from the copy), page checksums as detection only (PG data_checksums mixing in the block number, InnoDB crc32c, innochecksum/pg_checksums), prevention by never overwriting in place (LMDB, ZFS, or disabling doublewrite on atomic-write storage), and fsyncgate, where Linux dropping dirty pages after an fsync error forced PostgreSQL to PANIC rather than retry (data_sync_retry).
subtopics.visual: A compact non-interactive strip replays the tear the learner already produced in Part 1 (half-old, half-new sectors) and hands it to the real exercise: stepping each repair protocol's write sequence — the post-checkpoint full-page image landing in the WAL then replay overwriting the torn page, the doublewrite area written and fsynced before the in-place write with recovery choosing the intact copy, and copy-on-write allocating elsewhere so the tear can only hit a page nothing points at — with a crash insertable at any step and a bytes-written meter per protocol, plus a checksum-only run that detects the tear and can do nothing about it.

subtopics.title: Log retention, archiving and logical decoding internals
subtopics.covers: Everything that pins a WAL segment against recycling: the last checkpoint's redo pointer, wal_keep_size, physical and logical replication slots' restart_lsn, and an archive_command that has not yet succeeded, with max_slot_wal_keep_size as the escape hatch before the disk fills; InnoDB's circular redo (never retained) versus the binlog as its retained stream; and the internals of PostgreSQL logical decoding: building a consistent snapshot, the reorder buffer accumulating changes per transaction and emitting at commit, spilling large transactions to disk or streaming them in progress, replica identity deciding the old-row image, unchanged TOAST columns and two-phase decoding (consumers such as physical streaming and Debezium-style CDC are covered in the replication and logs-streams modules).
subtopics.visual: A strip of WAL segments carries retention pins (checkpoint redo point, archive cursor, slot restart_lsn); the learner pauses a consumer or makes archive_command fail and watches segments pile up until the disk-full alarm, while a second pane shows interleaved records entering the reorder buffer and being emitted as whole transactions at commit, with a replica-identity toggle changing which old-row columns appear in UPDATE events.

modules.title: Crash Recovery: ARIES, Recovery Time and What Survives
modules.why: Recovery is two questions at once: which consistent state can be rebuilt from the bytes that were durable at the instant of the crash, and how many minutes or hours that rebuild takes while the service is down or half-open — ARIES answers the first, redo rate and the undo tail answer the second, and every durability knob is a bet on the loss window between them.

subtopics.title: Shadow paging and copy-on-write recovery: SQLite journals and LMDB
