subtopics.covers: Recovery without replay by never overwriting live pages: System R shadow paging, SQLite's rollback journal (copy original pages to the journal, fsync, write in place, fsync, delete the journal; a hot journal found on open is rolled back) vs WAL mode (append frames with salt and checksum, the shared-memory wal-index, checkpoint copying frames back, one writer with concurrent readers, and checkpoint starvation), LMDB's copy-on-write B+tree with two alternating meta pages and a freelist gated by reader transaction IDs, and the costs of the approach: write amplification up to the root, single-writer designs and no sequential log to ship to replicas.
subtopics.visual: A copy-on-write tree beside a file view: the learner updates a leaf and watches a new path allocate up to the root and the meta page flip atomically; switching to SQLite rollback-journal or WAL mode replays the exact sequence of file writes and fsyncs for one commit, and a crash inserted at any step shows which recovery path (hot-journal rollback, WAL frame-checksum truncation, or the older meta page) restores a consistent file.

subtopics.title: ARIES recovery: analysis, redo and undo with compensation log records
subtopics.covers: The analysis pass rebuilding the transaction table (lastLSN, status) and dirty page table (recLSN) by scanning forward from the last checkpoint; redo repeating history from min(recLSN) and skipping records when the page is absent from the dirty page table, its recLSN is later, or its pageLSN is already at or past the record; undo of loser transactions in reverse LSN order across all losers via prevLSN chains, writing redo-only compensation log records whose undoNextLSN makes repeated crashes bounded and idempotent; nested top actions and logical undo for index splits; the real-engine variants (PostgreSQL redo-only with losers simply never marked committed in clog, InnoDB redo apply followed by undo-log rollback of active transactions, SQL Server as a direct ARIES descendant); and the non-ARIES alternative for in-memory engines — restore the newest snapshot or checkpoint file pair, then deterministically re-execute the command log (VoltDB, Hekaton, Redis AOF after RDB) with no dirty page table, no pageLSN tests and no undo pass, only CPU-bound replay.
subtopics.visual: The learner builds a log of interleaved transactions with a fuzzy checkpoint mid-way, chooses a crash LSN, then steps through analysis, redo and undo watching the transaction table, dirty page table and page images rebuild and CLRs append with undoNextLSN arrows pointing past already-undone work; crashing again in the middle of undo and restarting shows the second recovery skip the compensated records instead of re-undoing them; a side-by-side lane runs the identical workload as a checkpoint plus command log and replays it by re-execution, so the learner compares log bytes, passes performed and wall-clock recovery time between the two designs.

subtopics.title: How long recovery takes: redo rate, prefetch, parallel apply and the undo tail
subtopics.covers: Recovery as a time budget rather than only a correctness protocol: RTO ≈ checkpoint distance (WAL bytes since the redo pointer) ÷ effective replay rate, and why that rate is usually far below the write rate that produced the log — PostgreSQL's single-threaded startup process doing synchronous random reads of every referenced block not in cache (post-checkpoint full-page images make early redo read-free, which is why a short checkpoint interval buys recovery time twice), recovery_prefetch in PG 15 issuing readahead for blocks the log is about to touch, InnoDB's scan/parse-into-per-page-hash/apply phases bounded by innodb_redo_log_capacity, SQL Server parallel redo and LSM/in-memory engines whose replay is CPU-bound instead; then the undo tail that the steal/no-force quadrant buys: rollback cost is roughly proportional to the work the killed transaction did and can exceed it (it re-reads cold pages and writes its own CLRs), so an InnoDB instance killed during a huge DELETE comes up, accepts connections and then spends hours rolling back effectively unusable, with innodb_force_recovery a data-loss gamble rather than a fix; the engines' differing answers — SQL Server's Accelerated Database Recovery with a persistent version store making rollback near-constant-time, PostgreSQL's MVCC abort being O(1) with the bill deferred to vacuum (see the vacuum module), LSM engines having no undo at all; and the operational consequences: the detect/decide/promote/cut-over RTO decomposition in backups-incidents-disaster-recovery omits this replay-plus-undo term and must have it added, and 'the instance restarted and still will not accept writes' is a triage branch in database-incident-response whose answer is reading the redo progress and the rollback counters, not restarting again.
subtopics.visual: A recovery clock: the learner sets checkpoint distance, WAL bytes, cache-hit ratio and device latency and watches the redo pass advance LSN by LSN with an ETA, then toggles prefetch and parallel apply to see the rate and the ETA change; a second phase kills a transaction that has modified a chosen number of rows and runs the undo tail after the instance is nominally 'open', with a writes-accepted indicator staying red and a per-engine switch (InnoDB undo rollback, SQL Server ADR persistent version store, PostgreSQL abort-and-defer-to-vacuum) replacing the tail with its constant-time or deferred equivalent and showing where the same work reappears later.

subtopics.title: Engine durability designs compared and what each knob actually loses
subtopics.covers: A side-by-side of what 'committed' means per engine and setting under three fault classes (process kill, OS crash or power loss, primary loss): PostgreSQL synchronous_commit off/local/remote_write/on/remote_apply over a redo-only WAL plus clog; InnoDB innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit 0/1/2 and sync_binlog with the redo/binlog two-phase commit that can leave the binlog ahead of or behind redo; SQLite journal_mode and synchronous OFF/NORMAL/FULL (WAL+NORMAL loses recent commits on power loss but never corrupts); RocksDB WriteOptions.sync, disableWAL and manual_wal_flush; WiredTiger journaling with j:true; the command-logging family — VoltDB synchronous vs asynchronous command logging against its snapshot interval, Hekaton's log records plus checkpoint file pairs, and Redis appendfsync always/everysec/no versus RDB-only where the loss window is the whole save interval; and Kafka relying on replicated acknowledgement rather than fsync (see the logs-streams module), all framed as loss windows versus corruption, since async commit shrinks durability but never consistency.
subtopics.visual: An engine-by-knob matrix where the learner picks a setting and then triggers kill -9, power cut or primary loss against a timeline of acknowledged commits; recovery replays (redo, or snapshot-plus-command-replay for the in-memory rows) and marks each acknowledged transaction survived or lost, while a throughput gauge shows what the stricter setting would have cost, so the learner reads off the exact loss window of every configuration.

subtopics.title: Testing crash consistency: ALICE, CrashMonkey and fault injection
subtopics.covers: The crash-state space a single-node engine must survive: kill -9 (page cache intact) versus power loss (only fsynced bytes), reordering of writes between fsyncs, non-atomic appends, and the directory fsync needed for a rename or create to be durable; the tools that enumerate it: ALICE's abstract persistence models (which found dozens of vulnerabilities across LevelDB, SQLite, PostgreSQL and others), CrashMonkey and bounded black-box crash testing that surfaced ext4 and btrfs bugs, dm-flakey and dm-log-writes, RocksDB db_stress with kill points and sync fault injection, SQLite's simulated-power-failure harness and pg_test_fsync; and the classic bug classes they catch (missing directory fsync, assumed ordering, swallowed fsync errors), distinct from the distributed-history checking of the verification module.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a commit protocol (rollback journal, WAL append, rename-based atomic replace), a crash point in its syscall sequence, and which filesystem persistence assumptions to relax (ordering across fsyncs, append atomicity, directory persistence); an enumerator fans out the possible on-disk states and colors each as recovers-cleanly or violates-invariant, and removing the directory fsync makes a committed file vanish on the reboot branch.

parts.title: Using the Database Well
parts.summary: Advanced SQL, application access paths, modeling and per-store usage, application data patterns, and zero-downtime schema evolution on a single database.

modules.title: Advanced SQL for Engineers
modules.why: Window functions, grouping sets, LATERAL, time-series operators, event-analytics patterns and recursive CTEs turn application loops and N+1 round trips into single statements the planner can optimize, and each has precise semantics (frames and peers, bucket and counter-reset rules, session-gap and conversion-window definitions, working-table iteration) that a senior engineer must know to get correct results, not just fast ones.

subtopics.title: Set-based thinking: replacing loops and N+1 with joins, arrays and VALUES
subtopics.covers: Rewriting per-row application loops as joins, aggregates and bulk statements — WHERE id = ANY($1) with array parameters, UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...) AS v(id, val) for batch updates, INSERT ... SELECT, unnest() to turn arrays into rows, DELETE ... USING, and DuckDB/PostgreSQL array_agg/string_agg to collapse child rows — because each eliminated round trip removes network latency, parse/plan cost and a separate snapshot, while giving the optimizer one plan (hash join, memoize) instead of N index probes it cannot batch; the same rewrite is what ORM eager loading and MySQL's Batched Key Access do internally.
subtopics.visual: Side-by-side runner: the learner sets N (rows in the outer set) and network RTT with sliders and picks the procedural version (loop of SELECTs, loop of UPDATEs) or the set version (one join, ANY(array), UPDATE FROM VALUES); the component animates each statement crossing the wire, counts round trips, parses and rows touched, and plots total time as N grows so the linear-vs-constant gap and the single-plan shape become visible.

subtopics.title: Window functions: frames, peers, ranking and running aggregates
subtopics.covers: OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) semantics: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK on ties, the default frame RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW that makes SUM() OVER (ORDER BY) include all peers, ROWS vs RANGE vs GROUPS frames with EXCLUDE clauses and RANGE offsets on dates (PG 11+, MySQL 8, SQLite 3.28+, DuckDB), LAG/LEAD/FIRST_VALUE/NTH_VALUE with IGNORE NULLS, named WINDOW clauses, why window functions evaluate after WHERE/GROUP BY and cannot be filtered without a subquery, and the gaps-and-islands idiom (ROW_NUMBER differences, LAG-based flags with a running SUM) that replaces cursor-driven code.
subtopics.visual: A frame inspector: the learner edits a small partitioned table (including tied ORDER BY values and NULLs), picks a frame clause from a builder (ROWS/RANGE/GROUPS, offsets, EXCLUDE TIES/GROUP), and steps the current row through the partition while the component highlights exactly which rows fall in the frame and which are peers, showing the resulting SUM/RANK/LAG value change — the same query switched from ROWS to RANGE visibly changes the running total on tied rows.

subtopics.title: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE and FILTER
subtopics.covers: Computing several aggregation levels in one scan with GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP (a prefix hierarchy) and CUBE (all 2^n combinations), using GROUPING(col) bits to tell a subtotal NULL from a data NULL, how PostgreSQL implements them with one sort plus multiple hash sets (MixedAggregate) versus rewriting to UNION ALL, FILTER (WHERE ...) conditional aggregates as the clean form of the CASE-inside-SUM pivot, ORDER BY inside aggregates (string_agg, array_agg), WITHIN GROUP ordered-set aggregates (percentile_cont, mode), and the equivalents in MySQL (WITH ROLLUP), ClickHouse (WITH TOTALS/CUBE) and SQL Server.
subtopics.visual: A grouping lattice: the learner sees the powerset of grouping columns as a Hasse diagram, clicks nodes to compose a GROUPING SETS clause or presses ROLLUP/CUBE to auto-select nodes, and watches the result table fill with rows tagged by their GROUPING() bitmask (subtotal NULLs colored differently from data NULLs), while a plan strip shows how many sort or hash passes over the input the selection costs.

subtopics.title: LATERAL joins and top-N-per-group
subtopics.covers: LATERAL (and CROSS APPLY/OUTER APPLY in SQL Server, Oracle) lets a derived table or set-returning function reference columns of preceding FROM items, so 'the 3 most recent orders per customer' becomes a correlated subquery with ORDER BY ... LIMIT 3 that the planner runs as an index nested loop with an early-terminating inner scan; LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON TRUE to keep outer rows with no match, comparing it to ROW_NUMBER() OVER ... WHERE rn <= N (a full sort of every group) and DISTINCT ON (PostgreSQL), when each wins (few outer rows with a good (customer_id, created_at DESC) index vs a whole-table pass), and LATERAL for calling set-returning functions like unnest and jsonb_array_elements per row.
subtopics.visual: An outer-row stepper: the learner sets N, the number of groups and rows per group, and whether a composite index exists, then steps through outer rows while the component shows the correlated inner subquery evaluating for that row (index descent, stop after N) and its rows attaching to the output; a toggle switches to the ROW_NUMBER formulation and shows the full sort of every group instead, with a rows-scanned counter for each approach.

subtopics.title: Time-series SQL: buckets, gap filling, rates and ASOF joins
subtopics.covers: Time bucketing with time_bucket/date_trunc/toStartOfInterval and time-zone-correct boundaries, gap filling with LOCF and interpolation (time_bucket_gapfill, generate_series left joins), counter semantics (rate/increase, counter-reset detection, irate versus rate windows), ASOF joins for as-of-time alignment in DuckDB/ClickHouse/Timescale versus the LATERAL top-1 rewrite, and rollup correctness — avg-of-avg errors, weighted aggregates and mergeable aggregate states (hyperfunctions, ClickHouse -State/-Merge).
subtopics.visual: The learner places irregular sensor readings and a counter containing a reset on a timeline, then toggles bucket size, gap-fill mode, rate-versus-delta and ASOF-versus-LATERAL join, watching the emitted rows change while a red flag appears exactly where avg-of-avg or an undetected counter reset corrupts the rollup.

subtopics.title: Funnels, retention and sessionization over event tables
subtopics.covers: Sessionization by inactivity gap (LAG plus a running SUM of new-session flags) and why the gap threshold changes every downstream metric; funnels as ordered event matching with a per-user conversion window, expressed as window functions or as engine primitives (ClickHouse windowFunnel/sequenceMatch/retention, Snowflake MATCH_RECOGNIZE, BigQuery arrays), with strict versus any-order step semantics and repeated-event dedup; cohort retention matrices built from first-event date plus generate_series so empty cells appear; first- and last-touch attribution with FIRST_VALUE and IGNORE NULLS; and the cost model — why these are one pass per user partition when the table is sorted by (user, ts) and a sort-and-spill catastrophe when it is not, and why funnels resist pre-aggregation.
subtopics.visual: An event timeline per user where the learner drags the session-gap threshold and the funnel conversion window and watches sessions split and merge and each funnel step's count and drop-off change, with a plan strip showing whether the query stayed a single ordered pass over the user partition or fell back to a sort plus self-joins as rows scanned climbs.

subtopics.title: Recursive CTEs: hierarchies, graphs and series
subtopics.covers: WITH RECURSIVE evaluation as a working-table fixpoint — the anchor term seeds it, the recursive term joins only against the previous iteration's rows (semi-naive), UNION dedupes to prevent infinite loops on graphs while UNION ALL does not — with depth counters, path arrays (ARRAY[id] || path) and PG 14's CYCLE ... SET ... USING and SEARCH DEPTH/BREADTH FIRST clauses for cycle detection and ordering, generating series and calendars without a table (generate_series vs recursion in MySQL/SQLite), why recursive CTEs always materialize and cannot be pushed into, and the exponential blowup of path enumeration on DAGs; representation trade-offs (closure table, ltree, nested sets) belong to data-modeling-and-per-store-usage.
subtopics.visual: A fixpoint stepper: the learner draws a small directed graph (optionally adding a cycle), writes the anchor and recursive terms, chooses UNION vs UNION ALL and a CYCLE/depth guard, and presses 'iterate' to watch the working table, the intermediate table and the cumulative result fill in per iteration, with the frontier highlighted on the graph and a warning when the working table stops shrinking.

modules.title: Advanced SQL II: Documents, Text and the Write Side
modules.why: This module sits immediately after Advanced SQL because the rest of the part is written on top of it: data modeling's JSONB attribute bags, document stores' embed-versus-reference decision, search's relevance tuning over tsvector, write-side patterns' idempotent upserts and schema evolution's trigger-maintained backfills all assume this vocabulary already exists. JSONB, full-text search and pattern matching put semi-structured and human text inside the same statement as relational columns, while upserts, updatable views, data-modifying CTEs and triggers decide what a single write actually does to the database — and each has exact semantics (containment, lax versus strict jsonpath, lexeme pipelines, automaton evaluation and sargability, arbiter indexes and speculative insertion, view-translation rules, trigger and constraint timing) that separate a statement that is merely fast from one that is correct under concurrency and adversarial input.

subtopics.title: JSONB: operators, jsonpath and modeling in SQL
subtopics.covers: PostgreSQL jsonb as a parsed binary tree (keys sorted, duplicates dropped, numerics normalized, whitespace lost) versus json text, extraction with -> / ->> / #>> and subscripting (PG 14), containment @> semantics (object containment is recursive-subset, array containment is any-order subset, scalars-in-arrays match), existence ? / ?| / ?&, SQL/JSON path queries with @? and @@ and jsonpath filters and lax vs strict mode, mutation with jsonb_set / jsonb_insert / || / - that rewrite the whole value (and re-TOAST it), unpacking with jsonb_array_elements / jsonb_each / jsonb_to_recordset, and the modeling rule of relational columns for typed, constrained, hot fields with jsonb for sparse or user-defined attributes; MySQL JSON and JSON_TABLE, SQLite json1 and DuckDB as comparison points, with indexing covered in index-selection-strategy and the schema-level custom-field and embed-vs-reference decisions in data-modeling-and-per-store-usage and document-graph-and-key-value-store-usage.
subtopics.visual: A document-and-query lab: the learner edits a JSON document rendered as a tree and types a right-hand operand or jsonpath expression; the component evaluates @>, ?, @? and -> step by step, lighting up the matched nodes (and showing why an array containment matches out of order), then a mutation panel lets them run jsonb_set with a path and watch which node is replaced or created and how many bytes of the value are rewritten.

subtopics.title: Full-text search in SQL: tsvector, tsquery, ranking and trigrams
subtopics.covers: The text-search pipeline in PostgreSQL — parser tokens, per-configuration dictionaries (stop words, snowball stemming, synonyms, thesaurus), to_tsvector producing lexemes with positions and A–D weights, tsquery operators & | ! and phrase <-> / <N>, plainto/phraseto/websearch_to_tsquery, ts_rank vs ts_rank_cd (cover density) and the normalization bitmask, ts_headline, keeping a generated tsvector column current, and pg_trgm trigram similarity, word_similarity and % operators for fuzzy and LIKE '%x%' matching, with a comparison to Lucene/Elasticsearch BM25 and when to leave the database for a search engine; the GIN/GiST index structures underneath are in indexes-beyond-the-b-tree and production relevance tuning, hybrid retrieval and reindexing are in search-and-vector-retrieval.
subtopics.visual: A pipeline visualizer: the learner types a document and a search string, picks a configuration (english/simple), and watches the text split into tokens, pass through dictionaries (stop words dropped, stems produced), become a tsvector with positions and weights, and then match the tsquery operator tree node by node with phrase distances checked; a rank panel recomputes ts_rank/ts_rank_cd as they edit, and a trigram tab shows both strings' trigram sets and the similarity fraction.

subtopics.title: Pattern matching in the database: automata, backtracking and index acceleration
subtopics.covers: How LIKE and regex predicates are actually evaluated — Thompson NFA/DFA simulation with linear worst case (PostgreSQL's hybrid engine, RE2 in ClickHouse and Spanner) versus backtracking engines whose exponential blowup makes a user-supplied pattern a denial-of-service — which shapes are sargable (an anchored prefix rewritten to a range scan under C collation or text_pattern_ops, everything else a scan), extracting required literals and trigrams from a pattern so pg_trgm GIN, ClickHouse ngrambf and Elasticsearch wildcard fields can prefilter candidates before the automaton runs, how case-insensitivity and collation disable those rewrites, and statement_timeout plus pattern allowlists as the only real backstop against adversarial input.
subtopics.visual: The learner types a pattern and watches it compile into an automaton and run over sample rows with a step counter that explodes on a catastrophic-backtracking case while the DFA simulation stays linear, then flips on trigram extraction to see the required n-grams highlighted in the pattern, the plan become an index prefilter, and candidate counts before and after the automaton's verification pass.

subtopics.title: The view update problem: which views you can write through
subtopics.covers: Why an update against a view needs a unique, side-effect-free translation back to base rows (Bancilhon-Spyratos's constant-complement framing and why joins, aggregates, DISTINCT and set operations destroy it), the rules engines actually enforce — PostgreSQL auto-updatable simple views with WITH CHECK OPTION and INSTEAD OF triggers or rules for the rest, MySQL's updatable-view conditions, SQL Server's single-base-table restriction and indexed-view limits, Oracle's key-preserved-table rule — why a materialized view is never writable, how WITH CHECK OPTION interacts with row-level security so a tenant cannot write a row it then cannot read, and the practical pattern of exposing a view as a stable API surface while the base schema migrates underneath it (the full expand/contract choreography is in schema-evolution-and-migrations).
subtopics.visual: The learner composes a view with toggles for join, aggregate, DISTINCT and UNION while the tool reports auto-updatable or not and names the exact clause that disqualified it, then writes through it and steps the translation into base-table statements — showing a row that disappears from the view after its own update until WITH CHECK OPTION rejects the write, and an INSTEAD OF trigger supplying the translation the engine could not infer.

subtopics.title: Upserts, MERGE, RETURNING and data-modifying CTEs
subtopics.covers: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (arbiter index or constraint) DO NOTHING / DO UPDATE SET ... = EXCLUDED.col with WHERE, its concurrency guarantee via speculative insertion (insert-or-update always succeeds under races, but partial unique indexes and multiple arbiter matches are traps), the arbiter rule that with a conflict target only that arbiter's violation is handled — any other unique index still raises 23505 and aborts the statement, while only ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING without a target absorbs all of them and it cannot be combined with DO UPDATE; MySQL INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE and REPLACE (a delete plus insert), SQLite upsert, MERGE (SQL:2003, PG 15+) with WHEN MATCHED/NOT MATCHED [BY SOURCE] actions and its weaker concurrency (can raise unique violations under concurrent inserts), RETURNING to fetch generated keys and old values, and data-modifying CTEs (WITH ... DELETE RETURNING chained into INSERT) where every statement sees the same snapshot, cannot observe each other's writes, run in unspecified order and are executed exactly once even if unreferenced; building an idempotency or dedup key table on top of these primitives is write-side-data-patterns.
subtopics.visual: A two-session race: the learner writes an upsert against a table carrying two unique indexes (say email and username), launches two sessions attempting the same key, and steps through each session's speculative insert token, index check and wait/retry to see one insert and one update land — then makes the second session collide on the non-arbiter index and watches the statement abort with 23505 instead of updating; switching the statement to MERGE reproduces the unique-violation failure, and a second tab steps through a multi-CTE write statement showing the shared snapshot, each CTE's RETURNING rows feeding the next, and which CTE cannot see another's effect.

subtopics.title: Triggers, constraints and server-side execution order
subtopics.covers: BEFORE/AFTER/INSTEAD OF triggers, row- vs statement-level firing and transition tables (REFERENCING OLD/NEW TABLE) as the set-based alternative to per-row work, BEFORE triggers rewriting or suppressing a row by returning NEW/NULL, alphabetical trigger firing order (and what silently changes when someone renames one), the after-trigger queue and when it drains — end of statement, or COMMIT for deferred ones; referential integrity implemented as system AFTER triggers with their row-lock modes (FOR KEY SHARE on the parent) and the write amplification of ON DELETE CASCADE recursing down a graph; DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED constraints and violations surfacing at COMMIT instead of at the statement, recursion depth and trigger loops, session_replication_role = 'replica' and which triggers do and do not fire on logical-replication apply, COPY and bulk load; MySQL's immediate-only constraints and lack of deferral, and CHECK/EXCLUDE/NOT NULL as cheaper declarative alternatives to trigger logic — with trigger-maintained dual-write backfills during a migration covered in schema-evolution-and-migrations.
subtopics.visual: A cascade tracer: the learner builds a small parent/child schema with FKs, chooses ON DELETE CASCADE/SET NULL/RESTRICT and attaches row- or statement-level triggers, then fires one UPDATE or DELETE and watches it fan out level by level — each level showing rows written, triggers queued and locks taken (KEY SHARE on parents) with a per-row-vs-transition-table counter — while a separate deferred-queue lane holds the deferred constraint checks until the learner presses COMMIT, where the violation finally surfaces instead of at the statement.

modules.title: Data Modeling in Practice
modules.why: Most production data bugs are modeling bugs that only surface at scale or a year later — a schema nobody documented whose real join edges are folklore, a duplicated copy nobody reconciles, an orphaned child row whose parent was deleted out from under it, a customer-defined field that can never be constrained or migrated, a translation that silently falls back to English on a list page, a drag-to-reorder list that rewrites ten thousand rows per move — so a senior engineer needs an explicit discipline for reading an inherited schema and for derived data, type hierarchies, tenant-defined attributes, locales, trees and manual order.

subtopics.title: Inheriting an undocumented schema: archaeology and profiling
subtopics.covers: Reconstructing the model from information_schema and pg_catalog when no constraints were declared — inferring join edges from naming plus value-overlap sampling between candidate column pairs, profiling every column for cardinality, null fraction, distribution and format anomalies to expose the undeclared enum, the sentinel date (9999-12-31), the '' that means NULL and the number stored as text, separating live tables from dead ones with pg_stat_user_tables, idx_scan and sys.schema_unused_indexes read over a full business cycle including quarter-end jobs, attributing each table's writer from application code plus pg_stat_statements, recognising the fossilised antipatterns (comma-separated lists, EAV bags, half-honoured soft deletes, hand-synced shadow copies), and recording the result as COMMENT ON plus a checked-in data dictionary and a CI-generated ERD so the reconstruction does not rot back into folklore.
subtopics.visual: The learner is dropped into an unfamiliar 30-table schema with no foreign keys and must rebuild it: sampling value overlap between column pairs proposes join edges with a confidence score, column profiles surface an undeclared enum and a sentinel date, and usage counters advanced through a simulated business cycle mark tables live or dead — then the tool grades their reconstructed ER diagram and dead-table list against the ground truth hidden in the application code, flagging the table that looked dead until the quarterly job ran.

subtopics.title: Denormalization and read models
subtopics.covers: Duplicate data when join cost exceeds write-time maintenance and the consistency burden moves to writers: same-transaction fan-out, triggers and counter caches, generated columns, Postgres materialized views with REFRESH CONCURRENTLY (full recompute, requires a unique index), incremental view maintenance (pg_ivm, Materialize), CQRS read models fed by CDC with an explicit staleness window, and reconciliation jobs that detect drift between derived counts and source rows — the reporting-schema discipline for derived tables (declaring a fact grain, star schemas, conformed dimensions and slowly changing dimension types) is owned by data-engineering-warehouse-pipelines.
subtopics.visual: The learner toggles a social-feed schema between normalized and denormalized and picks a sync strategy (same transaction, trigger, async CDC, periodic refresh), then runs a mixed workload and watches write amplification per post, read fan-out per feed page, the staleness window, and a drift detector flagging rows when an async update is dropped.

subtopics.title: Schema for embeddings: chunks, model versions and re-embedding
subtopics.covers: Chunk table design (document id, chunk ordinal, content hash, model name and version, dimension, plus the metadata columns that filters will need), treating the embedding as derived state that must be recomputed whenever chunking or the model changes and doing it as a shadow column or shadow table with a throttled backfill and an atomic switch, propagating source deletes and updates to chunks and to the index (content-hash-based skip of unchanged chunks), dimension and quantization choices against storage and recall (index internals live in indexes-beyond-the-b-tree), and the decision of keeping vectors in the OLTP database versus a dedicated store based on transactional consistency with the source rows.
subtopics.visual: The learner edits source documents and watches chunking, hashing and embedding jobs fan out into a chunk table, then switches the embedding model to trigger a shadow-column backfill with progress, cost and dual-index storage meters, and finally deletes a source row to see the delete propagate into chunks and the index — or, with the propagation off, leave orphaned vectors that keep surfacing in results.

subtopics.title: Polymorphic associations and type hierarchies
subtopics.covers: The layouts for 'a comment belongs to a post or a photo' and what each buys: the untyped (commentable_type, commentable_id) Rails/Django pair, which forfeits foreign keys, ON DELETE CASCADE, a single index the planner can drive a join with, and leaves orphan rows only a nightly job finds; the exclusive arc of one nullable FK per parent type plus a CHECK that exactly one is non-null, keeping referential integrity at the cost of a column per type and a wide partial-index set; table-per-type (class-table inheritance) with a shared supertype table carrying identity and per-type child tables, giving typed FKs and NOT NULL on type-specific columns at the cost of a join per read; single-table inheritance with sparse nullable columns plus a CHECK per type, cheap to read and impossible to constrain; and a typed JSONB payload column for the genuinely open-ended tail with the promote-to-a-column rule — scored on which invariants the engine enforces versus which move to application code, index count and write amplification, the cost of 'fetch a child with its parent' and 'list all children of one parent', and what happens when a fifth parent type appears.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a layout for a comments-on-posts-and-photos schema and the panel renders the DDL, a green/red grid of which invariants the database itself enforces, and the plan plus buffers for the two canonical queries; an orphan-injector button deletes a parent row and shows which layouts reject or cascade it and which silently leave dangling children, while an 'add a new parent type' button replays the migration cost for each layout side by side.

subtopics.title: Custom fields: EAV, JSONB bags, sparse columns and DDL per tenant
subtopics.covers: Four layouts for tenant-defined attributes — an EAV triple table whose every report is a pivot with one join per field and whose values are untyped and unconstrained, a JSONB attribute column with expression or GIN indexes and no per-field statistics, a pool of reserved sparse typed columns with a metadata catalog mapping field ids to physical columns plus per-field index tables (the Salesforce approach), and real DDL per tenant with its catalog bloat and migration fan-out — compared on filtering and sorting by a custom field, enforcing required, unique and type constraints, planner estimates over untyped values, index entries written per row, and what happens when a customer changes a field's type, adds the 200th field or deletes one that data still references; plus the promote-to-a-real-column rule once a field becomes hot and universal.
subtopics.visual: The learner defines custom fields for two tenants under each layout and runs filter, sort and aggregate queries, watching pivot join count, rows scanned, index entries per insert and the planner's estimate-versus-actual gap, then attempts a uniqueness rule and a type change on a populated field and sees which layouts enforce them in the engine, which only validate in application code and which require a rewrite.

subtopics.title: Translatable content: per-locale rows, jsonb maps and fallback chains
subtopics.covers: The three layouts for localized fields — a translations table keyed by (entity_id, locale, field) or one row per locale, a jsonb map per column, and a column per locale — scored on which constraints the engine still enforces (NOT NULL on a required translation, uniqueness of a slug that must be unique per locale rather than globally), index entries written per insert as locales multiply, and the cost of rendering a list page in one locale; fallback chains (fr-CA → fr → default) resolved by COALESCE, LATERAL or a materialized resolved view and what each does to the plan; treating a translation as derived state with a coverage metric and a staleness window when it comes from a translation pipeline; per-locale ICU collation for ORDER BY and its interaction with the collation-version trap; per-language text-search configurations and which layout can actually feed them; and the boundary rule that pluralization, date and currency formatting belong in the application's message catalog while only content belongs in the database.
subtopics.visual: One entity list page renders under each layout for a chosen locale while a scoreboard counts rows joined, bytes read and index entries written per insert; adding locales grows each layout's storage and write cost at visibly different rates, requesting a locale with a missing translation walks the fallback chain with the extra lookups highlighted in the plan, sorting switches collation per locale, and an attempt to reuse a slug in a second locale is accepted or rejected depending on whether the layout can express per-locale uniqueness.

subtopics.title: Hierarchies and graphs in relational databases
subtopics.covers: Adjacency list (recursive CTE cost per level, CYCLE detection), materialized path and Postgres ltree with GiST, nested sets (O(1) subtree read, O(n) renumber on insert), closure table (n x depth rows, transitive edges kept in sync), many-to-many junction tables indexed in both directions, and the tipping point at which variable-depth unpredictable traversals justify a graph store (recursive CTE syntax and evaluation live in advanced-sql).
subtopics.visual: The learner builds a tree, picks a representation, and runs 'all descendants', 'path to root' and 'move subtree' side by side across representations, watching rows touched, recursion iterations or joins per query, and rows rewritten by the move.

subtopics.title: User-defined ordering: fractional indexing and reorderable lists
subtopics.covers: Storing an order the user drags rather than one the data implies — the integer position column whose every move rewrites the tail under a lock, float or decimal midpoints exhausting double precision after roughly fifty insertions at the same point, lexicographic fractional keys (Jira's LexoRank, Figma-style fractional indexing) that insert between any two keys in one row write at the cost of unbounded key growth, the rebalance job and running it without breaking cursors held by in-flight clients, two users dropping at the same position producing identical keys and the per-actor tiebreaker suffix that resolves it (the same fix CRDT list ordering uses), and the linked-list and array-in-one-row alternatives with their contention, size and pagination consequences.
subtopics.visual: The learner drags rows under each scheme and watches the rows actually written per move (a tail rewrite under integer positions against a single row under fractional keys), the key string grow character by character as they repeatedly insert at the same point until a rebalance fires and an open cursor breaks, then two simulated clients drop an item at the same position to produce colliding keys the tiebreaker separates.

modules.title: Using Document, Graph and Key-Value Stores
modules.why: Document, graph and key-value stores are not schemaless — each has a modeling discipline and a query language whose execution model decides whether a request is one pointer chase, one index probe or a full scan, and the wrong document boundary, traversal language, Redis structure or multi-model claim becomes the write-amplification, latency, runaway-bill or silently-lost-message bug that only shows up in production.

subtopics.title: Document and JSON modeling: embed vs reference
subtopics.covers: Embed 1:few data that is read together and bounded in growth, reference unbounded or many-to-many data, because MongoDB atomicity is per document (16 MB BSON limit, array growth forces document moves) and Postgres jsonb rewrites the whole value on any update with TOAST kicking in above ~2 KB; the subset, extended-reference and bucket patterns, and the hybrid rule of promoting hot, indexed or constrained fields to real columns (jsonb operators and jsonpath live in sql-documents-text-and-writes, the choice of index over a JSONB column in index-selection-strategy).
subtopics.visual: The learner drags a comments array into or out of a post document and grows it with a slider, watching document bytes climb toward the 16 MB limit, the round trips needed to render one post page, bytes rewritten per single-comment edit (whole document vs one row), and a count of duplicated fields that now have to be kept consistent.

subtopics.title: MongoDB usage: documents, aggregation pipeline and indexes
subtopics.covers: CRUD with update operators ($set, $push, $inc, arrayFilters) and upsert/findAndModify, aggregation stages ($match, $group, $unwind, $lookup, $project, $facet) where stage order decides index use and memory ($match/$sort pushed first, 100 MB per-stage limit and allowDiskUse), compound indexes under the ESR rule, multikey indexes (one array field per compound), partial, TTL and wildcard indexes, explain executionStats (IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN, totalKeysExamined), JSON Schema validation, and multi-document transactions on WiredTiger snapshots (engine internals in the MongoDB case study).
subtopics.visual: The learner assembles a pipeline from stage blocks over a sample collection and reorders them; each stage shows its intermediate documents and the count flowing through, whether it hits an index (IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN) given the indexes the learner has defined, and a memory bar approaching the 100 MB stage limit.

subtopics.title: Firestore and mobile-backend document stores
subtopics.covers: The constraints that shape a Firestore or Realtime Database schema — every query must be served by an index so composite indexes are declared rather than optional and index count drives write cost, query shapes limited to what an index can answer (one range field, restricted inequality and OR combinations, no joins) forcing denormalized duplicates kept in sync by client writes or Cloud Functions, the per-document sustained write limit and the sequential-key hotspot that monotonic ids create, realtime listeners billed per document read and re-delivering on reconnect with their own offline cache and latency compensation, security rules as the query-time authorization layer that rejects a query whose result set the rules cannot prove is permitted (and that must itself be unit-tested), transactions as bounded optimistic retries, and a cost model counted per document so one unbounded collection query is the runaway bill.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes a query that fails until the required composite index is declared, then attaches a listener and edits documents to watch per-document reads billed on every change and replayed after a simulated disconnect, drives a monotonic key pattern until the per-document write limit throttles, and tightens a security rule so the same query is rejected at the index rather than filtered on the client.

subtopics.title: Neo4j and Cypher: property graphs and traversal
subtopics.covers: Nodes, relationships, labels and properties; Cypher MATCH patterns, variable-length paths [*1..3], OPTIONAL MATCH, shortestPath and MERGE; index-free adjacency where each node record stores pointers into its relationship chain so a hop costs O(1) regardless of graph size, versus a relational join whose per-hop cost grows with the edge index; label and property indexes for anchor-node selection, the supernode problem, and where relational still wins (aggregations, bulk scans, strong constraints).
subtopics.visual: The learner draws a small property graph and runs a Cypher pattern beside the equivalent SQL join; the traversal frontier highlights per hop with cost counters that stay constant for pointer chasing but grow for index probes as the learner scales the edge table with a slider.

subtopics.title: Gremlin, SPARQL and SQL/PGQ: languages and their execution
subtopics.covers: Gremlin's imperative traversal steps with barriers, side effects and lazy evaluation versus declarative Cypher pattern matching, RDF triple stores and SPARQL basic graph patterns answered by joins over SPO/POS/OSP permutation indexes, the GQL standard and SQL/PGQ property-graph queries in Oracle, DuckDB and Postgres extensions, and how each lowers to joins so hop cardinality, path explosion and LIMIT pushdown can be predicted.
subtopics.visual: One three-hop question ships pre-written in all four languages (Cypher, Gremlin, SPARQL, SQL/PGQ) with two editable fragments — hop count and edge predicate — and all four lower to one shared traversal-plan model over a single graph, so changing a fragment re-animates each language's frontier or join order side by side with rows-touched and intermediate-result size per hop.

subtopics.title: Redis data structures and usage patterns
subtopics.covers: Strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets (dict + skiplist, ZRANGEBYSCORE leaderboards), streams (consumer groups, XACK, pending entries list), HyperLogLog and bitmaps; small-object encodings (listpack to hashtable/skiplist at size thresholds), TTL with lazy plus active sampled expiry, eviction policies and approximated LRU/LFU; atomicity from single-threaded command execution, MULTI/EXEC, Lua scripts (EVALSHA) and functions for token-bucket rate limits and locks; PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE and PSUBSCRIBE pattern channels as fire-and-forget fan-out with no persistence, acknowledgement, replay or backlog, so a subscriber that is disconnected, slow (client-output-buffer-limit pubsub kills it) or not yet connected loses those messages permanently, the connection entering subscribe mode and accepting almost no other commands (hence a second connection per subscriber), RESP3 push messages lifting that restriction, sharded pub/sub (SSUBSCRIBE) versus plain pub/sub broadcasting to every Cluster node, and keyspace/keyevent notifications as pub/sub over expiry and eviction events and therefore an unreliable trigger — the decision line being pub/sub for presence, cache-invalidation hints and live fan-out where loss is acceptable, Streams with consumer groups, XACK and the pending-entries list for anything a worker must not drop; plus keyspace hygiene (hash-tags in cluster, big keys, never KEYS). Persistence and cluster internals live in the Redis case study; counters, quotas and rate limits in hot-rows-counters-quotas-and-ledgers.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a data structure and a pattern (leaderboard, session cache, sliding-window limiter, stream with consumer groups), issues commands, and watches the internal encoding flip at thresholds, memory bytes, TTL countdowns and expiry sweeps, and two interleaved clients showing where a Lua script or MULTI makes a check-and-set atomic versus a lost update, with a pub/sub tab where publishing into a channel while one subscriber is dragged offline and back shows those messages vanishing without trace until the same traffic is flipped onto a stream and the reconnecting consumer replays and acknowledges its pending entries.

subtopics.title: Multi-model engines: what is shared and what is bolted on
subtopics.covers: Engines exposing several models over one storage layer — ArangoDB's documents, graph traversal and ArangoSearch over one RocksDB instance, Cosmos DB's SQL/Mongo/Cassandra/Gremlin APIs over one ARS engine with a single partitioning and RU model, SurrealDB, SingleStore rows plus columns plus vector plus full text, Oracle and Db2 as converged databases, MongoDB Atlas Search and Vector Search as co-located but separately maintained indexes — judged on the questions that decide it: is a cross-model write one transaction or two systems, is the secondary model's index synchronously maintained or an asynchronously replicated copy with its own lag and rebuild path, does one query plan span models or does the engine fan out internally, and does one backup, one failover and one ops surface really cover all of it; set against Postgres-plus-extensions and against separate stores fed by CDC, with the migration risk of a proprietary multi-API layer.
subtopics.visual: One dataset is queried as documents, as a graph traversal and as a search query in a multi-model engine and in an equivalent polyglot stack side by side, with each query annotated as one engine hop or a cross-store fan-out, each write annotated transactional or eventually consistent with its lag, and a counter tallying the operational surfaces (backup jobs, failover units, index rebuild paths) each architecture carries.

modules.title: Search in Production: Relevance, Analysis and Clusters
modules.why: The curriculum builds inverted indexes, BM25 and analyzers but never how a search system is shaped, tuned, measured, paginated, kept fresh or defended — and those are exactly the questions a senior who owns a search box is asked: why is this result third, did the change help, why did two conditions on different children produce a false hit, why did facet counts melt the cluster, why does Japanese return nothing, and why did one client's regexp take the tier down. This module is the declared owner of document modeling for an index, relevance evaluation, analysis chains, reverse search over stored queries, search topology and search-tier admission control; the vector, hybrid and embedding half of the old module now lives in its sibling vector-and-hybrid-retrieval, Part 2's indexes-beyond-the-b-tree owns the static inverted-index structures, index-selection-strategy only points forward, and query-scheduling-and-admission-control owns the SQL-engine version of load shedding rather than the search tier's.

subtopics.title: Modeling documents for a search index: flattening, nested and parent-child
subtopics.covers: Why a search index is a denormalized projection rather than a schema — object fields that flatten arrays and cross-match (the classic first/last-name false hit), Lucene nested documents stored as hidden child docs in the same block so any child edit rewrites the whole block, Elasticsearch join fields with same-shard routing and their query-time cost, Solr block joins, and denormalized copies kept current by CDC whose update amplification explodes when a parent field changes — judged by update rate, whether a filter must apply within one child, reindex cost and the aggregation shapes each layout still permits.
subtopics.visual: The learner models a product-with-variants document as flattened, nested or parent-child and runs a query that must match two conditions on the same variant, watching the flattened layout return a false positive the others reject, then edits one variant and one parent field to see documents rewritten per layout with index operations per write and per-query latency counted side by side.

subtopics.title: Relevance tuning and evaluation
subtopics.covers: BM25's k1 and b and field-length normalization, per-field boosts and dis_max/multi_match scoring, synonyms and stemming trading recall against precision, recency and popularity signals, index-time versus query-time decisions, judgment lists with precision@k, MRR and NDCG, interleaving and A/B evaluation, and learning-to-rank plugins.
subtopics.visual: The learner edits a small judged corpus and query set, drags k1, b, field boosts and a recency weight, and watches each document's score decomposition (tf, idf, length norm, boost, recency) re-rank the list live while NDCG@10 and MRR recompute against the judgments.

subtopics.title: Stored queries and reverse search: percolate and alerting rules
subtopics.covers: Inverting retrieval so thousands of saved queries are matched against each arriving document — Elasticsearch's percolator extracting each stored query's required terms into an ordinary term index so only candidate queries run against an in-memory Lucene index of the single document, Lucene MemoryIndex as the primitive, Prometheus and Loki rules evaluated per interval as the metrics analogue, Flink CEP and Rete-style matching for streams — plus candidate-selection recall, the per-document latency budget as rule count grows, rule versioning and shadow evaluation, and the dedup, suppression and grouping windows that stop one document firing the same alert a thousand times.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes a set of saved queries and drops documents in, watching each query's required terms get extracted into the candidate index and then, per document, the candidate set narrow from all N queries to a handful before full matching runs, with queries-evaluated versus queries-matched counters and a rule-count slider that makes naive all-rules matching climb linearly while the extracted-term filter stays flat.

subtopics.title: Multilingual and CJK analysis: segmentation, folding and per-language fields
subtopics.covers: Tokenization where whitespace fails — dictionary and n-gram segmentation for CJK (kuromoji, nori, smartcn, the ICU tokenizer, jieba, bigram fallback), German decompounding, Turkish dotted-i case folding and ICU diacritic/accent folding, stemming versus lemmatization and stopword lists that make no sense in agglutinative languages, transliteration and romaji matching, the per-language-field versus single-analyzer versus language-detection-at-index-time decision and its effect on relevance and index size, why PostgreSQL text search configurations cover only stemmed European languages so CJK needs pg_bigm, pgroonga or zhparser, and the rule that index-time and query-time analyzers must match so changing either invalidates the index.
subtopics.visual: The learner steps through a committed analyzer fixture — about eight sentences per language across English, German, Japanese and Turkish, each chain's stage-by-stage output generated offline and shipped with tool, dictionary and ICU versions recorded — watching tokens, foldings and the resulting postings and matched documents build up stage by stage, then swaps the analyzer to see previously matching documents silently stop matching until a reindex is run, with recall and index-size counters per strategy; build spec: every stage is badged fixture or live, and only genuinely browser-native stages accept typed input (Turkish dotted-i via toLocaleLowerCase('tr'), diacritic folding via normalize('NFD') plus mark stripping, optionally a ~20KB TinySegmenter for Japanese).

subtopics.title: Facets, aggregations and deep pagination
subtopics.covers: Doc values as per-field column storage for aggregations versus heap-eating fielddata, roaring-bitmap filter caches, terms, cardinality (HyperLogLog) and percentile (t-digest) aggregations with their approximation error and shard-level top-N inaccuracy, post_filter versus filter for facet counts, and deep pagination limits (from+size ceilings, search_after with a unique tiebreaker, scroll and point-in-time contexts that pin segments and delay merges).
subtopics.visual: A query over a segmented index shows the matching docid bitset while the learner toggles facet fields and watches doc-values columns being scanned and counts accumulating per segment then merging at the coordinator, with a pagination slider comparing from+size cost against search_after's constant cost and a badge showing which segments a PIT has pinned.

subtopics.title: Autocomplete, fuzzy and did-you-mean
subtopics.covers: Lucene FST term dictionaries walked by prefix, edge n-gram versus completion-suggester versus search-as-you-type indexes, Levenshtein automata intersected with the FST for bounded edit distance, pg_trgm similarity and phonetic matching, spelling correction from term frequencies and query logs, why prefix queries bypass analyzers, and per-keystroke latency and index-size budgets.
subtopics.visual: The learner types into a search box while the component walks the FST character by character, overlays the edit-distance-1 and -2 automata and highlights which terms the intersection admits, with per-keystroke latency, candidate count and index size shown for edge n-gram, completion suggester and fuzzy-FST approaches.

subtopics.title: Search index topology and zero-downtime reindex
subtopics.covers: Shard count and size targets against heap, segment and FST memory, refresh_interval trading indexing throughput against visibility lag, merge policy and force-merge for read-only indices, replicas for query throughput versus indexing cost, alias-based reindex when a mapping or analyzer changes including the dual-write catch-up window, lifecycle rollover for time-based data, and hot/warm/cold plus searchable-snapshot tiers.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets shard and replica counts and refresh interval under a mixed index-and-query load and watches indexing throughput, segment count, visibility lag and query latency respond, then changes an analyzer and must order the alias-based reindex steps correctly — mis-ordering the dual-write window visibly loses documents.

subtopics.title: Search under load: thread pools, circuit breakers and expensive queries
subtopics.covers: How a search cluster sheds load rather than falls over — fixed search thread pools with bounded queues returning 429s, parent/request/fielddata circuit breakers tripping on memory accounting rather than latency, the expensive query classes a client can send (leading wildcards and regexp, script queries and script fields, thousand-id terms lists, high-cardinality terms aggregations, deep from+size) and the guard for each (allow_expensive_queries, search.max_buckets, result-window caps, persisted or allowlisted query templates), per-request timeouts returning partial results with a timed_out flag and shard failures the caller must check, and PIT/scroll contexts leaked by clients until segments can no longer merge.
subtopics.visual: A cluster serving mixed traffic where the learner fires one expensive query class at a time and watches the search thread-pool queue fill, rejections appear, a circuit breaker trip with its memory accounting shown, and a timed-out request return a partial result the client silently treats as zero hits — then applies guards one at a time to see exactly which class each stops.

modules.title: Geospatial Data: Types, Queries and Cell Indexing
modules.why: Geospatial appears in the curriculum only as R-tree and GiST mechanics, yet distances are silently wrong under the wrong projection, invalid geometries make predicates lie, spatial plans are the one place an index returns candidates that must be rechecked, most production 'find nearby' runs on a sorted-key store with no R-tree at all, 'how do I get there and how long will it take' is answered by a precomputed graph index no bounding box can substitute for, and the dense raster and array side of the domain fits neither row nor column storage.

subtopics.title: Spatial types, projections and predicates
subtopics.covers: geometry (planar, SRID-bound) versus geography (spheroidal) and the projection choice that decides whether distance and area are correct, ST_Intersects/ST_Contains/ST_DWithin semantics, validity and repair (self-intersections, ring winding, ST_MakeValid), coordinate precision and snapping, WKB/EWKB storage with TOASTed geometries, and the equivalents in MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle Spatial and MongoDB 2dsphere.
subtopics.visual: Over the module's committed fixture — a simplified GeoJSON city extract of roughly 200 polygons plus ~2k POIs, drawn as SVG paths under a fixed local projection with no runtime fetch of any kind — the learner draws and drags polygons while flipping between geometry-4326, geography and a projected CRS, watching computed distance, area and predicate results change, with a validity checker highlighting a self-intersecting ring that ST_MakeValid repairs and a byte panel showing the stored WKB and its TOAST status.

subtopics.title: Filter-and-refine, spatial joins and nearest neighbour
subtopics.covers: The two-stage index-assisted plan (bounding-box filter from GiST or R-tree then exact geometry recheck), why ST_Intersects and ST_DWithin are sargable while ST_Distance(...) < x is not, ST_Subdivide for oversized polygons whose MBR defeats filtering, spatial joins as index nested loop over MBRs versus partitioned or grid joins (PBSM, Sedona, warehouse geography joins), and index-ordered KNN with the distance operator.
subtopics.visual: The learner drags a query window over a polygon layer and watches the MBR filter select candidates and the exact recheck discard false positives with live counters, then subdivides a country-sized polygon and sees the candidate count collapse, with a second tab toggling index nested loop against a grid-partitioned join and counting geometry comparisons.

subtopics.title: Cell-based spatial indexing on sorted keys
subtopics.covers: Mapping 2D space to a 1D sortable key with Z-order and geohash prefixes, S2's Hilbert-curve cell hierarchy with region covering parameters and Uber H3's hexagons with k-rings and non-nesting parents, turning a covering into range or IN queries against DynamoDB, Cassandra, Bigtable or Elasticsearch, the boundary problem requiring neighbour cells, client-side exact-distance rechecks, and hot-cell skew in dense cities.
subtopics.visual: The learner drags a search radius across the same committed city fixture (SVG paths, fixed local projection, no runtime fetch) while the tool computes geohash, S2 and H3 coverings at a chosen level, shows the generated key ranges and the number of store queries issued, marks the false positives filtered client-side and the neighbour cells that must be added, and shades a density grid computed in-page from the fixture's POIs where one cell becomes a throttled hot partition.

subtopics.title: Moving objects: geofences, proximity and trajectories
subtopics.covers: High-rate location updates and their write amplification on spatial indexes, geofence matching as a reverse spatial join (point against many polygons) with cell prefiltering and in-memory indexes, nearest-available-unit queries with expanding k-ring search, trajectory storage and simplification, map matching, and dwell/crossing semantics that decide whether an event fires once or repeatedly.
subtopics.visual: Simulated vehicles run generated trajectories over the committed city fixture (SVG only, no basemap request) while the learner picks a geofence-matching strategy (per-update polygon test, cell-prefiltered candidates, in-memory R-tree) and an update rate, watching per-update CPU proxy, index churn and the crossings each strategy misses when updates are sampled too coarsely.

subtopics.title: Routing on a road network: shortest paths, precomputation and isochrones
subtopics.covers: The geospatial question no bounding-box index can answer — Dijkstra and A* with a geographic heuristic, bidirectional search, and why continental door-to-door routing at interactive latency needs precomputation (contraction hierarchies with shortcut edges, hub labeling, ALT landmarks) that turns a query into a fraction of a traversal, turn restrictions and one-ways forcing an edge-based rather than node-based graph, time-dependent and live-traffic weights that partially invalidate that preprocessing, isochrones and many-to-many matrix queries as the expensive relatives that dominate the bill, and the placement decision between pgRouting inside the database and a dedicated in-memory engine (OSRM, Valhalla, GraphHopper) with the data-refresh pipeline each implies.
subtopics.visual: On the road graph committed with the city fixture (a few thousand edges as SVG, no runtime fetch) the learner drops a start and end and races plain Dijkstra, A* and a contraction-hierarchy query with nodes-settled counters, watches the CH build add shortcut edges level by level and then a query expand only upward from both ends, then edits one edge's weight and a turn restriction to see which precomputation survives, which must be rebuilt and how an isochrone's cost scales.

subtopics.title: Serving maps: tiles, generalization and precomputation
subtopics.covers: Vector tiles and the tile pyramid, generating tiles on the fly with ST_AsMVT versus precomputing and caching them, geometry simplification and attribute dropping per zoom level, clustering and server-side aggregation for dense point layers, and the cache and CDN layer that makes a map read path affordable.
subtopics.visual: The page cuts its own tile pyramid in-browser from the committed fixture (clip, simplify, encode — no tile server and no network request), and the learner pans and zooms it while each tile shows whether it hit the in-page cache or re-ran the cut, with sliders for simplification tolerance and zoom-dependent attribute sets trading rendered detail against real measured bytes per tile and build time.

subtopics.title: Chunked arrays and rasters: tiles, chunk shape and pyramids
subtopics.covers: Dense N-dimensional data stored as chunked tiles (Zarr, cloud-optimized GeoTIFF, HDF5, NetCDF, TileDB, PostGIS raster with in-db versus out-db tiles) with a chunk manifest and per-chunk compression, chunk shape as the access-pattern decision where a layout tuned for time-series extraction makes a spatial slice read every chunk, overviews and pyramid levels serving zoomed-out reads at a fraction of the bytes, HTTP range reads against object storage where too-small chunks become per-request cost and latency and too-large chunks become read amplification, sparse arrays and the alternative of shredding into tall (index, index, value) rows in a relational or columnar store with its per-cell overhead, and array engines and readers (TileDB, xarray plus Dask, DuckDB spatial) versus a database extension.
subtopics.visual: A 3D array whose chunk shape the learner sets, then slices along each axis in turn and watches chunks fetched, bytes read, useful-bytes ratio and HTTP request count change as the slice axis fights or matches the chunking, with an overview toggle serving a zoomed-out read from a pyramid level and a tall-table mode showing the same query as a row scan with its per-cell storage overhead.

modules.title: Time-Series and Observability Stores
modules.why: Every senior operates a metrics, logs and traces stack, eventually causes or debugs a cardinality explosion, and is asked to cut its bill; purpose-built time-series engines differ from both OLTP and general analytics in their partitioning, compression, label indexing and downsampling. The module is self-contained: it introduces the two ideas it needs from general partitioning — time as the partition key, and retention implemented by dropping a whole partition instead of deleting rows — in its first subtopic rather than assuming them, so it can be read before or after the application-side partitioning material. It stops at the single-node mechanism: the scale-out metrics stack (remote write, compactor downsampling, cross-replica dedup) is the Part 9 case study.

subtopics.title: Time-series engine designs: chunks, hypertables and TSM
subtopics.covers: Time as the primary partitioning key so that a row's timestamp alone decides which chunk it lands in and a time predicate prunes whole chunks unread, retention implemented as dropping an expired chunk rather than deleting rows (a metadata operation that leaves no dead tuples and no vacuum debt), columnar compression of closed chunks, append-mostly write paths and how out-of-order and late-arriving points are absorbed, and the design differences between TimescaleDB hypertables, InfluxDB TSM, Druid segments and a plain partitioned table.
subtopics.visual: The learner ingests a stream with adjustable lateness and cardinality and watches chunks being created, closed, compressed and dropped by retention, with a query panel showing exactly which chunks a time predicate prunes, a side-by-side counter of rows reclaimed by a chunk drop versus a DELETE, and what a late point costs when it lands in an already-compressed chunk.

subtopics.title: Prometheus TSDB internals: head block, chunks and postings
subtopics.covers: The storage mechanism of a single Prometheus: samples appended into in-memory head chunks backed by a WAL, head chunks m-mapped out to disk as they fill, delta-of-delta timestamp and XOR value (Gorilla) encoding inside a chunk, two-hour compaction of the head into an immutable block of index plus chunks plus tombstones, the labels-to-postings inverted index and matcher evaluation as posting-list intersection followed by chunk decode, and remote write as the handoff to the scale-out systems studied in Part 9.
subtopics.visual: With cardinality fixed by a preset so encoding is the only variable, the learner steps scrapes forward and watches individual samples land in a head chunk with the bit-level delta-of-delta and XOR encoding shown, head chunks m-mapped to disk, the WAL truncated as a two-hour compaction emits an immutable block, then runs a matcher and single-steps the postings intersection and chunk decode that answer it.

subtopics.title: Cardinality: label design, churn and enforcement
subtopics.covers: The decision surface over that same engine: active cardinality as the product of label value sets and why one unbounded label (user id, URL, pod name, request id) multiplies memory and postings size, series churn from short-lived pods and redeploys, relabelling and dropping at scrape or ingest time, per-tenant active-series limits and what a rejected sample looks like to the producer, exemplars and traces as the correct home for high-cardinality identifiers, and the query-side cost of a matcher that touches a million series.
subtopics.visual: A relabel-rule and limit editor over a running instance: each rule the learner writes is applied live to the incoming scrape, showing series admitted versus dropped, active series against the configured tenant limit and which queries the drop just made unanswerable — with the finding that after adding a drop rule, head memory and postings size fall only once the churned series age out of retention, not at the moment the rule lands.

subtopics.title: Rollups, downsampling, retention and continuous aggregates
subtopics.covers: Recording rules and continuous aggregates computing rollups on write versus downsampling jobs rewriting blocks after the fact, retention tiers moving older data to coarser resolution and cheaper storage, which queries may read a rollup and which must read raw, and the aggregates that do not merge — percentiles and distinct counts — requiring t-digest and HyperLogLog sketches to be stored instead of scalars.
subtopics.visual: A long-range query switches between raw, five-minute and one-hour resolutions showing samples scanned and latency, while a percentile computed from naively averaged rollups visibly diverges from the raw answer until the learner swaps in a stored sketch and the two converge.

subtopics.title: Sampling and aliasing: what a monitoring graph cannot show
subtopics.covers: Metrics as a sampled signal with the Nyquist consequence that a spike shorter than twice the scrape interval is either invisible or aliased into a phantom slow wave, why rate() and increase() need a window several times the scrape interval to be stable and return nothing when a scrape is missed, the extrapolation, counter-reset and staleness rules (Prometheus lookback delta, range-edge extrapolation) that make a graph disagree with an exact count, the downsampling decision to retain max and min beside avg so a rollup preserves the peaks an average erases, why percentiles cannot be averaged across series or recomputed from rollups and what a histogram, t-digest or KLL state stores instead, and the alerting consequences of a for-duration shorter than the resolution or an SLO measured from a signal that cannot see the outage.
subtopics.visual: The learner draws a true load signal containing a short spike, then sets scrape interval, rate window and rollup resolution and watches the rendered graph and the alert evaluation on top of it as the spike vanishes, smears across bins or aliases into a slow oscillation, with a side panel comparing avg-only against max-preserving rollup storage as the same alert fires or stays silent.

subtopics.title: Logs, traces and wide events at scale
subtopics.covers: Index-everything (inverted index, high write amplification and storage multiple) versus label-index-plus-brute-force scan (Loki-style chunk grep) versus columnar with skip and bloom indexes (ClickHouse, wide-event stores), trace storage as spans keyed by trace id with service and operation indexes, head versus tail sampling and what each makes unanswerable, retention tiering into object storage, and the cost model of bytes ingested versus bytes scanned versus index size.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets log volume, field cardinality and a query shape (needle-by-trace-id, or an aggregate over a high-cardinality field) and runs the same query against all three designs, comparing index size, bytes scanned, latency and monthly cost, with a sampling slider that makes specific traces vanish from the result.

modules.title: Application Access: ORMs, Generated APIs, Protocols and Drivers
modules.why: Most OLTP latency is spent outside the executor: in the ORM session or generated API layer that actually emits the SQL, in the driver that encodes and decodes every value, and in round trips and handshakes that are invisible unless you can read the wire protocol, so this module makes the client-to-backend path as legible as a query plan — and makes each statement attributable back to the endpoint, tenant and deploy that emitted it.

subtopics.title: The round-trip tax: ORMs, lazy loading and the N+1 problem
subtopics.covers: Lazy loading issues one query per parent row so page latency becomes N x RTT, JOIN-based eager loading (select_related, Hibernate JOIN FETCH) fans out one-to-many rows into duplicated wide result sets, batched IN loading (prefetch_related, Rails includes, Hibernate @BatchSize, GraphQL DataLoader) keeps shape at k round trips, and ORM-generated SQL carries its own traps (implicit casts defeating indexes, unbounded IN lists, OFFSET pagination, SELECT * over-fetching, save() on detached entities) that query-count assertions in tests and the set-based rewrites from the advanced-sql module catch.
subtopics.visual: The learner renders a page of N posts with authors and tags, drags a network-RTT slider and toggles lazy / JOIN / batched-IN loading, and watches a Gantt timeline of round trips, a rows-transferred meter that balloons under JOIN fan-out, and the total page latency recompute live.

subtopics.title: ORM internals: identity map, unit of work and flush ordering
subtopics.covers: The write side of the session machinery that the previous subtopic only reads through — a per-session identity map and first-level cache, snapshot-based dirty checking at flush, the fixed flush order (inserts, then updates, then deletes) that ignores your call order and so trips FK and unique constraints, autoflush before queries, cascade and orphan-removal rules, JDBC batch sizing (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, Django bulk_create) and why IDENTITY key generation disables batching, second-level and query caches with their invalidation, detached entities and open-session-in-view, @Version optimistic locking against the version-column pattern from serializability-without-blocking, and the escape hatches (raw SQL, sqlc, jOOQ, query builders) across Hibernate/JPA, SQLAlchemy, Django ORM, ActiveRecord and Entity Framework.
subtopics.visual: The learner mutates an object graph in a simulated session (insert a parent, edit a child, delete a sibling) and steps to flush: the identity map fills, dirty checking diffs each snapshot, and the emitted SQL reorders into insert/update/delete phases — firing a unique violation until an explicit flush is inserted — while counters for statements, round trips and batch size respond to toggling batching, cascades and the ID-generation strategy.

subtopics.title: Compiling REST and GraphQL to SQL: PostgREST, Hasura and the arbitrary-query problem
subtopics.covers: How auto-generated data APIs (PostgREST, Hasura, Postgraphile, Supabase) emit one statement instead of resolver-per-field round trips (lateral joins with json_agg or row-to-JSON aggregation), the authorization model where the API assumes a per-request role or sets JWT claims as session settings so row-level-security policies decide visibility — making SET LOCAL and role switching mandatory under a transaction-mode pooler — the arbitrary-shape query risk (unbounded nesting, expensive filters and sorts on unindexed columns, aggregates and counts a client can request at will) and the guards that contain it (persisted or allowlisted operations, depth and complexity limits, per-role statement_timeout and row caps, cursor-based pagination, estimated counts), subscriptions implemented as polled queries or logical-replication streams and their fan-out cost, and the point where a hand-written service is the right answer.
subtopics.visual: The learner issues a nested query and watches it compile into a single SQL statement with lateral joins and JSON aggregation, side by side with a resolver trace showing the N+1 round trips it replaced, then raises nesting depth and filter cost until the generated plan explodes and applies depth limits, persisted queries, a statement timeout and an index one at a time to see which guard actually catches it, with an RLS panel showing the policy predicate injected per request role.

subtopics.title: Wire protocols: PostgreSQL simple vs extended, MySQL and pipelining
subtopics.covers: The PostgreSQL message flow (StartupMessage, Query vs Parse/Bind/Describe/Execute/Sync, RowDescription/DataRow/CommandComplete/ReadyForQuery, errors discarding everything until the next Sync), text vs binary parameter and result encoding, named vs unnamed statements and portals, libpq pipeline mode (PG 14) and its ordering rules, MySQL COM_QUERY vs the COM_STMT_PREPARE/EXECUTE binary protocol and its lack of pipelining, Redis RESP pipelining, and why a per-statement round trip on a 0.5 ms datacenter link dominates a 50 us index lookup (plan caching of prepared statements is owned by execution-engines-and-resource-control).
subtopics.visual: A client/server sequence diagram with adjustable RTT: the learner types a parameterized statement, picks simple / extended / pipelined mode and steps message by message, watching bytes per message, the wall clock, and, when an error is injected mid-pipeline, the queued messages being discarded until Sync.

subtopics.title: Inside the driver: type mapping, statement caches and the errors they produce
subtopics.covers: How a driver turns wire bytes into language values and back — psycopg3/pgx/JDBC/node-postgres type registries, binary versus text result formats, NUMERIC arriving as a string or a lossy double, BIGINT beyond JavaScript's 2^53, UUID/bytea/array/JSON/interval mappings and timestamptz rendered through the driver's or the session's zone — plus the per-connection server-side statement cache that produces 'cached plan must not change result type' (0A000) after a deploy's DDL and 'prepared statement s1 already exists' through a transaction-mode pooler, driver pool defaults and validation queries, fetch-size and autocommit defaults that decide whether a large result streams or buffers into an OOM, and driver TLS, DNS caching and keepalive settings that decide how quickly a failover is noticed.
