subtopics.visual: A round-trip inspector where the learner picks a driver and a column set and watches each value cross the wire in text or binary and land as a concrete language type with precision loss flagged in red, then runs an ALTER TABLE behind a cached prepared statement to reproduce the exact 0A000 error, and flips the pooler into transaction mode to watch named statements collide across clients.

subtopics.title: Seeing the database from the application: query tags, spans and per-endpoint budgets
subtopics.covers: Emitting sqlcommenter/OpenTelemetry key-value comments carrying route, controller, tenant and release so a statement in pg_stat_activity, the slow log or Performance Insights is attributable to an endpoint (with normalization and cardinality rules that keep the tag from fragmenting pg_stat_statements or leaking PII), client spans that split a call into pool checkout wait, network, server execution and row fetch so pool exhaustion is distinguishable from a slow plan, pool gauges (in-use, wait time, checkout timeouts, evictions) exported as first-class metrics, and per-endpoint query-count and DB-time budgets enforced in production so a lazy load introduced by a refactor pages someone instead of quietly adding 200 round trips (server-side pg_stat_statements and wait events belong to operating-observability-tuning-capacity, CI query-count gates to dev-and-test-environments).
subtopics.visual: One request's waterfall decomposes into pool wait, network, server time and row streaming while the emitted comment travels into the server's own activity view; the learner toggles tagging to watch attribution appear and vanish, injects a lazy load so the per-endpoint query-count budget trips, and saturates the pool so the latency that a server-side view attributes to nothing shows up entirely as checkout wait.

modules.title: Moving Data and Routing Requests: Bulk Load, Streaming, Replicas and Retries
modules.why: Once the connection path is understood, the remaining client-side work is moving bytes in bulk without holding locks or snapshots too long, streaming results that do not fit in memory, sending each query to the right role, wiring change notifications through the same pooling and replica plumbing, and surviving the timeouts and in-doubt commits that every one of those paths eventually produces.

subtopics.title: Batching, pipelining and bulk loading: multi-row INSERT and COPY
subtopics.covers: Throughput climbs from single-row INSERT through multi-row VALUES, prepared batches (JDBC reWriteBatchedInserts), pipelining, to COPY FROM STDIN (text/binary) and MySQL LOAD DATA / multi-value INSERT as per-statement overhead and round trips are amortized, while batch size trades against transaction and lock duration, WAL volume, and per-row index maintenance versus drop-and-rebuild, with DEFERRABLE constraints, disabled triggers, UNLOGGED tables and the wal_level=minimal same-transaction WAL skip, ON CONFLICT upsert cost, synchronous_commit, ANALYZE after load, and checkpointed idempotent loaders that survive a mid-load failure (index bulk build itself belongs to b-trees-and-variants).
subtopics.visual: Load one million rows: the learner picks the method (single / multi-row / prepared batch / pipelined / COPY), a batch-size slider, and toggles indexes, FKs and UNLOGGED, then watches gauges for rows per second, round trips, WAL bytes, lock hold time and rebuild time, with a crash button that shows how much work a checkpointed loader must redo.

subtopics.title: Export, Arrow Flight and cross-engine data sharing
subtopics.covers: The egress direction of bulk movement: COPY TO and server-side export formats, writing Parquet/Arrow for downstream engines, Arrow Flight SQL and ADBC as columnar wire protocols that skip the per-row driver conversion which usually dominates a dataframe load, JDBC/ODBC fetch size and type-mapping losses, warehouse unload patterns (Snowflake COPY INTO stage, Redshift UNLOAD, BigQuery extract) with file sizing tuned for parallel readers, zero-copy sharing (Snowflake shares, Delta Sharing, Iceberg catalogs) that avoids copying at all, and verifying an export by row count and checksum.
subtopics.visual: The learner exports the same result set three ways — CSV over the row protocol, Parquet files, and Arrow Flight — and watches the cost split per stage (server serialization, network bytes, client deserialization into a dataframe), while a file-count and file-size slider changes downstream parallel read time.

subtopics.title: Read/write splitting in the application framework
subtopics.covers: The plumbing that actually routes a query: one connection pool per role with separate credentials and sizes (Rails connects_to/connected_to, Django database routers, Spring @Transactional(readOnly) with a routing DataSource, Hibernate replica hints, Prisma read replicas), the rule that any read inside an open write transaction must stay on the primary, how an ORM lazy load or a serializer touching an unloaded association after the transaction closes silently escapes to a replica, sticky-for-N-seconds and per-request pinning as the framework's approximation of the LSN/GTID staleness tokens the replication module defines, migrations and background jobs that must never resolve to a replica, connection-count multiplication across roles and pods against the backend budget, and the test harness that hides all of it by pointing both roles at one database.
subtopics.visual: A request timeline where the learner marks each ORM call read or write and picks a routing rule, watching queries land in the primary or replica pool while a lag slider makes a post-write render return stale data, then enabling per-request pinning and adding an association that lazy-loads after the transaction closes to watch it escape the pin and read stale anyway.

subtopics.title: Wiring LISTEN/NOTIFY through the client stack: pooling, payload limits and the re-read
subtopics.covers: The client-side plumbing a change notification has to survive, taking delivery semantics as given from caching-and-client-side-data: LISTEN is session state, so a transaction-mode pooler hands the listening session to another client and the application silently receives nothing while every health check still passes (session mode or a dedicated direct connection is the fix, at the cost of one pinned backend per listener); the 8000-byte payload ceiling and the pg_notify queue make shipping row state in the payload wrong, so the convention is to notify a table name and row id and have the handler re-read; and that re-read is a fresh query subject to the routing rules above, so on a replica-routed pool the hint outruns the row and the handler reads the pre-commit version or nothing at all — hence re-reading on the primary, or carrying the commit LSN in the payload and waiting for the replica to reach it, plus the job-table wake-up pattern where a missed notification is merely a slower poll rather than lost work.
subtopics.visual: A three-lane request trace — application handler, pooler, database — where the learner commits a write and watches the NOTIFY travel: switching the pooler between session and transaction mode makes the LISTEN registration land on a borrowed backend and the notification vanish with no error anywhere, a payload-size slider pushes past 8000 bytes into a failing commit until the learner switches to notify-an-id, and a routing toggle plus lag slider shows the re-read hitting a replica and returning the stale row until the handler is pointed at the primary or made to wait for the payload's LSN.

subtopics.title: Server-side cursors, portals and result streaming
subtopics.covers: A PostgreSQL portal executed with a row limit, DECLARE CURSOR, and WITH HOLD (materialized into a tuplestore at commit) stream large results while pinning the transaction's snapshot (holding back the vacuum xmin horizon) and its locks, JDBC fetchSize only streams with autocommit off, psycopg named cursors and MySQL useCursorFetch / mysql_use_result stream where the defaults buffer the whole result client-side into an OOM, cursor_tuple_fraction steers the planner toward fast-start plans, and a cursor left open in a transaction is an idle-in-transaction session as far as the server is concerned.
subtopics.visual: A ten-million-row query where the learner chooses buffer-all / fetchSize N / WITH HOLD and steps through fetches, watching client memory, the server tuplestore, the portal's position, the pinned snapshot holding back a dead-tuple counter that vacuum cannot reclaim, and the plan flipping between fast-start and full-throughput as cursor_tuple_fraction changes.

subtopics.title: Timeouts, retries and error handling from the client
subtopics.covers: A request passes through layered deadlines (pool checkout timeout, socket read timeout and tcp_user_timeout, server statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout) and the client must classify what it sees: serialization failures (40001) and deadlocks (40P01) are safe to retry, a connection refused before the first byte is safe, but a timeout during COMMIT is in-doubt and only safe with the idempotency keys from application-data-patterns, while cancellation travels on a separate CancelRequest connection with a secret key, dead peers after failover need TCP keepalives to detect, and retry budgets plus exponential backoff with jitter and deadline propagation keep retries from becoming the retry storms covered in backups-incidents-disaster-recovery.
subtopics.visual: A request timeline from pool to backend where the learner sets each timeout and injects a fault at a chosen point (lock wait, slow query, network drop before or after COMMIT), then watches which timeout fires first, the error class the client receives, whether the transaction actually committed, and a retry loop with backoff, jitter and budget replayed against a database QPS meter.

modules.title: Caching Tiers, Stampedes and Client-Side Data
modules.why: Every read the application does not send to the database lives in a cache tier, a change notification or a client-side replica, and all three are correctness systems disguised as performance systems: invalidation races, stampedes, slab fragmentation, dropped notifications and offline mutation rebase all decide what a user actually sees, so this module makes the staleness window, the delivery guarantee and the memory behaviour of that layer explicit instead of accidental.

subtopics.title: Caching patterns: cache-aside, read-through, write-through and invalidation races
subtopics.covers: Cache-aside (lazy population on miss), read-through, write-through and write-behind differ in who writes the cache and when, delete-on-write beats update-on-write for ordering, and the canonical race (a read-miss fetches the old DB value, a concurrent write commits and invalidates, then the stale set wins and lives for the whole TTL) is closed by Facebook-memcache leases, versioned compare-and-set, or delayed double delete, while TTL bounds staleness, negative caching absorbs misses on absent keys, in-process caches versus Redis/Memcached shift the consistency window, and that window is a product decision to document (log-driven invalidation via CDC is owned by logs-streams-derived-data).
subtopics.visual: A three-lane timeline (app threads, cache, database) where the learner drags read and write operations to interleave them under a chosen strategy, watches cache and DB values diverge with stale reads highlighted and a staleness-window bar, then enables leases or versioned set and sees the race close.

subtopics.title: Stampedes, thundering herds and request coalescing
subtopics.covers: A hot key expiring or a cold cache after a deploy or flush sends every concurrent request to the database at once, and the defenses are TTL jitter, request coalescing (Go singleflight, Guava LoadingCache) so one fetch serves all waiters, lock-and-serve-stale recompute, memcache leases, background refresh and hot-key warming, and probabilistic early expiration (XFetch: recompute when now - beta x delta x ln(rand) exceeds expiry) that spreads recomputes before the cliff, each trading extra work for a flattened QPS spike.
subtopics.visual: One thousand clients hammer a hot key with a visible expiry countdown; the learner enables jitter, singleflight, leases or XFetch (with a beta slider) and watches the database QPS spike flatten, the miss count fall and the per-request latency histogram shift.

subtopics.title: Inside the cache tier: slabs, admission and topology
subtopics.covers: Buffer-pool replacement theory does not transfer to a remote cache tier: memcached's slab allocator with size classes, slab calcification and the LRU crawler versus Redis's allocator and sampled eviction, admission policies that reject one-hit wonders (TinyLFU/W-TinyLFU in Caffeine with its frequency sketch), client-side consistent versus rendezvous hashing and the hit-rate cost of losing one node, hot-key replication across shards, and two-tier local-plus-remote caches with independent staleness windows — with the miss-ratio curve itself owned by the buffer-pool module (reuse distance / Mattson stack distance) and consumed here read-only as the evidence that turns a memory budget into an expected hit rate.
subtopics.visual: Reusing the buffer-pool module's trace generator and replacement engine as the substrate and displaying its reuse-distance miss-ratio curve as a fixed sizing reference, the learner drives only tier-specific controls — allocator mode (slab size classes versus generic) with a shifting object-size mix, admission policy on or off, and node count with a kill button — and watches per-size-class occupancy calcify and evictions spike under slabs, the TinyLFU frequency sketch fill and reject one-hit wonders, and the hit-rate dip on node loss differ sharply between modulo and consistent hashing.

subtopics.title: LISTEN/NOTIFY, change streams and realtime subscriptions
subtopics.covers: PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY — delivered only at commit, deduplicated within a transaction, an 8000-byte payload, a cluster-wide disk-backed SLRU queue under pg_notify with a bounded size (historically 8 GB, configurable via max_notify_queue_pages in 17) that warns when the slowest listener falls past roughly half of it and errors NOTIFY outright once it is full, monitored via pg_notification_queue_usage, nothing persisted so a disconnected listener loses events permanently, not available on physical replicas, and broken by transaction-mode pooling; MongoDB change streams with resume tokens over the oplog and the oplog window that invalidates a stale token; DynamoDB Streams and CockroachDB CHANGEFEED as resumable alternatives; Firestore and Supabase Realtime built on logical replication with per-client filters and row-level-security evaluation, and the fan-out and connection ceilings that follow; and the design rule that a notification is a hint that triggers a re-read at the client's own consistency level, never the data itself.
subtopics.visual: A client subscribes while the learner commits changes and watches events arrive, then disconnects the client and reconnects it to see LISTEN/NOTIFY events gone forever while a resume-token stream replays from its recorded position; stalling a listener fills the bounded pg_notify SLRU with a live pg_notification_queue_usage gauge that trips a warning near half and turns committing writers red at full, and a hint-then-re-read toggle restores correctness at the cost of an extra query per event.

subtopics.title: Databases in the browser: WASM engines, OPFS and hybrid execution
subtopics.covers: What actually runs client-side — SQLite compiled to WASM over the Origin Private File System with synchronous access handles, the fallback IndexedDB and in-memory VFSs and the durability guarantees they quietly drop, PGlite running a single-user Postgres in WASM with no processes or shared memory, DuckDB-WASM scanning remote Parquet through HTTP range requests on the footer, and MotherDuck-style hybrid plans splitting one query between client and server — under the constraints that decide feasibility: per-origin quota and eviction, one writer with cross-tab locking, wasm download and parse cost on cold start, and a storage layer the browser may revoke.
subtopics.visual: The learner loads a dataset and switches engine (SQLite-WASM, PGlite, DuckDB-WASM) and storage backend (OPFS, IndexedDB VFS, memory), watching bundle size and cold-start time, write durability across a simulated tab crash and a storage-eviction event, a second tab blocking on the write lock, and a remote-Parquet query issuing footer-then-column range requests with bytes fetched counted.

subtopics.title: Sync engines: shapes, buckets, optimistic mutations and rebase
subtopics.covers: The client-side end of the access path puts a partial replica in the browser or phone under a single server authority: partial replication defined by a query (ElectricSQL shapes served as a cacheable HTTP shape log, PowerSync's buckets with per-user sync rules and an upload queue), optimistic client mutators whose effects are re-applied and rebased when the server-authoritative response arrives (Replicache/Zero), and the hard parts — auth-scoped partial replication, rows moving out of a client's scope, client-side schema migration of the local store, server-rejected mutations and the rollback UX, and initial-sync cost on a cold device; multi-writer convergence without a single authority (Automerge, Yjs and the CRDTs beneath them) is owned by leaderless-quorums-crdts.
subtopics.visual: One offline client holding a shape makes local writes that render instantly while the server accepts a conflicting write from elsewhere; on reconnect the learner steps through the server's authoritative ordering, the rebase of each pending local mutation on top of it, one mutation rejected by a server rule and rolled back in the UI, and a row whose update pushes it out of the client's shape so it is evicted from the local store.

modules.title: Application Data Design Patterns
modules.why: Deletion policy, ID scheme, event-table layout, where ephemeral state lives, how fleet-wide configuration is distributed and the tenancy model are chosen once at design time and paid for forever — each has a default that looks fine at small scale and a failure mode (re-registration blocked by a unique index, random keys splitting every leaf, retention that can only be done by DELETE, a session table that becomes the WAL and vacuum bottleneck, one bad config row reaching every node in seconds, one tenant's migration fanning out across thousands of schemas) that appears only later, so the invariant behind the choice matters more than the pattern's name.

subtopics.title: Soft deletes, archival and retention
subtopics.covers: Contrasts a deleted_at flag with moving rows to a history/archive table and with partition-drop retention, showing how a plain UNIQUE(email) breaks re-registration until it becomes a partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL (or MySQL's generated-column trick, since MySQL has no partial indexes), how foreign keys and default scopes/views keep 'deleted' rows reachable, how never-purged rows inflate heap, indexes and every seq scan, and how batched purge jobs, DROP PARTITION and GDPR crypto-shredding actually remove data (backfill mechanics live in schema-evolution-and-migrations, bloat in mvcc-storage-vacuum-gc).
subtopics.visual: A users table where the learner switches among plain UNIQUE, partial unique index and archive-table designs, then re-registers a deleted email and runs 'list active users': the index entries, the constraint verdict, the query's injected predicate and the dead/live row counters change, and pressing 'purge' animates rows leaving the heap versus a partition being dropped in one step.

subtopics.title: ID generation: sequences, UUIDs, UUIDv7 and Snowflake IDs
subtopics.covers: Sequences and auto-increment are non-transactional (gaps on rollback, crash and CACHE, InnoDB auto-inc lock modes) and single-node, random UUIDv4 keys scatter inserts across every leaf of the B+tree (page splits everywhere, buffer-pool misses, doubled damage on InnoDB's clustered primary), time-ordered UUIDv7/ULID and Snowflake (41-bit ms timestamp + 10-bit worker + 12-bit sequence, with clock-rollback handling) append at the right edge but concentrate contention on one hot leaf, and coordinator-free schemes (Instagram's PL/pgSQL shard-embedded IDs, Flickr ticket servers, per-shard offset ranges) trade global ordering for availability while exposing enumeration risk.
subtopics.visual: N independent ID workers mint keys on a shared timeline under the chosen scheme — sequence (with CACHE size and auto-inc lock mode toggles), UUIDv4, UUIDv7, Snowflake — and the learner presses 'roll this worker's clock back' (Snowflake duplicate or stall), 'roll back a transaction' and 'kill the coordinator' while a read-only B+tree leaf strip reused from b-trees-and-variants merely reacts to the resulting key order, and a readout answers 'ORDER BY id == insertion order?', 'how many values were burned?', 'survives coordinator loss?' and 'enumerable by an attacker?'.

subtopics.title: Time-series, events and append-only tables
subtopics.covers: The generic append-only pattern: time-range declarative partitioning turns retention into DROP/DETACH PARTITION instead of DELETE plus vacuum, BRIN indexes fit only while physical order tracks time (out-of-order inserts and updates widen block ranges until every range matches), uniqueness constraints must include the partition key, thousands of partitions inflate planning and catalog lookups, and event-sourced append-only stores need snapshots and projections to stay readable (engine-specific designs — hypertables and chunks, TSM, compression on chunk close, rollups — are in time-series-and-observability-stores, partition pruning in execution-engines-and-resource-control, BRIN internals in indexes-beyond-the-b-tree, Cassandra bucketing in partitioning-and-sharding).
subtopics.visual: An event stream ingests into a table the learner configures as heap+B-tree versus time-partitioned+BRIN with partition-width and retention sliders: a 'last 24 hours' query highlights which partitions and BRIN block ranges are touched, dropping a partition versus deleting its rows shows freed pages versus dead tuples awaiting vacuum, and an out-of-order-insert toggle visibly widens BRIN ranges until the index scans everything.

subtopics.title: High-churn ephemeral state: sessions, presence, carts and view counts
subtopics.covers: What a row rewritten every few seconds actually costs in an MVCC engine (a new tuple version per update, non-HOT churn whenever an indexed column moves, WAL bytes shipped to every replica and into every backup, vacuum backlog and index bloat) and the InnoDB equivalent in undo growth and purge lag, set against the placement menu — Redis with TTL and an eviction policy, UNLOGGED or low-fillfactor tables, per-node memory with sticky routing and periodic flush, signed client-held state and its revocation problem, or a time-partitioned table dropped wholesale — with four questions that decide it (must it survive restart, must every node see it, must it be exact, what breaks if it evaporates) and the two failure modes each choice brings: expiry storms and the cold-start stampede after a restart.
subtopics.visual: One presence-and-session workload is driven simultaneously into a regular table, an UNLOGGED table and a Redis-style store while dead tuples, WAL bytes per second, replica lag, vacuum backlog and index bloat climb on the durable lanes and a memory ceiling with TTL sweeps governs the third, then a restart empties the ephemeral store and the learner watches the rebuild stampede hit the durable database behind it.

subtopics.title: Reference and configuration data: tiny tables, enormous fan-out
subtopics.covers: The data class that is small but read on every request on every node — feature flags, pricing and rate tables, routing and tenant config, id-to-name lookups — where the engineering problem is distribution and blast radius rather than storage: per-process in-memory copies refreshed by jittered polling versus a watch or change stream, versioned immutable snapshots swapped behind an atomic pointer so a reader never sees half a config, engine-level replicated copies (Citus reference tables, ClickHouse dictionaries, Kafka compacted topics and GlobalKTables, broadcast joins), an explicit staleness bound with last-known-good behaviour when the source is unreachable, and the three failure modes that make this class dangerous — a config that grows past a consumer's hard limit, one bad row fanning out instantly to every node with no canary, and a restart stampede where every process fetches at once.
subtopics.visual: The learner publishes a config change and watches it propagate to a fleet under each distribution mechanism with per-node staleness bars, then grows the config past a consumer's size limit to reproduce a fleet-wide failure, restarts the fleet to trigger a fetch stampede against the source, and applies mitigations one at a time — canary cohort, jittered polling, last-known-good, a size guard — to see which incident each actually prevents.

subtopics.title: Multi-tenancy layouts: shared schema, schema-per-tenant, database-per-tenant
subtopics.covers: Pooled shared-schema puts tenant_id first in every index and primary key (tenant_id, id) for locality and future sharding (Citus distributes on it) and leans on row-level security as a guardrail, schema-per-tenant multiplies catalog objects, search_path handling in connection pools and DDL fan-out on every migration, database-per-tenant gives real backup/restore and blast-radius isolation at the cost of connections and fleet operations, and hybrid cell/bridge models silo the largest tenants while pooling the long tail — with tenant moves between shards as the recurring operational task (RLS policies, quotas and noisy-neighbor controls are in security-and-tenant-isolation).
subtopics.visual: The learner drops tenants of different sizes into the three layouts side by side and fires the operations that actually differ by layout — run one migration, open pooled connections and set search_path, restore a single tenant from backup, move a tenant to another shard — watching catalog object counts, DDL statements issued, pool entries and per-connection session state, restore granularity and the rows copied plus locks held during the move.

modules.title: Write-Side Patterns: Side Effects, Idempotency and Background Work
modules.why: Retries, concurrent writers and crashes in the gap between a commit and an external side effect are where correct-looking application code loses money — double charges, orphaned objects, duplicated jobs, an order advanced twice from a stale read, a customer's CSV imported twice, a chunk swept out from under a live manifest, a recurring billing run that fires twice or silently skips a day — and each hazard has a specific mechanism (claim-before-effect, conditional transitions, leases and fencing, content-addressed immutability with safe reclamation, chunked resumable jobs, due-time indexes with catch-up policy) that a senior engineer is expected to reach for before inventing a worse one.

subtopics.title: Transactions in application code: boundaries and side effects
subtopics.covers: A transaction should span exactly one business invariant and contain no external call, because an HTTP request, email send or queue publish inside BEGIN/COMMIT holds row locks and an open snapshot for the remote system's latency (the vacuum/undo cost of that open snapshot is in mvcc-storage-vacuum-gc) and creates the dual-write hazard where the external effect succeeds but the commit fails, or the commit succeeds but its acknowledgement is lost and the caller retries; at the boundary the read-modify-write choice is a single atomic UPDATE SET x = x + 1 versus SELECT FOR UPDATE versus a version column (retry loops in serializability-without-blocking), and commit-then-publish is answered by the transactional outbox, previewed here and treated fully in logs-streams-derived-data (the client-visible transaction state machine — autocommit, savepoints, aborted state — belongs to transactions-and-isolation).
subtopics.visual: An annotated checkout flow where the learner drags BEGIN and COMMIT markers around the steps and places the 'charge card' call inside or outside the transaction: a timeline shows lock hold time and the concurrent transactions it blocks, and fault buttons (API hangs, commit ack lost, process crash after commit) reveal the outcome — double charge, orphaned order, or a clean outbox row waiting for a relay.

subtopics.title: Files and blobs: the database, the object store and the gap between them
subtopics.covers: Where the bytes live — bytea/BLOB and large objects inside the transaction (TOAST chunking, WAL and backup amplification, replication cost, but genuine atomicity with the row; storage internals in pages-tuples-heap-files) versus an object key plus a metadata row (presigned PUT/GET so bytes never traverse the app, CDN-friendly and cheap, but no transaction spanning the two systems) — and the protocol that closes the gap: upload the object first and commit the row second so a failure leaves a reclaimable orphan rather than a row pointing at nothing, or claim a 'pending' row then upload and confirm, plus content-addressed hash keys for dedup and idempotent retries, a new key per version instead of overwrite, soft delete with lifecycle expiry so a rolled-back transaction cannot destroy live bytes, a sweeper reconciling bucket against table, multipart resumption, range and streaming reads, derivative pipelines (thumbnails, transcodes) driven off the outbox, and deletion that must also reach caches, CDNs and backups for right-to-erasure.
subtopics.visual: An upload flow whose step order the learner chooses (object-first, row-first, two-phase pending) with a crash or lost acknowledgement injectable at each step — after the PUT, before commit, after commit, during rollback — resolving to an orphaned object, a dangling row or a correct pair, with a GC sweep plus lifecycle rule reclaiming orphans on a timer and a dedup toggle collapsing identical content onto one key, while a second lane stores the same files as bytea and tracks table size, WAL bytes per upload, replication traffic and backup duration climbing against the object-store variant.

subtopics.title: Content-addressed blobs: chunking, dedup and reference-counted GC
subtopics.covers: Storing bytes under their hash instead of a path — content-defined chunking with a rolling hash (Rabin, FastCDC) so an insertion in the middle of a file re-chunks only locally where fixed-size chunking re-stores everything, a chunk index from hash to location plus a per-object manifest, the chunk-size tradeoff between dedup ratio, index size and per-request cost on object storage, immutability making uploads idempotent so retries are free, and reclamation by reference counting versus mark-and-sweep with the race where a new manifest references a chunk the sweeper is about to delete (closed by a grace period or two-phase mark) — as shipped in Git packfiles, restic and borg, OCI image layers and S3-backed backup systems, with hash-collision and hash-migration as the closing questions.
subtopics.visual: The learner uploads a file, edits a few bytes in the middle and re-uploads, watching content-defined boundaries reform only around the edit while a fixed-chunking toggle re-stores every chunk, with dedup ratio, chunk count and index size updating live, then deletes a manifest and runs GC while a concurrent upload references a soon-to-be-swept chunk to produce the race and the grace period that closes it.

subtopics.title: Idempotency keys and deduplication tables
subtopics.covers: A dedup table keyed by a client-supplied idempotency key or request fingerprint with a UNIQUE constraint, storing status, request hash and the serialized response, where the correct order is claim-first (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING, or a 'processing' row that concurrent duplicates wait on or get 409 from) and the key row commits in the same transaction as the side effect, a mismatched request hash under a reused key is rejected Stripe-style, expired keys are purged by TTL, and natural idempotency comes from upserts and absolute (not incremental) updates; consumer-side dedup by message id is the same table applied to at-least-once delivery (producer-side exactly-once lives in logs-streams-derived-data).
subtopics.visual: A client fires the same payment request concurrently and again after a timeout; the learner toggles the dedup table off/on and chooses record-after-effect versus claim-before-effect, watching idempotency rows transition (processing → done with stored response), unique-violation rejections, waiting duplicates being served the cached response, and the server-side charge counter.

subtopics.title: Status columns, legal transitions and concurrent advancement
subtopics.covers: Modeling an entity lifecycle (order, payment, subscription, ticket) as one status column with an allowed-transition table or CHECK rather than a set of booleans that drift into impossible combinations; advancing it with a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND status = expected plus a rows-affected check so exactly one of two concurrent actors wins (versus the read-then-write that loses one), and where SELECT FOR UPDATE or a version column is needed instead; a transition history table as both the audit trail and the natural place to write the outbox row in the same transaction; partial indexes on non-terminal states so the pending-work query stays cheap as terminal rows accumulate, and partition-by-state or archival when they never stop accumulating; timeouts and expiries as scheduled transitions rather than derived-at-read predicates; enforcing that side effects fire on the transition and not on the state; and the point where the machine has enough branches and timers that a durable workflow engine replaces the column.
subtopics.visual: An order's state machine where the learner fires concurrent transitions from two sessions and watches the conditional UPDATE let exactly one succeed while a read-then-write variant produces an illegal state and a duplicated side effect, with a boolean-pair mode drifting into an impossible combination, a history-plus-outbox lane showing the event written in the same transaction, and a cost panel where the pending-work query's plan degrades as terminal rows pile up until a partial index restores it.

subtopics.title: Advisory locks and database-native mutual exclusion
subtopics.covers: pg_advisory_lock / pg_try_advisory_lock / pg_advisory_xact_lock and their (bigint) or (int,int) key space the application must partition itself (and the collisions from hashing a string key into it), session-scoped locks that outlive their transaction and leak through a transaction-pooled connection versus xact-scoped locks released at COMMIT, their participation in the same deadlock detector and visibility in pg_locks, the fact that they are not replicated to standbys and carry no fencing token so a paused holder is unprotected, the standard uses — serializing a migration runner, singleton cron and background jobs, per-entity critical sections that would otherwise need a row to lock — MySQL GET_LOCK/RELEASE_LOCK with its connection-scoped semantics, and the point at which an etcd/ZooKeeper lease with fencing is the right answer instead (failure-detection-leases-fencing).
subtopics.visual: Several workers race for the same advisory key while the learner switches between session and transaction scope, watches pg_locks fill and a holder's crash release (or fail to release) the lock, then routes the same workers through a transaction-mode pooler so a session lock is stranded on a shared backend and an unrelated client inherits it, and finally pauses a holder past its work to see the unfenced side effect run twice.

subtopics.title: Queues and job tables in the database: SKIP LOCKED
subtopics.covers: Workers claim jobs with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT n (or UPDATE ... RETURNING) over a partial index on (run_at, id) WHERE status = 'pending', hold a lease with a visibility timeout and heartbeat so a crashed worker's job is reclaimed, record attempts with exponential backoff and move exhausted jobs to a dead-letter table, and pay for it with vacuum pressure from high-churn rows, a hot head-of-queue page, polling cost (mitigated by LISTEN/NOTIFY) and a throughput ceiling in the low thousands of jobs per second — the design behind Oban, Que, Solid Queue and Graphile Worker and the point where Kafka or SQS takes over (lock semantics of FOR UPDATE/SKIP LOCKED/NOWAIT are in lock-based-concurrency-control).
subtopics.visual: A worker pool the learner scales polls a jobs table rendered as rows with state, lease expiry and attempt count; switching among no locking, plain FOR UPDATE and SKIP LOCKED shows duplicate processing versus lock waits versus parallel claims, killing a worker mid-job shows its lease expiring and the job being reclaimed, retried and eventually dead-lettered, while a dead-tuple meter and head-page contention counter track the hidden cost.

subtopics.title: Customer-facing bulk import and export
subtopics.covers: An upload landing in object storage with a job row per file, chunked parse into a staging table so validation failures become a per-row error report rather than one aborted transaction, chunk checkpoints that make a crashed worker resume rather than restart, dedupe of a re-uploaded file by content hash and of rows by natural key with explicit upsert-or-reject semantics, chunk sizing chosen against lock hold time, WAL volume and replica lag, progress and partial-success reporting to the user, and the export direction generating results asynchronously (server-side cursor or COPY straight to object storage, signed URL with expiry) instead of buffering a million rows inside a request handler.
subtopics.visual: The learner uploads a file containing invalid rows plus a duplicate of a previous upload, sets chunk size, and watches rows land in staging with an error table filling row by row and lock-hold and replica-lag meters responding to chunk size, then kills the worker mid-file to see the checkpoint resume exactly where it stopped, while an export lane races synchronous streaming (request timeout, app memory climbing) against async generation to a signed URL.

subtopics.title: Timers and schedules: due indexes, recurrence and catch-up
subtopics.covers: The durable timer store for work due later — a partial index on (due_at) WHERE pending with the claim query as one range seek plus FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, the hot head-of-index page and the dead-tuple churn of high-frequency status updates, bucketing by due minute or hour so a sweeper never scans the whole future, and partitioning or archiving terminal rows so the due index stays small; in-memory hierarchical timing wheels and Redis sorted sets as the low-latency complement to a durable index; the thundering herd when every schedule lands on the same round timestamp and jitter as the fix; recurring schedules stored as a cron or RRULE expression plus an IANA timezone and a materialized next-fire time, so DST moves them, some local times do not exist or happen twice, and next-occurrence computation must be idempotent and never drift; exactly-one firing under concurrent sweepers via leases plus an idempotency key on the effect, and clock skew between sweepers; catch-up policy after downtime (fire every missed occurrence, fire once, skip) and its business consequences; and the platform ceilings that force a timer table instead of a broker delay (pg_cron, Quartz, Temporal durable timers, SQS's 15-minute maximum, DynamoDB TTL's best-effort lateness, Kafka's lack of delayed delivery).
subtopics.visual: A store of millions of future timers where the learner sets the index shape, bucket granularity and sweeper cadence, schedules a spike on one round timestamp and watches index pages scanned per tick, firing lateness and the lock queue saturate until jitter spreads it, runs two sweepers to produce double firings until leases are enabled, then takes the pool down for an hour and picks a catch-up policy to see duplicate, once-only or silently skipped runs on the timeline, with a recurring rule dragged across a DST boundary firing twice or not at all unless its timezone is stored alongside the expression.

modules.title: Hot Rows: Counters, Quotas, Escrow and Ledgers
modules.why: A single row that every writer touches — a view counter, a rate-limit bucket, a stock level, an account balance — caps throughput at one update per lock hold time no matter how many cores or nodes you add, and the escapes (sharding, batched rollups, approximate sketches, budget leases across a fleet, escrow intervals, append-only balanced postings) each trade exactness, read cost or invariant strength in a way a senior engineer is expected to choose deliberately rather than discover under load.

subtopics.title: Counters, rate limits and aggregates
subtopics.covers: A single incremented row forms a lock convoy whose throughput is bounded by 1/lock-hold-time regardless of core count, so the fixes are sharded counters (random slot + SUM on read), client-side batching of deltas, insert-only delta rows periodically rolled up into a summary table, and approximate structures (HyperLogLog for distinct counts, Count-Min for frequencies) where exactness is not required; rate limiting compares fixed and sliding windows with a token bucket executed atomically in Redis via Lua versus in SQL, and COUNT(*) under MVCC must visit every version, which is why estimates from statistics or maintained aggregate rows replace it on large tables.
subtopics.visual: 100 clients hammer one counter while the learner switches among single hot row, 16 sharded slots, buffered rollup and a Redis token bucket: the lock queue depth and per-transaction hold timeline, the throughput gauge, and the read-side cost to reconstruct the total (one row versus SUM over shards versus summary plus recent deltas) update live.

subtopics.title: Fleet-wide rate limits and quotas: local buckets versus global truth
subtopics.covers: Why one central bucket becomes a hot key plus a round trip on every request once many nodes enforce it, and the alternatives that trade exactness for locality — per-node buckets holding a reallocated share of the budget, lease-and-batch reservations drawn from a central counter (escrow applied to quota rather than stock), sliding-window logs versus bucketed counters and their memory cost per key, per-tenant fairness so one caller cannot consume a shared pool, where the state lives (Redis Cluster with hash tags, a DynamoDB conditional update, in-memory counters reconciled by gossip), the fail-open versus fail-closed decision when the limiter store is unreachable, and how much over- and under-counting each design admits when the limit is a contractual number rather than a protection.
subtopics.visual: Traffic from a tunable number of enforcing nodes hits one limit while the learner switches between central bucket, per-node shares, lease-and-batch reservations and gossip reconciliation, watching requests per second at the limiter store, per-request added latency, and a ledger that tallies exactly how many requests were allowed above and refused below the true global limit, with a store outage flipping the fleet to fail-open or fail-closed.

subtopics.title: Escrow and commutative updates for hot rows with invariants
subtopics.covers: O'Neil's escrow method lets commutative increments and decrements on a quantity with a bound (non-negative balance, stock ≥ 0) run concurrently by keeping, per row, the committed value plus the sum of outstanding reservations as a [min, max] interval, admitting a transaction only if the invariant holds under every possible commit/abort outcome and adjusting the interval on its commit or abort; the application-level equivalents are reserve-then-confirm inventory holds with expiry (ticketing, checkout), the single-statement CAS UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock >= 1 with a CHECK constraint as backstop, DynamoDB conditional writes, and bounded CRDT counters — all of which avoid the read-set conflict that makes plain read-modify-write serialize.
subtopics.visual: An inventory row with stock 10 and a crowd of concurrent buyers where the learner toggles among FOR UPDATE, conditional UPDATE and escrow accounting: an escrow ledger shows the committed value, reserved-out amount and [min, max] interval moving as transactions reserve, commit or abort, each request is marked admitted-immediately, waiting or rejected, and a red invariant line at zero is never crossed while the throughput bar shows how much concurrency each strategy allows.

subtopics.title: Double-entry ledgers and transfer lifecycles
subtopics.covers: Append-only postings with balanced debit/credit pairs per transfer, balances derived by aggregation versus maintained materialized balance rows and the contention ceiling that creates, pending/posted/voided two-phase transfers and holds that expire back to the source account, idempotent transfer ids so a retried request posts once, integer minor units with currency codes and the prohibition on floats, per-account monotonic sequencing for auditability, reconciliation against external systems (card networks, banks) and TigerBeetle's purpose-built design of fixed-size transfers, batching and a deterministic state machine.
subtopics.visual: The learner posts concurrent transfers while toggling derived-versus-materialized balances and single-row-versus-escrow updates, watching a balance-invariant panel (sum of debits equals sum of credits), the lock queue and throughput, then replays a duplicated retry to see the transfer id suppress a double posting and lets a two-phase hold expire back to the source account.

modules.title: Schema Evolution and Zero-Downtime Migrations
modules.why: Every ALTER is a lock plus (sometimes) a full table rewrite, and rolling deploys mean two versions of the application share one schema at every moment; the expand/contract discipline, two-step online constraints, throttled backfills, idempotent data and seed migrations and generated-then-reviewed migration files are the mechanisms that turn a 30-minute outage into a boring change.

subtopics.title: What DDL locks and rewrites
subtopics.covers: Maps each ALTER TABLE form to the lock it takes and whether it rewrites the heap: PostgreSQL ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for most forms vs SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE for VALIDATE/SET STATISTICS and SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE for ADD FOREIGN KEY, metadata-only ADD COLUMN with a non-volatile default via attmissingval (PG11+) and DROP COLUMN via attisdropped versus full rewrites for non-binary-coercible type changes and volatile defaults, MySQL's metadata lock plus ALGORITHM=INSTANT (row-version limit) / INPLACE (row log) / COPY and LOCK=NONE, SQLite's rebuild-everything-except-add/rename/drop, and transactional DDL in Postgres versus MySQL's implicit commit.
subtopics.visual: A DDL matrix: the learner picks an engine, version and ALTER statement against a table of adjustable size, and sees the lock mode taken, rewrite yes/no with duration scaled to table size, and an animated traffic lane where SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE requests pile up or flow through for the lock's lifetime.

subtopics.title: The expand/contract pattern
subtopics.covers: The N-1/N compatibility invariant that rolling deploys impose (old and new code run against one schema simultaneously) and the sequenced recipe that satisfies it — expand (add nullable column or new table), deploy dual-writes, backfill, switch reads behind a flag, verify, then contract (drop) — including renames as add+copy+drop or via a view, dropping a column only after the ORM stops selecting it (Rails ignored_columns, Django), and the rule that schema and data changes never share a transaction because the lock is held for the whole backfill.
subtopics.visual: A deploy sequencer with app versions v1 and v2 running side by side against one schema: the learner drags schema steps and deploy steps into an order, and a compatibility grid turns red whenever a live version issues a query the current schema rejects (SELECT of a dropped column, INSERT missing a NOT NULL column), so the learner must find a legal ordering for a rename and a column removal.

subtopics.title: Adding constraints and indexes online: NOT VALID, CONCURRENTLY, lock_timeout
subtopics.covers: Two-step constraint addition — ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID checks only new rows under a brief lock, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT scans under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE — for CHECK and FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL via a validated CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) so SET NOT NULL skips the scan (PG12+), uniqueness via CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY then ADD CONSTRAINT USING INDEX, CONCURRENTLY's no-transaction rule and the INVALID index (pg_index.indisvalid=false) it leaves behind that still costs every write until dropped, the partitioned-table case where CONCURRENTLY is refused outright so the only non-blocking path is CREATE INDEX ON ONLY parent (metadata-only, arriving invalid) → CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on each partition → ALTER INDEX parent ATTACH PARTITION per child until the parent flips valid (detectable in pg_index/pg_partition_tree), with PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE on a partitioned table required to contain the partition key and a new partition's indexes pre-built before ATTACH PARTITION so the attach matches rather than rebuilds them, plus MySQL ADD INDEX INPLACE LOCK=NONE and FK adds under foreign_key_checks=0, and the lock_timeout-plus-retry loop that keeps a DDL from parking behind a long transaction and blocking everything queued after it (internals of CONCURRENTLY builds live in Indexes Beyond the B-Tree, lock queues in Lock-Based Concurrency Control).
subtopics.visual: A constraint runner over a table with some violating rows and continuous writes: the learner chooses one-step ADD CONSTRAINT versus NOT VALID + VALIDATE, sets lock_timeout and retry count, and watches a lock timeline showing which mode is held in each phase, which queries block, retry attempts bouncing off a long-running transaction, and a mid-build failure leaving an INVALID index that keeps absorbing writes until the learner drops it; a partitioned-table toggle switches the target to a parent with eight partitions where plain CONCURRENTLY is rejected, the ON ONLY parent index sits invalid in a catalog panel while each partition is built and attached, an unattached child keeps the parent invalid, a UNIQUE attempt without the partition key is refused, and attaching a partition whose index was not pre-built triggers a visible rebuild under lock.

subtopics.title: Backfills at scale
subtopics.covers: Batched, keyset-driven UPDATEs (WHERE id > last ORDER BY id LIMIT n, never OFFSET or one giant statement) each in its own short transaction, idempotent and resumable from a checkpoint, throttled adaptively on replica lag (pg_stat_replication write_lag, Seconds_Behind_Source) and WAL rate, with the hidden costs made explicit: every backfilled row is a new MVCC version (non-HOT if the column is indexed) feeding dead tuples, autovacuum pressure and xid consumption, per-index writes, trigger and FK-cascade amplification, burst-credit exhaustion on managed platforms, and verification counts before switching reads.
subtopics.visual: A backfill simulator with batch size, sleep and parallelism sliders over a table heat map that fills as rows convert; WAL MB/s, replica lag, dead-tuple count with autovacuum firing, and lock-wait spikes respond live, and a 'single giant UPDATE' button shows one long transaction pinning vacuum, holding row locks and blowing the replica lag budget.

subtopics.title: Data migrations and reference data as code
subtopics.covers: The half of a release that changes rows rather than structure: separating DDL migrations from data migrations (lookup and status catalogs, plan and price tables, country and currency lists, flag defaults, bootstrap roles, one-off corrections) and making each one idempotent and re-runnable so a retried or half-failed deploy cannot double-apply, keying seeds on a stable natural or explicitly assigned id rather than a serial that environments will disagree about so INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE plus an explicit setval beats a plain INSERT, ordering seeds and backfills against the expand/contract steps and against the app version that reads the new values, keeping anything long in a checkpointed job instead of inside the runner's transaction and advisory lock where it blocks every other replica's deploy, the merge policy when an operator edits a seeded row in production (seed authoritative, operator authoritative, or an ownership column that splits them) and retire-with-a-flag versus DELETE for a reference row that foreign keys still point at, the split between seed data that must exist everywhere, demo data that is dev-only and fixtures that are test-only (test fixtures and anonymized clones live in Developing and Testing Against Databases), a catalog test asserting the seeded rows match the code's enum, and the review rule that a data migration needs the same row-count assertion and rollback story as an ad-hoc production fix.
subtopics.visual: A deploy pipeline across dev, staging and production where the learner orders a lookup seed, a backfill and the app rollout: the version that reads an unseeded value fails, re-running the deploy makes a plain INSERT-based seed duplicate rows and strand the sequence while the upsert-on-natural-key form stays flat, an operator then edits one row and deletes another in production so the next release either overwrites the edit, resurrects the deleted row or fails on a foreign key depending on the chosen merge policy, and runner lock-hold time and blocked replicas move as the backfill is dragged in and out of the migration runner, with a per-environment drift report at the end.

subtopics.title: Migration tooling, linting and governance
subtopics.covers: Versioned migration frameworks (Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Django, Rails, Prisma, golang-migrate) with a schema_migrations table, checksums, forward-only bias and an advisory lock so concurrent app replicas don't race the runner; per-migration statement_timeout and lock_timeout; why a failing migration leaves a clean state under Postgres transactional DDL but a half-applied one under MySQL implicit commits; unsafe-statement linters that map SQL to lock consequences (squawk, strong_migrations, GitLab migration helpers, Atlas); CI against production-sized snapshots; running migrations as a separate job before the code deploy plus post-deploy migrations for contract steps; and rollback as forward-fix with a backup before any destructive step.
subtopics.visual: A migration-file editor with an inline linter: each statement gets annotated with its lock mode, blocked operations and rewrite flag, a CI lane replays the whole file against a simulated production-sized table with live traffic and reports outage seconds, a PG/MySQL toggle shows a mid-file failure rolling back cleanly versus leaving a partially applied schema, and the learner edits until the pipeline goes green.

subtopics.title: Autogenerated migrations and what the differ cannot see
subtopics.covers: How Alembic autogenerate, Django makemigrations, EF Core scaffolding and Prisma/Atlas migrate diff compare model metadata against the live catalog to emit DDL, the rename problem where a snapshot diff becomes DROP COLUMN plus ADD COLUMN and destroys the data unless the rename is declared, the constructs the differ does not model at all (data backfills, partial and expression indexes, views, triggers, grants, extensions, partitions, CONCURRENTLY which cannot run inside its transaction), the lock and rewrite consequence it never reports, the branch hazard where two PRs autogenerate against different baselines and produce a schema neither reviewed, and the working discipline of hand-editing every generated file, splitting schema from data steps and asserting the result against a production-sized clone.
subtopics.visual: The learner renames a column and widens a type in the model layer and watches the differ's emitted DDL sit beside the true diff, with a row-count meter showing exactly how many rows the generated DROP+ADD would destroy until a declared rename is added, then enables constructs the differ cannot model (partial index, trigger, extension, partition) and sees the generated schema drift from the real one while a lock-analysis panel labels each emitted statement with the lock mode and rewrite it will actually take.

subtopics.title: Branching databases: copy-on-write forks, deploy requests and ephemeral environments
subtopics.covers: Storage-level branching as a fork point in the version history (Neon branches as an LSN fork sharing existing layers, PlanetScale/Vitess branches, Turso database-per-branch) so a branch costs only the pages it diverges on, schema-diff-driven deploy requests that compute the DDL and apply it to the parent with online-DDL semantics on merge, seeding branches with subsetted or anonymized production data for PII safety, branch reset/expiry and cost control, and per-PR ephemeral databases that rehearse a migration's lock profile and backfill duration before it ever touches production.
subtopics.visual: A pull-request pipeline where the learner branches from production at a chosen point, runs migrations on the branch while a storage panel shows only diverged pages being copied, reads the computed schema diff and its lock analysis, resets the branch, then merges and watches the deploy request apply the same DDL online to the parent with its lock timeline replayed.

modules.title: Developing and Testing Against Databases
modules.why: Every backend engineer maintains a test suite that talks to a database and a pipeline that ships schema changes, and the recurring failures are mechanism questions the site otherwise teaches nowhere: tests passing on SQLite while production is Postgres, per-test isolation that silently breaks on code that commits, a 50-row fixture set that guarantees plan regressions reach production, two branches whose migrations apply in either order, and a change approved because 'staging looked fine'.

subtopics.title: Ephemeral test databases: containers, templates and per-test isolation
subtopics.covers: Running the real engine per suite (Testcontainers, docker-compose, pg_tmp) versus substituting SQLite and the dialect divergence that makes the cheap option lie, the three isolation strategies and where each breaks — wrap-in-transaction-and-rollback (invisible to code that commits, useless for triggers, DDL and deferred constraints), TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY between tests, and CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE with one database per parallel worker — plus throwaway-only speed knobs (fsync off, UNLOGGED tables, tmpfs) that invalidate any durability test, determinism (frozen clocks, seeded randomness, never asserting on physical row order or generated ids), and a guard that refuses to run against a non-local host.
subtopics.visual: A suite runner where the learner picks an isolation strategy and worker count and steps through tests including one that COMMITs, one that consumes a sequence and one that asserts row order: leaked rows, reused identity values and order-dependent flakes light up per test, a setup/teardown bar totals wall-clock, and switching the engine to SQLite re-runs the same suite showing which assertions now silently pass.

subtopics.title: Testing logic that lives in the database
subtopics.covers: Assertions that can only run against a real engine — proving a constraint by attempting the violation and asserting the SQLSTATE rather than the message, trigger and cascade behaviour including alphabetical firing order and what session_replication_role skips on logical-replication apply, row-level-security policies tested per role with the negative case that one tenant cannot read another's row and that a newly added table actually has RLS enabled, defaults, generated columns, function volatility and search_path, and a migration's own data transformation verified with before/after row assertions — written with pgTAP, utPLSQL or plain transactional cases in the application suite, plus schema-invariant tests that fail CI when someone adds a table with no owner, no tenant predicate in its indexes or no policy.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes assertions against a live schema — inserting a duplicate to prove the unique constraint's SQLSTATE, switching role to prove an RLS policy blocks a cross-tenant read, firing a cascade and counting the rows each trigger wrote — then a teammate's migration lands adding a table with RLS forgotten and a trigger whose new name reorders the firing sequence, and the panel shows which invariant tests caught each regression and which passed because they only ever exercised the happy path.

subtopics.title: Realistic test data: factories, subsetting, anonymization and branching
subtopics.covers: Why a tiny uniform dataset hides plan regressions because MCVs, histograms, n_distinct and correlation are all wrong, making a small clone plan like production by preserving distributions or importing the source's statistics, referentially complete subsetting that walks foreign keys to a closure instead of leaving orphans, deterministic pseudonymization so joins and uniqueness survive versus random masking that breaks them, quasi-identifier re-identification risk that makes hashing emails insufficient, copy-on-write branching (Neon, PlanetScale, Aurora clones, ZFS snapshots) for per-pull-request databases, and the rule that a masked clone is still personal data with production's access controls.
subtopics.visual: A clone builder where the learner picks a seed table and sampling fraction and watches the FK closure expand (orphans flagged when closure is skipped), assigns masking rules in deterministic or random mode and sees joins and unique constraints hold or break, then runs the same query against source and clone side by side so the plan flips when statistics are not carried over and snaps back when they are.

subtopics.title: Migrations in the pipeline: ordering, branching, preview databases and drift
subtopics.covers: Running migrations as a distinct stage before the app deploy, serialized by an advisory lock so parallel runners cannot race, with destructive contract steps in a post-deploy job; ordering across branches (timestamped versus sequential versions, two PRs that apply cleanly in either order but produce different schemas, checksum mismatches after a rebase, squashing to a baseline); keeping three sources of truth in agreement by diffing the migration-produced schema against the checked-in dump and against production with drift detection as a scheduled job; ephemeral per-PR databases from a template, a snapshot or a branch and what they cannot test; and merge gates that lint the statement and apply it against a production-sized clone under load.
subtopics.visual: A branch-and-pipeline simulator where two PRs each add a migration and the learner merges them in either order, watching the version table, checksums and resulting schema diverge until a drift check fails the build, then runs migrate → deploy → post-deploy with an injectable failure at each step to see which intermediate states the running app version tolerates.

subtopics.title: Capture and replay: validating a change against the real workload
subtopics.covers: Capturing the workload (pg_stat_statements aggregates versus full statement logs, MySQL slow and general logs, proxy-level mirroring) with its cost and privacy implications, replaying at original arrival times rather than as fast as possible because a closed loop reproduces coordinated omission and flatters the candidate, diffing a replay for correctness (result sets and warnings across versions) and for performance (per-statement p99, plan shape, buffers, statements whose plan flipped), gating releases on plan snapshots and hypothetical-index what-ifs, sizing a backfill or online schema change under replayed traffic, and the honesty constraints — same data and statistics, non-determinism under concurrency, no cache state, nothing about uncaptured traffic shapes.
subtopics.visual: The learner captures a trace from a running simulated workload and replays it against a candidate with one change applied (new major version, dropped index, changed memory setting), watching per-statement latency distributions and plan diffs align side by side with regressed statements ranked, and a mode switch between open-loop and as-fast-as-possible showing the tail distortion that makes the second mode lie.

subtopics.title: Regression gates in CI: query counts, plan snapshots and lock budgets
subtopics.covers: Turning database behaviour into assertions a pipeline can fail on — query-count assertions that catch an N+1 introduced by a lazy load, plan snapshots compared per statement with an allowed-shape list, a lock-time budget that rejects a migration whose ACCESS EXCLUSIVE window exceeds a threshold on production-sized data, row-count and bytes-read budgets for analytical queries, and how to keep these gates from becoming flaky (normalizing plan text, pinning statistics, tolerating cost drift while failing on shape changes).
subtopics.visual: A pull-request check panel where the learner introduces a lazy load, an index drop and a rewriting ALTER one at a time and watches exactly which gate trips — query count jumping from 2 to 200, a plan shape changing from Index Scan to Seq Scan, a lock held past its budget — with a knob for gate tolerance that shows false failures appearing when it is set too tight.

modules.title: Databases and AI Workloads
modules.why: LLM features are now shipped over production databases, and their failure mode is not a crash but a confidently wrong number, a cache that answers a paraphrase of a different question, a stale or over-permissive retrieval set, or an inference call inside the executor stalling ingest — all of which are database-side controls a senior is asked to design, while the privilege, row-level-security and tenant-isolation half of the problem (including agents holding SQL access) belongs to Part 10's security module.

subtopics.title: Text-to-SQL: schema linking, grounding and execution-guided validation
subtopics.covers: Retrieving the relevant schema subset (table and column descriptions, foreign-key graph traversal, embedding retrieval over the catalog) so the prompt is not the whole warehouse, value grounding by sampling distinct values and matching literals to real ones, execution-guided generation that runs EXPLAIN or a limited dry run to reject invalid joins and nonexistent columns, self-consistency across candidates, constraining generation to a semantic layer or view allowlist, showing the generated SQL and row counts for verification, the gap between benchmark accuracy and a real schema full of ambiguous and deprecated columns, and the split between guarding generation here and guarding execution with a restricted role, which Part 10's security module owns.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks one of eight recorded questions over a deliberately messy fixture schema, each carrying pre-recorded candidate statements (a correct one, a fan-out join, a hallucinated column, an ungrounded literal), and toggles guardrails — schema-subset retrieval, value grounding, EXPLAIN validation, row cap, view allowlist — while the page runs the real checks (catalog lookup against the schema, a genuine toy-planner EXPLAIN from the shared SQL engine, a literal-versus-distinct-values match) and shows exactly which guard rejects which candidate and which wrong-but-plausible answer is returned with no error once the guards are off.

subtopics.title: RAG data plumbing: chunking, freshness and permission-aware retrieval
subtopics.covers: Chunk size and overlap as a retrieval-quality knob, metadata columns that make filtering possible, keeping the index fresh from CDC or an updated_at cursor with a re-embedding queue, applying per-user and per-tenant permissions as a pre-filter (recall cost) versus a post-filter (leak and empty-result risk) versus separate per-tenant indexes, provenance and citation columns so an answer can be traced to a row, and deletion propagating to the index for right-to-erasure.
subtopics.visual: Over a fixed corpus embedded offline into six committed indexes (3 chunk sizes × 2 overlaps, the sliders snapping to exactly those settings and the page labelling every vector as a precomputed fixture), the learner selects a question from a committed bank and watches which chunks are retrieved and which a permission filter removes under a pre-filter/post-filter toggle that exposes both the recall cost and the leak, then applies one of the fixture's recorded source edits or deletions and follows it through the re-embedding queue with a staleness clock ticking on the served answer.

subtopics.title: Semantic caching: approximate keys, thresholds and invalidation
subtopics.covers: Caching answers keyed by embedding similarity rather than exact text, the similarity threshold trading hit rate against false hits where a paraphrase is not the same question, scoping entries by tenant and role so a cached answer cannot cross a permission boundary, invalidating on the underlying data version (snapshot id, max updated_at, a CDC signal) rather than TTL alone, negative caching and stampede control, and the contrast with an exact-keyed result or plan cache that is correct by construction.
subtopics.visual: The learner fires questions from a committed bank of about forty offline-embedded prompts — paraphrase clusters, near-miss pairs that must not hit, cross-tenant twins — and each probes the cache by real cosine similarity over those fixture vectors (labelled on-page as precomputed) against a draggable threshold, with a false-hit counter rising as the threshold loosens, a tenant-scoped entry refused to another role, and a data-change event invalidating exactly the entries whose source version advanced.

subtopics.title: Generating model output where the data lives
subtopics.covers: The three shapes for populating derived AI columns — a per-row UDF or trigger calling an external inference API (a network stall inside the executor holding a transaction open), a trigger-enqueued work table drained by a background worker or scheduled job with batching, backoff and rate limits, and an external CDC consumer — plus warehouse-native model functions (BigQuery ML, Snowflake Cortex, PostgresML), batching economics against per-request pricing, retry and partial-failure handling, and the freshness SLO that decides which shape is acceptable.
subtopics.visual: The learner inserts a burst of rows and picks a pipeline shape, watching the per-row UDF path stall the executor with open transactions and collapsing insert throughput while the queue-and-batch path drains a work table at a tunable batch size, with end-to-end freshness, token cost and failed-batch retry meters per design.

modules.title: Modeling Space, Time and Schema Change
modules.why: The modeling decisions that bite hardest a year out are the ones about where a thing is, when it was true, when we recorded it, and what the schema meant at the time — a location column that cannot serve the radius query the product later needs, a meeting that moves an hour when tzdata ships new DST rules, a correction that silently rewrites last quarter's history, a renamed field that a stale consumer reads as a default — so a senior engineer needs an explicit discipline for spatial representation, recorded time, bitemporal history and compatible schema change.

subtopics.title: Modeling location: which spatial representation a schema should store
subtopics.covers: The schema decision only — a numeric lat/lon pair, a PostGIS geometry column, a geography column, a geohash/S2/H3 cell-id column used as a sort-key or partition-key prefix on DynamoDB, Cassandra or Redis, or a denormalized combination of a geometry plus a cell id — scored on bytes stored per row, index bytes added, which predicates each can actually serve (radius, containment, KNN ordering, spatial join, tile fetch) versus which degrade to a scan or to application-side filtering, whether the store you already have can enforce the predicate at all, and when location belongs in a dedicated tile or search service rather than the transactional database; every mechanism behind these answers — SRIDs and projections, geometry-versus-geography distance semantics, filter-and-refine with GiST bounding boxes, ST_Subdivide, cell-based indexing on sorted keys — is owned by geospatial-data.
subtopics.visual: Every cell of the scoreboard is produced by a run, not a lookup: the learner picks a representation for a small committed point set and a fixed four-predicate workload (radius, containment, KNN order, tile fetch) executes against it, reporting per predicate the rows scanned, whether it reached an index or fell back to application-side filtering, and bytes per row measured off the actual encoded column — with geospatial-data's cell-covering panel embedded read-only on the cell-id row so the key-range expansion behind its numbers is visible, and a jump link there for the map and the mechanisms.

subtopics.title: Modeling time: recurrence, per-user days and the recording clock
subtopics.covers: The modeling decisions above the type level (storage, rendering, DST arithmetic and precision belong to sql-semantics-types-and-schema-design's temporal types page): why a future local event must store a local time plus an IANA zone id and a recurrence rule rather than a materialized instant, because a tzdata release is a change event that moves already-stored occurrences and forces a recompute pass; per-user and per-tenant date boundaries that make 'today' a query parameter rather than a constant, and what that does to daily aggregates and to a uniqueness constraint on a day; durations stored as integers of a fixed unit versus calendar intervals; and the clock source for created_at — client clock, statement_timestamp, or now() frozen for the whole transaction — with the ordering, tie-breaking and monotonicity assumptions each one silently buys.
subtopics.visual: A scheduling table holds recurrence rules plus materialized occurrence rows; the learner ships a tzdata release and watches exactly which stored occurrences the recompute pass must rewrite and which stale materialized instants would have drifted, then switches the created_at clock source among client, statement and transaction time under concurrent inserts to see ordering ties and inversions appear in a keyset-paginated feed, and drags a per-user day boundary to watch one daily-aggregate query return different row sets per viewer.

subtopics.title: Temporal modeling: history tables and bitemporal data
subtopics.covers: Valid time vs transaction time, SQL:2011 system-versioned tables (MariaDB, SQL Server), Postgres patterns using tstzrange with EXCLUDE USING gist (btree_gist) to forbid overlapping validity per key, temporal primary and foreign keys (PG 18 WITHOUT OVERLAPS), history tables maintained by triggers versus audit logs and CDC, AS OF queries, retroactive corrections that require bitemporal rows, and the storage and index cost of never deleting.
subtopics.visual: The learner edits an employee's salary along two axes, 'when it was true' and 'when we recorded it'; a 2D bitemporal plane shows rectangles being closed and opened, an AS OF query slicing the plane, a retroactive correction splitting a rectangle, and the EXCLUDE constraint rejecting an overlapping validity range.

subtopics.title: Schema evolution principles: Avro, Protobuf and compatibility
subtopics.covers: Backward, forward and full compatibility and their transitive forms as enforced by a schema registry; Protobuf field numbers, reserved, proto3 presence, defaults and unknown-field preservation; Avro writer's-vs-reader's schema resolution with defaults, aliases and union promotion; Iceberg column IDs; and the same rules applied to database columns (nullable-with-default adds, never reuse a name with new meaning) and to versioned documents with upgrade-on-read. Byte encodings live in hardware-os-durability; migration mechanics in schema-evolution-and-migrations.
subtopics.visual: A producer and a consumer with independently editable schemas plus a registry compatibility mode selector; the learner adds, removes, renames or re-types a field and watches each read resolve field by field (matched, defaulted, dropped, error) while the registry accepts or rejects the new version under each mode.

modules.title: Vector and Hybrid Retrieval in Production
modules.why: The curriculum builds ANN structures and BM25 separately but never how a retrieval system fuses them, decides whether it needs an index at all, measures recall as an SLO, re-embeds when the model changes or lays a vector collection across shards — and those are exactly the questions a senior who owns a RAG pipeline is asked: why did adding a filter destroy recall, why is brute force faster than our index, why did recall drop after the rebuild, and why does the coordinator lose true neighbours. This module is the declared owner of hybrid retrieval, the embedding lifecycle and vector topology: Part 2's tries-learned-and-vector-indexes owns the static ANN structures and the churn mechanism, search-and-vector-retrieval owns the lexical half these stages fuse with, index-selection-strategy only points forward, data-modeling keeps the chunk/version table shape and links here for re-embedding, and databases-and-ai-workloads and retrieval-toy-engines-and-frontier apply these rather than re-teach them.

subtopics.title: When a full scan beats an ANN index
subtopics.covers: Exact kNN as a columnar scan with SIMD distance kernels, batching and parallel workers, and the regimes where it wins — corpora in the low millions, per-tenant shards small by construction, filters selective enough that an ANN graph search degenerates or loses recall, guaranteed-recall requirements, and offline or batch scoring where latency is irrelevant; quantized or binary vectors as a cheap first pass with exact rerank over survivors; the implementations (pgvector with no index, ClickHouse and DuckDB distance functions, BigQuery VECTOR_SEARCH brute-force mode, Spark and NumPy batch scoring, Lucene's exact kNN); partition pruning and prefiltering as the real accelerator; and the cost model comparing bytes scanned per query against index build time, resident memory, staleness and rebuild cost.
subtopics.visual: Sliders for corpus size and filter selectivity race a brute-force scan against an HNSW index with live latency, recall, resident memory and build-time readouts, so the learner locates the corpus size where the index starts paying and then tightens the filter until the ANN branch's recall collapses and the scan wins again at the same size.

subtopics.title: Hybrid retrieval and reranking
