subtopics.covers: Lexical BM25 and dense ANN returning different candidate sets, why raw score scales are incomparable and how reciprocal rank fusion sidesteps normalization, Elasticsearch rrf/knn and OpenSearch hybrid pipelines, Vespa multi-phase ranking, pgvector plus tsvector fusion in one statement, cross-encoder reranking of the top-k, late interaction (ColBERT) and learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE), and pre-filter versus post-filter recall cliffs under selective metadata filters.
subtopics.visual: One query runs down two lanes — posting-list intersection and an HNSW graph walk — producing two ranked lists the learner fuses by RRF or weighted score with a slider, then reranks the top-k with a cross-encoder, watching recall@k, latency and cost accumulate per stage while a filter-selectivity slider makes post-filter recall visibly collapse.

subtopics.title: Embedding lifecycle and vector index operations
subtopics.covers: Choosing dimensionality and metric (cosine versus inner product versus L2 and the normalization requirement), build cost and memory budget for HNSW (M, efConstruction, per-segment builds), measuring recall against a brute-force ground truth as an SLO, quantization rollouts with full-vector rerank, re-embedding when the model changes via a shadow index and alias cutover — the single owner of that animation, which data-modeling's 'Schema for embeddings' links to rather than repeating — per-tenant index partitioning, and cost per million vectors in pgvector versus a dedicated store.
subtopics.visual: The learner loads a vector set, picks dimension, metric and quantization and watches build time, resident memory and measured recall against brute force, then triggers a model change and steps a zero-downtime re-embed — shadow index filling, recall-parity check, alias flip — with a cost and p99 meter per configuration; build spec: ship two precomputed embedding sets for the 'model change', since no model can run inside the page.

subtopics.title: Vector search topology: shards, replicas and per-shard top-k
subtopics.covers: Laying a vector collection across shards and replicas — routing by tenant or partition key so each shard's graph stays small, replicas buying query throughput at the price of duplicating a resident graph per copy, per-shard top-k fan-out and coordinator merge and why per-shard k must exceed the requested k or true neighbours are silently dropped, memory-mapped versus in-RAM graphs and DiskANN-style SSD serving as the capacity lever when the graph no longer fits, rebalancing cost when a shard splits, and how the per-segment churn and rebuild mechanism (owned by Part 2's tries-learned-and-vector-indexes) sets the per-shard maintenance budget.
subtopics.visual: A query fans out across a configurable number of shards and replicas, each returning its own top-k from a rendered graph walk, and the learner shrinks the per-shard k until true neighbours — highlighted against a brute-force ground truth — vanish from the merged result, while shard count, replica count and memory-mapped versus in-RAM mode move resident memory, p99 and recall.

modules.title: Connections and Pooling: Process Models, Poolers and Serverless Access
modules.why: A connection is the most expensive object an application creates and the one it manages worst: a PostgreSQL backend is a process with private memory and a handshake, the worker model (fork, threads or an event loop) silently decides how many of them a deploy demands, and the pooler that multiplexes them trades away exactly the session state your framework assumes — so connection budget, pooling mode and process model, not the executor, decide whether the database falls over under a traffic burst.

subtopics.title: Connection lifecycle and cost: TCP, TLS, SCRAM and process-per-connection
subtopics.covers: A fresh PostgreSQL connection pays TCP handshake + TLS 1.3 (1-RTT, 2 for TLS 1.2 without resumption) + the four-message SCRAM-SHA-256 exchange + startup parameters before the first query, then a fork()ed backend with private memory and cold catalog caches whose count inflates ProcArray snapshot cost and lock-manager contention (MySQL uses thread-per-connection with a thread cache or thread pool instead), so max_connections plus superuser_reserved_connections is a memory and contention limit rather than a throughput knob, throughput peaks near a few times core count and collapses beyond it, and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout is the rail against connections that hold snapshots and locks while doing nothing.
subtopics.visual: The learner dials app instances x connections-per-instance, core count and TLS settings, and watches backend processes spawn with memory bars, a handshake timeline decomposed into TCP / TLS / SCRAM / startup round trips (toggle session resumption), and a throughput-versus-connections curve that peaks and then collapses as contention and context-switch cost rise.

subtopics.title: Connections across process models: forks, threads and event loops
subtopics.covers: Why a socket inherited across fork() cannot be shared (interleaved request/response streams, 'server closed the connection unexpectedly', duplicate protocol state) and the post-fork hooks that dispose and rebuild pools in Gunicorn/uWSGI preload, Celery prefork, Rails/Puma and Passenger; thread-per-request pools versus async drivers (asyncpg, node-postgres, async SQLAlchemy) where concurrency rather than thread count sets backend demand; the sizing arithmetic of processes x threads-or-concurrency x replicas against max_connections and the pooler's own limits; connections held across await points, long CPU sections or external calls; and graceful-shutdown hooks that close connections so a rolling deploy does not strand idle-in-transaction backends.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a worker model and sets processes, threads and per-worker concurrency, watching total backends climb against the server and pooler budgets, then presses fork with the pool created before or after it — the first case showing two children interleaving on one socket until the protocol errors, the second showing clean per-child pools — while a blocking call dropped into the event-loop mode stalls every other task's checkout and inflates its wait-time gauge.

subtopics.title: Connection pooling: PgBouncer modes, session state and pool sizing
subtopics.covers: Session, transaction and statement pooling multiplex many clients over few backends at increasing cost to session state (SET vs SET LOCAL, temp tables, advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, named prepared statements now tracked by PgBouncer 1.21 max_prepared_statements, server_reset_query / DISCARD ALL), in-app pools (HikariCP) versus infrastructure poolers (PgBouncer, pgcat, Odyssey, RDS Proxy, ProxySQL multiplexing) sized by Little's law (connections = throughput x service time) and the cores-times-two-plus-spindles rule, with queueing versus rejecting at pool exhaustion and an idle-in-transaction client pinning a backend as the classic exhaustion cause.
subtopics.visual: Clients -> pooler -> N backends: the learner picks a pooling mode and fires BEGIN / SET / PREPARE / COMMIT sequences from several clients, watching each statement land on a backend, a session-level SET leak to another client in transaction mode, one idle-in-transaction client pin a backend while the wait queue grows, and a pool-size slider plotted against the Little's-law optimum.

subtopics.title: Serverless and edge access: connection management without a long-lived process
subtopics.covers: Per-invocation compute breaks every assumption of the pooling model — one backend per concurrent invocation, TLS and auth handshakes on every cold start, frozen containers holding sockets with no graceful close, connections leaking until an idle timeout — and the answers each cost something: external and regional poolers (RDS Proxy with its pinning rules, PgBouncer/pgcat/Supavisor sidecars, Cloudflare Hyperdrive with pooling plus opt-in query result caching, Prisma Accelerate), HTTP and WebSocket drivers (Neon's serverless driver, PlanetScale and D1 HTTP APIs, Aurora Data API, DynamoDB's HTTP model) that trade interactive transactions for one-shot round trips, module-scope client reuse across warm invocations, the session state and named prepared statements transaction pooling forbids, provisioned concurrency, idempotent retries for invocations that resume after a freeze, and the physics that running compute at the edge against one-region data moves latency rather than removing it.
subtopics.visual: A traffic burst hits four access paths — long-lived server with a pool, TCP per invocation, regional pooler, HTTP one-shot driver — from edge functions in three cities, while the learner raises concurrency and watches per-path backend-connection gauges hit max_connections, a per-request timeline decompose DNS / TLS / auth / query / RTT, sockets stuck idle-in-transaction after a container freeze, a pinning toggle silently degrade a transaction-mode proxy to session mode, and a cache toggle collapse repeat queries to near zero.

subtopics.title: Driver and client-library upgrades: auth plugins, TLS defaults and protocol negotiation
subtopics.covers: The client half of the upgrade matrix — authentication method changes that break old drivers (PostgreSQL md5 to scram-sha-256 requiring a libpq/JDBC minimum and a re-hash of every stored password, MySQL 8's caching_sha2_password and the mysql_native_password fallback), TLS defaults tightening (verify-full by default, dropped protocol versions, CA-bundle rotation on managed providers), driver major versions that change semantics rather than just API (psycopg2 to psycopg3 moving binding server-side, pgx statement caching, JDBC prepared-statement and reWriteBatchedInserts defaults), pooler compatibility for protocol-level prepared statements and session state, and the rollout discipline of upgrading clients ahead of the server requirement, keeping a fallback method open during the window and testing the client-by-server version matrix before either side moves (server-side and rolling cluster upgrades themselves belong to running-databases-capacity-platforms-upgrades).
subtopics.visual: A version matrix of client drivers against server versions where the learner upgrades one axis at a time and each cell replays the actual handshake — startup, auth method negotiation, TLS verification, prepared-statement setup through a pooler — turning green, degraded or failed with the exact error the application would log, and a rollout timeline shows which order of client-then-server (or the reverse) produces a window with no working combination.

modules.title: Migrating Large Live Tables and Non-Relational Stores
modules.why: Past a few hundred gigabytes the ordinary online-DDL tricks run out and the change has to be staged through a shadow or ghost table, a partition attach or a shadow column with its own trigger, backfill and cut-over — and outside the relational engines the schema lives in documents, gossiped table definitions and retained event streams where old versions never stop arriving; these are the mechanisms behind the largest, scariest and most common migrations a senior engineer will own.

subtopics.title: Schema evolution in NoSQL and event streams
subtopics.covers: Schema-on-read drift and the per-store DDL mechanics that manage it: a document version field with upgrade-on-read plus a background rewrite job (MongoDB, with $jsonSchema validators at validationLevel moderate), DynamoDB where adding attributes is free but key or GSI changes mean a new table or a throttled GSI backfill, Cassandra ALTER TABLE ADD propagated by gossip schema agreement (and schema-disagreement failures) with immutable primary keys, Iceberg column-ID evolution that makes rename and reorder metadata-only, and the operational consequence of retained and compacted topics keeping old event versions forever — deserializers must carry an upcaster chain from every historical version to the current one rather than assume readers were upgraded (registry compatibility rules and field-by-field resolution live in Data Modeling; the F1 state machine in Distributed Architectures).
subtopics.visual: A store holding documents at versions v1–v3 plus a compacted topic retaining old event versions: the learner adds, renames or removes a field and picks a strategy (upgrade-on-read, background rewrite, upcaster chain), then watches per-read upgrade paths light up, the rewrite job's progress and residual old-version count, and a store toggle showing the same change as a free attribute add in DynamoDB, a GSI backfill, a Cassandra gossip schema-agreement round, or an Iceberg metadata-only column-ID edit.

subtopics.title: Online schema change tools: gh-ost, pt-osc and InnoDB online DDL
subtopics.covers: Three ways to change a table nobody can lock: InnoDB INPLACE online DDL that builds the new structure while a row log captures concurrent DML and replays it under a brief exclusive MDL (and fails if innodb_online_alter_log_max_size overflows); pt-online-schema-change's shadow table with INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers on the original, chunked PK-range copy with chunk-time targeting, FK handling (rebuild_constraints vs drop_swap) and atomic RENAME; gh-ost's triggerless design that reads ROW binlog as a fake replica, interleaves binlog apply with row copy (INSERT IGNORE for copy, REPLACE for binlog so races converge), throttles on replica lag and thread counts, and cuts over with a sentry-table lock-and-rename dance; plus pg_repack and Vitess online DDL as the same shape elsewhere.
subtopics.visual: A ghost-table simulator with original table, ghost table and a binlog stream: the learner sets live write rate and throttle thresholds and watches the chunk cursor advance, binlog events land on the ghost table (with a race on the same row resolved by INSERT IGNORE vs REPLACE), replica lag pause the copy, and the final lock-and-rename cut-over; a pt-osc toggle replaces the binlog with triggers and shows added latency on every original-table write.

subtopics.title: Partitioning a large table that is already in production
subtopics.covers: Converting an unpartitioned hot table without a window — the copy route (create the partitioned parent, backfill in keyset-ranged chunks, mirror the tail by trigger or dual write, verify by counts and checksums, rename-swap in one short transaction) versus the attach route where the existing table becomes one partition under a matching CHECK constraint so ATTACH PARTITION skips its validation scan — plus the constraints the conversion forces (every unique and primary key must contain the partition key, inbound foreign keys, sequences and defaults, whether to have a DEFAULT partition at all, indexes built on each partition before attach), the tool equivalents (pg_partman's conversion helpers, pt-online-schema-change, gh-ost, MySQL ALTER TABLE ... PARTITION BY, Vitess), and the cheaper alternative of throttled batched archival deletes when retention rather than pruning was the actual requirement.
subtopics.visual: A 500M-row table under live writes that the learner converts by either route, watching chunk progress, trigger-mirrored tail rows, the lock mode and duration of every step and a running checksum diff, while a mis-ordered step — swapping before the tail has caught up, or attaching without the matching CHECK constraint — produces either silently lost rows or a full validation scan that blocks traffic for the length of the table.

subtopics.title: Key and type migrations: int to bigint and primary key changes
subtopics.covers: Sequence exhaustion at 2^31−1 (monitored via pg_sequences against the column's max) and why ALTER COLUMN TYPE bigint is a full rewrite plus index rebuild under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, so the recipe is a shadow column: ADD COLUMN new_id bigint, a sync trigger, batched backfill, CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, a NOT VALID/validated CHECK to prove NOT NULL, ADD CONSTRAINT PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX under a brief lock, sequence re-ownership, the same dance on every referencing FK column with ADD FOREIGN KEY NOT VALID → VALIDATE, and a single-transaction rename; with InnoDB's PK change rebuilding the clustered index and every secondary index, enum limits (ADD VALUE only, no removal), and partition-key changes needing a new table and copy.
subtopics.visual: A sequence counter racing toward 2^31 at the current insert rate with a countdown: the learner executes the shadow-column steps in order and each step shows the lock taken and its duration relative to table size, the trigger mirroring writes into new_id, referencing tables lighting up as they need their own conversion, and an out-of-order step (SET NOT NULL without the validated CHECK) triggering a full-scan lock that stalls the traffic lane.

parts.title: Distributed Foundations: Failure, Consistency, Time and Truth
parts.summary: Why distribute at all, the consistency model hierarchy, clocks and ordering, and failure detection with leases and fencing — the rules before the protocols.

modules.title: Why Distribute: Goals, Failure Models and the Rules of the Game
modules.why: Partial failure, tail latency and metastable overload are the new physics once data leaves one machine; this module fixes the goals, the timing and failure assumptions, and the vocabulary that every later protocol (consistency models, clocks, failure detection, replication, consensus) is judged against.

subtopics.title: Scale up vs scale out; shared-nothing vs shared-disk
subtopics.covers: Why a single box hits a wall (price/performance curve, NUMA and lock contention, one failure domain) versus scaling out over shared-nothing nodes (Cassandra rings, CockroachDB ranges, Postgres primary plus replicas), shared-disk (Oracle RAC cache fusion) and disaggregated storage (Aurora, Neon, Snowflake), with Amdahl's law and the Universal Scalability Law's contention (sigma) and coherency (kappa, glossed once as 'crosstalk') terms explaining why throughput bends over and eventually falls as nodes are added — fitting that model to measurements is deferred to performance-literacy-and-tradeoffs and the full architecture families to distributed-architectures.
subtopics.visual: The learner adds nodes to a cluster and watches individual requests animate through the coordination point each family forces — a router hop plus snapshot/lock acquisition for shared-nothing, a cache-fusion block transfer between peers for shared-disk, a log-service round trip for disaggregated storage — while the simulation meters per-node serialized time and cross-node coherency time and plots measured throughput against node count, so the knee and the retrograde tail emerge from the simulated hops rather than from a formula.

subtopics.title: The three goals: scalability, availability and latency
subtopics.covers: Load parameters (QPS, working-set size, read/write mix, fan-out ratio) that define what 'scale' means; availability as nines with MTBF/MTTR arithmetic, series vs parallel composition and the correlated-failure trap (rack, AZ, region, shared control plane, bad deploy) that makes redundancy worthless unless failures are independent and failover is correct; latency floors set by light in fiber (~5 us/km, 70-150 ms cross-region RTT) that bound any synchronous coordination, e.g. Spanner multi-region commit vs a single-region DynamoDB write; and, closing the loop, the first-look tension between the three — waiting for remote acknowledgements buys agreement while not waiting buys speed and uptime, so when a partition arrives a system either refuses (etcd, Spanner) or answers with possibly stale data (Cassandra, a Postgres async replica), with formal CAP/PACELC left to consistency-models and quorum arithmetic to leaderless-quorums-crdts.
subtopics.visual: The learner places replicas on a world map, chooses sync/async/quorum acknowledgement and a client location, then partitions or kills a region or AZ; computed write latency, read latency, read staleness and availability (nines) update live, a marker slides along a consistency-vs-availability axis showing whether each side refuses or answers stale, and a failure-correlation slider shows the nines collapsing as failures stop being independent.

subtopics.title: Fallacies of distributed computing and partial failure
subtopics.covers: Deutsch's eight fallacies made concrete: messages are lost, delayed, duplicated and reordered (TCP retransmits, head-of-line blocking, incast), nodes pause without warning (stop-the-world GC, VM migration, swap, fsync stalls) and partitions are common and often asymmetric (Bailis and Kingsbury, 'The Network is Reliable'), so every RPC has three outcomes — success, failure, unknown — and a timeout can never distinguish slow from dead (Two Generals), which is why at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handling is the default contract.
subtopics.visual: A two-node RPC simulator: the learner sends requests through a network with drop, delay, duplicate, reorder and server-pause knobs, and a split view contrasts what the client concluded ('timed out', 'ok') with what the server actually did (executed once, twice or never), tallying success/failure/unknown outcomes over time.

subtopics.title: Anatomy of a distributed request
subtopics.covers: Every hop of a write in a partitioned, replicated store — client library, router/coordinator (Cassandra coordinator, CockroachDB gateway, DynamoDB request router, Vitess vtgate), partition leader, follower replicas, storage, ack path — plus the cluster metadata (partition map, leader, epoch/term) that clients cache and that goes stale, producing NotLeader redirects, retries and the 'ack lost after commit' case where the client cannot know whether its write landed; client retry policy and idempotency keys are covered in application-access and application-data-patterns.
subtopics.visual: Step-through of one write across a 3-node, 2-partition cluster: the learner clicks each hop to reveal the message and the metadata it relies on, and can inject a failure at any hop (dropped request, dropped ack, stale partition map, leader change mid-flight) to watch redirects, retries and the final client-visible outcome — including a committed write the client believes failed.

subtopics.title: System models: synchrony, crash-stop and Byzantine
subtopics.covers: The assumptions a protocol is allowed to make: timing models (synchronous, asynchronous, partially synchronous with an unknown global stabilization time — Dwork, Lynch and Stockmeyer) and failure models (crash-stop, crash-recovery with stable storage, omission, Byzantine), guarantees stated as safety vs liveness, and what each combination permits — crash-tolerant consensus needs 2f+1 nodes and partial synchrony for liveness, Byzantine tolerance needs 3f+1 (PBFT), and practically all databases (Raft in etcd/CockroachDB/TiKV, Paxos in Spanner) assume crash-recovery, non-Byzantine nodes; FLP itself is treated in failure-detection-leases-fencing.
subtopics.visual: A model-picker grid (timing x failure) where the learner selects a cell and runs a small 'wait for k acks then commit' protocol against an adversary granted exactly that model's powers (delay unboundedly, crash, restart from stable storage, or lie); the tool animates which property — safety or liveness — the adversary can break, while the minimum cluster size (2f+1 vs 3f+1) and required k update with the selection.

subtopics.title: Tail latency, fan-out and hedged requests
subtopics.covers: Dean and Barroso's 'The Tail at Scale': with fan-out N the chance a request stays under the per-server p99 is 0.99^N, so a 100-shard scatter-gather hits its p99 on nearly every request; tail sources (queueing above ~70% utilization, GC and compaction pauses, hot keys, noisy neighbours, disk stalls, head-of-line blocking) and tail-tolerant techniques — hedged requests after the p95, tied requests with cross-server cancellation, micro-partitions and selective replication, latency-induced probation — and the extra load they cost (Bigtable, Cassandra speculative retry, gRPC hedging); percentiles and coordinated omission are measured in performance-literacy-and-tradeoffs.
subtopics.visual: A fan-out simulator where the learner sets N backends and each backend's latency distribution with a stall probability, watches the composite latency histogram's p99 climb as N grows, then enables hedged requests (tunable trigger percentile) or tied requests and sees the tail collapse alongside an 'extra load' meter showing the duplicated work.

subtopics.title: Metastable failures and cascading overload
subtopics.covers: Bronson et al.'s metastable failures: a transient trigger (deploy, traffic spike, one slow dependency) pushes the system into a state that a sustaining feedback loop keeps collapsed after the trigger is gone — retry amplification (r retries per layer gives r^depth requests), connection storms that exhaust pools and burn CPU on TLS/auth handshakes, timeouts that expire while work is still queued so completed work is wasted, and queue growth that raises latency and provokes more retries — countered by retry budgets (Finagle/Envoy ~10%), exponential backoff with jitter, deadline propagation and timeout budgets, bounded queues with load shedding (CoDel, adaptive concurrency limits), backpressure and circuit breakers, with goodput rather than throughput as the objective; incident-side handling lives in backups-incidents-disaster-recovery.
subtopics.visual: A closed-loop simulation of retrying clients in front of a bounded-capacity server queue: the learner fires a brief load spike, watches goodput collapse and stay collapsed after the spike ends (drawn as a hysteresis loop on a load-vs-goodput phase diagram), then toggles retry budgets, jittered backoff, deadline propagation, queue caps with shedding or a circuit breaker to see which interventions return the system to its stable state and how far load must otherwise drop.

modules.title: Networks, RPC and the Shape of Partial Failure
modules.why: Every distributed mechanism later in the course — replication streams, heartbeats, quorum messages, commit protocols — rides on an unreliable network that can drop, duplicate, reorder, delay and asymmetrically cut messages, and an engineer who has not internalized exactly which of those the wire permits will design protocols whose safety argument quietly assumes a network that does not exist.

subtopics.title: What the wire actually does: TCP, TLS, buffers and RTT
subtopics.covers: The path a database message takes from a write() through socket buffers, the congestion and receive windows, TLS record framing and the network, and why throughput is bounded by window over RTT rather than by link speed.
subtopics.visual: A packet-level animation of one request in flight with sliders for RTT, loss rate and window size, showing the congestion window sawtooth and the resulting effective throughput next to the link's nominal bandwidth.

subtopics.title: Message delivery: loss, duplication, reordering and head-of-line blocking
subtopics.covers: Which hazards a stream protocol removes and which it merely hides, how a single stalled message blocks everything queued behind it, and why application-level ordering assumptions break across connections.
subtopics.visual: A message channel with toggles for drop, duplicate, delay and reorder, feeding a receiver whose apply loop is shown step by step so the learner sees exactly which hazard corrupts its state.

subtopics.title: RPC semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once and idempotent servers
subtopics.covers: The three delivery guarantees, why a timeout leaves the caller unable to distinguish lost request from lost reply, and how a server-side dedup table plus a request id converts at-least-once into effectively-once.
subtopics.visual: A sequence diagram where the learner kills the request, the reply or the server between apply and acknowledge, and watches the dedup table decide whether the operation is executed once, twice or not at all.

subtopics.title: Retries, jitter and retry budgets: when retrying makes the outage
subtopics.covers: Retry amplification across a call fan-out, why synchronized backoff re-converges without jitter, and how budgets, deadlines and circuit breakers bound the extra load a struggling dependency receives.
subtopics.visual: A multi-tier fleet simulator with retry count, backoff, jitter and budget knobs that plots offered load against the amplification factor and shows the system tipping into a self-sustaining retry storm.

subtopics.title: Flow control and backpressure: bounded queues and where bytes pile up
subtopics.covers: How a fast producer and a slow consumer fill the queues between them, why unbounded buffering converts a throughput problem into a latency and memory problem, and where backpressure must be applied to be effective.
subtopics.visual: A pipeline of bounded queues between client, proxy and server where the learner sets each queue depth and consumer rate, watching latency and resident bytes explode when backpressure is disabled at any one stage.

subtopics.title: Partitions in the wild: asymmetric loss, gray failure and the one-way link
subtopics.covers: That real partitions are rarely clean cluster halves — one-way links, partial packet loss, an overloaded node that answers heartbeats but not work, and why these break protocols that assume symmetric connectivity.
subtopics.visual: A cluster topology editor where the learner cuts individual directed links and watches which nodes still believe they are leader, which can still form a quorum, and which pair of nodes disagrees about who is alive.

modules.title: Consistency Models and Impossibility Results
modules.why: A consistency model is a precise statement of which histories a replicated system may produce; linearizability and its weaker siblings are the only honest vocabulary for what a system promises, and CAP, PACELC, harvest/yield and the highly-available-transactions results only make sense once that vocabulary is in place.

subtopics.title: Histories, registers and linearizability
subtopics.covers: A history is a sequence of invocation/response events from concurrent clients against a sequential specification (read/write/CAS register), and it is linearizable iff a total order exists that respects real-time precedence of non-overlapping operations and the spec — equivalently each operation takes effect at a linearization point inside its interval — which makes linearizability compositional (local per object) unlike serializability, costs at least a majority or lease-holder round trip per operation, and is NP-complete to check in general (the automated search behind Knossos/Porcupine belongs to the verification module).
subtopics.visual: A manual linearization puzzle: the learner drags and resizes operation intervals (write x, read → v, CAS) on per-client timelines for a single register and then places the linearization point inside each interval by hand, while the tool only validates the two rules — real-time precedence and the register spec — circling the exact read that returns a value already overwritten before its own invocation when no placement can work.

subtopics.title: The hierarchy: sequential, causal, PRAM and eventual
subtopics.covers: Each weaker model is defined by which orderings it stops enforcing — sequential consistency keeps one total order and per-process order but drops real time (ZooKeeper reads), causal consistency keeps only happens-before so concurrent writes may be observed in different orders (COPS/Eiger dependency tracking, MongoDB causal sessions), PRAM/FIFO keeps only each process's write order, and eventual consistency promises only convergence with no bound on anomalies (Cassandra, Dynamo) — arranged in the Viotti–Vukolić / Jepsen lattice where 'strong consistency' in vendor docs may mean any of these.
subtopics.visual: A history editor with a strongest-model checker: the learner places reads and writes on several client timelines and the lattice lights the strongest node the history satisfies (linearizable → sequential → causal → PRAM → eventual), then a 'minimal edit' button shows the single operation move that drops the history exactly one level and why.

subtopics.title: Session guarantees: read-your-writes, monotonic reads and causal sessions
subtopics.covers: Terry et al.'s per-client guarantees — read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads, whose union is PRAM plus WFR = causal for one session — are honored by carrying a session token (a version vector, Postgres LSN, MySQL GTID set, or MongoDB clusterTime/operationTime) that a replica must catch up to before answering or else redirect, which is exactly why these guarantees are 'sticky' and cost nothing until the client switches replicas (the routing mechanics on real replicas live in the replication module).
subtopics.visual: A session-token tracer: the learner issues writes and reads from one client that a load balancer bounces between three replicas with independent lag sliders; the token with its version vector rides on every request, each guarantee can be toggled on individually, and the tool shows the replica either delaying the read until it has applied the token's version, redirecting it, or (guarantee off) returning the anomalous stale value flagged by name.

subtopics.title: CAP and PACELC done right
subtopics.covers: Gilbert–Lynch's formal CAP says a read/write register in an asynchronous network cannot be both linearizable and available (every request to a non-failed node eventually returns) once a partition occurs, and since partitions are not optional the real choice is per-operation behavior during one — so whole-system CP/AP labels and 'CA' are category errors — while Abadi's PACELC adds the everyday else-case where synchronous coordination trades latency for consistency (Spanner PC/EC, Cassandra and DynamoDB PA/EL, MongoDB PC/EC, an async Postgres replica PA/EC).
subtopics.visual: A two-replica register with a partition toggle where the learner plays the adversary: they pick a per-side policy (refuse, serve local, wait) and send reads and writes from clients on both sides, and the tool either counts a linearizability violation or a blocked request for every run, proving by exhaustion that no policy can achieve both once the partition is in place, and then shows the PACELC latency cost of each policy with the partition healed.

subtopics.title: Harvest, yield and degraded modes
subtopics.covers: Fox and Brewer's reframing of availability as yield (fraction of requests answered) times harvest (fraction of the data each answer reflects) turns CAP into an engineering knob — search and analytics fan-outs return partial harvest, transactional systems reduce yield instead — and gives the vocabulary for orthogonal, independently failing shards, circuit breakers as deliberate harvest reducers, and explicit degraded-mode contracts that callers can detect rather than silently stale results.
subtopics.visual: A query fans out to N shards drawn as a scatter-gather tree; the learner kills or partitions shards and chooses a policy (fail the whole request, return partial results with a flag, or serve a stale cached answer), and harvest and yield gauges plus a divergence-from-truth meter update per request while the response payload shows exactly which rows went missing.

subtopics.title: The availability boundary: which models survive a partition
subtopics.covers: Bailis's Highly Available Transactions result draws the line CAP only hints at, in three classes: totally available under partition with clients free to roam — read uncommitted, read committed, monotonic atomic view, item cut isolation and predicate cut isolation; only sticky available, meaning the client must stay pinned to one replica or carry its own version/causal-context token — read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads, PRAM and causal consistency; and provably unavailable — linearizability, sequential consistency, snapshot isolation, repeatable read over predicates and serializability; with the neighbouring results the classes are usually reaching for stated separately and attributed correctly, Mahajan–Setty–Alvisi showing that real-time causal consistency (real-time causal, not plain causal) is the strongest model achievable in an always-available, one-way convergent system, and Attiya–Ellen–Morrison proving lower bounds on the per-operation cost of highly available eventually consistent stores — which together are why Cosmos DB, Cassandra and Riak stop where they do and why the Jepsen map's availability classes are drawn where they are.
subtopics.visual: The lattice itself is the artifact: one generated workload runs simultaneously against every model under a single partition, and each lattice node is colored live as servable or blocking with the one offending request named inside it — flipping the stickiness switch is the discovery, moving the boundary so that read-your-writes, monotonic reads, PRAM and causal all go from red to green while RU/RC/MAV/cut isolation were green either way and linearizable, sequential, SI and serializable stay red.

subtopics.title: Coordination avoidance: CALM, I-confluence and which invariants really need it
subtopics.covers: The CALM theorem (a program has a coordination-free, eventually consistent implementation exactly when it is monotonic) explaining why set insertion, max and grow-only counters need no coordination while deletion-then-read, thresholds and unique assignment do, Bailis's I-confluence test asking whether merging two invariant-satisfying states can violate the invariant and its per-constraint verdicts (foreign-key insert and per-row CHECK are I-confluent; uniqueness, non-negative balance and global limits are not), the design consequences — append-only models, embedding the unique value in the partition key so all claims meet in one log, escrow for bounded quantities, read-only-ish home regions — and the Bloom/Bloom^L languages that check monotonicity statically, tying back to why CRDTs converge but cannot enforce a bound.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks an invariant and a pair of operations, runs them on two partitioned replicas that then merge, and the tool either shows every interleaving merging cleanly with the coordination-free path highlighted, or produces the merged state that violates the invariant and then offers the minimum fix — route the key through one partition, take an escrow reservation, or run a consensus round — with the latency each adds shown against the coordination-free baseline.

subtopics.title: Isolation meets consistency: strict serializability and friends
subtopics.covers: Transaction isolation (multi-object, no real-time constraint) and replica consistency (single-object, real-time) are orthogonal axes that must both be stated, combining into Jepsen's merged hierarchy where strict serializability = serializable + linearizable commit order (Spanner's external consistency via commit-wait, FoundationDB) sits above serializable-but-not-strict (CockroachDB's causal-reverse and stale-read anomalies under clock skew found by Jepsen) and 'strong' vs generalized snapshot isolation, and where replication introduces its own anomalies — stale-read-then-write, long fork, causal reverse — that Adya's graphs only capture once a real-time edge is added.
subtopics.visual: A two-axis picker (isolation level × replica consistency) drives scenario runs across two shards; for each run the tool draws the Adya dependency graph with an extra dashed real-time edge, highlights the cycle that appears only when that edge is included, names the anomaly (long fork, causal reverse, stale read), and overlays which real systems claim and which Jepsen observed at that grid cell.

subtopics.title: The latency price of consistency: Attiya-Welch and Lipton-Sandberg bounds
subtopics.covers: The formal result that in an asynchronous network with message-delay uncertainty u, linearizable read latency plus write latency is bounded below by roughly u (and sequential consistency lets you make reads OR writes local but never both, while causal and eventual consistency can make both local), why this is the theorem behind every real workaround — Raft leader leases and ReadIndex, CockroachDB closed timestamps and follower reads, Spanner's commit-wait paying the bound in clock uncertainty instead of messages, DynamoDB's eventually-consistent read at half price — and how to use it in a design review to reject 'local linearizable reads in every region' before reading the implementation.
subtopics.visual: A two-region register where the learner sets one-way delay and timing uncertainty and then tries to configure read and write latency below the bound, with a history checker generating the concrete violating interleaving every time the sum dips under u, and lease and stale-read toggles showing which guarantee had to be surrendered to buy the local read.

subtopics.title: Where you actually need linearizability
subtopics.covers: Uniqueness constraints, leader election and locks (which still need fencing tokens, in the failure-detection module), account balances and inventory reservations, exactly-once side effects and cross-channel timing dependencies (the image-resize race) genuinely require a linearizable operation such as CAS on a consensus log, at the price of a quorum or lease round trip — Raft read-index vs lease reads vs quorum reads in the consensus module — while feeds, counters, analytics and most reads can be safely downgraded to bounded-staleness or follower reads (Spanner stale reads, CockroachDB AS OF SYSTEM TIME, DynamoDB eventually consistent reads).
subtopics.visual: A username-registration service backed by three replicas whose consistency the learner selects from the lattice; they race two clients registering the same name, plus a cross-channel scenario that uploads then notifies via a side channel, and watch duplicate accounts or a not-found-on-resize appear or not per model while a latency meter shows what each stronger model costs per region.

modules.title: Time, Clocks and Ordering
modules.why: Ordering events without a trustworthy clock is the core trick behind every replication, conflict-resolution and distributed-transaction protocol.

subtopics.title: Physical clocks, NTP and their failures
subtopics.covers: Quartz oscillators drift tens of ppm (seconds per day), NTP corrects by slewing (adjtime, at most 500 ppm) or stepping when the offset exceeds 128 ms, leap seconds arrive as a repeated 23:59:59 unless smeared linearly over 24 h (Google, AWS), CLOCK_REALTIME can jump backwards while CLOCK_MONOTONIC only measures elapsed time, and VM live-migration, GC pauses and mis-configured NTP produce skews of seconds to minutes — the mechanism behind Cloudflare's 2017 leap-second outage (a negative duration from wall-clock subtraction) and behind Cassandra LWW timestamp mishaps, with PTP, GPS-disciplined clocks and cloud time services (AWS Time Sync, chrony) as the bounded-error remedies.
subtopics.visual: Three node timelines with per-node drift sliders (ppm), an NTP poll interval and a slew/step toggle: the learner watches the wall clocks fan apart between corrections and snap or slew back, injects a leap second or a 10 s VM pause, and sees a duration measured with the wall clock go negative while the monotonic clock's reading stays correct.

subtopics.title: Happens-before and why wall clocks cannot order events
subtopics.covers: Lamport's happens-before relation (program order, send-before-receive, transitivity) is the partial order every replication protocol must respect, two events are concurrent when neither reaches the other, and stamping events with skewed wall clocks yields the causal-reverse anomaly in which a write that causally followed another receives the earlier timestamp — the exact mechanism by which Cassandra's client-supplied last-write-wins timestamps silently discard the newer write (LWW versus siblings as a conflict-resolution choice is owned by leaderless-quorums-crdts).
subtopics.visual: One shared MessageTimeline primitive — three process lines, drag to send a message, click to add a local event, history serialized in the URL and reloadable on the four pages that follow — in its happens-before preset: its annotation slot answers a click on any two events with the highlighted causal path or a 'concurrent' verdict, and a skew slider stamps every event with its node's wall clock and reddens each pair whose timestamp order contradicts happens-before, tagging the write LWW would drop.

subtopics.title: Operating on assumed clock bounds
subtopics.covers: Turning "the clock is roughly right" into an operational contract: configuring ntpd/chrony or PTP (hardware timestamping, boundary clocks, sub-microsecond error versus NTP's milliseconds) and cloud time services (AWS Time Sync with ClockBound, GPS/atomic appliances), measuring rather than assuming skew via chronyc tracking, offset/dispersion/root-distance metrics and per-node clock-offset gauges scraped into alerts, how engines enforce the bound they assume — CockroachDB and YugabyteDB compare each node's measured offset against max_offset/max_clock_skew and self-terminate a node that exceeds roughly half of it, MongoDB signs cluster time so no client can push it forward, Cassandra and other LWW stores enforce nothing at all — and what a violated bound actually costs: stale or causally reversed reads, resurrected deletes and lost writes that no retry surfaces, which is why the clock-skew anomalies met earlier in consistency-models are diagnosed and bounded here rather than there.
subtopics.visual: A fleet dashboard where the learner picks a time source (bad NTP, chrony over WAN, PTP, cloud time sync), each source drawing its own error envelope, watches a live offset histogram across ten nodes with a max_offset threshold line, then injects drift or a poll failure on one node and sees the alert fire, the node cross the half-threshold and self-evict, and — with enforcement toggled off — the same skew instead silently reorder two writes on the timeline below.

subtopics.title: Lamport clocks and total order
subtopics.covers: The Lamport clock rules (increment on a local event, attach on send, max(local, received)+1 on receive) guarantee the clock condition a→b implies L(a)<L(b) but not its converse, so unrelated events are ordered arbitrarily by the (timestamp, node id) tiebreak into a total order consistent with causality — the primitive behind Lamport's mutual-exclusion algorithm and the monotone epoch counters in Raft terms, Kafka leader epochs and ZooKeeper's zxid, yet incapable of telling that two updates conflicted.
subtopics.visual: The same MessageTimeline in its Lamport preset, loadable with the history composed on the previous page: the annotation slot ticks a counter beside each event as messages are added, querying two events prints 'L(a)<L(b)' next to the true causal verdict so pairs that are concurrent yet ordered stand out, and a tiebreak toggle collapses every event by (timestamp, node id) onto a single total-order line.

subtopics.title: Consistent global snapshots: cuts and the Chandy-Lamport algorithm
subtopics.covers: A global state as a cut of the space-time diagram and the consistency condition that no received message appears without its send, the Chandy-Lamport marker rules (record local state on the first marker, then record each channel's state as the messages received between markers) that capture a consistent cut with no clock and no pause, why the recorded state may never have physically existed yet is reachable and satisfies every stable predicate (termination, deadlock, garbage), and its production descendants — Flink's aligned and unaligned checkpoint barriers, Spark Structured Streaming's offset commits, distributed deadlock detection — contrasted with timestamp-based snapshots (Spanner TrueTime, a Percolator/TiDB TSO, CockroachDB protected timestamps) that buy the same property by spending synchronized clocks instead of markers.
subtopics.visual: The same MessageTimeline in its Chandy-Lamport preset: pressing snapshot on any process steps markers along the channels while the annotation slot records each process's local state and each channel's in-flight messages and draws the resulting cut across the diagram, and a cut the learner hand-drags instead turns red, naming the received-but-never-sent message that makes it inconsistent.

subtopics.title: Vector clocks and version vectors
subtopics.covers: Vector clocks carry one counter per node and compare as dominates (every component ≤) or concurrent (incomparable), detecting concurrency exactly at the price of O(nodes) size (Charron-Bost shows nothing smaller characterizes causality); version vectors track the versions of one object rather than all events, back sibling detection in Dynamo, Riak and Voldemort, and suffer sibling explosion when clients act as actors and lost causality when truncated (Dynamo's 10-entry prune) — which dotted version vectors (Preguiça et al.) fix by tagging each write with its exact dot so servers keep one entry per replica.
subtopics.visual: The same MessageTimeline in its version-vector preset, the three process lines now three replicas of one object that named clients read and write with replication delay: the annotation slot shows each replica's vector as a column of per-node counters, a comparison panel returns dominates or concurrent for any two versions, concurrent writes visibly spawn siblings, and switching from per-client vectors to dotted version vectors collapses the sibling count under the identical history.

subtopics.title: Ordering without clocks: sequencers and timestamp oracles
subtopics.covers: A single timestamp oracle hands out monotonic integers — Percolator's TSO and TiDB's PD (a physical-ms prefix plus 18-bit logical suffix, an etcd-persisted allocation window renewed every 3 s so a restarted leader skips ahead and never repeats, client-side batching to millions of timestamps per second), Calvin's sequencer that batches inputs into 10 ms epochs for deterministic replay, and log positions used as time (Kafka offsets, Raft indices, Postgres LSNs, ZooKeeper zxid) — buying a total order at the cost of one extra round trip, a single point of failure and a hard throughput ceiling.
subtopics.visual: Clients fire timestamp requests at an oracle: the learner adjusts client batch size and the persisted-window length, watches per-request latency versus timestamps/second and the leader's persisted high-water mark, then kills the oracle and sees requests stall until the new leader resumes from the persisted mark, leaving a visible gap in the issued sequence.

subtopics.title: TrueTime: the interval API
subtopics.covers: Spanner's TT.now() returns an interval [earliest, latest] rather than a point and TT.after(t)/TT.before(t) are the only questions asked of it; ε is a sawtooth (about 1 ms right after a 30 s master poll, growing roughly 200 µs/s to about 7 ms) derived from GPS and atomic-clock time masters that a Marzullo-style algorithm cross-checks to evict liars; two events can be ordered iff their intervals are disjoint, which is how Paxos leader-lease disjointness and safe-time snapshot reads are proven, and AWS ClockBound/Time Sync expose the same interval abstraction (commit-wait itself lives in distributed-transactions).
subtopics.visual: An ε-over-time chart animating the sawtooth as the timeslave daemon polls masters, with knobs for poll interval, local drift rate and a 'liar master' injection; below it the learner places events on two nodes and the tool draws their TrueTime intervals, answering TT.after/TT.before with a definite order when intervals are disjoint and 'unknown' when they overlap.

subtopics.title: Hybrid logical clocks
subtopics.covers: HLC (Kulkarni et al.) keeps a tuple (l, c) where l tracks max(physical time, received l) and c counts events sharing the same l, so timestamps stay within a bounded distance of wall time, respect happens-before and fit in 64 bits; CockroachDB and YugabyteDB build on the max_offset bound operated in the earlier page to give every transaction an uncertainty interval [ts, ts+max_offset] in which any observed value forces a ReadWithinUncertaintyInterval restart, while MongoDB's cluster time is an HLC carried on every message so causality survives across sessions (the full transaction protocol is in distributed-transactions).
subtopics.visual: The same MessageTimeline in its HLC preset with per-node skew sliders: the annotation slot prints each event's (l, c) pair beside a drift meter showing |l − physical| staying bounded, and a read issued at ts against a value written at ts' inside the uncertainty window fires a visible ReadWithinUncertaintyInterval restart whose rate and window both grow as the learner widens max_offset.

modules.title: Failure Detection, Membership, Leases and Fencing
modules.why: Deciding who is alive and who holds authority is the mechanism behind failover, and getting it wrong is the origin of split brain.

subtopics.title: Failure detectors and FLP: why slow is indistinguishable from dead
subtopics.covers: Chandra-Toueg's completeness/accuracy taxonomy (P, eventually-perfect ◇P, the Ω leader oracle) and why only the eventually-perfect class is implementable in a partially synchronous network, the FLP result (no deterministic consensus in an asynchronous system with one crash) as the reason every real detector is a timeout, and how GC pauses, VM migrations and asymmetric partitions make a live node look dead so that every failover protocol must survive a false positive.
subtopics.visual: A cluster of nodes exchanging heartbeats where the learner drags a per-link latency distribution (median, variance, packet-loss) and a timeout slider, then injects a GC pause on one node; live counters show detection delay vs false-positive rate for each timeout, and the paused node is declared dead by its peers, resumes, and keeps acting while a red 'divergent world view' badge marks each peer that disagrees about who is alive.

subtopics.title: Heartbeats, timeouts and phi accrual detection
subtopics.covers: Fixed heartbeat timeouts versus the phi accrual detector (Hayashibara et al.) that turns the heartbeat inter-arrival sample window into a continuous suspicion level phi = -log10(P(no heartbeat by now)), Cassandra's phi_convict_threshold=8 and Akka's implementation with their max-sample-size and acceptable-heartbeat-pause knobs, how the application maps phi levels to actions (stop routing reads, then convict), and the failure mode where bimodal latency or an unbounded pause makes the fitted distribution useless.
subtopics.visual: A heartbeat arrival strip fed by a jitter slider and a 'drop next N beats' button: a phi curve climbs in real time after each missing beat, a draggable threshold line shows the exact instant of conviction, and a side-by-side fixed-timeout detector shows how many false convictions each scheme produces over the same arrival trace.

subtopics.title: Gossip protocols: epidemic dissemination and anti-entropy of membership
subtopics.covers: Push, pull and push-pull epidemic dissemination with O(log N) round convergence and fan-out/drop-rate tradeoffs, rumor mongering vs periodic anti-entropy exchange, Cassandra's gossip of per-endpoint state versioned by (generation, version) with heartbeat generations that detect restarts and a three-message SYN/ACK/ACK2 digest exchange, and failure modes such as stale generations after a restart with the same IP, schema-version disagreement and partial partitions where only some links are cut.
subtopics.visual: A 50-node graph where the learner seeds a state change on one node and steps rounds while tuning fan-out, push/pull/push-pull mode and link drop rate; each node colors in as it learns the rumor, a coverage-vs-round curve plots convergence against the log N prediction, and a partial-partition toggle shows the rumor stalling then leaking through the surviving links.

subtopics.title: Classic leader election and why it split-brains
subtopics.covers: The Bully algorithm (highest-id wins after O(N^2) election messages), ring election and the invitation algorithm as pre-consensus recipes that assume a perfect failure detector, the partition scenario in which both sides satisfy the algorithm's precondition and elect a leader that accepts writes, and the historical incidents that followed: Redis Sentinel promoting behind a partition, MongoDB's pre-3.2 election protocol, Elasticsearch clusters with minimum_master_nodes misconfigured, and the principle that a node cannot decide it is leader by itself — a majority must decide for it.
subtopics.visual: A Bully election stepper on 5 nodes where the learner kills the coordinator and watches ELECTION/ANSWER/COORDINATOR messages animate, then draws a partition line through the cluster and sees each side complete its own election; client writes to both leaders accumulate in two diverging logs until the partition heals and the tool highlights which writes must be discarded.

subtopics.title: Leases: time-bounded authority and the pause that breaks it
subtopics.covers: A lease as a lock with an expiry that grants unilateral authority until a deadline, renewal before expiry with a safety margin, the requirement that the holder checks against a monotonic clock while the grantor and holder tolerate bounded drift, expiration-based leases (GFS chunk leases, Chubby master lease, Raft leader leases for local reads) versus CockroachDB's epoch-based range leases tied to a node-liveness heartbeat, and the classic bug where a process checks the lease, pauses for GC or a stopped VM past expiry, resumes and writes as if it still owned the resource.
subtopics.visual: A timeline with two candidate nodes and a lease server: the learner sets lease length, renewal interval and per-node clock drift, then injects a pause of chosen length on the holder; the lease bar expires, the second node acquires it, and when the first node resumes its 'I own the lease' local belief is shown against the server's truth, with a counter of writes it issues while stale.

subtopics.title: Fencing tokens: making the storage layer the last line of defense
subtopics.covers: A monotonically increasing token issued with every lock or lease grant (ZooKeeper zxid, Chubby sequencers, HDFS NameNode epoch, Kafka leader epoch, Raft term, Patroni's etcd lease revision) that the resource itself must check and reject if lower than the highest seen, why Kleppmann's critique of Redlock holds — a lock without a token cannot protect against a paused client — and the storage-side enforcement mechanisms that implement it (conditional writes, S3 If-Match, CAS on an epoch column) contrasted with STONITH, which kills the old holder instead of ignoring it.
subtopics.visual: The lease-pause scenario replayed with a storage service in the picture: with fencing off, the resumed zombie's write lands and corrupts state; with fencing on, each grant carries a token, the storage panel shows its highest-seen token and rejects the stale writer's request with the comparison spelled out, and a third mode shows STONITH cutting the zombie's link instead.

subtopics.title: SWIM and Lifeguard: scalable membership in memberlist, Serf and Consul
subtopics.covers: SWIM's randomized direct ping then indirect ping-req via k peers to distinguish a dead node from a lossy link, the suspect-then-confirm state machine with a suspicion timeout, incarnation numbers that let a suspected node refute with a higher incarnation, infection-style dissemination piggybacked on ping traffic giving constant per-node load, and HashiCorp's Lifeguard refinements — self-awareness that lengthens a slow node's own timeouts, dogpile detection that scales the suspicion timeout by confirmers, and the buddy system that alerts the suspect first — all shipped in memberlist, Serf and Consul.
subtopics.visual: A SWIM ring where the learner pauses, partitions or slows one node and watches per-tick ping, ping-req and ack messages, a suspicion timer with its confirmer count, the incarnation number bump and refutation gossip when the node wakes, and a Lifeguard toggle that shows the same slow node avoiding a false declaration because its self-awareness score raised its own timeouts.

subtopics.title: Membership changes and quorum safety
subtopics.covers: Membership as replicated state that must be agreed before it is used, the disjoint-majorities bug when a cluster moves from 3 to 5 members in one step (a majority of C_old and a majority of C_new that do not intersect), the fix via single-server changes or joint consensus C_old,new whose full treatment lives in the consensus module, etcd learner promotion and Cassandra bootstrap/decommission with token ranges streamed before the node joins gossip as a member, and split-brain protection with odd-sized quorums, witness/tiebreaker nodes and why 2-node clusters cannot be safe.
subtopics.visual: A cluster-resize sandbox: the learner grows 3 to 5 nodes naively and then in staged single-server steps, drags a partition through the cluster mid-transition and tries to select two node sets that each form a majority under some configuration; the tool highlights the window in which two disjoint majorities exist, and a witness-node toggle shows the tiebreaker restoring a unique majority in a 2+1 layout.

parts.title: Replication, Partitioning and Consensus
parts.summary: How data is copied, split and agreed upon: leader-based replication, sharding with modeling for partitioned stores, Dynamo-style quorums and CRDTs, then Paxos, Raft and coordination services.

modules.title: Replication
modules.why: Replication is the first distributed mechanism most engineers operate, and lag, failover data loss and replica reads are its daily consequences; understanding where the ack sits, what the follower actually applies and what happens when the leader dies is the difference between a read replica and a silent data-loss incident.

subtopics.title: Why replicate and the three topologies: single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless
subtopics.covers: Why systems replicate (availability under node loss, read scaling, geo-latency, durability beyond one disk) and the three topologies every later mechanism sits inside — single-leader (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB replica sets), multi-leader (BDR/pgEdge, MySQL Group Replication multi-primary, DynamoDB global tables) and leaderless quorum systems (Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak: client writes to all N and waits for W acks, reads R and takes the newest version, read repair and hinted handoff as the repair path, no failover step because there is no leader) — plus the primary-backup vs state-machine-replication framing and what each topology does to write ordering; quorum arithmetic, anti-entropy and CRDTs get their full treatment in leaderless-quorums-crdts.
subtopics.visual: A three-node cluster with clients in two regions: the learner switches the topology (single-leader / multi-leader / leaderless with N=3, W=2, R=2), sends writes from both regions and steps the message timeline, watching each node's log, which writes wait on which acks, where a read fetches from, and the exact step at which ordering diverges or a conflict appears in each topology.

subtopics.title: Single-leader replication and log formats: physical, logical, statement
subtopics.covers: The leader's change stream in its three shapes and their trade-offs: statement shipping and its nondeterminism (NOW(), RAND(), auto-increment, triggers, UPDATE ... LIMIT without ORDER BY), row/logical changes (MySQL ROW and MIXED binlog, Postgres pgoutput with REPLICA IDENTITY controlling which old-row images are sent, no DDL or sequence replication, cross-version and selective), and physical WAL shipping (Postgres streaming replication, single-threaded startup-process replay, byte-identical same-major-version coupling, whole-cluster granularity, hot standby reads), with MySQL's parallel appliers (LOGICAL_CLOCK/WRITESET dependency tracking) as the way row-based replication escapes serial apply; logical decoding plumbing and CDC pipelines belong to write-ahead-logging-and-recovery and logs-streams-derived-data.
subtopics.visual: The learner types SQL on a leader (including a NOW() update and an auto-increment insert) and toggles statement / row / physical-WAL format, watching the bytes shipped per statement, how the follower applies them (re-execute vs apply row images vs replay page-level WAL records), which old-row fields appear as REPLICA IDENTITY changes, and the moment the statement-format follower silently diverges from the leader.

subtopics.title: Synchronous, asynchronous and semi-synchronous replication
subtopics.covers: Where the commit acknowledgement sits relative to follower persistence: async (ack after local fsync, the unreplicated tail is lost on failover), fully sync (commit latency equals the slowest required follower and commits stall when it dies), Postgres synchronous_commit levels (off/local/remote_write/on/remote_apply) and synchronous_standby_names FIRST n vs ANY n quorum forms, MySQL semi-sync AFTER_SYNC (lossless) vs AFTER_COMMIT and the rpl_semi_sync_master_timeout fallback to async, per-transaction durability overrides, and the production pattern of one in-region sync standby plus async cross-region replicas (RDS Multi-AZ as the managed form).
subtopics.visual: Three followers each with a sync/async toggle, a network-delay slider and a pause button: the learner drives a stream of commits and watches a per-transaction timeline of local-WAL-write, ship, remote-write, remote-flush and remote-apply events, a commit-latency histogram, the live set of 'acknowledged but not durable on any follower' transactions, and the fallback-to-async countdown when a required follower stalls.

subtopics.title: Replication lag anomalies and replica reads
subtopics.covers: What load-balanced replica reads break — read-your-writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix and writes-follow-reads, the session guarantees defined in consistency-models — and the concrete routing policies that cure them: leader or sticky-replica routing for a window after a write, LSN/GTID session tokens (compare pg_last_wal_replay_lsn to the write's commit LSN, MySQL WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET), remote_apply, bounded-staleness and follower reads (CockroachDB AS OF SYSTEM TIME, Spanner stale reads, Cosmos DB bounded staleness), plus measuring lag in bytes vs seconds, the cost each policy shifts onto the primary or the p99, why cross-partition causality still breaks under consistent prefix, and lag's bimodal behaviour under large transactions and DDL.
subtopics.visual: The consistency-models session-token tracer reused inside a policy-editor shell: the learner composes the routing rule (send to primary for N ms after a write / wait until a replica's pg_last_wal_replay_lsn passes the recorded commit LSN / require a GTID set via WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET / accept staleness under T / pin a sticky replica) and replays recorded traffic over lagging replicas, each routed request showing the real artifacts it compared rather than an abstract token, beside a scorecard tallying stale reads served, primary read load and added p99 per policy version.

subtopics.title: Failover, split brain and data loss on async failover
subtopics.covers: The three failover steps — detect (timeouts or an expired lease in etcd/ZooKeeper), choose (most-advanced LSN or GTID set, priorities), repoint (DNS TTLs, VIPs, proxies, connection storms) — and how each fails: promoting a stale follower discards the old leader's acknowledged-but-unreplicated commits (loss window equals the async tail), an unfenced old primary keeps accepting writes so the cluster forks (Postgres timelines, pg_rewind to rejoin, auto-increment collisions), the GitHub 2012/2018 and GitLab 2017 incidents, and why Patroni, Orchestrator, pg_auto_failover and STONITH exist; lease and fencing-token mechanics themselves are covered in failure-detection-leases-fencing.
subtopics.visual: A leader with a sync and an async follower and a lease in a coordination store: the learner partitions the leader at a chosen moment, watches the lease expire, the candidate chosen by log position and promoted onto a new timeline, then writes on both sides with fencing on or off and heals the partition to see which acknowledged commits are kept, rewound away or forked.

subtopics.title: Multi-leader replication and conflict resolution
subtopics.covers: Active-active replication for multi-region write latency and offline clients: star, ring and all-to-all topologies and how replication paths overtaking each other violate causality; the conflict taxonomy (concurrent updates, unique-constraint and auto-increment collisions, delete-vs-update, triggers); detection by version vectors vs wall-clock timestamps; and resolution by avoidance (home-region ownership per user), last-writer-wins (clock-dependent and silently discards updates — DynamoDB global tables), sibling retention, custom merge handlers and CRDTs (previewed here, built in leaderless-quorums-crdts), as implemented in BDR/pgEdge, MySQL Group Replication's certification, and CouchDB.
subtopics.visual: Two regional leaders with a controllable inter-region delay: the learner issues concurrent edits to the same row and colliding unique-key inserts during the delay, picks a topology and a resolver (LWW, keep siblings, custom merge, CRDT counter) and steps replication, watching each leader's version vector, the conflict detected on arrival and the converged value with any lost update highlighted.

subtopics.title: Chain replication and CRAQ
subtopics.covers: Chain replication's head-to-tail write propagation with the tail as the linearization point (reads at the tail are linearizable, read throughput scales with chain length, a master reconfigures the chain on head, middle or tail failure without losing acknowledged writes), CRAQ's clean/dirty version tracking that lets any node serve reads and forces a version query to the tail only when a dirty version exists, apportioned queries for eventual reads, and where the pattern ships — Azure Storage's stream layer, HDFS write pipelines, FAWN/Hibari and object-store replication paths — contrasted with primary-backup and Raft-style majority replication.
subtopics.visual: A four-node chain: the learner pushes writes and watches versions travel head to tail with acks flowing back, reads at each node under plain chain vs CRAQ showing exactly when a dirty version triggers a version query to the tail, then kills the head, a middle node or the tail and steps the master's reconfiguration to verify no acknowledged write is lost.

modules.title: Operating Replication: Slots, GTIDs and Apply Conflicts
modules.why: Understanding replication mechanisms is one thing and running them is another: the pages that actually wake engineers are a stuck apply worker filling the publisher's disk, a slot lost at promotion forcing a full re-snapshot, an errant GTID that quietly makes a replica unpromotable, and a standby cancelling queries because vacuum caught up with its snapshot — each a knob-level fault you can only fix if you know which artifact to read and which recovery action silently drops data.

subtopics.title: Replication in practice: Postgres slots and timelines, MySQL GTIDs, MongoDB replica sets
subtopics.covers: The states and knobs of real single-leader systems: Postgres streaming vs logical replication, replication slots pinning WAL retention (max_slot_wal_keep_size, a stalled consumer filling the disk), timelines and history files, follower bootstrap from a base backup plus catch-up, pg_rewind; delayed standbys (recovery_min_apply_delay, MySQL SOURCE_DELAY) as a tunable RPO for human error — a bad migration or an unqualified DELETE that a normal replica replays in milliseconds — and how to promote one by pausing at a target LSN or recovery_target_time, plus their interaction with hot_standby_feedback and WAL retention; cascading replication (replica-of-replica) to fan out beyond the primary's max_wal_senders; MySQL's binlog/relay-log pipeline, GTID sets for position-independent failover with MASTER_AUTO_POSITION, semi-sync and Group Replication's Paxos-based certification with ProxySQL routing; MongoDB replica sets' oplog, term-based elections with priorities, write concern w:majority and read concern majority, and rollback of writes never majority-acknowledged.
subtopics.visual: A four-pane replica lab: the learner detaches a Postgres subscriber and watches its slot pin WAL segments until the disk fills, runs a catastrophic DELETE and watches it land on the streaming and cascaded replicas instantly while the delayed standby still holds the pre-delete rows behind a countdown of remaining apply delay (then pauses it at a target LSN and promotes), promotes a MySQL replica and sees the GTID sets of every node reconcile which transactions each still needs, and partitions a MongoDB replica set to watch the term-based election and w:1 vs w:majority writes survive or roll back on reconnection.

subtopics.title: Adding and removing replicas without hurting the primary
subtopics.covers: What building a replica costs the running system — a base backup or snapshot restore saturating disk and network (pg_basebackup --max-rate, XtraBackup throttling, seeding from another replica or a storage snapshot instead of the primary), the WAL retained for the duration by the slot or wal_keep_size and the disk-full risk it creates, and the catch-up phase where apply must outrun the incoming write rate or never converge — then the admission decision that a replica is ready not when lag reaches zero but when its cache is warm and its lag sits inside the read-routing threshold, so warm-up queries or a gradual traffic ramp precede adding it to the pool, and the reverse path of draining it from the load balancer, letting in-flight cursors finish and dropping its slot so retention is released, closing with the arithmetic that a replica added for read throughput still consumes primary WAL bandwidth and can never exceed the apply rate of its single replay stream (routing policy itself lives in result-streaming-bulk-movement-and-client-reliability).
subtopics.visual: The learner adds a replica to a busy primary, choosing seeding source and throttle while primary IOPS, network saturation and retained WAL climb, then raises the write rate until the catch-up curve stops converging; routing traffic immediately versus after a warm-up ramp shows the cold-cache p99 spike and the stale reads it serves, and draining the replica with and without dropping its slot shows retention either released or silently pinned on the primary.

subtopics.title: Logical replication apply conflicts and the stuck subscriber
subtopics.covers: Logical replication's dominant production failure is on the apply side: the worker applies each publisher transaction all-or-nothing, so one duplicate key from a pre-seeded table, one missing row for an UPDATE or DELETE, a type, constraint, exclusion or partition-routing violation makes it error, restart and retry the same transaction forever — apply stops entirely, every later transaction queues behind it, the origin's confirmed_flush_lsn freezes and the publisher's slot pins WAL until pg_wal fills the disk; the diagnosis path (the error's context line naming the relation, the transaction's finish LSN and replication origin, per-conflict counters in pg_stat_subscription_stats, slot lag in pg_replication_slots), the recovery ladder (fix the offending row on the subscriber, then ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP (lsn = ...), then pg_replication_origin_advance(), then reseed the table), and the guardrails disable_on_error (PG 15), a slot-lag alert and max_slot_wal_keep_size — with the warning that every skip discards a whole transaction, so only a row-level comparison run proves the subscriber still matches.
subtopics.visual: A publisher streams a mixed workload into a subscriber that hits a duplicate key mid-transaction: the learner watches the error-restart-retry loop with the origin LSN frozen and the publisher's retained-WAL bar climbing toward a disk-full mark, toggles disable_on_error to compare a stopped subscription against infinite retry, then picks a recovery action (fix the row / SKIP the finish LSN / advance the origin / reseed) and sees a row-by-row diff against the publisher highlighting exactly which rows that action silently dropped.

subtopics.title: Slot failover, pg_createsubscriber and logical replication after promotion
subtopics.covers: Why a logical replication slot is primary-local, so promotion loses confirmed_flush_lsn and forces the consumer into a fresh table snapshot; PostgreSQL 17's failover slots and sync_replication_slots (and the pg_failover_slots extension before it) synchronizing slot state onto standbys, with standby_slot_names and hot_standby_feedback as the prerequisites; slot invalidation surfaced by wal_status and max_slot_wal_keep_size; PostgreSQL 17's pg_createsubscriber converting a physical standby into a logical subscriber without a new base backup; PostgreSQL 18's conflict detection, logging and per-conflict statistics in pg_stat_subscription_stats — including update_deleted detection backed by retaining dead tuples — with automatic conflict resolution still left to the application or an extension, plus origin filtering for bidirectional setups; and the perennial cutover gaps of sequences, DDL and large objects that every Debezium-behind-HA pipeline trips on.
subtopics.visual: A primary, a standby and a CDC consumer run side by side while the learner fails over with slot synchronization on or off, watching the consumer either resume at its confirmed_flush_lsn on the new primary or restart a full table snapshot, with live counters for duplicate events emitted, snapshot bytes re-read and time to catch up, plus a wal_status panel that invalidates the slot when retention is undersized.

subtopics.title: MySQL replication operations: errant GTIDs, skips and filters
subtopics.covers: The day-to-day faults of a GTID topology — an errant transaction executed locally on a replica that makes it unpromotable and poisons future topology changes (detected by diffing gtid_executed sets, repaired by injecting an empty transaction or rebuilding the replica), replicas left writable because super_read_only was never set, skipping a broken event correctly under GTIDs by committing an empty transaction for the offending GTID rather than sql_slave_skip_counter and why every skip hides divergence only pt-table-checksum will find, replication filters that silently drop statements and break failover symmetry, crash-safe applier settings (relay_log_recovery, sync_relay_log, the applier metadata tables) that decide whether a replica resumes correctly after power loss, multi-source replication with channel-scoped commands, and Seconds_Behind_Source lying under a stalled applier or one huge transaction.
subtopics.visual: A three-node GTID topology where the learner writes directly to a replica to create an errant transaction, attempts a promotion and watches the new topology refuse or diverge, diffs the gtid_executed sets to locate the offending GTID and repairs it with an empty transaction, then breaks the applier with a duplicate-key event to compare the correct GTID skip against sql_slave_skip_counter while a checksum run reveals the rows that silently diverged.

subtopics.title: Long transactions vs replicas: hot_standby_feedback and query conflicts
