subtopics.covers: Why physical replicas fight the primary's MVCC: replaying vacuum cleanup and btree page-recycle WAL records collides with standby snapshots that still need the dead versions, so the standby either delays replay (max_standby_streaming_delay, lag grows) or cancels the query (SQLSTATE 40001 'conflict with recovery'), alongside lock, tablespace and buffer-pin conflicts; hot_standby_feedback exports the standby's oldest xmin so the primary's vacuum retains those versions at the cost of table and index bloat, with idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement timeouts as the guardrails; InnoDB replicas' undo history-list growth under long read views is the MySQL analogue, and vacuum internals live in mvcc-storage-vacuum-gc.
subtopics.visual: A primary running updates and vacuum beside a standby with a long-running query: the learner steps WAL replay and sees a cleanup record collide with the standby snapshot's xmin, chooses delay or cancel via max_standby_streaming_delay and watches lag or a cancelled query result, then toggles hot_standby_feedback and watches the primary's dead-tuple count and the replay-lag curve trade off against each other.

modules.title: Partitioning and Sharding: Key Design, Placement and Rebalancing
modules.why: The partition key fixes where every byte lives, so it decides which queries stay single-partition, how much load skews even under a perfect hash, what a membership change costs to move, how requests find the right shard, and whether a rebalance or a celebrity key can be absorbed without taking foreground traffic down.

subtopics.title: Range vs hash partitioning and key design
subtopics.covers: Key-range partitioning (Bigtable/HBase regions, CockroachDB ranges, Spanner splits) keeps keys ordered so range scans touch few partitions but turns monotonic keys (timestamps, sequences) into one hot tail partition, hash partitioning (Cassandra murmur3 tokens, DynamoDB's hashed partition key, MongoDB hashed shard keys) spreads writes but turns every range query into a scatter, compound keys (partition key + sort/clustering key) recover order inside one partition, and directory/lookup-table partitioning buys arbitrary placement at the price of a metadata service; single-node declarative partitioning and pruning belong to the execution-engines module.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a key pattern (timestamp, UUIDv4, UUIDv7, user_id, (tenant_id, ts)) and a scheme (range, hash, compound) and streams inserts; a strip of partitions heats by write rate while a probe query such as 'last hour for user X' highlights how many partitions must be touched and whether it is a seek or a scatter.

subtopics.title: Consistent hashing, virtual nodes and alternatives
subtopics.covers: Karger's ring with successor ownership moves only about K/N keys on a membership change versus mod-N's near-total reshuffle; virtual nodes/tokens (Cassandra num_tokens, Riak ring_size, Dynamo tokens) shrink load variance roughly as 1/sqrt(vnodes), spread a dead node's rebuild across the cluster and allow heterogeneous weights but multiply range-repair and metadata cost; jump consistent hash and rendezvous/HRW hashing (Maglev) need no ring and O(1) memory but jump hash only supports removing the last bucket; replica placement walks the ring to N distinct racks/AZs (NetworkTopologyStrategy), and Chord-style O(log N) finger-table routing explains why databases prefer an explicit partition map over a pure DHT.
subtopics.visual: A ring with sliders for node count and vnodes-per-node where the learner adds or removes a node and watches keys recolor to their new owners, with a 'fraction of keys moved' bar and a per-node load histogram, toggling among mod-N, plain ring, ring with vnodes and jump hash to compare movement and balance.

subtopics.title: Balls into bins: why uniform hashing still gives you a hot shard
subtopics.covers: The maximum-load results that bound imbalance under perfect hashing (about log n/log log n for n keys into n bins, and m/n plus roughly sqrt(m log n / n) once m greatly exceeds n, so imbalance shrinks only as bins get heavily loaded) and the power-of-two-choices result that drops max load to log log n, applied to the decisions they actually govern — how many vnodes or tokens per Cassandra node, partitions per Kafka topic or Elasticsearch index, the ~16384 Redis Cluster slots, DynamoDB partitions per table — and the routing analogue where least-loaded-of-two-random beats both round-robin and random in proxies and client drivers.
subtopics.visual: The learner throws m keys into n bins under one, two or d choices and watches the max-load bar track the analytic curve while a per-bin histogram fills, then raises bins-per-node (vnodes) to see the imbalance ratio collapse while a metadata, gossip and repair-cost meter climbs, and switches a request router from random to least-of-two to see the tail of per-bin queue depth flatten.

subtopics.title: Placement as constrained optimization: balance, constraints and move cost
subtopics.covers: Framing replica and partition placement as an assignment problem with objectives (even bytes, even QPS, even leaseholders), hard constraints (rack, AZ and region diversity, residency pins, heterogeneous capacity) and an explicit move-cost term, then the two families that answer it — deterministic pseudo-random functions that store no map and recompute placement from a hash (Ceph CRUSH with its bucket types and non-minimal reshuffling, weighted consistent hashing) versus explicit maps produced by a heuristic or a solver (Cassandra's token-allocation algorithm for even ownership, CockroachDB's allocator scoring candidates on fullness, diversity and load, Kafka Cruise Control's multi-goal optimizer, Elasticsearch allocation deciders) — plus the theory that predicts their behaviour: minimal movement and perfect balance are in tension, greedy hill-climbing oscillates without damping or a move budget, and an over-constrained set is infeasible so a correct rebalancer reports rather than thrashes, while how a chosen move is actually executed safely belongs to the next subtopic.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets node capacities, failure-domain constraints and objective weights over a cluster and runs consistent hashing, CRUSH-style recomputation and a greedy constrained optimizer on the same topology, watching balance, constraint violations and bytes moved after adding a node, losing a rack and pinning a tenant, with an over-constrained configuration making the optimizer report infeasible while the hash-based scheme quietly places two replicas in one failure domain.

subtopics.title: Request routing and cluster metadata
subtopics.covers: Three routing topologies—partition-aware clients (Cassandra token-aware drivers, Kafka metadata fetches, Redis Cluster slot maps), a middleware/proxy tier and any-node coordinator forwarding (Cassandra coordinators, CockroachDB gateway nodes with a range cache)—each hold a partition map sourced from ZooKeeper/etcd, gossip or a strongly consistent meta range; the middleware tier is how an unmodified MySQL or PostgreSQL gets sharded—Vitess vtgate routing by its vschema over vanilla MySQL shards, the Citus coordinator with its distributed/reference/local table classes, MongoDB mongos plus config servers, and connection-level routers such as ProxySQL and pgcat—and it is chosen over a natively sharded engine when keeping the existing engine, dialect and ecosystem is worth an extra hop and the loss of cross-shard transactions and constraints (distributed-architectures compares the full family); stale maps surface as redirect errors that carry corrected metadata (Redis MOVED/ASK, CockroachDB NotLeaseHolderError, Kafka NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER with epoch-bumped refresh) so clients must refresh, bound retries and cap per-shard connection pools.
subtopics.visual: The learner fires a request from a client, then moves a partition's leader and fires again, stepping hop-by-hop through client-aware, middleware/proxy (vtgate- or Citus-style) and any-node forwarding while the client's cached map is shown going stale, receiving a redirect with new metadata and refreshing, with a hop and round-trip counter per topology.

subtopics.title: Rebalancing and resharding
subtopics.covers: Three partition-count strategies—a fixed large number of partitions moved whole (Riak, Elasticsearch shards, Redis Cluster's 16384 slots, Kafka partitions that can never be re-split), dynamic split/merge by size and load (HBase regions, CockroachDB ~512 MiB ranges with load-based splitting, Spanner splits, MongoDB chunks and the balancer) and partitions proportional to nodes (Cassandra vnodes)—plus the live-move protocol of snapshot copy, log catch-up, brief write freeze, atomic ownership switch and client redirect under bandwidth throttling to protect foreground traffic; application-level resharding (Vitess VReplication, Instagram/Notion-style migrations) uses dual-write or CDC backfill, verification and cutover, with the dual-write window's lost-write and ordering hazards, and pre-splitting avoids the single-empty-range startup hotspot.
subtopics.visual: The learner grows a table until ranges hit a split threshold and doubles the node count under each of the three strategies, watching partitions split and migrate with bytes-moved and foreground-latency gauges, then steps through a dual-write reshard (backfill, verify, cutover) and injects a crash or a write mid-window to see which rows diverge.

subtopics.title: Hot partitions, skew and adaptive capacity
subtopics.covers: Zipf-distributed keys (celebrity users, popular SKUs), monotonic keys and low-cardinality shard keys pin load on one partition's throughput ceiling (DynamoDB 3000 RCU/1000 WCU per partition, one Kafka partition per consumer), and the mitigations trade read fan-out for write spread: write-sharding with a bounded suffix plus scatter-gather reads, sharded counters, request coalescing and read caches (DAX), DynamoDB adaptive capacity (borrowing unused table throughput and split-for-heat isolating a hot item, never above the per-item ceiling), CockroachDB load-based range splits and lease rebalancing, Kafka's sticky partitioner; detection relies on per-partition metrics such as throttling errors, CloudWatch Contributor Insights and nodetool tablehistograms.
subtopics.visual: The learner shapes a key distribution with a Zipf-exponent slider and drives traffic at a partitioned table, watching per-partition heat and throttle counters climb, then toggles suffix salting (with fan-out cost shown), adaptive capacity, split-for-heat or a read cache and sees how much heat flattens and which requests still throttle.

modules.title: Querying and Modeling for Partitioned Stores
modules.why: Once the data is split, ordinary query shapes stop being free — joins, aggregates, pagination and lookups by a non-key attribute all become fan-out or remote-index problems — and DynamoDB and Cassandra modeling is exactly that discipline applied up front, designing the keys so the access patterns that matter stay single-partition.

subtopics.title: Cross-shard queries: scatter-gather, joins and aggregation basics
subtopics.covers: Queries lacking the shard key fan out to every shard so latency is the max of N and tail amplification grows with N; partial aggregation pushes SUM/COUNT/MIN/MAX and top-K/LIMIT to shards with a coordinator merge (AVG as SUM+COUNT, DISTINCT and percentiles needing full data or sketches) and ORDER BY becomes a merge of pre-sorted streams; joins run co-located when both tables share the shard key (Citus distributed tables on tenant_id, Spanner interleaved tables, Vitess keyspaces), broadcast when one side is small (Citus reference tables replicated everywhere) and otherwise need a shuffle whose exchange-operator mechanics belong to the distributed query module; cross-shard transactions cost coordination (distributed transactions module), so schemas are shaped to keep hot transactions single-shard.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes a two-table query, choosing each table's shard key, the join key and an aggregate; the executor animates whether it runs single-shard, co-located, broadcast or scatter-gather with partial aggregation at the shards, counting shards touched, bytes moved to the coordinator and the max-of-N latency.

subtopics.title: Pagination and cursors across shards
subtopics.covers: Single-shard keyset pagination does not survive fan-out: a globally ordered page of K rows needs K rows merged from every shard, so OFFSET costs (offset+K)×N rows scanned and engines cap deep paging outright (Elasticsearch index.max_result_window, with search_after plus a point-in-time or scroll as the alternatives); the cursor must encode the full sort tuple plus a unique tiebreaker—and per-shard positions when shards are heterogeneous—and be opaque or signed so clients cannot forge a position, shard splits and rebalances invalidate in-flight cursors, concurrent writes shift the global order and produce duplicated or skipped rows unless the read is pinned to a snapshot or timestamp (AS OF SYSTEM TIME, a PIT, a changefeed offset) which in turn pins MVCC versions, and total result counts degrade to estimates.
subtopics.visual: A four-shard table the learner pages through in a global order using OFFSET, search_after-style keyset cursors and a snapshot-pinned cursor, with rows scanned per shard and bytes returned to the coordinator counted as the page number climbs, while injecting concurrent inserts, a shard split and a rebalance shows rows duplicated, skipped or a cursor rejected—and the pinned mode holding the sequence stable at the cost of the retained versions it displays.

subtopics.title: Secondary indexes across partitions: local vs global
subtopics.covers: Document-partitioned (local) indexes live beside their partition so writes are cheap and synchronous but reads by the indexed attribute scatter to all N partitions (Cassandra native 2i and SAI, MongoDB non-shard-key indexes, DynamoDB LSI, Elasticsearch shards), whereas term-partitioned (global) indexes are sharded by the indexed value so a read hits one partition but every write must update a remote index partition—asynchronously with lag and eventual consistency (DynamoDB GSI with its own capacity whose throttling backpressures the base table, Cassandra materialized views) or transactionally via a distributed transaction (CockroachDB, Spanner, YugabyteDB secondary indexes); write amplification is 1 plus the number of global indexes, and cross-shard uniqueness needs a global index, a coordinator or the unique value embedded in the partition key.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes items and queries by a non-key attribute under local vs global indexes; the write path highlights which index partitions are updated synchronously or asynchronously with a lag clock, the read path counts partitions fanned out, and a read issued during GSI lag returns a visibly stale result.

subtopics.title: Global uniqueness across shards: claim tables and reserve-then-create
subtopics.covers: A unique index is only enforceable within the partition it lives in, so a username, email or slug must either be embedded in the partition key or routed to a single arbiter—a claims table keyed by the normalized value and claimed with a conditional write (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, DynamoDB attribute_not_exists inside TransactWriteItems, a Vitess consistent-lookup vindex, a single log partition per key as in the unbundled design)—and the two-step reserve-then-create protocol has a crash point at every step (an orphan claim with no row behind it, a row whose claim was lost) closed by claim TTLs, a reconciliation sweeper or one cross-shard transaction with its coordination cost; correctness also needs normalization before claiming (case folding, Unicode confusables and NFKC, plus-addressing, trailing dots) so two 'different' strings cannot both win, rename modeled as release-and-claim with a redirect record, a tombstoned reuse window after deletion that interacts with soft deletes and partial unique indexes, and the recognition that an asynchronously maintained global secondary index detects duplicates but can never prevent them.
subtopics.visual: Two clients race the same username against a sharded store while the learner picks the strategy—per-shard unique index, async global secondary index, claim partition with a conditional write, or a cross-shard transaction—and watches both succeed, one lose, or one abort with cross-shard hops and added latency counted per strategy, while injecting a crash between claim and create leaves an orphan the sweeper later reclaims (or does not) and a rename plus re-registration of the released name shows the old identity's references resolving to the new account until a tombstone window is enabled.

subtopics.title: Modeling for DynamoDB: access-pattern-first and single-table design
subtopics.covers: Enumerate every access pattern first and design PK/SK so each becomes a single-partition Query (begins_with and between on the sort key, item collections sharing a PK), overload generic PK/SK with entity prefixes (USER#, ORDER#), add inverted-key GSIs (GSI1PK=SK) for reverse lookups and sparse GSIs for filtered subsets, all under the hard limits—400 KB item, 10 GB item collection when an LSI exists, 1 MB per Query page, 3000 RCU/1000 WCU per partition—with capacity arithmetic (4 KB read units, eventually consistent reads at half price, 1 KB write units, GSI writes billed separately), write-sharded keys for hot collections, denormalized copies instead of joins, and conditional writes or TransactWriteItems for invariants; partition internals and Paxos are in the case studies module.
subtopics.visual: The learner assigns PK, SK and GSI keys to a set of entities against a checklist of access patterns; each pattern lights green (single Query), amber (GSI read with lag) or red (Scan with filter), items hash into partitions with size and heat bars, and a cost meter tallies RCU/WCU per pattern as the design changes.

subtopics.title: Modeling for Cassandra: partitions, clustering and time-ordered data
subtopics.covers: The partition key hashes to a murmur3 token and replica set while clustering columns fix the on-disk sort within the partition, so queries must supply the full partition key and a clustering-column prefix (ALLOW FILTERING is a cluster-wide scatter) and each query gets its own denormalized table; time-series keys are bucketed ((sensor_id, day) with CLUSTERING ORDER BY ts DESC for latest-first) to keep partitions under ~100 MB and ~100k rows; tombstones from DELETE, TTL expiry and null inserts are read until gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days) plus compaction, trip tombstone_warn/failure thresholds (1000/100000) and make the queue anti-pattern unusable; compaction strategy is a modeling decision—TWCS drops whole SSTables of expired TTL data, STCS for write-heavy, LCS for read-heavy—with compaction mechanics in the LSM module and Paxos-backed lightweight transactions (4 round trips) in the consensus module.
subtopics.visual: Sensor events stream into a table the learner defines by bucket granularity, clustering order, TTL and compaction strategy; partition size gauges trip the 100 MB warning, a per-read tombstone counter climbs toward the warn threshold as deletes and TTLs land, and TWCS time windows show whole SSTables expiring while STCS keeps tombstones lingering.

modules.title: Leaderless Replication, Quorums, Anti-Entropy and CRDTs
modules.why: Dynamo-style systems trade coordination for availability, and quorum math, repair and CRDTs are how they stay correct enough.

subtopics.title: The coordinator path and quorum arithmetic: N, W, R and consistency levels
subtopics.covers: Building on the leaderless overview in the replication module: the coordinator fans a write to all N replicas of the preference list but acks after W, a read collects R responses and returns the newest version, W+R>N guarantees at least one overlapping replica, and this arithmetic is exposed as Cassandra's ONE/TWO/QUORUM/LOCAL_QUORUM/EACH_QUORUM/ALL levels and Riak's n_val/r/w/pr/pw, with multi-datacenter quorums computed per DC and quorum latency equal to the k-th fastest replica (the basis for speculative retry).
subtopics.visual: Sliders for N, W, R (and a two-datacenter toggle with LOCAL_QUORUM/EACH_QUORUM) drive a replica ring where each write paints the acked replica set and each read paints the responding set; the intersection lights up green when W+R>N and empty-red when it does not, while a latency strip shows the coordinator's ack time as the k-th fastest of the per-replica latency dice the learner can reroll.

subtopics.title: Quorum systems: weighted voting, grids, load and availability
subtopics.covers: The design space above simple majorities: Gifford's weighted voting generalizing the intersection rule, the classic alternatives (grid, tree and crumbling-wall quorums, probabilistic quorums) and Naor-Wool's load/capacity/availability tradeoff showing that majority maximizes availability under independent failures while smaller quorums win on load, the observation that only write-write and read-write pairs must intersect (the licence behind Flexible Paxos's Q1+Q2>N, owned by consensus-and-coordination, Aurora's 4/6 write and 3/6 read quorums, owned by cloud-native-disaggregated-storage, and log-only or witness replicas that vote but do not store), and the correlated-failure caveat that makes AZ- and rack-aware placement part of the quorum definition rather than a deployment detail.
subtopics.visual: A node grid where the learner paints read and write quorums by hand or picks a scheme (majority, grid, tree, weighted, witness-augmented), the tool verifies every required intersection and refuses illegal configurations, and live meters show per-node load, system capacity and availability as a failure sampler kills nodes independently or by whole rack until no quorum can be formed.

subtopics.title: Why strict quorums are still not linearizable
subtopics.covers: Even with W+R>N the system violates linearizability (defined in consistency-models) through Kleppmann's in-flight-write race where one reader sees the new value before a later reader sees the old, partial writes that reach fewer than W replicas but are neither rolled back nor atomic, concurrent writes with no total order, and the read-repair race; the ABD register (Attiya, Bar-Noy, Dolev) shows the missing write-back phase that would make quorum reads linearizable, and Cassandra instead offers SERIAL/LOCAL_SERIAL via Paxos (owned by the consensus module), with the QUORUM anomalies documented by Jepsen.
subtopics.visual: A three-replica space-time diagram where the learner drags the per-replica arrival time of one write's messages and positions two client reads; a built-in history checker (Porcupine-style, but tiny) marks the resulting history linearizable or not and highlights the offending pair, and an 'ABD write-back' toggle adds the second read phase so the learner can see the same drag no longer produces a violation.

subtopics.title: Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff
subtopics.covers: When owners are unreachable, Dynamo and Riak let fallback vnodes further along the ring accept the write and count toward W (a sloppy quorum that breaks the overlap guarantee until handoff), whereas Cassandra keeps quorums strict and only stores hints on the coordinator (per-target hint files, max_hint_window_in_ms default 3h, throttled replay triggered by gossip UP events, hints never counting toward CL except CL ANY); the durability illusion of expired hints, hint storms on node return, and Riak's pr/pw primary quorums as the opt-out.
subtopics.visual: The learner kills one or two owner replicas on the ring and issues writes with a Dynamo/Riak-style or Cassandra-style handoff mode selected; hint files or fallback vnodes fill visibly, a read during the outage shows which replica set answers and whether it misses the data, and bringing owners back animates throttled replay, while advancing a clock past the hint window drops the hints and leaves the write unreplicated until anti-entropy.

subtopics.title: Read repair, digest reads and distributed tombstones
subtopics.covers: Cassandra's read path sends a full data request to the snitch-preferred replica and digest requests to the rest of the CL set, compares hashes, escalates to full reads on mismatch, resolves per cell by timestamp and writes the winner back as blocking read repair (background read_repair_chance was removed in 4.0), and Riak repairs by version-vector dominance; deletes are tombstone writes that must survive gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days) so every replica learns of them before compaction purges them, otherwise a replica that missed the delete resurrects the value, while tombstone accumulation trips tombstone_warn/failure thresholds (compaction-level tombstone mechanics belong to lsm-trees).
subtopics.visual: A read at a chosen CL animates the data request plus digest requests, the hash comparison, escalation to full reads, timestamp resolution and the repair mutation; then the learner deletes a key while one replica is down, drags a clock past gc_grace_seconds, runs compaction on the healthy replicas, restores the third and reads again to watch the zombie value come back.

subtopics.title: Anti-entropy with Merkle trees and repair scheduling
subtopics.covers: Each replica builds a hash tree over its token range (leaves hashing all rows in a subrange, 2^15–2^20 leaves in Cassandra, produced by a validation compaction that scans the data), peers compare roots and descend only into mismatched subtrees so the message cost is O(log n) while streaming granularity is one leaf range, which over-streams matching rows; Cassandra full vs incremental repair (repaired/unrepaired SSTable sets via anticompaction), subrange repair and Reaper scheduling inside gc_grace, Riak's persistent AAE hashtrees with periodic rebuilds, ScyllaDB's row-level repair that hashes row batches instead of fixed trees, and DynamoDB's internal anti-entropy.
subtopics.visual: Two replicas hold a key range; the learner flips a handful of keys to differ, watches both trees build bottom-up, compares roots, expands only the mismatched branches and sees the streamed key ranges, then drags a tree-depth slider to trade tree size against over-streaming and a schedule slider to see whether repairs finish inside gc_grace on every node.

subtopics.title: Conflict detection: last-write-wins, siblings and dotted version vectors
subtopics.covers: Applying the vector-clock rules from time-clocks-ordering to storage: Cassandra's per-cell LWW by microsecond client timestamps silently drops concurrent updates, depends on clock agreement, and can assemble a row from cells of different writes (a Jepsen-observed anomaly); Riak's causal context detects concurrency and surfaces siblings (allow_mult) for merge-on-read, sibling explosion under client retries with server-side ids is fixed by dotted version vectors (Preguiça/Baquero), and Dynamo's shopping-cart merge shows an application resolver plus its deleted-item-resurrection flaw and actor pruning limits.
subtopics.visual: Two clients do get-modify-put on the same Riak-style object across a partition while each replica's version vector is drawn as a live column; the learner switches the resolver among LWW, keep-siblings and an application merge to see what survives healing, then hammers retries with plain version vectors to grow a sibling explosion and flips on dotted version vectors to watch the siblings collapse to the true concurrent set.

subtopics.title: CRDTs I: convergence by construction with counters, registers and sets
subtopics.covers: Strong eventual consistency without coordination: state-based CvRDTs whose states form a join-semilattice with a commutative, associative, idempotent merge (G-Counter, PN-Counter, LWW- and MV-Register, G-Set, 2P-Set, OR-Set with unique tags, and the dot-based optimized OR-Set that needs no tombstones), operation-based CmRDTs that require causal delivery, delta-state CRDTs that ship only changes, the limit that CRDTs cannot enforce global invariants like non-negative stock (escrow lives in application-data-patterns), and deployments in Riak data types, Redis Enterprise Active-Active, Akka Distributed Data and Cosmos DB.
subtopics.visual: Three replicas of a chosen CRDT show their internal state (per-actor counter vectors, tag sets, causal contexts) as the learner applies operations offline on each, then wires the replicas together in any order and watches every merge land on the identical lattice join; a naive LWW-register mode drops an update for contrast and a delta-mode toggle shows how many bytes each sync ships.

subtopics.title: CRDTs II: sequences, collaborative text and garbage
subtopics.covers: Replicated sequences give every character a unique id and an insertion origin so concurrent inserts commute (RGA, Logoot/LSEQ position identifiers, Yjs's YATA, Automerge's columnar op log, and Fugue's fix for the interleaving anomaly that RGA and Logoot exhibit), deletes leave tombstones that can only be purged once causally stable, op-based delivery needs a causal broadcast layer, and the comparison with operational transformation explains why Google Docs needs a central server while CRDT editors merge peer-to-peer at the cost of per-character metadata.
subtopics.visual: Two replicas type into the same document during a partition while each character's (agent, counter, origin) id is drawn beneath it; on reconnection the learner steps through the integration algorithm to see exactly where each concurrent insert lands, switches between RGA and Fugue to expose the interleaving anomaly, and watches tombstones accumulate then vanish once the causal-stability frontier passes them.

subtopics.title: The Dynamo lineage compared: Dynamo, Riak, Cassandra, Voldemort, ScyllaDB and DynamoDB
subtopics.covers: Same paper, different choices: Dynamo's vector clocks, preference lists and per-range Merkle trees; Riak's sloppy quorums, DVV siblings and AAE; Cassandra's deliberate rejection of vector clocks for cell timestamps, coordinator-side hints, digest reads and Paxos LWT (owned by consensus-and-coordination); Voldemort's client-side routing and pluggable storage; ScyllaDB's shard-per-core hints and row-level repair; and DynamoDB the service, which the 2022 paper reveals as leader-based Multi-Paxos replication groups per partition rather than a Dynamo clone, with data modeling and case studies handled elsewhere.
subtopics.visual: A decision matrix where the learner picks a system and a scenario (owner down, concurrent writers, missed delete, clock skew) and the same three-replica animation replays it with that system's mechanisms, so the result cell shows sibling vs silent LWW loss, hint location, repair path and which guarantee held or broke for each system side by side.

modules.title: Consensus Foundations and Raft
modules.why: Consensus is the primitive that turns a set of machines into one linearizable log, and Raft is the implementation a senior engineer actually meets — etcd, Consul, TiKV, CockroachDB and Kafka's KRaft all run it — so this module establishes what consensus guarantees, why no deterministic asynchronous protocol can guarantee termination, and then walks Raft's safety argument, reconfiguration, snapshotting, flow control and read paths in enough detail to debug a real cluster.

subtopics.title: The consensus problem and total order broadcast
subtopics.covers: Agreement, validity, integrity and termination as safety versus liveness properties (FLP means liveness needs a failure detector, owned by failure-detection-leases-fencing), majority quorums as the intersection guarantee so 2f+1 nodes tolerate f crashes, and the equivalence chain consensus ≡ atomic/total-order broadcast ≡ a linearizable log ≡ state machine replication, from which linearizable registers, CAS and uniqueness constraints (consistency-models) fall out by assigning each operation a log position.
subtopics.visual: A quorum-and-log sandbox: the learner sets N, crashes up to f nodes and drags two quorum sizes, watching the shared acceptor cell light up or vanish (and a checker trying to get two different values 'chosen' when it vanishes); then concurrent client ops from three clients are stamped into one replicated log whose positions become their linearization points on a timeline.

subtopics.title: Impossibility results and how systems dodge them: FLP, consensus numbers and randomization
subtopics.covers: The shape of the FLP proof — an initially bivalent configuration always admits a schedule that preserves bivalence, so no deterministic asynchronous protocol guarantees termination with even one crash — and exactly which assumption each real system relaxes: partial synchrony plus randomized election timeouts (Raft, Multi-Paxos with a distinguished proposer), an eventually-strong failure detector (Ω), randomized consensus terminating with probability one (Ben-Or, HoneyBadger BFT), and leases that reintroduce timing; plus Herlihy's consensus numbers showing atomic registers cannot solve consensus while compare-and-swap can, which is why a correct lock or leader record needs a compare-and-set-capable store (etcd txn, DynamoDB conditional write, S3 If-Match) and not a plain PUT, and the invariant across all of them that safety is never traded, only liveness.
subtopics.visual: The learner plays an adversarial scheduler against a small consensus protocol, delaying exactly the messages that keep each reachable configuration bivalent (every configuration badged bivalent or univalent) until the protocol visibly fails to terminate; a panel of escapes — randomized timeouts, a failure detector, coin flips — then drives the adversary's success probability toward zero while every attempt to break agreement instead of termination is refused.

subtopics.title: Raft: election and log replication
subtopics.covers: Terms as a logical clock, randomized election timeouts, RequestVote with one vote per term and the up-to-date check (last term, then last index) that yields Leader Completeness, AppendEntries doubling as heartbeat with the prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm consistency check that truncates divergent follower suffixes, nextIndex/matchIndex backoff, the Log Matching property, advancing commitIndex only by counting replicas of a current-term entry (the Figure 8 counterexample), State Machine Safety, and client session/serial-number dedup for exactly-once apply; etcd/raft, TiKV, CockroachDB, Consul and Kafka KRaft.
subtopics.visual: A 5-node Raft simulator where the learner submits entries, pauses and partitions nodes and forces timeouts, watching per-node term/votedFor/log/commitIndex and the leader's nextIndex/matchIndex arrays update per RPC; a scripted Figure 8 scenario lets them switch off the current-term commit rule and watch an entry that was 'committed' by count get overwritten by a newer leader.

subtopics.title: Raft: membership changes, snapshots, log retention and disruptive rejoiners
subtopics.covers: Configuration changes as log entries under joint consensus (C_old,new needs majorities of both) versus single-server changes and the disjoint-majorities bug (fixed by allowing one uncommitted change at a time), learners/non-voting members caught up before promotion (etcd learner, CockroachDB), snapshots with last-included index/term, InstallSnapshot and safe log truncation with compaction interacting with slow followers, leader-side flow control — inflight and byte limits per follower (etcd/raft maxInflightMsgs, maxSizePerMsg), pipeline depth, CockroachDB quota pools — and the log-retention rule that the leader must keep entries the slowest follower still needs, so one paused replica pins the leader's memory and disk until the retain-versus-snapshot threshold trips and pays a full state transfer instead ('raft log too large'), which is the mechanism behind one slow node degrading a whole group; plus PreVote, CheckQuorum and leader transfer against disruptive rejoiners and term inflation.
subtopics.visual: One 5-node Raft simulator run as three separate presets, each exposing a single knob and a single meter so every effect is attributable: (a) Resize — grow 3→5 naively versus under joint consensus, with the transition window highlighted and a 'find two disjoint majorities' challenge that can only be won in the naive mode; (b) Lag — pause one follower while a pipeline-depth/inflight-limit slider runs, watching the leader's log-retention and memory meter climb until the retain-versus-snapshot threshold fires InstallSnapshot with its bandwidth cost shown; (c) Rejoin — partition a node, let its term inflate, and return it with PreVote/CheckQuorum on and off to see whether it deposes a healthy leader.

subtopics.title: Raft: linearizable reads — log-write, ReadIndex and leader leases
subtopics.covers: Why a leader that has silently lost its leadership will happily serve stale reads, and the three strategies that fix it: appending a no-op read entry to the log (correct, one fsync + one round trip per read), ReadIndex (record commitIndex, confirm leadership with a heartbeat quorum, wait for applied ≥ that index — no disk write), and clock-dependent leader leases (etcd, TiKV, CockroachDB range leases) that make reads local at the cost of assuming a bounded clock drift and a bounded pause; plus follower/learner reads served safely via a ReadIndex from the leader, and the staleness window each choice actually exposes (lease/fencing theory lives in failure-detection-leases-fencing).
subtopics.visual: The learner partitions the current leader away from its followers and then issues reads under each of the three modes side by side, watching a timeline mark exactly which reads return stale data and for how long as the lease clock counts down and the new leader commits fresh writes; sliders for clock skew and a stop-the-world pause on the old leader show the lease mode breaking while ReadIndex and log-write reads simply stall.

modules.title: Paxos, Leaderless Consensus and Byzantine Faults
modules.why: Paxos is the language the literature and the big systems are written in — Chubby, Spanner's Paxos groups, Cassandra LWT — and its variants map the design space Raft deliberately narrows: where the message-delay floor really is, whether a distinguished leader is needed at all, and what changes when a node may lie; a senior engineer needs this to read the papers and view-change protocols, to answer 'why does this commit cost two inter-region round trips and can any design make it one?', and to explain why a database inside one trust domain still budgets for crashes and corrupt disks rather than tripling replicas.

subtopics.title: Paxos: single-decree
subtopics.covers: Proposers, acceptors and learners; totally ordered ballot numbers; phase 1 prepare/promise (an acceptor promises to ignore lower ballots and returns its highest accepted ballot and value), phase 2 accept/accepted, the rule that a proposer must adopt the highest-ballot value among its promises (P2c) so that once a value is chosen by any majority every higher ballot re-proposes it, 'chosen' being a fact no single node may know, dueling proposers livelocking and the distinguished-proposer fix; used by Chubby, Spanner's Paxos groups and Cassandra LWT.
subtopics.visual: A hand-driven round runner: the learner controls two proposers with chosen ballot numbers against five acceptors, dropping, delaying and reordering individual prepare/promise/accept/accepted messages while each acceptor shows (promisedBallot, acceptedBallot, acceptedValue); a 'chosen' detector fires when a majority accepts one ballot, and challenge mode dares them to get a second value chosen, highlighting the overlapping acceptor whose promise forces the higher ballot to adopt the old value.

subtopics.title: Multi-Paxos and log replication
subtopics.covers: A sequence of instances (slots) with one stable leader whose single phase 1 covers all future slots so each write costs one phase-2 round trip, out-of-order slot completion and holes filled with no-ops on leader change, learn/commit messages and in-order state-machine apply, batching and pipelining of in-flight slots with per-slot fsync as the latency floor, Flexible Paxos (only Q1 + Q2 > N is required, allowing tiny phase-2 quorums) and Mencius rotating leaders, contrasted with Raft's stricter contiguous log; multi-group placement and heartbeat coalescing are owned by distributed-architectures.
subtopics.visual: A slots-by-acceptors grid where the leader appends with message drops and a pipeline-depth slider (throughput vs in-flight count), a 'kill leader' button that triggers the new leader's prepare over all slots, showing recovered highest-ballot values and no-op fills for holes; a Flexible Paxos toggle lets the learner pick Q1/Q2 sizes and see whether intersection holds and how write latency changes.

subtopics.title: How many message delays a commit must take: consensus latency lower bounds
subtopics.covers: The two-message-delay lower bound for a leader-based decision and Lamport's result that learning in a single delay requires fast quorums larger than a majority (the source of Fast Paxos's quorum inflation and EPaxos's F+⌊(F+1)/2⌋ fast path, with Atlas and Tempo trimming it under weaker assumptions), the f+1-round lower bound for synchronous agreement, why every leaderless one-RTT design must either enlarge the quorum or keep a slow-path fallback that contention forces it onto, and how these delays compose with speed-of-light RTTs to set the floor that Spanner, CockroachDB and Aurora DSQL commit latencies all sit above.
subtopics.visual: A region map where the learner picks a protocol, quorum sizes and replica placement, and the tool counts message delays to decide and to learn, refuses configurations whose quorums fail to intersect, prints the resulting commit latency from the RTT matrix, and raises a conflict-rate slider so the fast path's abort-to-slow-path rate erodes the theoretical saving in front of them.

subtopics.title: Zab, Viewstamped Replication and Paxos Made Live lessons
subtopics.covers: Zab's epochs and zxid = (epoch, counter), discovery/synchronization/broadcast phases with TRUNC/DIFF/SNAP catch-up and its primary-order (per-client FIFO, prefix) guarantee; Viewstamped Replication (Oki–Liskov 1988, VR Revisited 2012) with view numbers, op-numbers, DoViewChange/StartView selecting the log with the highest (last-normal-view, op-number) and recovery from peers without disk; the key contrast that Raft elects only up-to-date logs while Zab/VR pull the best log to the new leader; and Paxos Made Live's engineering lessons—disk-corruption markers, master leases, snapshots, group membership, runtime invariant checks, fault-injection testing and the gap between paper and system.
subtopics.visual: A side-by-side stepper that runs one identical crash-and-partition scenario under Raft, Zab and VR from the same initial logs, letting the learner step election/view change and watch which replica's log wins, which entries get truncated and the message count per protocol, with a 'corrupt this replica's disk' toggle showing how Paxos Made Live's marker prevents a corrupted node from breaking its promises.

subtopics.title: EPaxos and leaderless consensus
subtopics.covers: Every replica leads its own commands, which carry dependency sets and sequence numbers; PreAccept to a fast quorum of F+⌊(F+1)/2⌋ commits in one round trip when all replies agree on dependencies, otherwise a Paxos-Accept slow path via a majority; execution by strongly connected components of the dependency graph ordered by seq; conflict defined as non-commutative operations on the same key; geo benefits (nearest replica, no leader bottleneck) against the costs—protocol complexity, unbounded dependency chains under contention, the execution-linearizability bug found by TLA+ model checking—and successors Atlas, Tempo and Cassandra's Accord (CEP-15).
subtopics.visual: The learner submits keyed commands from three regions on a map: non-conflicting commands animate the one-RTT fast path to the nearest quorum while conflicting ones fall to the slow path, and a dependency graph on the right grows edges and collapses SCCs into execution order; a conflict-rate slider shows the fast-path share and tail latency degrading.

subtopics.title: Byzantine faults: PBFT, 3f+1 and why databases assume crashes
subtopics.covers: Why arbitrary behavior needs 3f+1 replicas and 2f+1 quorums (any two quorums intersect in f+1 nodes, at least one honest), PBFT's pre-prepare/prepare/commit rounds with signed messages and view changes, the linear-communication successors behind permissioned ledgers (HotStuff, Tendermint), and the engineering argument databases actually make — inside one trust domain the expected faults are crashes, corrupted disks and buggy code, so the budget goes to checksums, protocol-aware recovery, replica consistency checks and deterministic simulation rather than tripling replicas and signing every message — plus where the Byzantine model does surface: cross-organization ledgers, untrusted cloud storage verified by proofs, client-supplied timestamps in Cassandra, and a partially-partitioned coordination node behaving arbitrarily as in Cloudflare's 2020 etcd incident.
subtopics.visual: A replicated log driven by a fault dial that moves from crash to omission to arbitrary: a 2f+1 crash-tolerant cluster stays correct until one node starts sending different values to different peers and the replicas visibly diverge, then the same fault is replayed against a 3f+1 PBFT run where the liar is outvoted at the prepare quorum, with per-write message counts, signature cost and replica bill displayed so the price of the upgrade is explicit.

modules.title: Coordination Services and Recipes
modules.why: Almost nobody implements a consensus protocol, but nearly every distributed system leans on one through ZooKeeper, etcd or a conditional write, and that is where the failures actually happen — a paused lock holder, a watch that fired while nobody was listening, a log entry that never reached the disk — so a senior engineer needs the primitives, the correct recipes and their pitfalls in one frame.

subtopics.title: ZooKeeper: znodes, sessions and watches
subtopics.covers: The data-tree model with persistent, ephemeral and sequential znodes, sessions maintained by heartbeats with a negotiated timeout, expiry that atomically deletes a client's ephemerals, and session migration across ensemble servers; ordered one-shot watches as edge notifications rather than a change feed; linearizable writes funnelled through the Zab leader with per-client FIFO order, reads served locally by any server (so possibly stale) and sync() to force a read forward; observers for read scaling and the small-value, small-request design point (jute.maxbuffer).
subtopics.visual: A three-server ensemble the learner drives: two clients create ephemeral and sequential znodes and set watches, then one client's heartbeats are paused past the session timeout so its ephemerals vanish and every watcher's notification fires; a 'read from this follower' toggle shows a read lagging the leader's latest write until sync() pulls it forward.

subtopics.title: etcd v3: revisions, leases, txn and watch streams
subtopics.covers: The MVCC key space with a global revision counter plus per-key create/mod revisions and version, range reads at a past revision, txn compare-and-set as the raw linearizable CAS primitive (and the compare targets: value, version, create/mod revision), leases with keepalive that expire whole sets of attached keys at once, watch streams resumed from a revision and the compaction that invalidates them, defrag plus the DB-size and request-size limits, and Kubernetes' dependence on all of it (one key per object, informers as watches from a revision, the 'too old resource version' failure).
subtopics.visual: A revision-timeline explorer where each write advances the global revision: the learner opens a watch from an old revision and replays its event stream, then runs compaction and watches that stream fail with 'revision compacted'; a lease panel lets them stop keepalives and see every attached key disappear together, and a txn builder shows a compare-and-set succeeding or failing against a concurrent writer.

subtopics.title: Chubby and what a coordination service is for
subtopics.covers: Chubby's five-replica Paxos cell behind a filesystem-like namespace of coarse-grained locks and small files, sessions with client-side caching that the master must invalidate before acknowledging a write, sequencers handed to external services so they can reject stale lock holders, the deliberate design choice of coarse locks and metadata (elect a leader, publish config, name a service) rather than fine-grained locking or a data store, the client library as the real consumer of consensus, and how ZooKeeper and etcd inherited or diverged from each of those choices.
subtopics.visual: A coarse-lock versus fine-lock comparison under the same workload: the learner raises lock rate and client count and watches the coordination cell's round trips, cache-invalidation traffic and failure blast radius grow, with a caching toggle showing the master blocking a write until every cached copy is invalidated.

subtopics.title: Recipes: leader election, herd-free locks, barriers and membership
subtopics.covers: Leader election as the lowest sequential ephemeral znode (or an etcd lease-backed key claimed by a txn compare-and-set), the herd-free lock where each waiter watches only its predecessor instead of the parent, read/write locks, single and double barriers, membership and service discovery through ephemeral nodes plus a directory watch, config distribution and the re-read-on-notify discipline; each recipe carried across ZooKeeper and etcd primitives, and the same correctness argument every time — the store decides, the client only observes what it decided.
subtopics.visual: A recipe runner where the learner starts N contending clients on a lock and toggles between watch-the-parent and watch-your-predecessor, seeing the O(N²) notification herd collapse to O(N) as each client's watch arrow re-pins to the node ahead of it; a mode switch replays the same clients as a leader election and as a double barrier, showing which znode each client is waiting on at every step.

subtopics.title: Coordination pitfalls: paused holders, watch gaps and misuse
subtopics.covers: The lock holder that GC-pauses past its session expiry while a second client legitimately acquires (only fencing tokens at the storage layer protect the data — theory in failure-detection-leases-fencing), the gap between a one-shot watch firing and being re-registered in which changes are missed (so never trust the event payload, always re-read state), session-expiry handling as the most-fumbled path in every client library, treating ZooKeeper as a queue or blob store, the reconnect herd after an ensemble restart, etcd's request and DB size limits and compaction/defrag pauses, and the availability coupling created when every service's liveness depends on one cell.
subtopics.visual: A fault lab: the learner pauses the lock holder past its session expiry, watches a second client acquire, then resumes the first and lets it write to a store with fencing tokens on or off (write accepted versus rejected with the stale token); a second dial drops the client's watch re-registration for a few events so a change is visibly missed, and switching on re-read-after-fire recovers it.

subtopics.title: Consensus under storage faults: fsync vs replication durability
subtopics.covers: Raft and Paxos assume persisted state survives a crash, so a node that loses or corrupts its log (power loss without fsync, fsyncgate-style errors, bit rot) can vote or lead in ways that erase committed entries—the Protocol-Aware Recovery paper (CTRL) shows ZooKeeper, LogCabin and etcd either crash, truncate (spreading the loss via a new leader) or, with PAR, repair from peers by distinguishing locally-lost from globally-uncommitted entries; TigerBeetle implements this model; contrasted with Kafka's replication-only ISR durability (detailed in logs-streams-derived-data), Redpanda's and BookKeeper's per-write fsync, and correlated rack/AZ power loss where replication alone fails.
subtopics.visual: A 3-node replicated log where the learner sets each node's durability policy (fsync per entry, fsync every N ms, replication only) and injects faults—power-cut one node, flip bits in one entry, or cut a whole rack—then watches which acknowledged entries survive and steps the recovery: naive truncate-and-rejoin letting a damaged follower elect a leader missing committed entries versus PAR's per-entry repair from peers.

subtopics.title: Recovering from permanent quorum loss
subtopics.covers: The on-call path when a majority is gone for good (two of three members' disks destroyed) and the cluster can never commit again: the wait-versus-force decision and how to tell a slow member from a dead one, the per-system tools that deliberately violate the protocol's quorum precondition—etcd's `snapshot restore --force-new-cluster` and the single-member `--force-new-cluster` restart, CockroachDB's `debug recover make-plan`/`apply-plan` for ranges with unavailable replicas, ZooKeeper reconfig from a surviving snapshot—the loss they can cause (entries committed on the dead majority but never replicated here, unbounded in principle because the survivor cannot know what it missed), the requirement to fence every ghost member and network path first and run the tool exactly once on exactly one node, and the rebuild path afterwards (fresh member ids, re-seeded data, reconciliation against downstream state), with unclean leader election in Kafka (logs-streams-derived-data) as the same availability-versus-safety knob and restore mechanics in backups-incidents-disaster-recovery.
subtopics.visual: A 3-node cluster where the learner kills two members and watches writes hang with no leader, then runs force-new-cluster on the survivor and sees exactly which acknowledged entries vanish (each entry tagged with where it was replicated), followed by resurrecting a dead member with fencing off—two clusters claiming the same identity and diverging—versus fenced, where it can only rejoin as a fresh empty member.

subtopics.title: Lightweight transactions: Paxos inside Cassandra
subtopics.covers: A per-partition Paxos instance behind INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS / UPDATE ... IF: prepare/promise with timeuuid ballots, read of the current row, propose/accept, commit as a normal mutation stamped with the ballot—four round trips at SERIAL or LOCAL_SERIAL, incomplete rounds finished by the next proposer via the system.paxos table, contention causing ballot retries and throughput collapse, the rule that mixing non-LWT writes on the same key breaks the guarantee, SERIAL reads to observe in-flight commits, Cassandra 4.1's Paxos v2 (fewer round trips, linearizable reads) and Accord as the successor; contrasted with DynamoDB's leader-based conditional writes and etcd's txn compare-and-set.
subtopics.visual: The learner races two clients' INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS on one partition across three replicas, stepping ballots through prepare/read/propose/commit with adjustable message delays until exactly one applies and the other receives [applied]=false with the existing row; a 'mix in a plain write' button shows a non-LWT write's later timestamp clobbering the LWT result, and a contention slider drives visible retry storms and latency growth.

parts.title: Distributed Transactions, Architectures, Streams and Verification
parts.summary: Atomic commit and distributed SQL protocols, cloud-native and disaggregated architectures, distributed and analytical query execution, logs and derived data, and how distributed claims are verified.

modules.title: Distributed Transactions: Atomic Commitment Across Partitions
modules.why: Every multi-partition write has to answer the same question — who holds the commit decision, and what happens to the other partitions when that holder dies mid-flight — and the answers run from classic 2PC and its blocking window, through replicated coordinators and Percolator's primary-key trick, to protocols that give up ordering transactions against each other in exchange for never blocking or aborting at all.

subtopics.title: Two-phase commit
subtopics.covers: The coordinator's prepare/vote/decide protocol with force-written PREPARE and COMMIT records, participants holding locks in the in-doubt window when the coordinator dies after they voted yes, presumed-abort and presumed-commit log optimizations and the read-only-participant shortcut, XA as practiced (Postgres PREPARE TRANSACTION, MySQL XA, JTA) with orphaned prepared transactions blocking vacuum and heuristic completion breaking atomicity, and why 2PC is atomic commitment rather than consensus.
subtopics.visual: A coordinator and three participants rendered as message lanes plus each node's log, lock table and state (working / prepared / in-doubt / committed): the learner crashes any node at any message boundary, watches which locks stay held and which force-writes happened, then toggles presumed-abort to see which log records and ACK messages disappear from the trace.

subtopics.title: Write paths in Cassandra and DynamoDB
subtopics.covers: Cassandra's single-partition atomicity from commitlog plus memtable, logged batches written to batchlog replicas and replayed after a coordinator failure versus unlogged batches that can half-apply, LWT as per-partition Paxos (mechanism in consensus-and-coordination), and DynamoDB TransactWriteItems' timestamp-ordered two-phase protocol from the 2023 paper where a transaction coordinator ledger drives prepare (condition checks and per-item timestamp validation, no locks held) and commit, ConditionCheck failures cancel the whole set, isolation between transactions is serializable but plain GetItem can observe partial application, and client tokens make retries idempotent.
subtopics.visual: The learner submits a three-item write to a three-partition cluster and switches the mode among Cassandra logged batch, unlogged batch and DynamoDB TransactWriteItems, watching the batchlog entry, fan-out and replay after a dropped replica, the coordinator ledger record and per-item prepare timestamps, a conditional check failing and canceling everything, and a non-transactional reader probing mid-flight to see exactly which items are visible.

subtopics.title: Read-atomic isolation and RAMP: atomic visibility without two-phase commit
subtopics.covers: The fractured-read anomaly where a multi-partition write becomes half-visible (a row and its global secondary index, both directions of a friendship edge, a denormalized copy), read-atomic isolation as the guarantee that forbids exactly that without ordering transactions against each other, Bailis's RAMP protocols — RAMP-Fast attaching sibling-key metadata so a reader detects a missing version and repairs it in a second round, RAMP-Small's two-round timestamp intersection, RAMP-Hybrid's Bloom-filter middle ground — all coordination-free, partition-independent and abort-free, and where the same shape already appears in practice as Cassandra logged batches, DynamoDB GSI lag, and the per-write sibling metadata distributed stores attach to make multi-shard reads coherent.
subtopics.visual: A two-partition write is read mid-flight so the learner sees the fractured result directly (index hit, base row missing), then RAMP metadata is enabled and the reader's first round detects the missing sibling version and issues its repair fetch, with round trips, added latency, metadata bytes per write and an abort counter pinned at zero shown beside a 2PC lane performing the same write with locks and a commit round.

subtopics.title: 3PC, Paxos Commit and replicated coordinators
subtopics.covers: Three-phase commit's pre-commit phase removes blocking only under synchronous crash-stop and produces split decisions when a partition leaves one side pre-committed and the other timing out to abort; Gray and Lamport's Paxos Commit replicates each participant's vote through 2F+1 acceptors so any node can learn the outcome; and the practical fix used by Spanner (coordinator is a Paxos group), CockroachDB (transaction record on a Raft range) and TiKV (primary lock on a Raft region) turns the in-doubt window into ordinary consensus latency at the cost of extra quorum round trips.
subtopics.visual: The same commit-time crash scenario runs side by side under 3PC and under a Raft-replicated coordinator: the learner injects a coordinator crash or a network partition at any step and watches 3PC's two sides reach conflicting commit/abort decisions while the replicated coordinator's newly elected leader reads the decision from the replicated log and drives participants to completion, with a round-trip and fsync counter for each protocol.

subtopics.title: Percolator and TiDB
subtopics.covers: Snapshot isolation over Bigtable's single-row atomicity using lock, write and data column families, a timestamp oracle issuing start_ts and commit_ts, prewrite (primary first, then secondaries, rejecting on a newer write or an existing lock) and commit where committing the primary is the single atomic point and secondaries are rolled forward lazily, readers that hit a lock checking the primary's status and TTL to roll it forward or back, and TiKV's async commit (commit_ts derived from max min_commit_ts across secondaries so the client need not wait for the primary), 1PC for single-region writes, and TiDB's pessimistic locks.
subtopics.visual: A key-by-column-family grid: the learner steps a two-key transaction through prewrite and commit watching lock, write and data cells fill with timestamps, kills the client between primary and secondary commit, then dispatches a reader that follows the orphaned secondary lock to the primary and resolves it, and toggles async commit to see min_commit_ts computed instead of a primary-first commit.

modules.title: Timestamp-Ordered and Deterministic Distributed Transactions
modules.why: Once the commit decision is safe, the remaining problem is order: Spanner, CockroachDB and Calvin are three different answers to how machines with unsynchronized clocks agree on one transaction order — pay for it with commit-wait, with uncertainty restarts, or with a replicated input log — and each answer sets what anomalies survive, how contention is arbitrated and when old versions can finally be reclaimed.

subtopics.title: Spanner: TrueTime commit-wait and external consistency
subtopics.covers: Tablets replicated by Paxos groups with TrueTime-disjoint leader leases, read-write transactions using 2PL with wound-wait on the leader's lock table and 2PC whose coordinator is itself a Paxos group, a commit timestamp s chosen at or above TT.now().latest and commit-wait until TT.after(s) so timestamp order equals real-time order (external consistency, i.e. strict serializability), lock-free snapshot reads at t_safe = min(Paxos safe time, lower bound of prepared-but-uncommitted transactions), and bounded-stale reads; the TrueTime interval API itself lives in time-clocks-ordering.
subtopics.visual: Two Paxos groups under an epsilon slider: the learner commits T1 and then a causally dependent T2 on the other group and watches each transaction's TrueTime interval, chosen timestamp and commit-wait bar; disabling commit-wait lets an external observer read them in inverted order, while a snapshot reader shows t_safe being held back by an in-flight prepared transaction.

subtopics.title: CockroachDB transactions: intents, HLC and parallel commits
subtopics.covers: Write intents stored as provisional MVCC versions in Pebble pointing at a transaction record on the first-written range, HLC commit timestamps pushed above the read-timestamp cache so no write lands below a served read, conflict handling by pushing the other transaction (priorities) or refreshing the read spans forward instead of restarting, uncertainty intervals of max_offset producing ReadWithinUncertaintyInterval restarts, parallel commits where a STAGING record plus all acknowledged in-flight writes makes the commit implicit and a recovery process reconstructs the outcome, and asynchronous intent resolution after commit.
subtopics.visual: Two ranges and two transactions: the learner steps T1's writes across ranges watching intents, the STAGING transaction record and parallel-commit acknowledgments, then sends a concurrent reader into an intent (push), a writer below the timestamp cache (refresh succeeds or fails), and a read inside the uncertainty window (restart), with the retry counter and the exact client-visible error shown.

subtopics.title: Calvin and deterministic databases
subtopics.covers: A sequencer batches inputs into epochs and replicates the batch order via Paxos, schedulers acquire locks strictly in log order so every replica computes the same result without 2PC or per-transaction replication, dependent transactions use an optimistic reconnaissance read with a re-check, aborts arise only from logic never from contention, FaunaDB as the production descendant, Aria's batch execution with reservations and VoltDB's single-threaded partitions, and the cost that interactive transactions and unknown read/write sets do not fit.
subtopics.visual: The learner submits a batch of transactions with declared read/write sets; the sequencer numbers them and two replicas each with two partitions execute in lockstep with a lock manager granting strictly in log order and a cross-partition message counter comparing against 2PC, while adding a dependent transaction shows the reconnaissance read re-executing when its read set changes.

subtopics.title: Distributed deadlock detection and priorities
subtopics.covers: Global waits-for cycles that no single shard can see, edge-chasing probe detection (Chandy-Misra-Haas) versus centralized graph collection versus timeout-based aborts, wound-wait with transaction priorities as used by Spanner and by CockroachDB's push mechanism and per-range transaction wait queue with distributed cycle detection, wait-die as the alternative, deadlock probability growing with the number of shards touched, and how the choice interacts with client retry loops and idempotency.
subtopics.visual: Three shards where the learner builds a cross-shard lock cycle among three transactions and picks the strategy: under detection, probe messages travel the waits-for edges until one returns to its origin and a victim is chosen; under wound-wait, the priorities decide who is wounded and when, with lock hold time and wasted work compared across strategies.

subtopics.title: Clock-skew anomalies: causal reverse and stale reads
subtopics.covers: How a skewed physical clock lets a causally later write receive an earlier timestamp (causal reverse) and how uncertainty intervals, commit-wait, HLC max_offset enforcement and node self-eviction on excess skew prevent it, stale follower reads that lack a closed or safe timestamp, the difference between serializable and strictly serializable when clocks drift, and the CockroachDB and YugabyteDB clock findings whose Jepsen methodology lives in verification-jepsen-simulation.
subtopics.visual: Two shards with independently skewable clocks: the learner performs a write on one shard and a causally dependent write on the other, watches the timestamps come out reversed and a snapshot reader see the second without the first, then enables uncertainty intervals and watches the read restart at a higher timestamp instead of returning the anomaly.

subtopics.title: Isolation across shards and cluster-wide MVCC garbage collection
subtopics.covers: A consistent cross-shard snapshot needs one global timestamp (TSO, HLC or TrueTime) plus each shard's safe or resolved time, write skew across partitions under SI is only caught with global conflict tracking (CockroachDB timestamp cache plus refresh, TiDB's SI-based repeatable read), and reclaiming old versions needs a cluster-wide low watermark: TiKV's PD safepoint from the oldest active start_ts with GC workers deleting below it and the ErrGCTooEarly failure for long transactions, CockroachDB's gc.ttlseconds with protected timestamps pinning versions for backups and changefeeds, and Spanner's version-retention windows.
subtopics.visual: A cluster timeline over several ranges' version chains: the learner opens transactions with different start timestamps, starts a backup, and drags the GC safepoint watermark, watching which versions become reclaimable, how an active transaction or protected timestamp pins the watermark in place, and a snapshot read that reaches below the safepoint failing with the engine's error.

modules.title: Distributed SQL Architectures: Sharded Raft, Shared-Disk and Compatibility
modules.why: Range-sharded Raft clusters, sharding middleware and shared-disk clusters are the families a senior engineer picks among when one machine stops being enough, and each one moves the durability point, the failover unit and the coordination tax somewhere different; on top of that almost every new entrant sells 'Postgres compatibility', a layered claim you have to be able to take apart before you bet an application on it.

subtopics.title: Architecture families: one write, four systems
subtopics.covers: Traces the same single-row write through the four dominant families — shared-nothing Raft-per-range (CockroachDB, TiKV/TiDB, YugabyteDB, Spanner), disaggregated log-shipping storage (Aurora, Neon, AlloyDB), sharding middleware over unmodified engines (Vitess, Citus) and leader-replicated cloud KV partitions (DynamoDB) — naming for each the durability point (Raft quorum fsync, 4/6 storage-node ack, single-primary WAL fsync plus async replica, 2/3 Paxos replicas), the number of network hops before ack, the failover unit and its RTO, and the coordination tax that makes a single large PostgreSQL beat all four for workloads under one machine's ceiling.
subtopics.visual: Learner submits one write and steps it hop-by-hop through four stacked lanes (client → router → leader/primary → replicas/storage → ack) with a latency meter per hop, then clicks any box to kill it mid-flight and watches which lanes lose the write, which stall until a lease or election timeout, and which keep serving, filling a comparison table of durability point, ack hops, failover unit and consistency as they go.

subtopics.title: 'Postgres-compatible': which layer is actually compatible
subtopics.covers: The distinct layers a compatibility claim can stop at — wire protocol (startup, extended query, COPY, cancel key), SQL dialect and type system, pg_catalog emulation that ORMs and migration tools introspect, session semantics (temp tables, advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, prepared statements through poolers), PL languages and extensions, and operational surface (EXPLAIN shape, pg_stat_statements, pg_dump round-trip) — traced through CockroachDB, Yugabyte's reuse of the real PostgreSQL query layer, AlloyDB and DSQL, Spanner's PG interface, and analytics engines that speak the protocol without being relational-OLTP at all.
subtopics.visual: Learner picks an engine and a probe — driver handshake, ORM catalog introspection, a prepared statement through a pooler, SELECT FOR UPDATE, LISTEN/NOTIFY, CREATE EXTENSION, a recursive CTE — and steps it message by message through the wire-protocol stepper reused from application-access (Startup/Auth, Parse, Bind, Describe, Execute, RowDescription/DataRow, ErrorResponse), watching it either complete or stop dead at one specific message carrying that engine's real error text; changing the client library version or flipping the pooler from session to transaction mode replays the identical probe to a different verdict, and the layer at which the claim ended (wire, catalog, session, dialect, extension) is read off the message where it stopped rather than asserted by a table.

subtopics.title: Range-sharded KV with Raft: CockroachDB, TiKV, YugabyteDB
subtopics.covers: The keyspace is cut into ranges (~512 MB CockroachDB ranges, ~96 MB TiKV regions, YugabyteDB tablets) each replicated by its own Raft group; range descriptors are found through a two-level meta range (meta1/meta2) cached at the gateway, a leaseholder (epoch-based lease tied to node liveness, or expiration lease for meta ranges) serves reads without a Raft round trip, ranges split on size or on load (hot-key splitting) and merge when small, an allocator (or TiDB's Placement Driver) rebalances replicas and leases by store fullness, diversity and QPS, and multi-Raft costs are controlled by coalesced heartbeats and quiescing idle groups.
subtopics.visual: Learner sees a cluster map of stores holding colored range replicas with leaseholders starred; they push traffic at one key and watch a load-based split, a meta-range lookup being cached at the gateway, a leaseholder transfer moving the star and reads following it, then kill a store to see each affected Raft group elect a new leader, the lease expire and be reacquired, and the allocator up-replicate onto surviving stores while a quiescence counter shows idle groups stop heartbeating.

subtopics.title: Geo-distribution, follower reads and placement
subtopics.covers: Table locality choices — REGIONAL BY TABLE, REGIONAL BY ROW (home-region column pinning the leaseholder and voting replicas), GLOBAL tables that pay a future-timestamp write to give every region non-stale local reads — plus survival goals (zone vs region), non-voting replicas, closed timestamps that let any replica serve AS OF SYSTEM TIME reads, Spanner's bounded/exact staleness reads and placement directories, follow-the-workload lease movement, and the alternative of DynamoDB global tables with last-writer-wins conflict resolution, all governed by the fact that a quorum write costs at least one inter-region RTT.
subtopics.visual: Three region columns hold replicas each labeled voter, non-voter or leaseholder against a fixed RTT matrix, and per range a closed-timestamp watermark ticks forward: the learner fires reads and sees which ones a follower may answer (and how stale) versus which must cross to the leaseholder, watches follow-the-workload hand the lease to another column as traffic shifts, flips the table to GLOBAL to see the write bar stretch by a future-timestamp interval while the read bars collapse to local, and kills a region to watch quorum arithmetic (votes surviving of votes required) decide which ranges keep committing and which stall.

subtopics.title: Shared-disk clustering: Oracle RAC cache fusion
subtopics.covers: Every node mounts the same storage and the Global Cache Service masters each block on one node by hash so that a block held in another node's buffer cache is shipped over the interconnect instead of re-read from disk, with null/shared/exclusive block modes, current versus consistent-read block transfers, two-hop versus three-hop message patterns, past images retained for instance recovery, redo threads per node replayed on crash after resource remastering, and block pinging on hot index blocks as the classic scaling failure; DB2 pureScale contrasts with a centralized coupling facility holding the global lock table and group buffer pool accessed over RDMA.
subtopics.visual: Learner opens sessions on two or three nodes sharing one disk and has them update and read the same block, watching the master lookup, block-mode transitions, the block shipping across the interconnect as a two-hop or three-hop transfer, a past image being kept and a ping counter climbing as contention grows, then kills a node to see remastering and redo-thread recovery, with a toggle that redraws the same trace against pureScale's central coupling facility.

subtopics.title: Online schema change in distributed SQL: the F1 state machine
subtopics.covers: Because nodes cache schema versions under leases, F1/Spanner and CockroachDB never let more than two consecutive versions be live and move a new index through absent → delete-only (deletes maintained, writes ignored) → write-only (all mutations maintained, not readable) → backfill of existing rows → public, with drops walked in reverse, the lease duration bounding how long each transition must wait; skipping delete-only leaves orphaned index entries after deletes, skipping write-only lets the backfill miss concurrent inserts, and CockroachDB implements this as a schema-change job over descriptor leases with the backfill running as a distributed, resumable, MVCC-timestamped scan.
subtopics.visual: Learner adds an index on a three-node cluster where each node shows the schema version it holds a lease on; they step the version forward and run concurrent inserts, updates and deletes on nodes at different versions while the index panel stays consistent, then flip a 'skip state' switch and repeat to see orphaned or missing index entries light up red, with the lease timer showing why each transition waits for the previous version to drain.

modules.title: Cloud-Native and Disaggregated Architectures: Aurora, Object Stores and Serverless
modules.why: Once storage is a service rather than a disk, the durability point moves off the compute node entirely — into a redo quorum, a journal, or an immutable object — and everything an engineer cares about (commit latency, recovery time, branch cost, cold starts, the monthly bill) is decided by how many requests, bytes and inter-AZ hops sit between the client and that point.

subtopics.title: Aurora: the log is the database
subtopics.covers: Only redo log records leave the compute node: each 10 GB protection group is six segments across three AZs with a 4/6 write quorum and 3/6 read quorum, storage nodes materialize pages on demand from the redo they hold and gossip missing records to each other for repair, compute tracks the Volume Complete LSN and Volume Durable LSN (VDL) and truncates above the VDL on crash so recovery needs no redo replay and no checkpoints, read replicas receive the same redo stream only to invalidate their buffer caches, and the design is single-writer with a 64 KB-per-batch log-write bottleneck and cross-region physical replication as its known limits.
subtopics.visual: Learner commits transactions and watches redo records fan out to six storage segments in three AZ columns with the VCL/VDL markers advancing as acks arrive, then kills an entire AZ to see the 4/6 quorum still complete and gossip repair backfill the missing records, and finally crashes the compute node to watch recovery consist only of reading the VDL and truncating, with a page-read request showing a storage node materializing the page from its log.

subtopics.title: Object stores as substrate: S3 semantics and erasure coding vs replication
subtopics.covers: What an engine can and cannot assume from S3-class storage — strong read-after-write and list-after-write (since 2020), no append and no rename, immutable objects with multipart upload, conditional PUT via If-None-Match/If-Match ETag as the only atomic primitive (used for manifest and lock files by Iceberg, SlateDB and Delta), ~10–100 ms first-byte latency with per-request pricing, and expensive LIST — and beneath it how 11-nines durability comes from Reed-Solomon (k+m) erasure coding across failure domains rather than 3× replication, with reconstruction fan-in reads, repair traffic amplification, degraded-read latency and local reconstruction codes (Azure LRC, HDFS EC) as the trade-offs, contrasted with Colossus and Ceph.
