subtopics.visual: Learner sets 3× replication or an RS(k,m) stripe with sliders and fails drives one by one, watching storage overhead, the surviving-failure budget, the reconstruction reads fanning in from k fragments and the repair bytes crossing the network, then switches to the API panel and races two engine nodes on a conditional PUT of the same manifest key to see one 200 and one 412.

subtopics.title: Durability math: AFR, repair windows and what eleven nines means
subtopics.covers: Turning device and failure-domain statistics into a data-loss probability rather than an availability figure — annualized failure rate under the exponential model, why loss requires a second and third failure inside the repair window so MTTDL scales with repair bandwidth rather than with copy count, replication against erasure coding at equal overhead (three copies versus RS(6,3) versus RS(10,4)), the repair-traffic term that makes wide codes slower to heal and the local reconstruction codes that buy repair cost back with storage — then the assumption that actually breaks every calculation, independence, since a correlated batch, a shared power domain, a firmware bug, one operator or one control plane makes the correlated term dominate regardless of redundancy, and the closing observation that software deletion, a bad migration and a lost encryption key outrank disks entirely, which is why an immutable off-account copy and a proven restore move the answer more than any coding scheme.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets AFR, replica count or coding scheme, repair bandwidth and cluster size and watches modelled annual loss probability and MTTDL recompute with every term shown, then raises a correlated-failure fraction and sees the nines collapse no matter how much redundancy is added, while a second panel adds operator-error and software-deletion rates that dwarf the device term until an immutable off-account copy is introduced.

subtopics.title: The object-storage tier ladder and what each tier makes possible
subtopics.covers: Storage classes as a design input rather than a billing detail — S3 Standard's ~10–100 ms first byte and per-request pricing versus S3 Express One Zone directory buckets at single-digit milliseconds with single-AZ durability and different request economics, the GCS and Azure equivalents, regional caches and instance-store NVMe as the rungs above, archive classes with minutes-to-hours retrieval below — then the designs each rung newly permits or forbids: a WAL or commit path on object storage (SlateDB, turbopuffer, diskless brokers), spill and shuffle to objects instead of local disk, per-request cost and small-file overhead as the real limit on commit frequency, and the cross-AZ transfer a single-AZ tier removes and reintroduces on failure.
subtopics.visual: The learner assigns each part of an engine's I/O (WAL append, checkpoint, spill, cold read, archive) to a storage tier and runs a workload, watching p50/p99 per operation, requests per second by class, monthly cost and the durability envelope change, with an AZ-failure button showing exactly which single-AZ-tier data becomes unavailable and what the engine does about it.

subtopics.title: Disaggregated storage engines: Neon, SlateDB, WarpStream, Snowflake
subtopics.covers: Neon replaces PostgreSQL's disk with safekeepers (a Paxos-style WAL service that acks commits) and a pageserver that ingests WAL into delta and image layers and answers get_page@LSN by reconstruction, enabling copy-on-write branches; SlateDB runs an LSM entirely on object storage with a batched WAL of small objects, a manifest advanced by conditional PUT and no local disk; WarpStream makes Kafka brokers stateless agents that batch records into S3 objects sequenced by a metadata service, trading hundreds of milliseconds of latency for zero inter-AZ transfer cost; Snowflake keeps immutable micro-partitions on S3 with per-warehouse SSD caches and metadata/transactions in FoundationDB — all sharing one cost model of request count, batching interval, inter-AZ bytes and cache-miss latency.
subtopics.visual: Learner picks a layout (Neon safekeepers+pageserver, SlateDB LSM-on-S3, WarpStream agents, Snowflake warehouses) and drags a batching-interval slider while writes and reads animate through compute cache, buffer and object-store tiers with live p50/p99 latency, PUT/GET rate, inter-AZ bytes and dollars per hour; on the Neon layout a 'branch at LSN' button shows the new branch sharing existing layers and a get_page@LSN request reconstructing a page from an image layer plus delta layers.

subtopics.title: The shared-storage OLTP family: Socrates, PolarDB, AlloyDB and the swing back to local NVMe
subtopics.covers: Aurora and Neon as two points in a family read off one comparison spine — Azure SQL Hyperscale/Socrates splitting compute, log service, page servers and XSTORE archive with the log as the only durable write path, Alibaba PolarDB sharing one PFS volume across nodes over RDMA with no redo shipping between them, Google AlloyDB layering a log-processing service that materializes pages plus a columnar engine and tiered cache — compared on who materializes pages, what a commit waits for, what a replica must do to observe a write, failover cost and whether a second writer is possible, then the counter-move where latency-sensitive teams went back to local NVMe (PlanetScale Metal) because a network page fetch has a hard floor.
subtopics.visual: One write and one cold page read traced through four stacked lanes (Aurora redo quorum, Socrates log service plus page servers, PolarDB shared volume over RDMA, local-NVMe primary) with per-hop latency and the durability point marked on each, plus buttons to kill a compute node, a page server and a whole AZ so the learner sees which lane keeps serving, which stalls, and which loses exactly the cache it needed.

subtopics.title: Zero-disk analytics and search: shared storage under ClickHouse, Elasticsearch and StarRocks
subtopics.covers: The rewrite of shared-nothing analytical and search engines onto object storage — ClickHouse Cloud's SharedMergeTree replacing per-replica ReplicatedMergeTree state with one shared part set and a coordination service, Elasticsearch's stateless/serverless split of a single indexing tier from search tiers reading segments out of object storage, OpenSearch remote-backed storage with segment replication, StarRocks and Doris shared-data modes and Pinot/Druid deep-store decoupling — together with what compute-compute separation buys (isolated ingest and query clusters over one copy, scale-out with no data movement, replica count decoupled from durability) and what it costs (commits routed through a metadata service, cache warm-up after every scale or failover event, per-request object-store bills and small-part pressure).
subtopics.visual: The learner runs one ingest-plus-query workload against a shared-nothing cluster and its shared-storage rewrite side by side, then adds a replica, kills a node and doubles query concurrency, watching bytes moved, time until the new capacity serves its first query, local-cache hit rate, commit-path hops and object-store request counts diverge — the shared-nothing lane rebalancing terabytes while the shared-storage lane serves immediately but entirely from a cold cache.

subtopics.title: Aurora DSQL: adjudicators, journals and OCC at region scale
subtopics.covers: DSQL's split of Postgres-compatible query processors on Firecracker microVMs from an adjudicator that validates each transaction's read and write sets against concurrent commits, a Journal service that is the only durable write path, and independently scaled storage shards that apply asynchronously, with EC2 TimeSync-derived timestamps providing strong snapshot isolation and cross-region commits, plus the constraints that fall out (no foreign keys, ~5-minute/10k-row transaction limits, aborts instead of waits, no session-pinned connections).
subtopics.visual: The learner fires concurrent transactions from two regions and steps each commit through adjudicator conflict validation against overlapping key ranges, journal durability and asynchronous storage apply, watching one transaction abort with an OCC conflict while sliders for transaction duration, write-set size and contention drive live abort-rate and cross-region commit-latency meters.

subtopics.title: Serverless and elastic scaling internals
subtopics.covers: How capacity follows load in Aurora Serverless v2 (ACUs resized in place by growing and shrinking the buffer pool with scaling lag and a scale-to-zero pause), Neon (compute suspended after idle, state safe in pageserver, resume costs a cold VM plus an empty local file cache that must re-warm from the pageserver), DynamoDB on-demand (partition throughput doubling, the previous-peak rule, split-for-heat and hot-partition throttling) and connection handling through a pooler; the recurring failure modes are cold-start latency on the first request, cache-loss latency cliffs after resume or downscale, throttling when a spike outruns scaling and cost that tracks provisioned rather than used capacity.
subtopics.visual: Learner draws a traffic curve with spikes and idle gaps and runs it against Aurora Serverless, Neon and DynamoDB on-demand side by side, watching capacity units chase demand with visible lag, a cold-start stall on the first request after idle, the cache hit-rate graph collapsing after a suspend or downscale and recovering, throttled requests appearing where a spike exceeds twice the previous peak, and a running cost meter per system.

modules.title: Distributed Query Execution: Joins, Exchange and Shuffles
modules.why: MPP join strategy, exchange placement, skew handling and shuffle fault tolerance decide analytical cost and latency by orders of magnitude.

subtopics.title: Distributed join strategies: co-located, broadcast, shuffle and semi-join reduction
subtopics.covers: Co-located (partition-aligned) joins that move nothing, broadcast joins that replicate the small side to every node (Spark autoBroadcastJoinThreshold 10 MB, Trino REPLICATED distribution, Citus reference tables, ClickHouse GLOBAL JOIN vs local JOIN), shuffle/repartition joins hashing both sides on the join key, and semi-join reduction where the build side's Bloom filter or min/max range is pushed into the probe-side scan before any shuffle (Trino dynamic filtering, Spark runtime filters, Oracle Bloom pruning), all decided by a cost model that adds network bytes (|S|×N for broadcast vs |R|+|S| for shuffle) to CPU and I/O.
subtopics.visual: Two tables with adjustable sizes and partitioning keys spread over four nodes; the learner picks co-located, broadcast or shuffle (or lets the cost model choose) and watches bytes flow over each network edge with per-node build/probe work bars, then enables dynamic filtering and sees the Bloom filter shrink the probe side before it crosses the wire.

subtopics.title: Skew, salting and adaptive query execution
subtopics.covers: Why hashing a Zipfian join or group key sends one partition 100× the rows of the others so the stage finishes when its slowest reducer does, and the fixes: salting the hot key (append salt 0..k-1 and replicate the other side k ways), skew-aware repartitioning that splits hot partitions into sub-ranges, hybrid plans that broadcast only the hot keys, sampled range partitioning (TeraSort-style split points), and Spark AQE re-planning at shuffle boundaries from observed map-output sizes (coalesce tiny partitions, split skewed ones, demote sort-merge to broadcast when the real size is small), plus Trino's skewed-partition and Redshift's distribution-key skew diagnostics.
subtopics.visual: The learner slides a key distribution from uniform to Zipf and watches per-reducer input bars grow lopsided with stage makespan pinned to the tallest bar; applying a salt factor k, a sampled range partitioner or AQE animates the hot partition splitting and small partitions coalescing, with total-work and makespan meters showing the extra CPU bought for lower latency.

subtopics.title: Exchange operators, plan fragments and distribution properties
subtopics.covers: Graefe's exchange operator that encapsulates parallelism so other operators stay single-threaded, plan fragmentation into stages at exchange boundaries with gather, broadcast, hash-repartition, round-robin and range exchange types, the optimizer treating data distribution like an interesting order with Cascades physical-property enforcers that insert exchanges only where a required partitioning is unmet (CockroachDB DistSQL, SQL Server, Greenplum Motion nodes, Trino AddExchanges), pipelined streaming shuffles where the whole DAG runs concurrently (Trino, Impala, Greenplum) versus materialized shuffles written to local disk stage by stage (Spark sort-based shuffle, MapReduce), and Trino's phased scheduling that launches build-side stages first under per-resource-group memory limits.
subtopics.visual: A logical plan tree where the learner drags exchange operators onto edges, or lets the property enforcer place them, and sees the plan split into colored fragments deployed across nodes; stepping execution shows row batches streaming across exchange edges concurrently in pipelined mode versus accumulating in shuffle files and running one stage at a time in materialized mode.

subtopics.title: Distributed aggregation, DISTINCT, top-N and mergeable sketches
subtopics.covers: Two-phase aggregation with partial pre-aggregation inside the scan fragment and final aggregation after a hash repartition on the group key, adaptive disabling of partial aggregation when it fails to reduce rows (Trino) and memory-bounded flushing of the pre-aggregation hash table, aggregation trees and Dremel's serving tree merging partials level by level, COUNT(DISTINCT) rewritten into a repartition on (group, distinct) pair or replaced by mergeable sketches (HyperLogLog, KLL/T-Digest quantiles, Count-Min) whose associative union lets partials merge exactly, ClickHouse -State/-Merge combinators persisting partial states in tables, and ORDER BY LIMIT executed as per-node top-N heaps merged once at the coordinator (the sketches' own internals and error bounds are dissected in analytical-query-platforms).
subtopics.visual: Rows on four nodes under a GROUP BY; toggling partial aggregation collapses the rows crossing the exchange to one per group per node, and switching COUNT(DISTINCT) between the exact repartition plan and HLL shows per-node registers merging by max at the coordinator with the error bound plotted against bytes shipped.

subtopics.title: Scan splits, columnar batches and late materialization across the wire
subtopics.covers: Scan scheduling in units of splits (Parquet row groups, Hive file byte ranges, MergeTree granule ranges, CockroachDB ranges) handed to workers with locality preference and work stealing, columnar batches (Arrow record batches, Velox vectors, Trino pages) crossing exchanges with dictionary encoding preserved and LZ4 on the wire, column pruning and filter pushdown fixing the projection that ships, late materialization across fragments where only join keys and row positions cross the join exchange and wide payload columns are fetched afterwards (Dremel, Vertica, Photon/Velox), and the crossover where a remote re-fetch of payload rows costs more than shipping the columns up front.
subtopics.visual: A wide table and a join; the learner selects the referenced columns and early versus late materialization, then watches the split queue drain across workers (with a slow worker being stolen from) while per-edge column-width bars show bytes crossing the exchange before the join, after it, and in the deferred payload fetch.

subtopics.title: Graph analytics: vertex-centric, linear algebra and worst-case optimal joins
subtopics.covers: Vertex-centric BSP execution (Pregel/Giraph/GraphX supersteps, message combiners, supernode-induced stragglers), linear-algebra formulations (GraphBLAS, sparse matrix-vector PageRank), edge-cut versus vertex-cut partitioning (PowerGraph, METIS) and their communication costs, and worst-case optimal join algorithms (Leapfrog Triejoin in DuckDB, RelationalAI, Umbra) whose intermediate sizes stay bounded on cyclic queries where binary hash joins explode.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs PageRank on a power-law graph under edge-cut versus vertex-cut partitioning, watching per-partition message volume and superstep makespan skew from one supernode, then switches to a triangle-counting tab comparing binary hash joins against leapfrog triejoin with live intermediate-result-size curves.

subtopics.title: Cancellation, stragglers and fault tolerance across fragments
subtopics.covers: Coordinator-driven cancel fan-out (Trino task abort, Spark killTask, CockroachDB flow cancellation through context propagation) and the orphaned tasks and leaked memory left when a node misses the message, straggler mitigation by speculative execution (MapReduce backup tasks, Spark speculation triggered by task-duration quantiles), fault tolerance by lineage-based recomputation of lost partitions over materialized shuffle files (Spark, MapReduce) versus fail-the-whole-query in pipelined MPP engines (classic Trino, Impala, Greenplum), Trino fault-tolerant execution spooling exchange data to object storage for task-level retries, and cluster-wide memory accounting that kills the query when any node's pool overflows.
subtopics.visual: A three-stage fragmented query runs while the learner kills a worker or injects a slow node and switches engine mode: pipelined MPP aborts the whole query, Spark recomputes only the lost partitions from lineage, Trino FTE retries the task from spooled exchange data, speculative copies race the straggler, and a cancel button fans out with a chosen node dropping the message and leaking a task.

modules.title: Analytical Query Platforms: Warehouses, Federation and Approximation
modules.why: Above the execution layer, what actually decides analytical cost is how much data is pruned, where the query runs, which plan fragments are pushed into another engine, and whether an approximate or precomputed answer is good enough.

subtopics.title: Cloud warehouse query path: pruning, caches, virtual warehouses and slots
subtopics.covers: How Snowflake serves a query: cloud-services metadata (per-micro-partition min/max, ndistinct and null counts held in FoundationDB) prunes files before compute touches S3, the result cache returns identical query text for 24 hours while the table version is unchanged, virtual-warehouse nodes cache files on local SSD with consistent hashing so the same node reuses the same files after resizes, spills go to local SSD then remote storage, and multi-cluster warehouses scale out on queue depth; contrasted with BigQuery's Dremel serving tree over Capacitor with slot scheduling and per-byte-scanned billing, and Redshift's shared-nothing DISTKEY/SORTKEY model (storage design itself lives in distributed-architectures).
subtopics.visual: A table shown as micro-partitions with min/max metadata; the learner types a predicate and picks a clustering key to watch the pruned fraction, bytes scanned, cache tier hit (result, local SSD, remote) and query cost update, then resizes or adds a cluster and watches file-to-node assignments re-hash and the warm-cache fraction drop.

subtopics.title: Federated queries and connector pushdown
subtopics.covers: postgres_fdw's deparser that ships WHERE clauses only when built from shippable (immutable, built-in or whitelisted-extension) operators with matching collations, use_remote_estimate issuing remote EXPLAIN versus local default costs, join pushdown only when both foreign tables share a server and user mapping, aggregate/ORDER BY/LIMIT pushdown, async_capable parallel foreign scans (PG14) and fetch_size cursor batching; Trino's connector SPI (applyFilter, applyProjection, applyAggregation, applyLimit/applyTopN, ConnectorSplitManager with dynamic filters delivered into splits), Spark DataSource V2 pushdown, Iceberg manifests as a statistics source, and why a join across two sources with no remote statistics degrades to fetch-everything nested loops.
subtopics.visual: A query over two remote sources where the learner toggles each pushdown capability (filter, projection, join, aggregate, limit) and remote statistics on or off, watching the generated remote SQL text rewrite itself, estimated versus actual rows crossing the connector, and the plan flip between remote execution and a local hash join over full fetches.

subtopics.title: Composable engines: Arrow, ADBC/Flight SQL, Substrait and reusable executors
subtopics.covers: Arrow as the shared columnar memory format with ADBC and Flight SQL replacing row-at-a-time ODBC/JDBC transfer and their zero-copy/streaming implications for result delivery, Substrait and Calcite as portable plan representations that let one optimizer drive another engine, reusable execution kernels (Velox, DataFusion, DuckDB-as-a-library, Photon) and the real recompositions built on them (InfluxDB 3 on DataFusion plus Parquet, Gluten pushing Spark stages into Velox), and the seams where composition leaks — type system and decimal semantics, NULL and collation rules, function-behavior mismatches and pushdown fidelity.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks operators and types to build a query, and the page renders the real artifacts side by side — the Substrait plan as inspectable JSON with its type and function-reference fields expandable, and the result as an honest Arrow record batch byte grid (validity bitmap, offsets buffer, values buffer, 64-byte-aligned padding) with a bytes-on-the-wire and per-row-conversion counter against a modeled row-protocol path — then the learner injects a seam mismatch (decimal precision/scale, or NULL ordering) between plan producer and kernel and watches a wrong answer emerge with the offending field and the buffer bytes behind it highlighted.

subtopics.title: Approximate answers: sketches, samples and error bars
subtopics.covers: How each sketch works and what it guarantees — HyperLogLog's leading-zero registers, harmonic-mean estimator, sparse/dense modes and HLL++ bias correction (Redis PFCOUNT, ClickHouse uniqHLL12, BigQuery APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT, postgresql-hll), Count-Min and Space-Saving for heavy hitters, KLL and t-digest for quantiles and why t-digest is accurate at the tails, Theta and MinHash sketches for set operations, similarity and dedup — all mergeable so partials compose associatively, set against sampling as the other lever: TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (block, correlated, biased) versus BERNOULLI (row), ClickHouse's SAMPLE requiring a sampling expression in the primary key, stratified samples for skewed groups, confidence intervals on sampled aggregates, and the lower bound (Charikar et al.) proving no estimator recovers distinct counts accurately from a small sample, which is why engines keep sketches for COUNT DISTINCT and samples for SUM.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a data distribution and a query (COUNT DISTINCT, p99, top-k, SUM), dials sketch size or sample rate, and watches the estimate and its error band converge on the exact answer while bytes-of-state and merge cost are counted; a block-versus-row sampling toggle clusters correlated rows and visibly biases the estimate that row sampling got right, and merging two sketches shows the union being exact where merging two samples is not.

subtopics.title: Segments and set membership: bitmaps, intersections and incremental updates
subtopics.covers: Treating membership as the stored object — Roaring bitmaps over dense surrogate ids with their array/bitmap/run containers, the id-densification mapping that makes it possible, evaluating a segment expression as word-level AND/OR/ANDNOT in milliseconds over tens of millions of members, engine support (ClickHouse groupBitmap and bitmapAnd, Pinot bitmap columns, Redis bitfields, roaringbitmap for Postgres), incremental maintenance as members enter and leave versus nightly rebuild, HyperLogLog when only the count is needed, and the second serving shape this workload always grows — answering 'is this one user in segment S' per request, which needs a per-user membership row or bitmask rather than the segment bitmap.
subtopics.visual: The learner composes a segment expression from clauses over a population and watches each clause's Roaring bitmap render as containers and the intersections execute word by word with live cardinality and bytes, compares the same question as a SQL predicate scan and as an HLL estimate, then streams membership changes to see incremental updates against a full rebuild and flips to the per-user lookup to watch the segment bitmap fail to serve it.

subtopics.title: Materialized views: query rewrite, incremental maintenance and HTAP replicas
subtopics.covers: Answering queries using views via containment-based view matching (Calcite, Oracle QUERY_REWRITE, BigQuery and Snowflake automatic MV rewrite), refresh strategies from full rebuild through REFRESH CONCURRENTLY diffing to incremental maintenance by the delta rules Δ(R⋈S)=ΔR⋈S ∪ R⋈ΔS ∪ ΔR⋈ΔS with per-group counts so SUM/COUNT survive deletes while MIN/MAX and outer joins fall back to recomputation (pg_ivm), ClickHouse materialized views as insert triggers that see only the inserted block (the JOIN-blindness gotcha), Snowflake dynamic tables with target lag, and HTAP columnar replicas where TiFlash joins as a Raft learner and waits on a read index for freshness while a router picks row or column replica per query; full incremental dataflow engines (Materialize) belong to logs-streams-derived-data.
subtopics.visual: The learner edits base rows beneath a joined and aggregated view and watches the delta rules fire, each changed view row highlighted by the term (ΔR⋈S, R⋈ΔS, ΔR⋈ΔS) that produced it, against a full-recompute panel with per-write work and staleness meters; deleting a group's last row shows count-based cleanup and deleting a MIN shows the recompute fallback.

subtopics.title: Single-node vectorized vs cluster: when DuckDB beats MPP
subtopics.covers: The fixed per-query cost of a cluster (planning, fragment scheduling, network round trips, shuffle serialization) that an in-process vectorized engine over Parquet on local NVMe or S3 with all cores never pays, the working-set threshold where one machine's memory and NVMe bandwidth run out (the roughly 1 TB-per-node region), Amdahl and shuffle-bound speedup limits, cloud cost per query of one large VM versus N small nodes, DuckDB/Polars/Photon single-node TPC-H results, Tigani's finding that most warehouse queries scan under 100 MB, and the cases MPP still wins: many concurrent users, data that must stay put, and federation.
subtopics.visual: Sliders for data size, selectivity, cores per node, node count, network bandwidth and shuffle fraction drive a live latency-and-cost chart comparing DuckDB on one box against an N-node MPP cluster, with the crossover point sliding as fixed scheduling overhead and shuffle cost change.

modules.title: Logs, Streams and Derived Data
modules.why: The log unifies replication, CDC, messaging and derived views; knowing what a broker acknowledgement, an offset commit and a rebalance actually promise is what keeps data moving between systems without loss or duplication.

subtopics.title: The log as the universal primitive
subtopics.covers: An append-only, totally ordered sequence addressed by position (Postgres LSN, Kafka offset, Raft index) is the one abstraction behind the WAL, the replication stream, a Kafka topic and a CDC feed: state machine replication (same log + deterministic apply = same state), every consumer is just a cursor whose lag is its distance from the head, log compaction (Kafka compacted topics, LSM compaction) keeps the latest value per key so the log stays bounded yet replayable, and the stream-table duality (Kreps' 'The Log', Kafka Streams KTable) lets a compacted stream be read back as a table.
subtopics.visual: A central append-only log the learner appends key/value records to, fanning out to four consumers (a B-tree materialized view, a replica, a cache, a search index) each with its own cursor and adjustable apply speed; crashing a consumer and replaying from its saved offset shows convergence, and a compaction toggle visibly shrinks the log while the rebuilt final state stays byte-identical.

subtopics.title: Change data capture and the outbox pattern
subtopics.covers: The dual-write problem (a DB commit and a broker publish cannot be made atomic) is solved by writing an outbox row in the same local transaction and having a relay such as Debezium read it from the log (Postgres pgoutput logical decoding, MySQL row-format binlog, DynamoDB Streams), which gives at-least-once delivery ordered per aggregate key, requires an idempotent/inbox consumer, needs snapshot-plus-stream handoff without gaps (watermark-based incremental snapshots), and has the operational teeth of replication slots pinning WAL until the disk fills, REPLICA IDENTITY controlling which old-row values UPDATE/DELETE events carry, and DDL, sequences and unchanged TOAST columns not appearing in the stream (decoding mechanics are covered in write-ahead-logging-and-recovery).
subtopics.visual: An order service the learner runs in dual-write or outbox mode, injecting a crash at any numbered point (after DB commit before publish, after publish before marking sent, relay restart) and watching whether the event is lost, delivered once or duplicated; enabling a consumer dedup table absorbs the duplicate, and pausing the consumer makes the slot-lag and retained-WAL gauges climb.

subtopics.title: Queues that are not logs: SQS, RabbitMQ, Pulsar, NATS and Redis compared
subtopics.covers: This module owns the delivery-semantics comparison for every messaging substrate, including Redis: how a visibility-timeout or per-message-ack broker differs from a replayable log — SQS standard (at-least-once, unordered, receive/visibility-timeout/delete, heartbeat extension for long work, long polling, redrive to a DLQ after maxReceiveCount) versus SQS FIFO (message-group ordering, dedup ids, throughput limits), RabbitMQ exchanges/bindings, prefetch, manual ack versus auto-ack, publisher confirms, quorum versus classic mirrored queues and their split-brain history, priority and delayed delivery, Pulsar's BookKeeper-backed shared/key-shared/failover subscriptions with per-message ack, NATS core versus JetStream, Redis pub/sub (fire-and-forget fan-out with no persistence or replay, a disconnected subscriber losing everything published meanwhile, slow readers disconnected by client-output-buffer-limit, and sharded pub/sub in Cluster) and Redis Streams (consumer groups via XREADGROUP, XACK, the pending-entries list, XAUTOCLAIM for stuck messages, MAXLEN/XTRIM capped retention) — all set against Kafka's partitioned log and the database queue table (application-data-patterns) on the axes that actually decide the choice: ordering scope, redelivery and poison-message handling, retention and replay, fan-out, delay/priority, and consumer-scaling limits (Redis's data structures, single-threaded atomicity, memory model and persistence options stay in document-graph-and-key-value-store-usage).
subtopics.visual: A worker pool the learner points at SQS standard, SQS FIFO, RabbitMQ, Pulsar, NATS JetStream, Redis pub/sub, Redis Streams or Kafka while setting consumer count, prefetch/visibility timeout and a failure rate: in-flight timers count down until a slow worker's message reappears and two consumers process it, a poison message's receive count climbs until it lands in the DLQ (or ages in the Streams pending-entries list until XAUTOCLAIM reassigns it), disconnecting a subscriber under Redis pub/sub silently drops every message published meanwhile while the same disconnect under Streams or Kafka replays from stored entries, ordering marbles arrive shuffled until message groups or key-shared subscriptions are chosen, and a scaling slider shows where each system's ordering scope or partition count caps throughput.

subtopics.title: Kafka consumer groups, rebalancing and offset semantics
subtopics.covers: The group coordinator (elected per group from a __consumer_offsets partition) runs JoinGroup/SyncGroup with a generation id that fences stale members while the group leader computes an assignment (range, round-robin, sticky, cooperative-sticky); heartbeats and session.timeout.ms detect death while max.poll.interval.ms evicts a consumer whose processing is merely slow, eager stop-the-world rebalancing pauses every partition where cooperative incremental rebalancing moves only the affected ones, static membership (group.instance.id) suppresses rebalances across rolling restarts, offsets live in the compacted __consumer_offsets topic with auto.offset.reset earliest/latest/none, committing before versus after processing is exactly the at-most-once versus at-least-once decision (with sendOffsetsToTransaction the only way to fold the commit into a transaction), lag is the backpressure signal, consumers cannot exceed partitions, and KIP-848 moves assignment into the broker with incremental reconciliation while KIP-932 share groups add queue-style per-record acks beyond the partition ceiling.
subtopics.visual: A rebalance stepper where the learner adds and kills members, slows one past max.poll.interval.ms and switches between eager, cooperative-sticky and KIP-848 protocols: assignment bars redraw at each generation bump with a stop-the-world consumption gap under eager mode, per-partition lag climbs during the pause, moving the commit before or after processing makes a crash produce visible duplicates or skipped records, and enabling static membership makes a rolling restart pass with no rebalance at all.

subtopics.title: Batch processing: MapReduce, shuffles and reprocessing
subtopics.covers: MapReduce's map → shuffle (hash-partition by key, sort, spill to local disk) → reduce pipeline gets fault tolerance from deterministic re-execution over immutable HDFS inputs and speculative execution for stragglers; joins are reduce-side sort-merge, map-side broadcast or pre-partitioned, with salting for hot keys; Spark/Flink-batch/Tez cut a DAG into stages at shuffle boundaries and recover via lineage instead of materializing every intermediate; and reprocessing (Lambda's dual batch/speed layers vs Kappa's replay-from-the-log) relies on backfilling into a fresh derived table with idempotent outputs and an atomic swap.
subtopics.visual: The learner drops a small input into a word-count-plus-join job and watches map outputs get partitioned and sorted into reducer buckets, kills a worker mid-shuffle to see only its tasks re-execute, flips a skew toggle to make one reducer balloon until salting splits it, then switches to Spark mode where the same DAG collapses into stages and a backfill panel replays the log into a shadow table with a catch-up curve ending in an atomic swap.

subtopics.title: Kafka replication internals: ISR, leader epochs, acks and fsync
subtopics.covers: A partition leader appends while followers fetch, ISR membership is dropped after replica.lag.time.max.ms, the high watermark is the minimum log-end-offset of the ISR and consumers only see below it, acks=0/1/all combine with min.insync.replicas to define what an acknowledgement promises, leader epochs plus OffsetForLeaderEpoch truncation (KIP-101) fixed the log-divergence and data-loss bugs of high-watermark-based truncation, unclean.leader.election trades availability for lost acked writes, the default relies on replication rather than fsync for durability (flush.messages/flush.ms), and the KRaft controller quorum replaced ZooKeeper as the metadata log (segment and index layout is covered in the Kafka case study).
subtopics.visual: A 3-replica partition where the learner produces under a chosen acks/min.insync.replicas, slows a follower until it drops from the ISR, then kills the leader and watches the LEOs, high watermark and epoch table decide which acknowledged messages survive; a truncation-mode switch contrasts KIP-101 epoch-based truncation with the old high-watermark rule that leaves replicas divergent.

subtopics.title: Exactly-once semantics: idempotent producers and transactions
subtopics.covers: Delivery is at-least-once and only effects can be exactly-once: Kafka's idempotent producer stamps a PID and per-partition sequence numbers that the broker dedups within its last-five-batches window (OutOfOrderSequence otherwise); the transactional producer registers a transactional.id whose epoch fences zombie producers, the transaction coordinator logs state in __transaction_state, commit runs as prepare then COMMIT/ABORT control markers written into every touched partition and into __consumer_offsets (sendOffsetsToTransaction), and read_committed consumers stop at the last stable offset while a transaction is open, so a hung transaction stalls everyone; Flink's two-phase-commit sink rides the same markers, and external side effects (payments, emails) stay at-least-once behind idempotency keys (see application-data-patterns).
subtopics.visual: A producer sending through a lossy network with retries, where toggling idempotence shows sequence numbers deduplicating the redelivered batch; enabling transactions reveals the coordinator's state log, the markers landing in each partition and __consumer_offsets, a read_committed consumer's LSO frozen on an open transaction, and a zombie producer fenced by an epoch bump.

subtopics.title: Shared-log abstractions: Corfu, Delos, BookKeeper/Pulsar vs Kafka
subtopics.covers: Corfu separates ordering from storage with a sequencer that hands out positions and clients that write striped, chained replicas to flash units, filling holes on reconfiguration; Delos' virtual consensus wraps loglets (ZooKeeper-backed, native) behind a VirtualLog so the consensus implementation can be swapped live via seal-and-reconfigure; BookKeeper ledgers use ensemble/write-quorum/ack-quorum with fencing and a last-add-confirmed pointer so stateless Pulsar brokers can serve any segment; whereas Kafka couples serving and storage in a partition leader so rebalancing copies data (WarpStream and tiered storage move that boundary and are covered in distributed-architectures).
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a Corfu, BookKeeper or Kafka layout, appends records and watches sequencer ticket → striped quorum writes versus leader-append-then-follower-fetch, then kills a storage node to compare recovery paths (hole-filling, ledger fencing plus new ensemble, or ISR shrink plus a data-copying rebalance); a Delos mode swaps the loglet implementation mid-stream through the seal step.

subtopics.title: One copy of the bytes: Kafka topics as Iceberg tables
subtopics.covers: Materializing a topic directly as an Iceberg table (Confluent Tableflow, Redpanda Iceberg Topics, WarpStream/AutoMQ S3-native brokers, Kafka Connect and Flink Iceberg sinks) collapses the CDC-to-lake hop: schema-registry subjects map to Iceberg schemas evolved by column id, exactly-once commits are aligned so each table snapshot records the offset range it contains, frequent streaming commits create small-file and compaction pressure, and replay, backfill and analytical scan end up reading the same objects instead of three separately maintained copies (the Iceberg format itself is covered in column-stores-analytical-storage).
subtopics.visual: Producers append to a topic whose segments land as Parquet in object storage while the learner tunes commit interval and watches Iceberg snapshots appear carrying offset ranges, replays a consumer from a snapshot instead of the log, and lets small files accumulate until a compaction job rewrites them, with freshness, file-count, request-count and cost meters moving against each other.

modules.title: Data Engineering: Warehouse Modeling, Ingestion and Pipelines
modules.why: The site teaches columnar storage, lakehouse formats, CDC and MPP execution but never how analytical tables are shaped, extracted, loaded or scheduled — and the classic failures (a wrong grain that double-counts, a fact joined to the current rather than the then-current dimension, a rerun that duplicates rows, an API extract whose watermark silently skips rows, a partner file delivered twice) are modeling and pipeline problems that no amount of engine knowledge fixes; this module opens the site's data-platform track, which sits after the streaming and verification thread rather than inside it, and it is the single owner of dimensional modeling and slowly changing dimensions, because the grain, the SCD type and the load that maintains them are one decision and Part 5's data-modeling-and-per-store-usage only raises the grain question and points here.

subtopics.title: Dimensional modeling: star schemas, grain and fact tables
subtopics.covers: Declaring a fact table's grain before anything else, transaction versus periodic-snapshot versus accumulating-snapshot facts, additive, semi-additive and non-additive measures, conformed dimensions and the bus matrix, surrogate versus natural keys, degenerate, junk and role-playing dimensions, factless fact tables, snowflaking and why it is usually avoided, and the modern counterweight of one-big-table denormalization where joins are expensive and columnar compression makes width cheap — this page being the site's home for the material that the OLTP modeling module deliberately stops short of.
subtopics.visual: The learner declares a grain and drags dimensions onto a fact table, then runs three analytical questions that each become answerable, double-counted or impossible with the offending fan-out highlighted, while a toggle re-runs the same questions against a one-big-table layout showing bytes scanned and joins eliminated.

subtopics.title: Slowly changing dimensions and incremental loads
subtopics.covers: Type 1 overwrite, Type 2 with validity ranges and a surrogate key so facts join to the version true at event time, Type 3 and hybrid forms, late-arriving dimensions and inferred members, the MERGE that implements them on Snowflake, BigQuery, Delta and Iceberg with its real cost (copy-on-write file rewrite versus merge-on-read delete files), snapshots as the packaged form, and choosing the incremental predicate (updated_at high-water mark, CDC stream, partition overwrite) with its hazards: clock skew at the watermark, invisible hard deletes and non-idempotent reruns.
subtopics.visual: A source row changes three times while the learner selects an SCD type and an incremental strategy: the dimension animates rows closing and opening with validity ranges, an as-of query joins to the correct or the wrong version, and running the same load twice produces visible duplicates until the merge key or partition overwrite makes it idempotent, with bytes rewritten shown per strategy.

subtopics.title: Ingesting from APIs and SaaS sources: incremental extraction without a log
subtopics.covers: Sources with no WAL to tail — REST and GraphQL APIs, SaaS exports, partner feeds — extracted by full refresh, an updated_at high-water mark or a provider cursor, and the hazards of each: server clock skew or a timestamp set before commit letting rows slip under the watermark, records mutated without touching updated_at, hard deletes invisible to every incremental strategy and detectable only by periodic full reconciliation, offset and cursor pagination duplicating or dropping rows under concurrent writes, rate limits and retry budgets that shape the schedule, resumable checkpoints so a failed run does not restart from zero, landing raw immutable payloads before parsing so a schema change is replayable, and vendor schema drift between runs.
subtopics.visual: The learner extracts from a simulated API with configurable rate limits, clock skew and mutation behaviour, watching the watermark advance while rows written just before it are silently skipped, a page shift under concurrent writes duplicate and drop records, a hard delete survive in the warehouse until a full reconciliation finds it, and a mid-run failure resume from its stored checkpoint rather than the beginning.

subtopics.title: Landing zones: ingesting partner files from SFTP and object storage
subtopics.covers: Detecting arrivals by object-created event versus polling a prefix, manifests and checksums that say a delivery is complete, a processed-file registry keyed by name plus content hash so a re-delivery is skipped and a corrected re-send is recognized as superseding, landing raw bytes immutably before any parse so an encoding or schema surprise is replayable, the partial-file and ordering hazards (a multipart upload read mid-write, late days, out-of-order periods) and the watermark or partition-overwrite strategy each implies, quarantine plus per-file error reporting back to the partner, and back-pressure and concurrency limits when a year of history lands at once.
subtopics.visual: A landing prefix the learner drops files into — an exact duplicate, a truncated upload, an out-of-order day and a corrected re-send — while choosing the detection strategy (filename, content hash, manifest) and watching which loads are skipped, quarantined, double-counted or silently overwritten downstream, with the registry showing the exact reason each file was accepted or rejected.

subtopics.title: One-time imports: onboarding a legacy or customer dataset
subtopics.covers: The re-runnable import pipeline that engine migrations and streaming ingestion both assume away — landing supplied files immutably and surviving their defects (encoding detection and mojibake, delimiter and quoting quirks, BOMs, Excel-mangled dates, leading-zero identifiers and comma decimals), loading into an all-text staging table so nothing is rejected at the door, then validation and mapping passes that classify every row accepted, quarantined or rejected with a per-rule counter and a report the supplier can act on, a crosswalk table from source id to generated id so a re-run is idempotent and a later file references the same rows, parents-before-children ordering with deferred constraints and post-load index and statistics builds, and a cutover gate of row-count plus financial-total reconciliation against the source before anyone is allowed to use the data.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs a deliberately dirty supplier file through the staged import and watches rows split into accepted, quarantined and rejected buckets per validation rule, fixes one mapping rule and re-runs the same file to see the crosswalk table make it idempotent instead of doubling the data, and finishes at a reconciliation panel where row counts match but a currency total does not until the Excel-mangled decimal column is found.

subtopics.title: Zero-ETL and managed replication: what the provider actually runs
subtopics.covers: The managed OLTP-to-warehouse pipelines that replaced hand-built CDC for many teams — Aurora and RDS zero-ETL into Redshift, Datastream into BigQuery, Snowflake's managed connectors, Fivetran and Airbyte as the third-party form — all of them log-based capture plus apply with the plumbing hidden, and the questions that decide whether hiding it is safe: real end-to-end latency, DDL and type-change handling, deletes and TRUNCATE, whether history or only current state survives, backfill and re-seed behaviour, per-table failure isolation, replication-slot and WAL pressure on your primary, cost per changed row versus compute-hour, and the transformation and schema control you give up against running Debezium yourself.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs one source workload through a managed zero-ETL path and a self-run CDC path side by side and then injects the events that separate them — an ALTER TABLE, a column type change, a mass DELETE, a primary failover, a paused consumer — watching target freshness, rows diverging, slot lag on the primary and a cost meter respond on each path.

subtopics.title: Loading the warehouse: staged files, streaming ingest and clustering upkeep
subtopics.covers: Staging compressed files in object storage for bulk COPY versus event-notification auto-ingest versus streaming write APIs with their buffering and dedup semantics, the file-size sweet spot with too-small files inflating request cost and metadata and too-large files starving parallelism, the true cost of MERGE against immutable files and how repeated merges degrade clustering, the maintenance jobs that repair it (compaction, reclustering, OPTIMIZE and VACUUM, statistics refresh), declared-but-unenforced warehouse constraints, and bad-row handling via rejected-record tables.
subtopics.visual: The learner produces files with adjustable size and arrival rate and picks an ingestion mode: loader slots fill in parallel (idle on oversized files, request-bound on tiny ones), the micro-partition layout accumulates until clustering depth degrades and a test query's pruned fraction collapses, then a compaction job restores it while a cost meter splits spend across ingest, storage and repair.

subtopics.title: Orchestration and idempotent pipelines: schedules, backfills and watermarks
subtopics.covers: A task DAG with a scheduler, partition or execution-date semantics that make each run a pure function of its interval, catchup and backfill across many partitions under concurrency limits, retries with backoff and the requirement that every task be idempotent (write-then-swap a partition rather than append), sensors and event triggers versus fixed schedules, freshness SLAs, late data handled with watermarks and grace periods, partial-DAG failure and restart, poison partitions and quarantine, and the CDC connectors feeding it with their snapshot resume, slot lag and schema-change events.
subtopics.visual: A DAG timeline of partition-scoped runs where the learner launches a thirty-partition backfill with a concurrency cap and watches the scheduler queue and warehouse load meter, injects a mid-DAG failure and reruns to see non-idempotent tasks double rows while partition-swap tasks stay exact, then delays a source past the watermark so a run silently emits incomplete output.

subtopics.title: The transformation layer: models, materializations and incrementality
subtopics.covers: ELT's transformation half as versioned SQL — ref and source building a DAG the tool topologically sorts, materializations (view, table, ephemeral CTE, incremental, materialized view) and their rebuild cost, per-engine incremental strategies (append, merge, delete+insert, insert_overwrite with partition pruning) and the predicate that decides what is scanned, snapshots implementing Type 2, tests compiled into count-of-failing-rows queries, layering into staging, intermediate and marts, and the full-refresh-versus-incremental drift that makes a careless rebuild both expensive and different.
subtopics.visual: The learner edits a small model DAG and flips each node's materialization, seeing the compiled SQL change (a view inlining upstream, an incremental model wrapping MERGE with its filter), then runs the DAG for bytes scanned, rows written and runtime per node, changes upstream data to see which nodes recompute, and removes the unique key so the merge produces duplicates that the attached test catches.

subtopics.title: CI for the transformation layer: slim runs, PR environments and data diffs
subtopics.covers: The analytics counterpart to Part 5's OLTP pipeline gates — building only modified models and their children against a deferred production manifest (dbt state:modified plus --defer, or the equivalent selector in other tools) so a pull request never rebuilds the DAG, per-PR schemas or zero-copy clones created and dropped automatically, the split between unit tests over fixed fixtures that pin transformation logic and data tests that only assert on whatever rows happen to exist, data diffs comparing a model's output between the production and PR runs to catch grain and semantic changes no assertion covers, bytes-scanned and cost budgets per CI run, and the promotion path from development through staging to production with the state manifest as the shared artifact.
subtopics.visual: The learner edits one model in a DAG and watches slim CI select exactly that model and its descendants while a full-refresh lane rebuilds everything, with bytes-scanned, runtime and dollar meters diverging, then a data diff between the two runs surfaces a row-count explosion and a changed column distribution that every passing test missed.

modules.title: Analytics Delivery: Quality, Semantics, BI and Activation
modules.why: Once tables are modeled and loaded, the remaining half of a data platform is making them trustworthy and consumable, and this is where the failures a senior is actually paged for live — bad data travelling six hops before anyone notices, a customer table where the same person exists four times, three dashboards disagreeing about 'revenue' because each re-implemented the filter, a concurrency queue backing up behind scheduled deliveries with a surprise bill attached, and a warehouse-derived field quietly becoming the value an operational transaction depends on.

subtopics.title: Data quality, contracts and lineage
subtopics.covers: Validation at load (schema enforcement, not-null, range and enum expectations, referential checks a lake cannot enforce natively), frameworks and the choice between failing the run and quarantining rows to a dead-letter table, freshness, volume, nullness and distribution monitors with anomaly detection over their own history, reconciliation against the source by row counts and checksummed aggregates, data contracts as producer-side schema plus semantic guarantees enforced in CI and a registry, column-level lineage and impact analysis, and PII classification propagated along that graph.
subtopics.visual: A pipeline graph where the learner injects a source defect (a column arriving null, a unit change, a duplicated batch, a dropped field) and picks a defense, watching how many hops the bad data travels before detection, which downstream models and dashboards the lineage graph marks affected, and how quarantining rows differs from failing the whole run.

subtopics.title: Deduplication and record linkage: blocking, scoring and stable clusters
subtopics.covers: Normalization and standardization before any comparison, blocking or candidate generation that keeps the pairwise problem sub-quadratic (exact blocking keys, trigram and phonetic keys, MinHash/LSH banding, sorted-neighbourhood windows) and the recall lost by each blocking choice, pairwise scoring with Jaro-Winkler, token-set and numeric-tolerance comparators and probabilistic Fellegi-Sunter weights as implemented by Splink, Zingg and Dedupe, turning scored pairs into entities by connected components and the transitive-closure blowup where one bad link merges thousands of records (mitigated by graph clustering and score thresholds), survivorship rules for the golden record and the crosswalk table mapping source ids to it, stable cluster ids across incremental reruns so downstream keys do not churn, and evaluation with precision and recall on a labeled sample plus a human review queue.
subtopics.visual: A record set where the learner picks blocking keys and watches candidate pairs fall from N-squared to a tractable count while recall against known duplicates is tracked, then drags the match threshold to move precision and recall and clusters the surviving pairs, with one over-merged transitive chain highlighted and a rerun with new records showing which cluster ids stayed stable.

subtopics.title: Semantic and metrics layers: definitions, join paths and pre-aggregation routing
subtopics.covers: Defining a metric once as versioned code — measure, aggregation, grain, entities, permitted dimensions, filters and declared join paths in dbt Semantic Layer/MetricFlow, Cube, LookML, Malloy, AtScale or warehouse-native metric views — and the compiler that turns a metric-plus-dimension request into SQL by walking that join graph with per-engine dialect differences, the fan-out trap where joining two fact tables through a shared dimension multiplies rows unless the layer emits symmetric aggregates or separate subqueries, time-grain and additivity rules that forbid summing a semi-additive measure across time and force a ratio to be computed after aggregation rather than averaged across rollups, an ambiguous join path made an error instead of a wrong number, pre-aggregations and rollup caches with their freshness and invalidation plus the routing decision that sends a request to a rollup or to raw facts, row- and column-level access filters enforced in the layer so every consumer inherits them, its role as the grounding surface for LLM-generated analytics (a metric to call rather than a schema to guess), the classic OLAP-cube lineage it re-invents (MDX, Mondrian), and its costs: another deployable, dialect gaps, and drift when people query the warehouse directly or paste CASE WHEN definitions into BI tools, notebooks and reverse-ETL syncs.
subtopics.visual: The learner defines one metric with its grain, entities and join path, requests it across several dimension sets and watches the compiled SQL change join path and aggregation while a fan-out guard blocks an illegal dimension, then adds a second fact table so the naive plan double-counts until the symmetric-aggregate rewrite fixes it, computes a ratio correctly and again by averaging pre-aggregated rows to see the two numbers diverge, and enables a rollup so a routing panel shows which requests hit it, which miss, and what bytes scanned, freshness and cost each choice carries after a late-arriving source row lands.

subtopics.title: Serving BI: dashboards, extracts, concurrency and the query bill
subtopics.covers: Live queries against the warehouse versus extracts and in-memory models (Tableau Hyper, Power BI import, Looker PDTs), result and metadata caching with cache keys that must include the row-access policy or leak across users, aggregate tables and pre-warm jobs for the first-load cliff, concurrency control (Snowflake multi-cluster warehouses, BigQuery slots and reservations, Redshift WLM queues) versus per-dashboard timeouts and row caps, scheduled deliveries and auto-refresh as the hidden load multiplier, filters that are unselective or wrapped in a function and so defeat partition pruning, and cost attribution by dashboard and user with the guardrails — query tags, per-user limits, a required partition predicate — that make a runaway panel visible before the invoice.
subtopics.visual: The learner builds a dashboard of panels over a partitioned table and sets refresh interval, concurrent viewers and cache mode, watching queue depth, bytes scanned, p95 panel latency and a running dollar meter respond, then adds an unselective filter that defeats pruning and switches the same panels to an extract or a pre-aggregated table to see which get faster and which go stale.

subtopics.title: Reverse ETL: pushing warehouse results back into operational systems
subtopics.covers: Syncing modeled tables out to CRMs, ad platforms, support tools and application databases (Hightouch, Census, hand-rolled jobs): diffing a snapshot against the previous run so only changed rows are emitted, idempotent upserts keyed on a stable external id with a mapping table for provider-assigned ids, destination rate limits and batch sizes with backoff and per-record partial-failure handling so one rejected row does not fail the sync, error surfacing and replay, the freshness contract that a warehouse-derived field is hours stale inside a system whose users assume it is live, the full resync a model change triggers and the quota it burns, and the ownership rule that an activated field must never become the system of record for anything a transaction reads.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs a sync between a modeled table and a destination with configurable rate limits and failure rate, watching the diff emit only changed rows while batches throttle, retry and queue per-record errors for replay, then edits the upstream model so every row changes and sees the full resync blow through the destination's quota while a staleness clock shows how out of date the destination field had been all along.

modules.title: Stream Processing, Derived State and Durable Execution
modules.why: Derived state is only as correct as the semantics that maintain it: windows and watermarks, incremental views, sagas and durable workflows, tamper-evident history and end-to-end checks are what keep an unbundled system honest.

subtopics.title: Sagas and compensations
subtopics.covers: A saga (Garcia-Molina & Salem) breaks a long-lived cross-service transaction into local ACID steps with compensating actions, run by choreography over events or by an orchestrator whose state machine is durably logged (Temporal, Step Functions) so it can resume after a crash; steps are classified compensatable/pivot/retriable and must be idempotent; the lost isolation produces lost updates and dirty reads across services, countered by semantic locks, commutative updates, pessimistic views and re-read-before-act; and the honest comparison with 2PC across services says to keep data that truly needs atomicity inside one database.
subtopics.visual: A flight+hotel+car booking saga the learner can fail at any step or crash the orchestrator mid-flight, watching compensations execute in reverse and the orchestrator resume from its persisted state; racing a second saga or reader against it exposes the intermediate-state anomaly, and enabling a semantic lock shows the race being blocked instead.

subtopics.title: Auditing derived state against its source log
subtopics.covers: Derived stores drift from the log that feeds them through buggy appliers, skipped or reordered messages and silent corruption, so an auditor periodically replays a range of the source log, recomputes a rolling digest over the expected output and compares it with the derived store's own digest to locate the first divergent offset, then repairs by rebuilding the affected key range from the log; the auditor's lag behind the head is the central knob (too short and in-flight writes look like corruption, too long and detection is slow), and the tamper-evident primitives this reuses — hash chains, Merkle inclusion and consistency proofs, WORM retention such as Certificate Transparency, QLDB digests and S3 Object Lock — are built in Part 10's 'Tamper-evident audit' page and taken here as given, along with the threat model they do and do not cover: replay audits catch applier bugs and corruption, never a writer who legitimately appended bad data.
subtopics.visual: The learner corrupts, drops or reorders rows in a derived store while a periodic audit job replays the source log, folds a rolling digest over the recomputed output and binary-searches down to the first offset where the two digests part, then triggers a range rebuild; an auditor-lag slider shows short lags raising false alarms on writes still in flight and long lags stretching time-to-detection, with detection-time and false-alarm counters per setting.

subtopics.title: Stream processing semantics: time, windows, watermarks and state
subtopics.covers: Event time vs processing time, watermarks as a heuristic completeness bound (bounded out-of-orderness, per-source watermarks combined by minimum, idle-source handling), tumbling/hopping/sliding/session windows with triggers, allowed lateness and retraction/update outputs (the Dataflow model), keyed operator state in embedded RocksDB backed by changelog topics (Kafka Streams) or Flink checkpoints taken with Chandy-Lamport barriers (aligned vs unaligned) and restored by key-group range on rescaling, and the join family: buffered stream-stream, stream-table and temporal joins.
subtopics.visual: A windowing sandbox where the learner drags events onto an event-time axis with chosen arrival delays, sets window type, watermark delay and allowed lateness, and watches windows fire, late events get dropped or emit retractions, and the keyed-state panel change; injecting a checkpoint barrier then crashing an operator shows restore from the last snapshot and replay of the source from the checkpointed offset.

subtopics.title: Enriching a stream: async lookups, caches and pushing back on the source
subtopics.covers: Joining events to reference data three ways with different failure modes — per-record synchronous lookups that serialize the operator and saturate the operational store, asynchronous I/O with bounded in-flight requests and ordered versus unordered emission (Flink AsyncDataStream, and Kafka Streams' lack of an equivalent), and streaming the dimension in by CDC into local keyed state or a broadcast stream so lookups are local and versioned — plus the cross-cutting decisions: a per-key cache whose TTL is exactly the staleness contract, retry and timeout policy for a failed lookup, whether enrichment must use the dimension as of the event time or as of now, and the backpressure path that makes an overloaded lookup store stall the source rather than silently drop records.
subtopics.visual: One event stream is enriched by each strategy side by side while the learner raises event rate and lookup latency, watching synchronous lookups stall the operator and drive the database's queue depth up, async I/O hold throughput until its in-flight cap, and CDC-into-local-state stay flat, with a cache-TTL slider trading lookups per second against how often the output carries a stale attribute and a toggle replaying a record whose dimension changed mid-stream under as-of-event versus as-of-now.

subtopics.title: What a stream cannot compute: space lower bounds and predicting state size
subtopics.covers: The streaming model's hard constraint that exact distinct counts, exact quantiles and stream-stream joins over unbounded time need state proportional to the input (the Alon-Matias-Szegedy space lower bounds), which is exactly why every engine forces a window, a retention TTL or a sketch onto unbounded operators — Flink state TTL and interval joins, Kafka Streams window retention and changelog size, Materialize arrangement memory, RocksDB state backends — how watermarks and allowed lateness convert 'unbounded' into 'bounded by lateness', why keyed aggregation state grows with key cardinality rather than event rate (so a user-id key is fine and a request-id key is not), and the arithmetic for predicting state bytes, checkpoint duration and rescale time before deploying instead of after.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs one query three ways — unbounded stream-stream join, windowed join, and sketch-based approximation — while state size, checkpoint duration and answer error are plotted over time, then moves a key-cardinality slider that grows state without bound and an event-rate slider that leaves it flat, making the real driver visible before a TTL is applied and the curve finally levels off.

subtopics.title: Dataflow, incremental computation and event sourcing
subtopics.covers: Timely dataflow tracks progress with frontiers over logical timestamps so operators know when a time is complete, and differential dataflow represents collections as (data, time, diff) updates flowing through arrangements so joins, reductions and even iterative computations are maintained incrementally (Naiad, Materialize, DBSP) instead of recomputed; event sourcing applies the same idea to application state, with commands validated against an aggregate that is a fold over its event stream, snapshots to bound replay, CQRS projections rebuilt from the log, event versioning/upcasting and the deletion problem (crypto-shredding), while SQL-level materialized views are covered in distributed-and-analytical-query.
subtopics.visual: The learner edits base rows and watches a differential-dataflow join-plus-count propagate only (row, time, ±1) diffs through arrangements while a side-by-side batch panel recomputes everything; an event-sourcing mode lets them append commands to an account aggregate, see state as a fold over events, take a snapshot, and rebuild a projection by replay.

subtopics.title: Choosing a streaming database: Materialize, RisingWave, Flink SQL, ksqlDB
subtopics.covers: Materialize's differential-dataflow views with strict serializability and real-time recency guarantees, RisingWave's actor model checkpointing state to object storage so compute scales independently of state size, Flink SQL's changelog model (append vs upsert streams, retractions) with a RocksDB state backend, incremental and unaligned checkpoints and savepoint-based rescaling, and ksqlDB/Kafka Streams' changelog-topic-backed local state, compared on the axes that bite: view consistency versus event-time watermarking, state size and storage cost, join and retraction semantics, and whether changing a query means rebuilding state from the source.
subtopics.visual: The same continuous join-plus-aggregate runs in three simulated engines while the learner injects late and retracted events and watches each emit retractions or upsert overwrites, then rescales workers to see state redistribute from local RocksDB versus being fetched from object storage, with freshness, state-size and cost meters diverging per engine.

subtopics.title: Durable execution: workflow histories, deterministic replay and versioning
subtopics.covers: Temporal, Restate, Inngest and DBOS persist an append-only event history per workflow so a worker crash is recovered by replaying that history to rebuild in-memory state without re-running completed activities, which imposes determinism constraints on workflow code (no wall clocks, randomness or unguarded I/O; timers, signals and queries become durable events), leaves activities at-least-once so external side effects still need idempotency keys, requires versioning/patching for executions already in flight, and in DBOS's variant keeps the history in Postgres beside the application's own tables so workflow state is queryable and transactional with business data — the mechanism that replaced most hand-written sagas.
subtopics.visual: A multi-step order workflow renders its event history as a log while the learner kills the worker mid-step and watches replay re-derive local variables from history without re-invoking completed activities, then edits the workflow code to break an in-flight execution's replay until a version patch is applied, with a counter showing how many activities were replayed versus actually re-executed.

subtopics.title: Unbundling the database and end-to-end correctness
subtopics.covers: Kleppmann's 'turning the database inside out': the log as integration backbone with caches, indexes and warehouses as asynchronously maintained derived views, the resulting problem of reading your own writes across derived stores, the end-to-end argument (Saltzer) that dedup and exactly-once must live at the application layer via operation IDs, enforcing uniqueness and other constraints by routing all claims for a key through one log partition instead of a distributed transaction, multi-partition atomicity via a single log record plus idempotent appliers, the split between integrity (non-negotiable) and timeliness (negotiable), and trust-but-verify auditing against silent corruption.
subtopics.visual: An end-to-end request tracer where the learner submits a payment with retries through a load balancer, a service, the log and two derived stores; toggling operation IDs shows duplicate side effects suppressed, sending two concurrent username claims shows the partitioned-log constraint letting exactly one win, and injecting corruption into a derived store shows whether the periodic audit catches it.

modules.title: Verifying Data Systems: Jepsen, Simulation and Formal Methods
modules.why: Vendor claims are checked by generating histories under faults, by fuzzing the engine for wrong answers and by exhaustively exploring protocol state spaces; seniors must read Jepsen reports critically, verify their own replicas and clusters, and know which method (black-box history checking, query oracles and differential testing, model-based property testing against a reference model, deterministic simulation, model checking) finds which class of bug.

subtopics.title: Jepsen: history generation and fault injection
subtopics.covers: Jepsen's architecture — a control node driving concurrent client processes against a real cluster, generators composing operation streams (mix, stagger, phases, limits) over workloads such as register, set, bank and list-append, a nemesis injecting iptables partitions (majority/minority, bridge, partial), SIGSTOP pauses, kills, clock bumps/strobes, disk faults and membership changes — and the recorded history of :invoke/:ok/:fail/:info events where an indeterminate :info result must be treated as possibly-applied, plus why a 'pass' only certifies one configuration, version and fault schedule.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a simulated store model (async-primary, majority-quorum, Raft), a generator mix (read/write/CAS rates, client count) and a nemesis schedule, presses run, and watches per-client invoke→response bars fill a timeline with partition and pause bands overlaid, responses dropped by the nemesis turning into dashed :info intervals and the EDN history scrolling beneath.

subtopics.title: Chaos engineering and game days
subtopics.covers: Hypothesis-driven fault injection in production or staging (Netflix Chaos Monkey, Gremlin, LitmusChaos, AWS FIS): define a measurable steady state, state the hypothesis, minimize blast radius with canaries and abort conditions, inject primary kill, added latency, disk full, DNS and dependency failures, then validate failover automation (Patroni, Orchestrator, MongoDB elections), runbooks and alerting while measuring MTTR — with Jepsen-style consistency checks of your own deployment as the complement to availability-only experiments (restore and multi-region drills are owned by backups-incidents-disaster-recovery).
subtopics.visual: A chaos console over a simulated LB→app→primary/replica→cache stack with a live SLO gauge: the learner writes a hypothesis (fault, expected p99 and error budget, recovery deadline), sets blast radius as a traffic percentage and an abort threshold, fires the fault, and watches the failover sequence, request errors and runbook checklist tick off until the hypothesis is stamped confirmed or refuted (or the experiment auto-aborts).

subtopics.title: Linearizability checking: Knossos and Porcupine
subtopics.covers: Checking a history against a sequential model by search — Wing–Gong and Lowe's just-in-time linearizability as used by Knossos and Porcupine, memoizing visited (linearized-set, model-state) pairs, treating :info operations as pending with infinite response time, partitioning the history by key because linearizability is compositional, why the problem is NP-complete (Gibbons–Korach) so checkers time out on long contended histories, and how etcd, TiKV and FoundationDB's clients use Porcupine in-house with witness visualizations of the failing read.
subtopics.visual: The learner drags read/write/CAS intervals on per-client register timelines and the checker animates its search tree — each node a partial linearization with the model value, branches only for operations whose invocation precedes every pending response, backtracks in red, and either a linearization-point placement snapped onto the timeline or the contradicting read circled with an explored-state counter that balloons as contention grows.

subtopics.title: Elle and Adya cycles: checking isolation from histories
subtopics.covers: Elle's trick of a list-append workload where every append is unique so each key's version order is recoverable from any read, inferring ww edges from prefix order, wr edges from what a reader saw and rw anti-dependency edges from what it missed, then finding strongly connected components and naming them by Adya class — G0 (ww cycles), G1a aborted read, G1b intermediate read, G1c, G-single (one rw edge), G2-item, G-nonadjacent — adding process and realtime edges to test strict serializability, internal-consistency and cyclic-information anomalies, Hermitage for single-node levels, and the PostgreSQL 12.3 G2-item bug under 'serializable' that Elle found.
subtopics.visual: The learner sees only what a black-box client observed — each transaction's list-append writes and the read lists it got back, never the engine's true version order — and steps Elle's inference one rule at a time: recover each key's version order from the longest observed read, derive ww edges from that prefix order, wr edges from what a read contained and rw edges from what it was missing, with edges the observations cannot justify drawn grey as uninferable; toggling process and realtime edges then turns a history that passed serializability into a strict-serializability violation, and only after the cycle closes does a panel name its Adya class and list which isolation levels legitimately permit it.

subtopics.title: Replica consistency verification: checksums, pt-table-checksum and repair
subtopics.covers: Detecting silently diverged replicas — CockroachDB's consistency queue sending a ComputeChecksum command through Raft so every replica hashes its range at the same log index and a mismatched replica is fataled or reported, MVCC-stats recomputation, Percona pt-table-checksum computing chunked CRC32/xxHash over primary-key ranges as statements that replicate so each replica hashes its own copy and pt-table-sync repairs, PostgreSQL amcheck (bt_index_check, verify_heapam) on standbys plus pg_checksums, and the drift sources under logical replication (triggers, sequences, non-deterministic functions, missing REPLICA IDENTITY, TOAST) — Cassandra's Merkle-tree repair is owned by leaderless-quorums-crdts.
subtopics.visual: Three replicas of one key range shown as row grids: the learner injects a divergence (bit flip, dropped row, trigger-side-effect drift, torn write), chooses the CockroachDB mode (checksum command marches through the Raft log and all replicas hash at the same index) or the pt-table-checksum mode (chunk checksums replicate as statements and each replica compares), watches matching hashes turn green and the mismatched chunk turn red, then runs repair and sees the rows reconciled.

subtopics.title: Finding wrong answers: sqlsmith, SQLancer oracles and differential testing
subtopics.covers: Random query generation against the live catalog to build type-correct statements (sqlsmith) and what it can and cannot detect — crashes and assertion failures yes, wrong results no, because there is no oracle; the three oracles that solve that without a reference implementation: pivoted query synthesis (construct a query that must return a chosen row, so its absence is a bug), non-optimizing reference engine construction (evaluate the predicate as a projection with optimizations disabled and compare against the optimized plan), and ternary logic partitioning (the results of p, NOT p and p IS NULL must union to the unpartitioned result, which is what catches three-valued-logic and index-path bugs); differential testing across engines and across optimizer settings (enable_indexscan off, forced sequential scan, JIT on/off) as the poor man's oracle; automatic test-case reduction down to a minimal failing query; and how to apply this in practice before trusting a new extension, a custom operator class or a newly adopted engine.
