subtopics.visual: An oracle lab: the learner writes a predicate over a small table with NULLs and the tool builds the TLP partitions and the NoREC pair, runs them against a simulated optimizer carrying an injectable bug (a NULL mis-handling in an index path, an over-eager predicate pushdown), highlights the exact rows the partitions fail to reconstitute, and then minimizes the failing query clause by clause until only the smallest reproducer remains.

subtopics.title: Model-based property testing: a reference model, generated sequences and shrinking
subtopics.covers: Testing a storage or data-access layer against an executable specification rather than expected outputs — writing a tiny in-memory reference model, generating operation sequences from a state machine so only legal calls are produced, comparing the real system's response against the model after every step, and letting the framework shrink a 400-operation failure down to the three calls that matter (Erlang and Haskell QuickCheck state machines, Hypothesis stateful testing, jqwik, Rust proptest, and the same idea in-house at FoundationDB and TigerBeetle) — with the invariants worth encoding for a database client (an upsert is idempotent, a retried transaction takes effect exactly once, keyset pagination visits every row exactly once under concurrent inserts, a cache and its source agree after a flush), seeded deterministic replay so a CI failure reproduces, and where this sits between unit tests, differential query oracles and full deterministic simulation.
subtopics.visual: The learner defines a reference model and an operation set and the generator fires randomized legal sequences against both the model and a simulated engine carrying an injectable bug, so a divergence is caught and then shrunk step by step in front of them from a long trace to a minimal three-call reproduction, with counters for sequences run, sequences that found the bug and shrink steps taken.

subtopics.title: Deterministic simulation testing: FoundationDB, TigerBeetle, Antithesis
subtopics.covers: Running an entire cluster single-threaded over a simulated network, disk and clock driven by one seeded PRNG so every failing interleaving replays exactly — FoundationDB's Flow actors and BUGGIFY fault macros, TigerBeetle's VOPR with state-machine and liveness checkers and its rule against wall clocks, threads or unseeded randomness, Antithesis' deterministic hypervisor for unmodified software, swarm testing across thousands of seeds, and why DST explores rare interleavings that Jepsen's real-cluster timing cannot reach while sharing its blind spot for bugs outside the modeled fault set.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets a seed and sliders for message drop, disk latency, fsync lies and clock jumps on a single-threaded three-node Raft, watches the simulated event queue pop timestamped events and the simulated clock jump ahead, and when an invariant breaks the same seed replays step by step with an identical interleaving; toggling a code fix and rerunning the same seed turns it green while a seed grid shows swarm results across many runs.

subtopics.title: TLA+ and model checking protocols
subtopics.covers: Specifying a protocol as Init/Next state machine with safety invariants and fairness-conditioned liveness, TLC exploring states breadth-first with fingerprinting, symmetry sets and small finite models, reading a counterexample trace, and the real specs — Lamport's TwoPhase and Paxos, Ongaro's Raft, Amazon's DynamoDB/S3 use, MongoDB's replication spec, CockroachDB's parallel commits — plus Apalache symbolic checking, PlusCal, the spec-to-code gap closed by trace validation and conformance testing, and why IronFleet/Verdi-style proofs remain rare.
subtopics.visual: A model-checker explorer over a fixed two-phase-commit state machine (TM and RM states, an 'all RMs agree' invariant) whose guards are exposed as toggles and small predicate dropdowns — 'TM may commit when: all RMs prepared / any RM prepared / always', 'RM may abort after preparing: yes/no', message loss on/off — and pressing check runs a genuine explicit-state breadth-first search over the bounded product with real fingerprinting, so the states-found, distinct-states and diameter counters tick honestly as the graph grows level by level until a real violating path from the initial state to the bad state lights up, with a symmetry-reduction toggle measurably collapsing the interchangeable RMs and shrinking the graph.

subtopics.title: Famous Jepsen findings and the bug classes behind them
subtopics.covers: Mapping landmark reports to mechanisms — MongoDB's stale reads and lost writes under default w:1/read-concern-local and the 4.2.6 retryable-write rollback bug, Kafka's acknowledged-write loss under unclean leader election that motivated leader epochs, Redpanda's duplicated and lost records around leader changes, CockroachDB's clock-skew stale reads beyond max offset, PostgreSQL 12.3's G2-item under serializable, etcd 3.4's lease and stale-read issues, Cassandra LWT Paxos bugs, TiDB and YugabyteDB auto-retry lost updates, Redis-Raft and Elasticsearch split-brain — distilled into recurring classes: unsafe defaults, retrying indeterminate operations, log truncation on election, lease and clock assumptions, membership changes, and docs that overclaim.
subtopics.visual: A report gallery: the learner picks a finding and a mini-cluster replays its minimal reproduction message by message (e.g. w:1 write acknowledged, primary partitioned, new election, write rolled back on rejoin) alongside the anomalous history it produced, while a systems-by-bug-class matrix fills in as findings are explored.

parts.title: Real-System Case Studies
parts.summary: One page per engine, tying every mechanism module to how a shipping system actually assembles storage, query, transactions and replication.

modules.title: Case Studies: Relational, Embedded and Disaggregated Engines
modules.why: PostgreSQL, InnoDB, SQLite, DuckDB, RocksDB and Aurora are the engines seniors actually run, and each is a distinct design point; every page here assembles mechanisms already taught in Parts 2-8 into a whole engine and never re-derives them, so a case study only adds the engine's own configuration, its seams and the operational consequences of its choices.

subtopics.title: PostgreSQL end to end
subtopics.covers: One UPDATE traced through the postmaster's process-per-connection model, the extended protocol and plan cache, Selinger/GEQO planning, a clock-sweep shared_buffers frame, the heap tuple's xmin/xmax/ctid with the HOT-or-not decision and Lehman-Yao index maintenance, WAL records with full-page images after a checkpoint, group commit and synchronous_commit, the clog bit and ProcArray snapshot that make it visible, SSI's SIREAD locks catching a dangerous structure, then walsender streaming the bytes to a hot standby and logical decoding turning them into pgoutput row changes through a slot, with the well-known pain points (xid wraparound, bloat, connection limits, subtransaction overflow, slot WAL retention) shown as consequences of exactly these choices.
subtopics.visual: Where Part 1's anatomy page showed schematic boxes, this page shows the artifacts: the learner runs an UPDATE on a two-index table alongside a SERIALIZABLE reader and inspects the real decoded objects the statement produced — a field-by-field WAL record (resource manager, block references, the full-page image that appears or vanishes with checkpoint distance), the before and after heap tuple headers with xmin/xmax/ctid/infomask, the touched index leaf entries, the clog bit flipping at commit, the ProcArray snapshot the reader holds, the SIREAD lock that forms the dangerous structure, and the pgoutput message the slot emits — with toggles for whether the updated column is indexed (HOT chain vs new index entries) and synchronous_commit changing which artifacts exist and when the client is acknowledged.

subtopics.title: Extending PostgreSQL: extensions, hooks and access methods
subtopics.covers: What an extension actually is — a control file, versioned SQL scripts with upgrade paths and optionally a shared library, installed by CREATE EXTENSION as catalog rows owned by an extension object so pg_dump emits the CREATE rather than its contents — plus shared_preload_libraries with shared-memory requests and background-worker registration (why pg_stat_statements needs a restart and pg_trgm does not), the hook surface that makes behavior pluggable without forking (planner_hook, ExecutorStart/Run/End, ProcessUtility, ClientAuthentication, emit_log_hook) mapped to what real extensions do with it (auto_explain, pg_hint_plan, pg_stat_statements' queryid normalization, pgaudit, Citus rewriting into distributed plans), the extensible type system where operators, operator classes and families are what make a new predicate indexable (PostGIS on GiST, pg_trgm, bloom), custom index access methods (pgvector's HNSW and IVFFlat), table access methods, CustomScan nodes, TimescaleDB's hypertable chunking, pg_cron and pgmq as background workers and FDWs as an access method for remote data, and the operational edges: extension versions pinned per database, ABI coupling to the major version that blocks pg_upgrade until a compatible build exists, managed-provider allowlists that decide which extensions exist at all, untrusted languages and non-superuser installs as a privilege-escalation surface (see security-and-tenant-isolation), and the maintainer risk of depending on out-of-tree code.
subtopics.visual: A server diagram reusing the anatomy module's query-lifecycle lanes where the learner enables extensions one at a time and watches exactly where each attaches — a hook node splicing into the utility, planner or executor lane, a CustomScan node replacing a subtree, a new opclass row appearing in the catalog and flipping a previously unusable predicate from Seq Scan to Index Scan, an index-AM call, a background worker process starting, a shared-memory segment being claimed — with a restart-required badge on preloaded libraries, a major-version bump that marks which extensions block the upgrade, and a DROP EXTENSION step showing which catalog objects vanish with it.

subtopics.title: MySQL and InnoDB end to end
subtopics.covers: The same UPDATE through InnoDB's clustered primary-key B+tree with secondaries storing PK values, a mini-transaction emitting redo into the circular ib_logfile ring, an undo record with rollback pointer in undo tablespaces that read views traverse and purge trims (history list length), change-buffer merges for non-unique secondaries, the adaptive hash index and midpoint-LRU buffer pool with adaptive flushing, doublewrite before in-place page writes, REPEATABLE READ's next-key and gap locks (and the write skew RR still permits), and the binlog–redo XA two-phase commit with flush/sync/commit group-commit stages, row-format binlog, GTIDs, semi-sync and multi-threaded appliers, with gap-lock deadlocks and metadata locks on DDL as the classic production failures.
subtopics.visual: Four InnoDB-specific panels with no Postgres counterpart — the undo record and its roll-pointer chain back through prior versions that a read view walks and purge trims, the circular redo ring with checkpoint age and the LSN wrap point, the doublewrite area filling before any in-place tablespace write, and the prepare→binlog-write→binlog-sync→commit state machine — driven by the same UPDATE, with innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit and sync_binlog as knobs and, as the page's centerpiece, a crash injected precisely between binlog write and InnoDB commit so the learner watches recovery scan the binlog to decide whether the prepared transaction is committed or rolled back, and sees which settings turn that into silent data loss or a replica that diverges.

subtopics.title: SQLite
subtopics.covers: The single-file pager and B-tree file format (rowid table b-trees with overflow chains, index b-trees, WITHOUT ROWID tables, freelist), the lock ladder SHARED→RESERVED→PENDING→EXCLUSIVE and why SQLITE_BUSY and BEGIN IMMEDIATE exist, rollback-journal mode (copy old pages to -journal, fsync, overwrite in place) versus WAL mode (append frames to -wal, wal-index hash in -shm, readers pin an mxFrame snapshot while one writer appends, checkpoint copies frames back and truncates), the VDBE register-machine bytecode the NGQP planner emits, and how serializable-by-construction single-writer semantics plus a frozen file format and exhaustive testing explain why it is the most deployed database on earth.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs BEGIN/UPDATE/COMMIT from one connection while a second connection reads, toggling journal vs WAL mode, and watches the main file, -journal, -wal and -shm byte maps grow and shrink, each connection's position on the lock ladder, the wal-index and mxFrame the reader holds, and a checkpoint copying frames back; a crash button at any step shows the recovery path, and a side pane steps the statement's VDBE opcodes and registers as it executes.

subtopics.title: SQLite everywhere: WAL shipping, embedded replicas and local-first sync
subtopics.covers: Turning the single-file engine into a replicated, edge-deployed, per-tenant store and what each design actually guarantees: Litestream's continuous WAL-frame shipping to object storage with generation files and point-in-time restore (and its asynchronous loss window), LiteFS replicating whole transactions at the FUSE layer behind a Consul-held primary lease with write forwarding, rqlite/dqlite putting SQLite behind Raft, libSQL/Turso embedded replicas that read a local file and forward writes to a primary with a frame-number read-your-writes token, Cloudflare D1's read replication through Sessions and Durable Objects' per-object SQLite with point-in-time recovery; then the sync layer above — ElectricSQL/PowerSync partial replication with shape subscriptions, server-side row filters that double as authorization, CRDT versus server-authoritative merge, per-device change logs, and applying schema migrations to clients that were offline for several versions — plus the database-per-tenant pattern these enable and its backup, migration and noisy-tenant consequences.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes on two offline devices and a primary while choosing the replication design (Litestream restore, LiteFS lease-and-forward, Raft, libSQL embedded replica, shape-based sync with CRDT or server-authoritative merge), then kills the primary mid-stream and reconnects the devices to see which acknowledged transactions survive, which writes conflict and how each design resolves them, how stale each reader is, whether a read-your-writes token forces a wait or a redirect, and what happens when a migration reaches a device that missed two schema versions.

subtopics.title: DuckDB
subtopics.covers: An in-process OLAP engine: single-file columnar storage in 122,880-row row groups with per-segment lightweight compression (bit-packing, dictionary, RLE, FSST for strings, ALP for floats) plus zone maps, ART indexes for primary/unique keys, push-based vectorized execution over 2048-row DataChunks with selection vectors, morsel-driven parallelism scheduling pipelines across threads, out-of-core hash join, aggregation and sort that radix-partition and spill to temp when the memory limit is hit, optimistic MVCC with transaction-local storage and undo buffers for appends, a WAL checkpointed into the file, and direct Parquet/CSV/Arrow scans with projection and filter pushdown, which is why it replaces pandas-scale pipelines rather than a warehouse.
subtopics.visual: The learner submits a join-aggregate over a table wider than a memory-limit slider and watches the pipeline DAG execute: DataChunks pushed source→filter→hash-join→aggregate, a thread-count knob spreading morsels across workers, hash-table partitions turning red and spilling to disk as the limit is crossed, and a storage pane showing which compression each column's segments chose and how many row groups the zone maps pruned.

subtopics.title: RocksDB
subtopics.covers: The library LSM: column families sharing one WAL with their own memtables and SSTs, WriteBatch atomicity and pipelined write groups, skiplist memtable → immutable memtable → L0 flush, leveled compaction with dynamic level bytes, the three stall triggers (L0 file count, pending compaction bytes, memtable count) with slowdown and stop thresholds, block-based tables with partitioned index/filter, Bloom and ribbon filters and prefix extractors, LRU/HyperClock block cache versus the OS cache, snapshots as sequence numbers that hold versions through compaction, iterators merging memtables and levels while skipping tombstones, MANIFEST/VersionSet crash safety, pessimistic and optimistic TransactionDB, the rate limiter, and how MyRocks, TiKV, Kafka Streams and Flink each configure it.
subtopics.visual: A live internals panel where the learner issues Put/Get/Delete/Iterate/Snapshot against chosen column families and watches the WAL, memtables, per-level SST tiling, block-cache occupancy and compaction-backlog gauge; pushing writes past the L0 and pending-bytes thresholds turns the write meter to slowdown then stop, holding a snapshot shows compaction forced to keep old versions, and sliders for write_buffer_size, level multiplier and Bloom bits move the read/write/space amplification counters.

subtopics.title: LMDB, WiredTiger, Badger and Redwood: same trace, different engines
subtopics.covers: One script (write, overwrite, delete, read at an old snapshot, crash, reopen) executed on four designs: LMDB's mmap copy-on-write B+tree with two alternating meta pages, a freelist DB, one writer, readers that never block but pin free pages via the reader table and no log or compaction; WiredTiger's in-memory pages with skiplist update chains reconciled to on-disk pages, checkpoints plus a journal, and timestamp-based snapshot isolation; Badger's WiscKey split with keys in an LSM and values in a value log that needs its own GC; and FoundationDB Redwood's versioned B+tree with prefix compression, short-lived versions and delta pages, with bytes written, pages read and version-retention cost compared.
subtopics.visual: Four parallel lanes step through the same script; at each step the learner sees which file regions each engine writes (meta page flip, reconciled page, value-log append, versioned page), how an old snapshot held open blocks page reuse or forces version retention differently in each, and after the crash which recovery path each takes, while a scoreboard tallies bytes written and pages read per engine.

subtopics.title: Aurora and Neon as an operator
subtopics.covers: What changes for a Postgres user when storage is disaggregated, assuming (and never re-deriving) Part 8's mechanism pages for Aurora's log-is-the-database quorum and Neon's safekeepers and pageserver layer map: which familiar knobs disappear or invert — checkpoint and full_page_writes tuning, fsync and WAL sizing, pg_basebackup and physical slots, shared_buffers versus Aurora's survivable cache or Neon's local file cache, superuser and the provider's extension allowlist, connection limits and where a pooler must sit; what each operation costs — writer failover and cold replica cache, an AZ loss, Aurora backtrack and fast clone versus Neon branch-at-LSN as environments, pageserver restart and compute autosuspend cold starts, logical-slot and branch retention that pins storage; and which metrics expose the mechanism rather than the symptom (IO:XactSync and commit-latency wait events, replica lag, storage read IOPS and write amplification per commit, GetPage latency and layer-map depth, safekeeper WAL lag), plus where each ceiling actually binds (single-writer write throughput, cross-network page reads, per-request billing).
subtopics.visual: An operator console rather than an engine diagram: the learner runs a chosen workload against an Aurora or Neon deployment, moves only the knobs the platform still exposes and watches the metric panel respond, then injects failures (AZ loss, writer failover, pageserver restart, compute autosuspend, a forgotten replication slot or branch) and sees error budget, recovery time, replica staleness, retained storage and bill move — with a side panel naming which Part 8 mechanism each metric is the visible edge of.

subtopics.title: Vitess: sharding MySQL
subtopics.covers: How VTGate parses each query and routes it by the vschema (keyspaces, keyspace_id ranges, hash, lookup and consistent-lookup vindexes, sequences replacing auto-increment) to VTTablets fronting MySQL shards with query pools and ACLs; resharding with VReplication (copy phase, binlog catch-up, VDiff verification, SwitchTraffic with reverse replication for rollback) and MoveTables; the cross-shard limits of scatter-gather, lookup-vindex consistency and the opt-in atomic-transaction 2PC, plus the semantics that change for the application (transactions spanning shards, cross-shard joins) as run at YouTube, Slack, GitHub and PlanetScale.
subtopics.visual: The learner defines a vschema over a small schema, types queries and watches VTGate's route plan highlight one shard, a lookup-vindex hop or a scatter across all shards; then splits a shard 2→4 and watches VReplication's copy-phase progress bar, binlog catch-up lag, VDiff row comparison, SwitchTraffic flipping routing while reverse streams keep the old shards current, and a rollback that switches back.

modules.title: Case Studies: Distributed OLTP, Wide-Column and NewSQL Stores
modules.why: Bigtable, Cassandra, DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, MongoDB, graph engines, CockroachDB/TiDB, Spanner and FoundationDB each pick a different point in the operational design space — master vs masterless, quorum vs consensus, single-row atomicity vs strict serializability, pointer chase vs shard hop, and in the cloud offerings a metered currency that prices every one of those choices — and seeing how each assembles the storage, replication and transaction mechanisms of earlier modules into a shipping system is what lets a senior engineer predict its failure modes, read its Jepsen report and choose it for the right job.

subtopics.title: Bigtable and HBase
subtopics.covers: The (row key, column family:qualifier, timestamp) → cell model over sorted row keys with per-family retention/versioning and locality groups with per-group compression as the ancestor of column families everywhere, tablets as key-range splits addressed through the three-level Chubby-file → root tablet → METADATA hierarchy that clients cache and refresh on a miss, exactly-one-server-per-tablet enforced by a Chubby lock file with master election and reassignment when a lock expires, the write path of commit-log append then memtable then minor compaction to SSTables on GFS/Colossus with merging and major compactions and reads merging memtable plus SSTable stack behind a bloom filter, one shared commit log per tablet server recovered by sorting it on (table, row, log sequence) so each reassigned tablet replays only its own records, single-row atomicity as the entire transactional contract and what that forced Megastore, Percolator and Spanner to build above it, and the lineage split into HBase as near-clone (RegionServers, HDFS, ZooKeeper), Cassandra taking the data model but rejecting the master, and Spanner keeping the tablet/SSTable substrate and adding Paxos.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes keyed rows onto a tablet map over a sorted key space and watches a tablet split at the size threshold and rewrite its METADATA row, then kills a tablet server so its Chubby lock expires and the master reassigns its tablets and replays the sorted shared commit log into them, while a second pane steps one read merging memtable and SSTables with a locality-group toggle showing how many files and bytes a narrow column-family projection actually touches and a major compaction dropping superseded versions and deleted cells.

subtopics.title: Cassandra and ScyllaDB
subtopics.covers: The token ring with vnodes and gossip membership, the per-node write path (commit log then memtable then SSTable flush with STCS/LCS/TWCS compaction, partition index and key/row caches), the coordinator read path using digest requests, cell-timestamp reconciliation and read repair, tombstones bounded by gc_grace_seconds and the resurrection hazard when repair is late, full vs incremental Merkle-tree repair, and how ScyllaDB rebuilds the same design on Seastar's shard-per-core with per-shard memtables, userspace I/O scheduler and no shared locks — LWT, quorum arithmetic and data modeling are pointed to consensus-and-coordination, leaderless-quorums-crdts and partitioning-and-sharding.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes and deletes rows at a chosen consistency level against a 6-node two-datacenter ring, toggles nodes down, then reads: watching the coordinator fan out, hints queue for the down node, digests mismatch and the read-repair merge across each node's memtable and SSTables, and drags a gc_grace/repair timeline to see a tombstone purged before repair resurrect a deleted row.

subtopics.title: DynamoDB
subtopics.covers: The 2022 paper's architecture: request routers consulting a partition-map metadata service, ~10GB partitions with three replicas across AZs whose Multi-Paxos leader appends to a replicated log, B-tree storage replicas plus log-only replicas for cheap durability and fast repair, admission via per-partition and global (GAC) token buckets that implement adaptive capacity and burst, split-for-heat and split-for-size, GSIs maintained asynchronously with their own capacity and lag, Streams and PITR derived from the replicated log, TransactWriteItems via a two-phase coordinator with timestamp ordering, global tables with last-writer-wins, and the failure lessons (2015 metadata outage) that drove MemDS caching.
subtopics.visual: The learner drives traffic at a table and watches the router consult partition metadata, the leader Paxos-replicate to two storage replicas and a log replica, partition and GAC token buckets drain and throttle, a hot partition split-for-heat redistribute load, and a GSI's replication lag trail the base table while a strongly consistent read of the base and an eventually consistent read of the GSI diverge.

subtopics.title: Azure Cosmos DB: request units, partitions and five consistency levels
subtopics.covers: The service's real contract — logical partitions keyed by the partition key with a hard 20GB ceiling sitting inside physical partitions with their own throughput cap, request units as the single currency for reads, writes, queries and index maintenance so a cross-partition fan-out query costs orders of magnitude more than a point read and a 429 with retry-after is the normal backpressure signal, provisioned versus autoscale versus serverless throughput and how a container's RUs divide across physical partitions, an indexing policy that indexes every JSON path by default and bills write RUs for it until paths are excluded, the five named consistency levels (strong, bounded staleness, session with its continuation token, consistent prefix, eventual) mapped to the RU cost, latency and cross-region behaviour of each, multi-region writes resolved by last-writer-wins or a stored merge procedure, the change feed as the built-in derived-data path, and the MongoDB and Cassandra wire-protocol surfaces emulated over the same engine — the underlying consistency definitions themselves are owned by consistency-models and conflict resolution by leaderless-quorums-crdts.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a partition key for a sample workload and fires point reads, filtered queries and writes while an RU meter charges each one and logical partitions grow toward the 20GB limit until one hot key starts returning 429s with retry-after, then switching consistency level and write region moves read latency, observed staleness and RU cost together, and toggling index paths off visibly drops the write RU charge.

subtopics.title: MongoDB and WiredTiger
subtopics.covers: WiredTiger's B-tree pages with in-memory skip-list update chains, MVCC via snapshot and commit timestamps with oldest/stable timestamps, 60-second checkpoints plus journaling and recover-to-stable-timestamp, the oplog as an idempotent capped collection, replica-set elections with terms and priorities, write concern w:majority advancing the majority commit point that gates stable timestamp and rollback, read concerns local/majority/snapshot/linearizable, causal-consistency sessions via cluster time, sharding through config-server replica sets, chunks, the balancer and mongos targeted vs scatter-gather routing, multi-document transactions on WT snapshots with a two-phase coordinator across shards, and the Jepsen lesson that the pre-5.0 w:1 default lost acknowledged writes.
subtopics.visual: The learner writes through a 3-member replica set with chosen write and read concern, partitions the primary and watches oplog entries replicate, the majority commit point and stable timestamp advance, an election bump the term, and the old primary roll back entries beyond its stable checkpoint on rejoin, toggling read concern to see which reads had exposed the now-lost writes.

subtopics.title: Neo4j, JanusGraph and distributed traversal
subtopics.covers: Neo4j's fixed-size record stores with doubly linked relationship chains (index-free adjacency), relationship group records for supernodes, page cache and store-file layout, transaction log and causal-cluster Raft core with read replicas and bookmarks; contrasted with JanusGraph/HugeGraph serializing adjacency into wide Cassandra/HBase rows with vertex-centric indexes, Neptune and TigerGraph, and the structural limit that distributed traversal converts pointer chases into network hops.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs a four-hop traversal on a single-node record-store engine, stepping through relationship-chain pointers and page-cache hits, then reruns the identical traversal on a partitioned adjacency store where each hop crosses shards, comparing pointer dereferences, network messages and latency, with a supernode toggle that engages relationship-group indirection.

subtopics.title: Serving a social graph: objects, associations and the cache tier
subtopics.covers: The read-dominated graph-serving design that neither a graph database nor plain sharded SQL gives you — Facebook TAO's typed id-keyed objects and typed, time-ordered associations kept as per-(id1, type) lists with maintained counts over sharded MySQL, a follower/leader lookaside cache where the leader is the single writer per shard and serializes cache fills and invalidations, the deliberately tiny API (assoc_range, assoc_time_range, assoc_count) that is the only thing the layout can answer cheaply, read-after-write in the writing region against eventually consistent followers, and the failure modes — celebrity association lists, miss stampedes on the leader, cross-region lag — set against index-free adjacency and against a plain join.
subtopics.visual: The learner issues assoc_range and assoc_count queries against a rendered object/association store with follower cache, leader cache and sharded MySQL, watching hits, leader-serialized fills and write invalidations travel, then makes one object celebrity-hot to produce a miss stampede at the leader, and replays the identical workload as a normalized join for comparison.

subtopics.title: CockroachDB and TiDB
subtopics.covers: The full CockroachDB stack: Cascades-style optimizer and DistSQL flows of processors placed on leaseholders, ranges of ~512MB each a Raft group with epoch-based leases tied to node liveness, meta1/meta2 addressing and the range cache, Pebble per store, load-based split/merge and the allocator's rebalancing, closed timestamps for follower reads; versus TiDB's stateless SQL servers over TiKV's ~96MB Regions with Raft, PD as central placement driver and timestamp oracle, coprocessor pushdown of filters and aggregates, and TiFlash columnar Raft learners for HTAP — contrasting HLC plus decentralized placement against a central TSO/PD, with the transaction protocols themselves owned by distributed-transactions.
subtopics.visual: The learner types a two-table join on a 3-node cluster and steps it in CockroachDB mode (gateway resolves keys via meta ranges and range cache, DistSQL places processors on leaseholders, each proposes through Raft into Pebble) then TiDB mode (fetch a TSO from PD, route by Region, push filters to TiKV coprocessors), watching a per-hop latency breakdown and what changes when a leaseholder or PD is in another region.

subtopics.title: Spanner
subtopics.covers: Universe, zones and spanservers with tablets on Colossus, directories as the unit of placement and movedir migration, long-lived Paxos leaders with disjoint leases hosting the lock table and transaction manager, coordinator/participant 2PC layered over Paxos groups, interleaved parent-child tables that keep a hierarchy in one split, size- and load-driven splits, read-only transactions served at safe time without locks, schema changes as timestamped non-blocking transactions, the 2017 SQL layer with distributed query execution and range extraction, and F1's lessons (hierarchical schema, client-side OCC, protobuf columns, global indexes, change history) — commit-wait and TrueTime are owned by distributed-transactions and time-clocks-ordering.
subtopics.visual: The learner draws an interleaved schema (Customers → Orders → Items), inserts rows and watches keys co-locate into one directory and split, then drags a split boundary or triggers a movedir to another zone's Paxos group and re-runs a parent-child join to see it change from a single-group read to a cross-group 2PC with the extra round trips highlighted.

subtopics.title: FoundationDB
subtopics.covers: The unbundled transaction system: coordinators holding configuration via Paxos, a cluster controller, the sequencer assigning read and commit versions, GRV and commit proxies, resolvers partitioned by key range checking read/write conflict ranges for optimistic strict serializability, transaction logs fsyncing the commit before acknowledgement, storage servers pulling from tLogs and serving MVCC reads within a 5-second version window, whole-generation recovery that rebuilds the transaction subsystem in seconds while storage keeps serving, data distribution of shards, the 5s/10MB transaction limits, and layers (record layer, document layer) built on the ordered KV API — deterministic simulation is owned by verification-jepsen-simulation.
subtopics.visual: The learner submits a transaction and watches its read version fetched from a GRV proxy, reads served by storage servers at that version, then the commit flow through proxy → sequencer version → resolvers checking conflict ranges (a concurrent overlapping write turns the transaction red) → tLogs fsync → storage servers pull; killing a resolver or tLog shows the entire transaction subsystem recover as a new generation while reads continue.

modules.title: Case Studies: Streaming, Search, Caching and Real-Time Analytics
modules.why: Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch, ClickHouse, Druid/Pinot, the time-series engines and the Spark job that feeds half of them are what engineers reach for when the system of record is not enough — a cache, a log, a derived search index, a warehouse, a sub-second serving tier, a metrics database, a batch compute engine — and each one buys its speed by giving something up, so knowing exactly which mechanism pays for that speed is what keeps a derived store from being trusted as a system of record and a tuning knob from being turned by superstition.

subtopics.title: Redis
subtopics.covers: The single-threaded ae event loop (epoll/kqueue) that makes every command atomic and serializes Lua/EVAL and MULTI blocks, 6.0 I/O threads that parallelize only socket read/write, fork()-based RDB snapshots paying copy-on-write memory under write bursts, AOF with appendfsync always/everysec and the 7.0 multi-part rewrite, PSYNC2 replication IDs plus backlog for partial resync, Sentinel failover vs Cluster's 16384 CRC16 hash slots with config epochs and ASK/MOVED slot migration, maxmemory eviction by sampling 5 keys against a 24-bit LRU clock or LFU counter, active-sampling plus lazy key expiry, and why Redlock's lease-without-fencing argument (Kleppmann vs antirez) matters.
subtopics.visual: The learner fills a maxmemory-bounded instance with keys carrying TTLs under a chosen eviction policy and watches the event loop dequeue one command at a time, each eviction sample five keys' 24-bit LRU clocks and evict the oldest, active-expire cycles sweep, and a fork() RDB snapshot's copy-on-write pages balloon as a write burst hits the parent.

subtopics.title: Kafka storage: segments, indexes and tiered storage
subtopics.covers: A partition as a directory of segment files (.log, sparse .index of relative offsets every index.interval.bytes, .timeindex, .txnindex) rolled by segment.bytes/segment.ms, record batches carrying producer id/epoch/sequence and batch compression, reliance on the OS page cache with sendfile zero-copy for fetches, time/size retention deleting whole segments, the log cleaner's dirty-ratio-driven compaction that keeps the last value per key and drops tombstones after delete.retention.ms, __consumer_offsets as a compacted topic, and KIP-405 tiered storage offloading closed segments to object storage with remote log metadata while the local hot set stays small — ISR, leader epochs and acks belong to logs-streams-derived-data.
subtopics.visual: The learner produces keyed messages of chosen sizes and watches segments roll, sparse index entries append at the byte interval, a fetch-by-offset binary-search the index then scan forward in the .log, then runs the compaction cleaner (dirty ratio threshold, tombstone retention) and tiered offload of closed segments to see which bytes remain on local disk.

subtopics.title: Elasticsearch and Lucene
subtopics.covers: Lucene's immutable segments (FST term dictionary, postings with skip lists, doc values, stored fields, live-doc bitsets for deletes) merged by the tiered merge policy, near-real-time refresh creating searchable segments every second vs flush (Lucene commit plus translog truncation) with index.translog.durability=request fsync, a shard as one Lucene index replicated primary-backup using primary terms, sequence numbers, local/global checkpoints and in-sync allocation IDs so a promoted replica can replay from its translog, master election and cluster state publication (Zen2, Raft-like since 7.0), two-phase query-then-fetch search, and the Jepsen findings (lost writes, dirty reads, split brain) that make it a derived index rather than a system of record.
subtopics.visual: The learner indexes and deletes documents and watches each land in the translog and in-memory buffer, become searchable only when refresh writes a new segment, get merged with deletes dropped via live-doc bitsets; then fails the primary after partial replication so the new primary bumps its primary term, computes the global checkpoint from sequence numbers and replays or rejects operations, showing which acknowledged writes survive.

subtopics.title: ClickHouse
subtopics.covers: How the assembled system runs on top of MergeTree (owned by column-stores-analytical-storage): query analysis into a processor pipeline with PREWHERE, index-driven mark-range selection and parallel part reading as vectorized blocks, two-level GROUP BY with partial aggregation states merged at the initiator, Distributed tables with sharding keys and one-replica-per-shard fan-out, ReplicatedMergeTree coordinated through Keeper's replication log with parts fetched from peers, insert deduplication by block hash and quorum inserts, materialized views as insert-time triggers rather than query-time views, mutations as asynchronous part rewrites, async inserts, and why point updates and unbatched inserts are anti-patterns.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs a GROUP BY over a 2-shard by 2-replica cluster and steps the initiator fanning to one replica per shard, each replica selecting parts and mark ranges, running PREWHERE and partial aggregation as vectorized blocks and shipping aggregation states back to merge; then kills a replica mid-insert and watches the Keeper replication log entries queue and the part fetch bring it back in sync.

subtopics.title: Apache Druid and Pinot: real-time OLAP serving
subtopics.covers: The serving tier between a warehouse and a KV store: Druid's time-chunked segments of dictionary-encoded columns with roaring-bitmap inverted indexes per dimension, the ingestion split where real-time tasks serve fresh rows from memory before handing segments off to deep storage, historical nodes with tiered segment caching, broker scatter-gather with time-chunk and dimension pruning, a coordinator balancing segments, and ingest-time rollup trading raw fidelity for size; Pinot's star-tree pre-aggregation plus inverted/sorted/range/JSON indexes, upsert tables keyed by a primary-key-to-record-location map for mutable event streams, and its tight Kafka coupling; and why sub-second high-concurrency user-facing dashboards need this shape and where ClickHouse overlaps.
subtopics.visual: The learner streams events into a real-time task and watches the segment become queryable immediately, hand off to deep storage and load onto historical nodes, then issues a filtered group-by and steps broker segment pruning by time chunk, per-segment roaring-bitmap intersection or star-tree lookup and partial-aggregate merge, with rollup granularity and star-tree dimension splits as sliders trading storage against rows scanned and p99 latency.

subtopics.title: Prometheus TSDB and TimescaleDB: time-series engines
subtopics.covers: Why a time-series store indexes label sets rather than a primary key: Prometheus's head block of in-memory chunks with its own WAL and checkpoints, m-mapped head chunks, 2-hour persistent blocks holding index/chunks/tombstones/meta, postings lists per label pair intersected to resolve a selector, delta-of-delta and XOR chunk encoding, block compaction over time ranges and retention, remote write/read, and the memory-per-active-series model that makes cardinality (series count, not row count) the dominant resource; contrasted with TimescaleDB's hypertable chunk routing by time and space, chunk exclusion at plan time, compressed columnar chunks with segmentby/orderby, and continuous aggregates maintained through invalidation logs.
subtopics.visual: One ingest stream and one range query run down two lanes side by side — the Prometheus lane embedded read-only at a fixed preset (head chunks m-mapping into 2-hour blocks, postings lists intersecting for the selector) while every control acts on the TimescaleDB lane: chunk interval and space-partition count routing rows into hypertable chunks, plan-time chunk exclusion against the query's time and space predicates, a compression policy rewriting older chunks into columnar batches under chosen segmentby/orderby columns, and a continuous aggregate refreshed from its invalidation log so the same query can be answered from the rollup — with chunks touched and bytes read per lane as the shared meter.

subtopics.title: Apache Spark as an engine: executors, memory regions and shuffle files
subtopics.covers: The units an operator actually tunes — driver versus executors, cores per executor and the task slots they create, the unified memory model splitting execution and storage with its spill when execution wins, off-heap and overhead memory that decides whether YARN or Kubernetes kills the container, partition sizing from input splits and spark.sql.shuffle.partitions with AQE coalescing on top, sort-based shuffle writing index plus data files to local disk and the external (or object-store-backed) shuffle service that lets an executor die without losing them, persist/cache storage levels and their eviction, dynamic allocation and speculative execution, broadcast thresholds and the driver OOM from collect, and the write path's small-file and commit-protocol problem on object storage — the AQE rewrite rules, skew salting and distributed join strategies themselves belong to distributed-and-analytical-query, and lineage, reprocessing and the MapReduce heritage to logs-streams-derived-data.
subtopics.visual: One join-and-aggregate job the learner tunes by executor cores, memory fraction, shuffle partitions and dynamic allocation, watching task slots fill, per-executor memory split between execution and storage until spill files appear, shuffle map outputs land as index and data files and get fetched by reducers, then killing an executor with and without an external shuffle service to compare recomputation cost, with stage makespan and output file count shown per configuration.

parts.title: Production Practice
parts.summary: Securing, operating, tuning, sizing, backing up and recovering databases, plus the incidents that recur and what postmortems teach.

modules.title: Provisioning, Platform and Fleet Lifecycle
modules.why: The curriculum jumps from design straight to operating a database that already exists: nothing covers how it came to be, what the managed service takes away, what the network path between client and engine costs, how the bill decomposes, which account quota or missing AZ capacity will block the replacement instance at 3 a.m., why extensions block a major upgrade, how other teams get a database at all without each inventing its own topology, how a change reaches a thousand tenant databases, or how anything is ever retired — yet these are where unplanned restarts, accidental instance replacement, unowned unbacked-up instances and irreversible deletions actually come from.

subtopics.title: Provisioning as code: IaC, parameter groups, secrets and drift
subtopics.covers: Declaring instances, clusters, subnet and parameter groups in Terraform, Pulumi or an operator and reading the plan diff for attributes that force destroy-and-recreate versus an in-place update; static versus dynamic parameters (pending-reboot state, PostgreSQL context levels with ALTER SYSTEM and reload versus restart-required settings, MySQL SET PERSIST) and how a rolling restart is sequenced across replicas and primary without an unplanned failover; the single-source-of-truth problem where ALTER SYSTEM, a console hotfix and a parameter group all shadow the managed file; credential lifecycle with secrets managers, dynamic roles, IAM and workload identity, and dual-secret rotation with an overlap window; plus deletion protection, prevent_destroy and per-environment state.
subtopics.visual: A plan-and-apply sandbox classifies each changed attribute as in-place, requires-reload, requires-restart or force-replace with estimated downtime and a data-loss warning, then applies a parameter change showing which live sessions pick it up immediately, which wait for a reload and which need the animated rolling restart, while a side panel shows a console hotfix creating drift the next plan wants to revert and a credential rotation succeeding or dropping connections depending on the overlap window.

subtopics.title: Managed databases: what RDS, Aurora and Cloud SQL take away
subtopics.covers: The privilege ceiling (no filesystem access, no untrusted languages or custom collations, logs only through an API) and the supported alternative for each, extension and version allowlists that gate features and upgrade paths, maintenance windows and forced minor upgrades with their reboot, storage autoscaling, IOPS and burst-credit ceilings and instance-level throughput caps, managed backups and PITR with fixed retention plus why a cross-account immutable copy is still your job, Multi-AZ failover and endpoint DNS behaviour with connection draining and cached resolutions in long-lived pools, managed blue/green built on logical replication, proxies and what they pin, and the exit questions to ask before committing.
subtopics.visual: A control-plane simulator runs a live workload while the learner triggers a maintenance-window upgrade, a storage autoscale event and a Multi-AZ failover, watching DNS TTL expiry, dropped connections, pooler behaviour and per-request errors against a failover stopwatch, with a privileges panel where superuser-only actions are refused beside the supported alternative.

subtopics.title: Provider quotas, capacity and the limits you meet at 3 a.m.
subtopics.covers: The account- and region-level ceilings that block a recovery rather than a launch — instance-type capacity exhausted in an AZ so the replacement or larger class cannot be created, service quotas on instances, storage, provisioned IOPS, snapshots and cross-region snapshot copies, subnet IP and ENI exhaustion that prevents a new node or task from attaching, control-plane API throttling during a fleet-wide rollout or a mass snapshot copy, and cross-account copy limits that stretch a restore past its RTO — together with the practices that surface them in advance: quota dashboards alerting at a fraction of the limit, capacity reservations for the named replacement shape, a DR plan that states the exact instance type, AZ and subnet it needs, and a periodic drill that actually calls the provisioning API.
subtopics.visual: A recovery drill in which the learner must replace a lost primary and each attempt hits a different real ceiling — no capacity for that class in that AZ, an account quota already at its limit, a subnet with no free addresses, a throttled snapshot copy — with a stopwatch showing how many minutes each adds to RTO and a pre-flight panel that would have flagged every one of them the week before.

subtopics.title: The network path to the database
subtopics.covers: Every hop between client and engine — availability-zone placement with sub-millisecond round trips that are still billed per gigabyte in both directions versus cross-region tens of milliseconds, private endpoints and peering versus NAT and public endpoints, the proxy chain (mesh sidecar, load balancer, connection pooler, managed proxy) each adding a hop, a queue and a TLS termination, DNS-based endpoints whose client-side caching outlives a failover, TCP keepalive and user timeout versus load-balancer idle timeouts that silently reap pooled connections, MTU for bulk copy, and per-instance bandwidth ceilings that cap replication, backup and restore.
subtopics.visual: A topology canvas where the learner places app instances, proxies and replicas across zones and regions and then sends a read, a write and a backup stream, each hop adding latency and per-GB cost to a running total, while a failover flips the DNS record and a client with a cached entry keeps hammering the dead endpoint until its TTL expires and an idle-timeout slider starts killing pooled connections mid-flight.

subtopics.title: Cloud database cost models and the levers that move them
subtopics.covers: Reading a bill as an engineering signal — instance-hour plus storage plus provisioned IOPS plus backup plus transfer for managed instances, per-I/O charging versus an I/O-optimized tier and the utilization crossover, serverless capacity units with scale-to-zero and minimum floors, provisioned versus on-demand capacity plus reserved commitments and the separate cost of secondary indexes and streams, warehouse credits per second with auto-suspend and multi-cluster scaling, bytes-scanned versus slot reservations, object-storage request pricing that makes small files expensive, cross-AZ and egress that replication and scatter-gather silently multiply, and the tagging and showback that make any of it actionable.
subtopics.visual: A bill builder where one workload (QPS, dataset size, read/write mix, replicas, regions, retention) is configured across four platforms and stacked cost bars decompose by line item, then the learner pulls levers one at a time — I/O-optimized tier, auto-suspend, partition pruning, moving a replica out of a second AZ — seeing which line item each touches and where the ranking between platforms flips.

subtopics.title: Extensions and plugins: install, upgrade and the version trap
subtopics.covers: The separation between the installed shared library and the SQL-level extension version, so an image upgrade can leave the catalog version behind the binary and break function signatures until an extension update runs; preload-and-restart extensions versus on-demand ones; ABI compatibility with the server major version so every extension needs a build for the target before an upgrade can start, and the ordering between extension and server upgrades; extensions that change on-disk or index representations implying a reindex or a staged version path; how extension-owned objects survive dump/restore and logical replication; trusted extensions and non-superuser installs; and the same problem as MySQL plugins and search-engine plugin pinning.
subtopics.visual: An upgrade planner takes an extension set and a target major version and renders each extension's availability, required preload and restart, catalog-versus-binary version and any implied index rebuild; pressing 'upgrade the package only' replays an application call failing on a changed function signature, which an extension update clears while an index-format extension still shows a pending reindex.

subtopics.title: Running a fleet: staged rollouts, resumable fan-out and drift detection
subtopics.covers: Inventory and tagging as the precondition for any fleet action, the rollout shape that bounds blast radius (a canary, then percentage waves, with automatic halt on error rate, replication lag or migration duration), fanning a schema change across thousands of tenant schemas or databases with a bounded worker pool, per-tenant idempotency, checkpoints so a failed run resumes rather than restarts and per-tenant timeouts so one pathological tenant does not stall a wave, the version-skew window in which the application must tolerate both schema shapes until the slowest tenant finishes, drift detection that reports exceptions rather than the fleet, and telemetry designed around outlier ranking instead of one dashboard per instance.
subtopics.visual: A grid of five hundred tenant databases the learner rolls a migration across with configurable wave size, parallelism and halt thresholds: cells turn succeeded, failed or skipped while a version-skew histogram shows how long both shapes coexist, an injected failure trips the halt, a resume picks up exactly at the checkpoint, and a drift panel lists tenants matching no intended version.

subtopics.title: Databases as a paved road: self-service provisioning, guardrails and ownership
subtopics.covers: Turning the fleet lifecycle into a product other teams consume — a small catalog of supported shapes (engine, version, size class, topology, backup policy) generated from one module rather than copied per team, a request-to-running path that requires ownership, environment, data-classification and retention metadata before anything is created, guardrails expressed as policy that rejects a non-conforming plan at apply time (public endpoint, no backup, unsupported version, missing owner) instead of relying on review, per-team quotas and cost visibility, a deprecation path for shapes leaving support with a migration deadline, and a documented exception process for the workload that genuinely does not fit the road.
subtopics.visual: The learner provisions through the paved path and then tries to bypass it — an unsupported version, a public subnet, no owner tag, backups disabled — watching policy reject each plan by naming the rule and the exception route, while a fleet panel tracks how many instances conform, which carry exemptions and when each exemption expires, and how each team stands against its quota and cost budget.

subtopics.title: Decommissioning: proving it is unused, then taking it apart safely
subtopics.covers: Proving disuse before deleting anything — scan and index usage counters read over a full business cycle including monthly and quarterly jobs with a known reset point, statement-log greps for the identifier, and the rename-and-wait technique that gives an instant rollback DROP does not; the ordered teardown of a whole system — stop writers, verify no replication slot, CDC consumer, foreign-data wrapper, backup job, scheduled report or dashboard still reads it, take a final archival export readable without the original engine and prove it restores, fail the endpoint loudly rather than silently, retire replicas, monitors, alerts and runbooks, release storage and reservations; and the compliance tail of retention obligations, key destruction for residual encrypted copies, expiring cross-region and cross-account snapshots, and recording the disposal.
subtopics.visual: A decommission checklist runner over a live simulated system surfaces what the naive path misses — traffic found in a log grep after the 'unused' verdict, a quarterly job firing on day 31, an inactive replication slot on another cluster still pinning WAL, a downstream search index whose only source was this table, a snapshot copy in a second region — each blocking the final 'destroyed' state, with a rollback button available only while the rename-and-wait window is open.

modules.title: Security and Access Control: Identity, Privileges and Untrusted Callers
modules.why: Who can reach the listener, who the server believes they are, what privileges that identity carries, and what an attacker or a careless human can do once a statement reaches the parser are each a concrete mechanism inside the engine (a host-rule matcher, a SCRAM exchange, a privilege bitmask on a catalog row, a parse tree built from concatenated text, a search_path lookup in a definer function), and a senior engineer must know their exact semantics and bypass paths because exposed listeners, injected statements, standing human access and privilege-escalation chains are how real database breaches actually happen.

subtopics.title: Authentication: hba rules, password schemes, certificates and short-lived credentials
subtopics.covers: How a server decides who is connecting: PostgreSQL pg_hba.conf first-match evaluation over (type, database, user, CIDR) with trust/reject/scram-sha-256/cert/peer/ldap methods, why md5 is a pass-the-hash scheme while SCRAM-SHA-256 gives salted mutual proof and channel binding, MySQL caching_sha2_password vs mysql_native_password, clientcert=verify-full with CN-to-role maps, and cloud alternatives (RDS IAM auth tokens, Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, Vault dynamic roles) that replace long-lived passwords with 15-minute signed tokens and rotated leases.
subtopics.visual: An hba rule evaluator: the learner orders a stack of pg_hba rules and fires connection attempts (source IP, user, database, SSL on/off, method offered); the matcher walks rules top-down highlighting the first hit, shows accept/reject/wrong-method outcomes, then a side panel replays SCRAM vs md5 with a captured hash to show which one an attacker can replay.

subtopics.title: Authorization: roles, ownership, grants, default privileges and least privilege
subtopics.covers: Privileges as ACL bitmasks on catalog rows (pg_class.relacl, MySQL mysql.tables_priv) checked at bind time per object, role inheritance graphs with INHERIT/NOINHERIT and SET ROLE, the distinction between owner (implicit all + DROP/ALTER) and grantee, why PUBLIC's default CREATE on the public schema mattered before PG15, ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES vs GRANT ON ALL (only future vs only existing objects), column-level grants, and the per-service least-privilege pattern of app_rw / app_ro / migrator roles with NOLOGIN group roles owning objects.
subtopics.visual: A privilege-resolution explorer: the learner builds a role graph (edges = membership, flags = INHERIT/SUPERUSER) and grants on a schema of tables and columns; clicking any (role, object, operation) animates the resolver walking inherited roles, owner check and PUBLIC ACL until it finds a matching ACL entry or denies, and toggling ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES shows which future objects would or would not be covered.

subtopics.title: Exposure and hardening: the database's attack surface
subtopics.covers: The baseline and the attack each item stops — binding and firewalling (listen_addresses, bind-address, security groups, PrivateLink/VPC endpoints versus a public endpoint plus allowlist), TLS required and enforced server-side instead of left to client sslmode, elimination of default, shared and anonymous credentials (the open Redis/MongoDB/Elasticsearch incident class), host-based rules ordered so a permissive catch-all cannot shadow the strict ones, restricting the outbound and command-execution surface (COPY TO PROGRAM, LOAD DATA LOCAL, dblink and FDW egress, extension install, untrusted languages), separating admin and replication ports from the application path, and the verification loop of external scanning, a CIS-style benchmark run and an alert on any newly opened listener or rule.
subtopics.visual: A hardening scorecard over a simulated deployment where each control is a toggle and an attacker pane runs the matching attempt — connect from the public internet, force a plaintext downgrade and sniff the credential, log in with a shipped default, run COPY TO PROGRAM, reach the replication port — showing which attempt each control blocks, and demonstrating a strict rule rendered useless by a permissive one placed above it.

subtopics.title: Rotating credentials and certificates without an outage
subtopics.covers: Where database credentials actually live and leak (environment variables visible in process listings and crash dumps, .pgpass and my.cnf, base64-not-encrypted Kubernetes secrets, connection strings in logs and error messages) versus secret managers and short-lived IAM or Vault-issued credentials; the dual-credential rotation sequence that avoids downtime — create the new secret, roll app instances so both are accepted, verify no traffic on the old, then revoke — contrasted with a single-step change and with dynamic leases whose TTL must exceed the longest checkout; the pieces that must rotate in step (PgBouncer userlist or auth_query, ProxySQL credentials, replication and CDC users, backup and monitoring users, roles that own objects); TLS lifecycle as the higher-impact case — server certificate expiry failing every verify-full client simultaneously, CA rotation needing a trust-both window with both roots distributed before the switch, client-certificate and CRL handling, and provider CA-bundle updates that have caused fleet-wide outages; plus detection (expiry and credential-age monitoring, unused-role audits) and the containment playbook when a credential leaks.
subtopics.visual: A rotation timeline across app instances, pooler and database: the learner runs a naive single-step password change and watches authentication errors spike on every instance that has not yet redeployed, then repeats with the dual-credential sequence and with short-lived dynamic leases, seeing a lease shorter than the pool checkout produce mid-transaction failures; a parallel lane advances the clock toward certificate expiry with and without a trust-both CA window, showing the cliff where every verify-full client drops at once.

subtopics.title: Untrusted input in SQL: parameterization, dynamic SQL and defense in depth
subtopics.covers: Why Bind-time parameters make a value structurally incapable of becoming syntax while concatenation and hand-rolled escaping break (multibyte charset tricks, quoting functions applied to the wrong position), the positions that cannot be parameterized and their correct handling (quote_ident/format %I and %L, allowlists for ORDER BY and table names, LIKE wildcard escaping), second-order injection from previously stored values, dynamic SQL inside PL/pgSQL EXECUTE and ORM raw fragments, blind and time-based exfiltration via boolean predicates and pg_sleep, stacked statements and whether the driver's protocol even permits them, and the database-side blast-radius controls that survive a hole — a least-privilege role, RLS, statement_timeout and row caps, a read-only replica, and pgaudit or error-signature detection.
subtopics.visual: A vulnerable endpoint the learner attacks: each payload typed into a parameter re-renders the concatenated statement's parse tree gaining new nodes (tautology, UNION, stacked statement) beside the parameterized path where the identical plan is reused and the payload sits inert in the Bind message, then moving the injection point to an ORDER BY column or a table name shows parameterization no longer applying until an allowlist or %I quoting is added, while a defense panel replays one successful injection against each database-side control to show exactly how many rows it can still read, write or exfiltrate.

subtopics.title: Human access to production: break-glass, four-eyes DML and session recording
subtopics.covers: The principle that standing human logins to the primary are the vulnerability, and the machinery that replaces them — just-in-time time-boxed grants brokered with approval (Vault dynamic roles, Teleport, cloud IAM session policies), read-only-by-default routing to a replica behind masked views and RLS for support and analysts, a recording proxy or pgaudit session logging because a direct psql session on a bastion leaves no statement trail, a second-approver gate plus a linked ticket for any hand-written DML or DDL, export and result-size limits on what a human can download, and the review loop that audits who used break-glass, on what data and why.
subtopics.visual: An access broker where the learner requests a role and watches the grant path resolve (approval, TTL, target primary vs masked replica, permitted statement classes), then runs a support SELECT and a hand-written UPDATE under each configuration while a session-recording timeline captures or silently misses each statement, and the grant clock expires mid-transaction so the learner sees what revocation does to an in-flight session and its held locks.

subtopics.title: Privilege escalation paths inside the database
subtopics.covers: The chains by which an ordinary role becomes superuser: SECURITY DEFINER functions with an unset search_path hijacked by a shadowing function or operator in a writable schema, ALTER FUNCTION/trigger ownership tricks, pg_read_server_files / pg_execute_server_program and COPY ... TO PROGRAM, untrusted PL languages, extensions installed by non-superusers, dblink/postgres_fdw credentials in the catalog, MySQL FILE/SUPER privilege and LOAD DATA LOCAL, and the mitigations — SET search_path = pg_catalog, pg_temp on definer functions, REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public, predefined roles instead of superuser, and the cloud provider pattern of a hobbled rds_superuser.
subtopics.visual: An escalation-chain graph: the learner starts as a low-privilege role and picks from available actions (create a function in a writable schema, call a SECURITY DEFINER function, run COPY TO PROGRAM); the component animates each step's effect on the effective privilege set and the search_path lookup that made it work, and applying a mitigation (locked search_path, revoked CREATE) visibly cuts the edge so the chain no longer reaches superuser.

modules.title: Data Protection: Row-Level Access, Encrypted Data and Tenant Isolation
modules.why: Once identities and privileges are settled, the remaining question is what each caller may see of the data itself — which rows a predicate lets through, what a ciphertext still reveals to the server holding it, what an agent can pull out of a sandbox, and which tenant's workload can starve another's — and every one of these is a mechanism with an exact failure mode (a predicate the rewriter injects, a userset traversal served from a stale snapshot, a frequency histogram over deterministic ciphertexts, a shared buffer pool no quota can partition) that produces the cross-tenant leaks and data-exposure incidents senior engineers are expected to design against.

subtopics.title: Row-level security and data masking
subtopics.covers: CREATE POLICY ... USING (read filter) and WITH CHECK (write filter) predicates injected by the rewriter as implicit WHERE clauses per command type, how PERMISSIVE policies OR together and RESTRICTIVE ones AND, tenant context via current_setting('app.tenant_id') or session role, the bypass paths (table owner, BYPASSRLS, superuser, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY), the planner rules that only leakproof functions may run before the policy predicate (so a non-leakproof function in WHERE can leak via error messages and can defeat index use), security_barrier views, and masking via column grants, views, SQL Server Dynamic Data Masking and Postgres anonymizer-style extensions.
subtopics.visual: A policy playground: the learner writes USING/WITH CHECK predicates, sets the session's tenant setting and role, and issues SELECT/UPDATE/INSERT statements; the component shows the rewritten query with the injected predicate, the resulting plan (index scan on tenant_id vs seq scan with filter when the predicate is not sargable), which rows pass, and a leakproof toggle that moves the learner's own function before or after the policy filter.

subtopics.title: Encryption in transit and at rest: TLS, TDE and key management
subtopics.covers: Client sslmode semantics (disable/allow/prefer/require/verify-ca/verify-full) and why anything below verify-full accepts a MITM, server-side ssl_min_protocol_version and cipher policy, hostname vs CA verification; at rest the layered options — block-device/EBS encryption, filesystem, TDE (SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL keyring, Percona/EDB Postgres) with per-tablespace data keys wrapped by a KMS master key (envelope encryption), and application-level field encryption with deterministic vs randomized modes; key rotation as re-wrapping data keys vs re-encrypting data, crypto-shredding, and the honest map of where plaintext still exists (buffer pool, WAL in memory, logs, pg_dump output, replicas, temp files).
subtopics.visual: An encryption-boundary tracer: the learner toggles encryption at each hop of a request path (client, wire, replica stream, buffer pool, WAL, data files, backups, logs) and picks a layer (disk/TDE/field); a data value flows through the path and renders as plaintext or ciphertext at every point, with a threat panel (stolen disk, network sniffer, DBA with psql, compromised app) lighting up green or red for each configuration, and a rotate-key button showing envelope re-wrap vs full re-encryption cost.

subtopics.title: Searching encrypted columns: blind indexes, structured encryption and what leaks
subtopics.covers: The ladder from randomized encryption (secure but unqueryable) through deterministic encryption and keyed-HMAC blind indexes (equality and joins, but identical ciphertexts hand an honest-but-curious server a frequency histogram that recovers low-entropy columns like state, sex or diagnosis) to order-preserving and order-revealing encryption (range and sort, but ordering plus an auxiliary distribution recovers nearly everything, per the Naveed-Kamara-Wright attacks on CryptDB-style deployments) and searchable symmetric encryption with its access-pattern and volume leakage and the leakage-abuse attacks that exploit it, alongside the production compromises a senior actually picks among — MongoDB Queryable Encryption's structured-encryption equality and range indexes, SQL Server Always Encrypted with and without secure enclaves, client-side field encryption in DynamoDB and the AWS Database Encryption SDK, and a tokenization vault plus a surrogate plaintext index scoped by row-level security — plus what stops working (sorting, joins, aggregates, LIKE, planner statistics and therefore estimates), key rotation as a full re-encryption, and the rule that the column's entropy and query pattern, not the cipher's strength, determine what leaks.
subtopics.visual: The learner encrypts a column whose value distribution they shape under each scheme, runs equality, range, sort, join and aggregate queries to see which succeed, which degrade to a full scan and which are impossible, then takes the attacker's seat with a public auxiliary frequency table and watches plaintexts recovered from a ciphertext frequency histogram and from recoverable sort order, with the recovery rate falling as they raise the column's entropy or switch to a randomized scheme and rising again when they add a range index.

subtopics.title: Zanzibar-style authorization stores: tuples, checks and the new-enemy problem
subtopics.covers: Relationship tuples (object, relation, subject) with userset rewrites for groups, roles and inheritance as implemented by Google Zanzibar, SpiceDB, OpenFGA and Ory Keto; a permission check as a bounded graph reachability search with per-edge caching, request hedging and a depth limit, and why deeply nested groups force a denormalized reverse index (Zanzibar's Leopard); the list-objects direction — 'which documents can this user see' — and the choice between filtering in the authorization service (accurate but unpaginatable at scale), pushing a returned id set into the database (bounded list sizes), or duplicating authorization data into the database so it can be joined and paginated, with the consistency cost of the last; the new-enemy problem where a check served from a stale snapshot re-admits a just-revoked user, and snapshot tokens (zookies) that trade latency for correctness after a revoke; and the comparison with row-level security and plain application joins for simpler models.
subtopics.visual: A relationship graph where the learner runs a check and watches the traversal expand usersets hop by hop with cache hits and misses per edge and a depth cap firing on a deep group chain, then revokes a permission and issues the same check with and without a snapshot token to reproduce the stale allow, and finally runs a list-objects query whose fan-out the reverse index collapses while a database-join variant shows the same answer paginated but staler.

subtopics.title: Agents with SQL access: least privilege, budgets and injection through data
subtopics.covers: Scoping an agent or MCP server to a dedicated NOLOGIN-owned read-only role with RLS and column grants rather than the app role, enforcing statement_timeout, row and result-size caps and per-agent query/cost budgets, pointing it at a replica or a branch copy instead of the primary, allowlisted parameterized queries or a semantic layer versus free-form generated SQL, prompt injection arriving through stored rows and tool descriptions so retrieved data must never be treated as instructions, and audit logging plus human approval gates before any write or DDL.
subtopics.visual: An agent issues generated SQL against a sandbox where the learner toggles role privileges, RLS policies, statement timeout and row caps and watches each guard reject a runaway scan or a cross-tenant read; a poisoned row containing instructions then shows the agent following them into an attempted write, which an approval gate and a read-only role each stop at a different layer.

subtopics.title: Multi-tenant isolation and noisy neighbors
subtopics.covers: Given the shared-schema / schema-per-tenant / database-per-tenant layouts from application-data-patterns, the isolation mechanisms layered on them: RLS keyed on a session-scoped tenant id as the last line of defence, connection quotas per role and per database, statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, cgroup and container-level CPU/IO limits, workload managers (SQL Server Resource Governor, Redshift WLM, Snowflake warehouses, Citus tenant isolation onto dedicated shards), the shared-resource failure modes (buffer pool eviction, lock manager, WAL throughput, autovacuum starvation) that quotas cannot isolate, cell-based blast-radius design, and cross-tenant leak tests that assert every query plan carries a tenant predicate.
subtopics.visual: A shared-cluster stress bench: the learner places tenants of different sizes on one instance and cranks one tenant into an abusive workload (full scans, long transactions, connection floods); dashboards show buffer-pool share, lock waits and p99 latency for every other tenant, then the learner applies quotas, timeouts, a resource governor pool or migrates the tenant to its own cell and watches which of the neighbors' symptoms actually go away and which (WAL, vacuum) persist.

modules.title: Compliance, Auditing and Data Governance
modules.why: Retention, residency, anonymization and right-to-erasure obligations are not policy documents but concrete data-plane work — you cannot erase what you cannot find, a dataset with the names stripped out is not anonymous, a residency promise holds only if every replica, backup and support session obeys it, an audit trail that a privileged operator can silently edit proves nothing in the dispute it exists for, and a recorded access nobody alerts on is how a valid credential walks off with the customer table — so a senior engineer has to know the discovery, lineage, placement, retention-vs-hold, privacy, misuse-detection and tamper-evidence mechanisms, the honest limits of each, and how to turn them into evidence a third party will accept, before promising a regulator or a customer anything.

subtopics.title: Finding the PII: classification, catalogs and column lineage
subtopics.covers: Automated discovery by column-name heuristics plus value sampling with regex and NER classifiers (AWS Macie, Google DLP, open-source scanners) and its failure modes — confident false positives, and real personal data hiding in free-text notes, JSONB blobs and encoded identifiers; recording the verdict durably where it survives refactors (PostgreSQL COMMENT and security labels, dbt and Iceberg/Glue table properties, a catalog such as DataHub or OpenMetadata) rather than in a wiki page; column-level lineage that traces a field through every derived copy — CDC topics, materialized views and read models, search indexes, warehouse tables, exports, backups and logs — derived from query and pipeline metadata rather than drawn by hand; joining that graph to the erasure and retention workflow so every downstream node has a named owner and a concrete deletion mechanism (row delete, key destruction, partition drop, index reindex) and gaps are visible as stalls; and access governance on top of it — who may read tagged columns, break-glass paths, and the periodic review that catches drift.
subtopics.visual: A lineage explorer over a small platform: the learner runs the classifier over sample rows and watches columns acquire tags with confidence scores, including one false positive and one genuine identifier buried in a free-text column, then selects a tagged column so the graph highlights every downstream store it reaches, each node showing whether an erasure mechanism exists — with a simulated deletion request fanning out and stalling at the node that has none.

subtopics.title: Anonymization that holds: k-anonymity, l-diversity and differential privacy
