subtopics.covers: Why stripping direct identifiers fails against quasi-identifier linkage (the AOL and Netflix re-identifications), k-anonymity by generalization and suppression with its l-diversity and t-closeness patches and their utility cost, the differencing attack in which two aggregates differing by one predicate isolate an individual and thereby defeat any deterministic minimum-count threshold, differential privacy's formal guarantee with Laplace or Gaussian noise and an epsilon budget that depletes across repeated queries, and the shipping implementations a senior meets — BigQuery and Snowflake differential-privacy clauses, Google's DP libraries, per-group minimum-count rules in analytics products — plus the honest limit that DP answers are useless at small group sizes and that a masked clone is still regulated data.
subtopics.visual: A query console over a synthetic population where the learner runs a differencing attack (one aggregate, then the same aggregate with one extra predicate) to isolate a single person's value, watches a minimum-count threshold fail to stop it, then enables DP noise and sees the attack fail while an epsilon-budget meter drains with each query and the reported value's error bar widens as the group shrinks.

subtopics.title: Auditing, PII lifecycle and right-to-erasure
subtopics.covers: Audit mechanisms and their costs: pgaudit session vs object logging, MySQL audit plugin, trigger-based history tables, CDC-derived audit streams, and log volume/latency trade-offs; PII classification, tokenization and vault patterns; retention policies enforced by partition drop; and why GDPR/CCPA erasure is a graph problem across primary, replicas, WAL archives, backups, CDC topics, search indexes, warehouses and caches, where crypto-shredding (destroying the per-user key) is the only practical way to erase immutable copies, with break-glass access and periodic access reviews as the compliance loop.
subtopics.visual: An erasure-propagation simulator: the learner submits a delete for one user and watches the request fan out across a data-flow graph (primary, replicas, WAL archive, nightly backups, Kafka topics, Elasticsearch, warehouse, cache), each node turning green when erased or staying red with a retention countdown; switching to a per-user-key model and clicking shred flips all encrypted copies to unreadable at once, while an audit panel shows the pgaudit records produced by each action.

subtopics.title: Detecting misuse: bulk reads, anomalous access and alerting on query telemetry
subtopics.covers: Building detections over the audit records of the previous subtopic and pg_stat_statements rather than merely retaining them — rows returned per session against a per-role baseline (the signal that catches a slow drip where per-statement rules do not), first-time access to a PII-tagged table by a role that never touched it, predicate-free scans of a large customer table, COPY TO or a bulk export of a whole relation, access outside business hours or from a new source address, and a service role reading columns its feature never needed — wired to the response levers built elsewhere (row caps, statement timeouts, masked views from Data Protection, break-glass expiry from Security and Access Control) so a trip degrades access automatically, with the false-positive management that decides whether anyone acts on the alert and the honest limit that a compromised application role looks exactly like the application.
subtopics.visual: A telemetry stream of normal traffic carrying four seeded misuse patterns — an analyst paginating an entire customer table over an hour, a support engineer's one-shot unfiltered SELECT, a compromised service role reaching new columns, and a nightly job whose volume legitimately spikes — where the learner writes threshold and baseline rules and watches which patterns each rule catches, misses or falsely flags on a precision/recall scoreboard, with a response toggle that clamps a row cap the moment a rule trips.

subtopics.title: Retention, legal hold and subject access requests in conflict
subtopics.covers: The three colliding obligations over one dataset — a retention policy implemented as partition drops, TTLs and object-lifecycle rules, an erasure request that must delete sooner, and a legal hold that forbids deletion of anything touching a matter — resolved by a hold registry that gates every automated deletion path including backup expiry and object-lock retention, suppression plus a documented exception where erasure and hold collide, the unavailability of crypto-shredding while the key must be preserved, the release path when a hold lifts and deferred deletions must actually run, and the subject-access side: locating every record about one person across the lineage graph within a statutory deadline, producing a machine-readable export that does not leak co-tenants or counterparties joined into the same rows, and logging the request and its fulfilment as evidence.
subtopics.visual: A partitioned table whose partitions carry both a retention clock and a hold flag while the learner fires a retention sweep, an erasure request and a legal hold in different orders and watches which rows are deleted, blocked, suppressed or irretrievably destroyed — with backups, object-locked copies and CDC topics tracked separately — then runs a subject access request that walks the lineage graph to assemble an export while a redaction step flags every field belonging to another subject.

subtopics.title: Data residency and sovereignty: pinning rows, replicas, backups and reader location
subtopics.covers: Turning a jurisdictional requirement into enforced placement — region-pinned rows and tenants (CockroachDB REGIONAL BY ROW, Spanner placement policies, per-region shards or cells), the full copy inventory that must obey the same rule (read replicas, backups and cross-region snapshot copies, WAL and binlog archives, CDC topics, search indexes, warehouse tables, application logs and managed-service telemetry), key residency so any copy outside the boundary is unreadable without an in-region KMS key, transfer that is legally distinct from storage (cross-border support access, an on-call engineer or provider staff reading rows from another country, the sub-processor list), and the evidence the obligation actually demands: a per-data-class map of where bytes live and an alert when a new copy appears outside it.
subtopics.visual: A world map of one deployment where the learner tags a dataset with a residency rule and every copy lights green or red against it, then performs ordinary operational actions — enable a cross-region backup copy, add a global secondary index, open a support session from another region, ship logs to a central account — each spawning a new copy that the violation detector names along with the mechanism (key residency, region-pinned placement, log routing, support-access policy) that would have prevented it.

subtopics.title: Tamper-evident audit: hash chains, Merkle proofs and ledger tables
subtopics.covers: Making an audit trail that survives a compromised operator rather than merely recording events: append-only tables with UPDATE and DELETE revoked and INSERT-only grants, hash-chained rows storing H(prev_hash || payload) so any edit, deletion or reorder breaks the chain at a provable point, and the authenticated data structures behind the productized versions — Merkle trees with O(log n) inclusion proofs, Merkle Patricia tries, history trees giving append-only consistency proofs (the Certificate Transparency mechanism) and the inclusion vs consistency vs non-membership distinction — as shipped in Amazon QLDB journals and digests, SQL Server and Azure SQL ledger tables, Immudb and Git's object model; periodic roots anchored externally in WORM storage (S3 Object Lock, a signed digest) under credentials the application does not hold, verification jobs and the incident procedure when verification fails, the log-vs-database race when audit writes are not in the same transaction as the change, the GDPR tension that pushes PII out of the immutable log behind per-subject keys (crypto-shredding), and the honest limit that proofs bind history rather than the correctness of whatever the application wrote — the mechanism referenced from 'Unbundling the database and end-to-end correctness' in Stream Processing, Derived State and Durable Execution, where the same chains and proofs are applied to auditing a derived store.
subtopics.visual: An audit table rendering payload, previous hash and computed hash per row: the learner tampers with a historical row, deletes one or swaps two, then runs the verifier and watches the chain break exactly at the first altered record with every later row flagged, while leaf hashes fold upward into a Merkle root published to an external append-only anchor so re-verification draws an inclusion proof failing at the precise tree path, a consistency proof between two published digests separates an honest append from a rewritten history, and disabling the external anchor shows which tampering the in-database chain alone cannot catch.

subtopics.title: Audit readiness: mapping controls to database evidence
subtopics.covers: Turning every mechanism in this module into artifacts a SOC 2, PCI or HIPAA auditor will accept — access control (role and grant inventory, the dated access-review record, no shared accounts, break-glass grants with approver and expiry), change management (every DDL traceable to a reviewed change and ticket, plus the log proving no out-of-band change happened), encryption (key inventory and rotation records, the at-rest and in-transit configuration exported as evidence rather than asserted), backup and recovery (a dated restore test with measured RTO and a row-count comparison), logging and monitoring (audit retention, the tamper-evidence verification job, alert-to-response records from the misuse detections) and sub-processor documentation for managed services — plus generating each artifact continuously from the system instead of assembling screenshots the week before, and the procedure when the evidence and the claimed policy disagree; the evidence-not-assertion framing itself is owned by Lifecycle Checklists and Review Gates.
subtopics.visual: An evidence-collection run against a simulated deployment produces one artifact per control, and the learner sees which come back clean, which come back contradicting the stated policy (a DDL with no approval, a role granted directly rather than through a group, a restore test older than its interval) and which cannot be produced at all because nothing was configured to record them, with a remediation panel showing the single configuration change that converts each 'cannot produce' into a continuous artifact.

modules.title: Operating Databases: Observability and Tuning
modules.why: Every dashboard number, wait event and configuration knob is a window onto a mechanism you have already studied; this module maps the signals back to those mechanisms so you can diagnose a live system instead of pattern-matching, turns the signals into SLOs, pages and runbooks worth waking a human for, covers the scheduled maintenance clockwork whose silent failure is its own outage, and then works down the knob stack from engine parameters to the kernel and filesystem settings underneath them — ending with the automatic tuners that now turn those knobs for you and must be supervised.

subtopics.title: Metrics that matter: signals mapped to mechanisms
subtopics.covers: Applies USE/RED to a database and ties each signal to its mechanism — latency percentiles (p50/p99 per statement class, not averages), active vs idle-in-transaction connections against max_connections and pool size, buffer/OS cache hit ratio as a weak signal that hides working-set cliffs, replication lag in bytes (pg_stat_replication write/flush/replay LSN deltas, MySQL Seconds_Behind_Source and GTID gaps, Kafka under-replicated partitions and ISR shrink) vs seconds, checkpoint cadence (pg_stat_checkpointer/pg_stat_bgwriter checkpoints_timed vs checkpoints_req and the full-page-write burst after each), pg_stat_io and iostat await/queue depth for I/O saturation, RocksDB pending-compaction bytes and write-stall counters, autovacuum activity and oldest xmin — plus the exporter stack (postgres_exporter, PMM, sys schema, CloudWatch Enhanced Monitoring, Performance Insights) and the rule that alerts fire on saturation and invariant violations (quorum health, oldest-xmin age) rather than symptoms.
subtopics.visual: A live dashboard bound to a simulated engine under a mixed workload: the learner injects one hidden fault (lock pileup, requested-checkpoint storm, replica apply stall, compaction stall, connection storm, working set outgrowing cache) and watches which panels move first and in what order, then commits to a diagnosis before the fault is revealed with the causal chain from mechanism to metric drawn over the graphs.

subtopics.title: SLOs, burn-rate alerting and the runbook
subtopics.covers: Picking database SLIs a user actually feels — query success rate, p99 for a named statement class rather than for all traffic, replication lag measured against the read-routing threshold, freshness of a derived store — and setting SLOs with an error budget that gates risky change (migrations, upgrades, rollouts); multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts (a fast burn pages, a slow burn files a ticket) instead of static thresholds that fire on every checkpoint spike; the short list of database conditions genuinely worth a page (write unavailability, quorum or primary loss, wraparound countdown, disk days-to-full, backup age exceeding the RPO, replica lag past the routing threshold, connection saturation) and the long list that should only ever be a dashboard; symptom-based paging with cause-based dashboards behind it, dependency-aware suppression so one node failure produces one page, and alert hygiene (a runbook link on every alert, auto-resolution, deduplication, a weekly review of what fired and what it cost); and writing the runbook itself as a decision tree of copy-pasteable diagnostics with explicit mitigation side effects and abort criteria.
subtopics.visual: An alert-tuning bench where the learner sets SLO targets and burn-rate windows, then replays recorded incident traces — a slow burn from a lagging replica, a fast burn from a lock pileup, a checkpoint blip, a backup that silently stopped — and sees which configurations page, which stay silent and which are false positives, with a scorecard per configuration showing median detection time, pages per week and incidents missed entirely.

subtopics.title: Query-level telemetry and wait events
subtopics.covers: How per-statement and per-session instrumentation works and what it costs: pg_stat_statements normalization by queryid with total vs mean time vs calls, shared/local/temp block counters and wal_bytes to rank by I/O or WAL rather than time; log_min_duration_statement, auto_explain (with ANALYZE/BUFFERS sampling) and log_lock_waits for slow-plan capture; wait-event attribution in pg_stat_activity (Lock, LWLock, IO, IPC, BufferPin, Timeout, Client) sampled into Active Session History by pg_wait_sampling or RDS Performance Insights (average active sessions by wait class), MySQL performance_schema events_waits/statements summaries and the sys schema, the slow query log and InnoDB status, and Oracle ASH as the lineage; and query tagging with sqlcommenter/OpenTelemetry so a wait event on the database can be joined to a service trace.
subtopics.visual: An Active Session History sampler: the learner runs a workload mix and every simulated second the sampler polls the session table and stacks a wait-class area chart, then filters by wait class or queryid to discover which statement is spending its time in Lock:transactionid behind a long transaction versus LWLock:WALWrite during a fsync stall versus IO:DataFileRead after a cache miss, and toggles sampling frequency to see attribution accuracy trade against overhead.

subtopics.title: The database log as an operational artifact
subtopics.covers: Configuring the log for diagnosis rather than noise — log_line_prefix carrying timestamp, pid, user, database, application_name and a propagated request id so a line joins an application trace, log_connections/log_disconnections for connection-storm forensics, and log_checkpoints, log_lock_waits, log_autovacuum_min_duration and log_temp_files as the four settings that explain most incidents after the fact — plus log_statement and its cost, log_statement_sample_rate and log_min_duration_sample for high-QPS sampling, csvlog and jsonlog for machine parsing, rotation, retention and the log volume sharing a filesystem with data, credentials and PII appearing in statement text and bound parameters, and aggregate analysis with pgBadger or pt-query-digest as the complement to counter views.
subtopics.visual: A log console where the learner toggles each logging parameter under a running workload and watches lines per second and megabytes per hour climb alongside what becomes diagnosable, then replays one recorded incident three times — errors only, the four recommended settings, full statement logging — to see which configuration would have identified the cause, with a redaction toggle exposing a bound parameter value that should never have been written to disk.

subtopics.title: Monitoring vacuum, bloat, wraparound and history lists
subtopics.covers: The operational signals for the garbage mechanisms covered in the MVCC module — n_dead_tup vs n_live_tup and the autovacuum trigger (threshold + scale_factor × reltuples), cost-based throttling (autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay/cost_limit) and worker starvation across many tables, pg_stat_progress_vacuum phases, bloat estimation (pgstattuple exact vs the catalog-based estimator, index bloat via pgstatindex) and remediation (pg_repack, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM FULL locks), age(datfrozenxid) alert ladders (autovacuum_freeze_max_age at 200M, warnings at 1B, xidStopLimit read-only shutdown near 2^31) and the four horizon holders that block freezing (long transactions, idle-in-transaction sessions, stale replication slots, prepared transactions, plus hot_standby_feedback) — with InnoDB history list length, purge lag (innodb_max_purge_lag) and undo tablespace growth as the analogue, and Cassandra tombstone counts per read as the LSM version.
subtopics.visual: A dual-engine horizon dashboard: the learner runs an update-heavy workload and tunes scale_factor and cost_delay, then opens a long transaction, leaves a replication slot inactive, or sets hot_standby_feedback, and watches the Postgres side (dead tuples, bloat %, oldest xmin pinned, age(datfrozenxid) counting toward the shutdown line) and the InnoDB side (history list length climbing while purge stalls) diverge and recover when the holder is released.

subtopics.title: Scheduled maintenance: partition creation, retention and reindex windows
subtopics.covers: Pre-creating future time partitions well ahead of the boundary (pg_partman premake, scheduled DDL, the MySQL and ClickHouse equivalents) and what happens when the runway runs out — errors on insert, or rows accumulating in a DEFAULT partition that can no longer be split without a lock and a rewrite — plus detach-and-archive or drop for retention, scheduled REINDEX CONCURRENTLY against index bloat, ANALYZE after bulk loads and on partitioned parents, and the scheduler decision itself (pg_cron or an event scheduler inside the database versus an external runner or Kubernetes CronJob) with the four ways each fails: a job that silently stopped, a run that overlapped itself, a run that held its lock into peak traffic, and no alert on last-success age.
subtopics.visual: A calendar-driven simulation where the learner sets premake depth and job cadence then advances time: inserts succeed until the last pre-created partition is passed, at which point they either error or fall into the default partition that the learner then tries and fails to split online, while a job-health board shows last success, overlap, lock window and the alert threshold each maintenance job would have tripped.

subtopics.title: Host, kernel and filesystem tuning for database servers
subtopics.covers: The OS settings that change database behaviour — transparent huge pages causing compaction stalls versus explicit huge pages shrinking page tables for a large buffer pool, vm.swappiness and why swapping the pool is worse than sizing it smaller, vm.dirty_background_ratio/dirty_ratio/dirty_expire_centisecs shaping writeback bursts that collide with checkpoints, the I/O scheduler (none/mq-deadline on NVMe), device readahead and nr_requests, NUMA interleaving and zone_reclaim_mode, CPU governor and C-states for tail latency, ulimits and max_map_count, filesystem choice and mount options (XFS vs ext4 vs ZFS, noatime, ZFS recordsize and its double copy-on-write with the WAL), and the network sysctls (somaxconn, tcp_keepalive, tcp_user_timeout) that decide how fast a dead peer is noticed.
subtopics.visual: A tuning console over a simulated host under a write-heavy workload where each toggle perturbs a named engine mechanism: THP injects periodic compaction stalls into the p99 trace, a raised dirty_ratio lets dirty pages accumulate until a writeback storm collides with the checkpoint curve, swappiness pushes buffer-pool pages to swap and collapses the hit rate, and each change is annotated with the metric that would have revealed it in production.

subtopics.title: Tuning knobs mapped to mechanisms
subtopics.covers: Treats configuration as parameters of mechanisms already studied and shows the knob-to-behavior transfer function: Postgres max_wal_size and checkpoint_completion_target set checkpoint frequency and therefore the full-page-write burst and recovery time, bgwriter_lru_maxpages and backend writes, wal_buffers/commit_delay and group commit, synchronous_commit levels, effective_io_concurrency and prefetch depth, random_page_cost on SSD and plan choice, fillfactor and HOT update rates, per-table autovacuum storage parameters; InnoDB innodb_io_capacity and adaptive flushing, redo log capacity vs checkpoint age, innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit, innodb_flush_neighbors, buffer pool instances; RocksDB write_buffer_size and max_write_buffer_number, level0 file-count triggers for slowdown and stop (write stalls), max_background_jobs, target_file_size_base and block cache sizing; Kafka replica fetchers and flush intervals — plus managed-service parameter groups that hide or clamp these.
subtopics.visual: A knob console wired to a live compact engine simulation: turning max_wal_size shortens the checkpoint interval and the learner watches full-page-write bytes and recovery-time bars respond; raising L0 trigger counts trades read amplification for fewer write stalls in an LSM panel; lowering work_mem turns a hash join into batches spilling to temp files — each knob highlights the internal component it parameterizes and overlays the predicted vs observed metric trace so the learner sees knobs as inputs to mechanisms rather than magic numbers.

subtopics.title: Self-tuning claims: automatic indexing, knob tuners and autonomous databases
subtopics.covers: What platform auto-tuning actually does and how to supervise it — Azure SQL automatic tuning creating, verifying and reverting indexes and forcing last-known-good plans, Oracle Autonomous Database's automatic indexing pipeline of candidate identification, invisible verification and rollback, Aurora and Redshift auto-WLM and automatic table optimization, hypothetical-index advisors, and the Bayesian and reinforcement-learning knob tuners (OtterTune, CDBTune) whose commercial failure is itself the lesson — judged on the questions that decide whether to trust it: which workload window the recommendation was fitted to and how sampling biased it, whether it is verified before adoption and revertible after, what it costs in write amplification, storage and plan stability, and why index creation is a safer automatic action than index dropping or a parameter change.
subtopics.visual: A tuner runs against a workload the learner can shift mid-experiment — add a month-end report, retire a query, double the write rate — while each recommendation moves through candidate, verification and adopted-or-reverted states with measured read gain, write cost and storage shown per index, so a recommendation fitted to last week's traffic visibly turns into a regression once the workload changes and the learner sets the guardrail or verification window that catches it.

modules.title: Running Databases: Memory, Capacity, Storage and Platforms
modules.why: Once you can read a database's signals and turn its knobs, the next layer of operational risk is resources and substrate: how RAM is really partitioned and who the OOM killer picks, which resource runs out first and what headroom costs, what an SRE actually does to the volume when the disk fills, where cold data goes when deleting it is not an option, and what a managed provider or a Kubernetes scheduler quietly took away from you.

subtopics.title: Memory sizing and the OOM killer
subtopics.covers: How a database's RAM is actually partitioned and how it overflows: shared_buffers vs the OS page cache (double caching, the 25% rule of thumb, effective_cache_size as a planner hint only), work_mem as a per-sort/hash-operation per-query allowance multiplied by hash_mem_multiplier, parallel workers and concurrent backends, maintenance_work_mem and autovacuum_work_mem, per-process overhead of process-per-connection; InnoDB's buffer pool (70–80%) plus per-thread sort/join/read buffers multiplied by threads and the redo/log buffers; RocksDB memtables × column families plus block cache plus index/filter blocks pinned outside it — the in-engine partition itself taken as given from the buffer-pool module and only sized here; then the Linux side this page owns — vm.overcommit_memory=2 and overcommit_ratio, the OOM killer's oom_score and oom_score_adj for the postmaster, why killing one backend forces a crash-recovery restart of the whole Postgres instance, huge pages, and cgroup memory limits counting page cache so containers get OOMKilled before the kernel would.
subtopics.visual: The buffer-pool module's memory treemap embedded read-only as the starting state, with every control on the OS beneath it: the learner sets vm.overcommit_memory and overcommit_ratio, oom_score_adj on the postmaster versus its backends, and a cgroup limit, then raises load until an allocation is refused outright or the OOM killer fires, and a timeline shows which process oom_score picked and the blast radius that follows — one backend killed still restarting the whole Postgres instance into crash recovery, the postmaster killed losing every session, and the container case where page cache counted against the cgroup limit triggers an OOMKill while the in-engine treemap still reports headroom.

subtopics.title: Capacity planning and cost modeling
subtopics.covers: Forecasting the resource that runs out first and what it costs: the working-set-vs-RAM cliff (cache hit and p99 are non-linear in dataset size), cloud I/O budgets (gp3 baseline 3000 IOPS/125 MB/s and paid provisioning, io2 and burst credits, instance-level EBS throughput caps, local NVMe with no durability, DynamoDB RCU/WCU and adaptive capacity, Cassandra compaction I/O headroom), WAL and binlog bytes per second as the true write budget that also sizes replication, backup and archive bandwidth, growth models that include index and TOAST multipliers, MVCC/tombstone overhead and backup retention, headroom targets near 60–70% utilization (queueing intuition owned by the performance module), days-to-full trend alerting rather than thresholds, and the order-of-spend ladder — vertical scaling, then indexes and caching, then read replicas, then sharding — costed against instance, storage and cross-AZ transfer pricing.
subtopics.visual: A growth-and-cost projector: the learner enters rows per day, row and index sizes, update ratio, replication factor and retention, and a timeline marks the dates the working set crosses RAM (cache hit and p99 curves bend), IOPS crosses the gp3 baseline, and disk fills, alongside a monthly cost curve; picking an intervention (add RAM, provision io2, add a replica, shard) moves the crossing dates and the cost line so they can compare cost per month of headroom bought.

subtopics.title: Growing, moving and reclaiming storage without downtime
subtopics.covers: The one-way and two-way doors under the data directory — online EBS/persistent-disk resize followed by a filesystem grow, the fact that block storage cannot shrink so reclaiming space means a new volume and a copy, IOPS and throughput that scale with volume size or must be provisioned separately, LVM and filesystem layouts that permit growth, moving relations between tablespaces under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock versus building the new index directly on the target, relocating a data directory or moving to a larger instance class via replica promotion, reclaiming space that VACUUM returns to the relation but not the filesystem (pg_repack, rebuild, dump and restore), keeping WAL and temp files on separate volumes so one runaway query cannot stop the server, and an ordering that leaves a checkpoint where the operation can still be aborted.
subtopics.visual: A host whose volume is filling while the learner chooses an intervention order — resize and grow the filesystem, move a table to a new tablespace, run pg_repack, promote a larger replica — each step showing the lock held, duration scaled to table size, space returned to the filesystem versus merely to the relation, and whether it can still be aborted, with an attempt to shrink the volume refused outright.

subtopics.title: Archival and tiering: keeping cold data cheap and still reachable
subtopics.covers: The hot/warm/cold ladder and the mechanism at each rung — detaching a time partition and moving it to slower storage (PostgreSQL tablespaces on cheaper volumes, InnoDB tablespace moves), exporting to columnar files in object storage that are still queryable in place (Parquet through DuckDB, Trino, parquet_fdw or ClickHouse S3 engine), Iceberg or Delta as the archive format so the data outlives the engine that wrote it, and engine-native tiering (ClickHouse TTL ... MOVE TO VOLUME, Timescale tiered storage, Kafka tiered storage, Snowflake and Redshift external tables); the decisions that make or break it — what Glacier-class retrieval latency and per-request pricing do to an occasional compliance query, keeping a searchable manifest of what was archived and where, preserving the schema and its evolution alongside the bytes, and proving a restore before the hot copy is deleted; and the collisions with the rest of the lifecycle, where an archive tier is exactly the copy that erasure requests and legal holds both reach for.
subtopics.visual: A data-age timeline with a per-tier cost and latency panel: the learner sets age thresholds and assigns a target per tier, then issues queries spanning different ages and watches which tiers each one touches, with bytes scanned, dollars per query and an added retrieval-latency penalty whenever a query reaches the archive tier; a 'delete the hot copy' button is blocked until a restore of the archived partition has been run and verified.

subtopics.title: Running on managed services: what the provider controls and what it hides
subtopics.covers: The operational surface of RDS/Aurora, Cloud SQL/AlloyDB and Azure Database — parameter groups with static versus dynamic parameters and reboot-to-apply, the absent superuser (rds_superuser, cloudsqlsuperuser) and the extensions, file access, replication slots and configuration it blocks, maintenance windows and forced minor-version upgrades, Multi-AZ standby failover as a DNS flip with a cold cache versus Aurora's shared-storage promotion versus read-replica promotion, snapshot restore creating a new instance whose blocks hydrate lazily from object storage so first reads are slow, backup windows and retention caps, storage autoscaling that can grow but never shrink, blue/green deployments built on logical replication, and the observability you lose (no host access, sampled Performance Insights, truncated logs) plus how to compensate.
subtopics.visual: A managed-instance console where the learner changes a static parameter and watches it queue until reboot, triggers a Multi-AZ failover and sees the DNS TTL, connection resets and cold-cache latency curve, restores a snapshot and observes first-touch reads paying lazy hydration until warmed, and attempts blocked operations (install an extension, read a server file, grant superuser) that return the provider's actual error and the reason behind it.

subtopics.title: Databases on Kubernetes: operators, volumes and eviction
subtopics.covers: How Kubernetes primitives interact with stateful engines: StatefulSet ordinal identity and PVC binding, local PersistentVolumes (fast, topology-pinned, node loss equals data loss unless the database replicates) vs network volumes (EBS/PD attach-detach latency on rescheduling, no multi-attach, fsync latency), StorageClass WaitForFirstConsumer binding, operators (CloudNativePG electing a primary via Kubernetes leases instead of Patroni, Zalando/Patroni, Vitess, Strimzi for Kafka/KRaft) and what their switchover and failover actually do, PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable expressed in quorum terms and the node-drain that evicts two of three, pod anti-affinity and topology spread across zones, cgroup memory limits that count page cache and produce exit 137 while shared_buffers looks safe, CFS CPU-quota throttling of checkpointer and compaction threads, and liveness probes that kill a pod mid-crash-recovery or mid-checkpoint and turn a slow recovery into a restart loop.
subtopics.visual: A three-replica database cluster scheduled on a four-node Kubernetes cluster: the learner chooses local vs network volumes, sets the PDB, memory limit and liveness probe timeout, then drains or kills a node and watches PVC rebinding time, the lease-based leader election, whether the drain is blocked or proceeds into quorum loss, and the cgroup meter that includes page cache climbing until the kubelet OOMKills the pod and the probe restarts it before recovery finishes.

modules.title: Failover Stacks, the Pooler Tier and Upgrades
modules.why: The last operational risks sit between the client and the engine and at the moments the engine changes version: the pooler tier every connection passes through and whose failure takes down every database behind it, the automation that actually performs your failovers and the routing layer that decides who the primary is, the security advisory that turns an upgrade into a deadline you did not choose, and the one-way doors of major-version upgrades, OS collation changes that silently corrupt indexes, and mixed-version clusters that pass the point of no return.

subtopics.title: Operating the pooler tier: PgBouncer and ProxySQL in production
subtopics.covers: Running the pooler as its own tier — sizing pool_size, max_client_conn, max_db_connections and reserve pools against the backend budget, reading SHOW POOLS/STATS/CLIENTS with client wait time as the true saturation signal, server_lifetime and server_idle_timeout recycling backends, PAUSE/RESUME and RECONNECT to hold client connections across a failover or restart instead of dropping them, the single-threaded process and the so_reuseport multi-process layout for CPU-bound instances and zero-downtime reloads, auth_query versus a static userlist and how a credential rotation must reach the pooler in step, TLS termination on both sides, HA placement as a sidecar per pod versus a shared pair behind a VIP and the blast radius of each, and the ProxySQL equivalents with query rules, mirroring and hostgroup failover.
subtopics.visual: A pooler tier under load where the learner sets pool sizes and timeouts and watches client wait time and backend count respond, then fails the primary over with and without PAUSE/RESUME to compare dropped connections and client errors, restarts the pooler with and without so_reuseport, and rotates a credential to see which path — static userlist or auth_query — keeps authenticating.

subtopics.title: HA stacks in practice: Patroni, Orchestrator and the routing layer
subtopics.covers: The moving parts of a real failover — Patroni's leader key with a TTL in etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper and the loop_wait/retry_timeout/ttl arithmetic that bounds detection, watchdog and demote-on-DCS-loss as fencing, synchronous_mode and synchronous_mode_strict trading availability for zero RPO, pg_rewind or full rebuild on rejoin; MySQL's Orchestrator topology graph with anti-flapping and hooks, InnoDB Cluster with MySQL Router, and MHA as the legacy; the routing layer clients actually hit (HAProxy health checks against primary/replica endpoints, VIP plus keepalived, service discovery, PgBouncer in front of or behind the VIP); and the drill matrix of planned switchover, unplanned failover, DCS partition and double failure with measured RTO and RPO for each.
subtopics.visual: A three-node Patroni cluster with etcd and an HAProxy lane where the learner sets ttl, loop_wait and synchronous mode, then partitions the leader from the DCS or kills its host: the leader key's TTL counts down, the old primary demotes or is killed by the watchdog, candidates race on LSN, health checks flip routing, and a stopwatch plus lost-transaction counter report RTO and RPO for that exact configuration, with a switchover button showing the zero-loss path for contrast.

subtopics.title: Security patches: CVE triage and the emergency upgrade path
subtopics.covers: Turning a published advisory into a decision — reading the attack precondition (pre- or post-authentication, requires a specific extension or a role the attacker already holds, client-side rather than server-side) and matching it to real exposure (no public listener, no untrusted roles, extension not installed), the classes that recur (PostgreSQL search_path and SECURITY DEFINER escalations, libpq and driver protocol flaws, MySQL privilege bugs, dependency CVEs inside search and streaming stacks, the container base image rather than the engine), the patch mechanics per platform (a minor version is binary-compatible and needs a restart or a rolling failover through the HA stack, a managed provider may schedule it for you, an extension fix needs ALTER EXTENSION UPDATE after the package, a driver fix is an application deploy), the mitigations that buy time (revoke a privilege, drop the extension, close a port, disable a feature) and the tracking loop of security-list subscriptions, a fleet version-and-extension inventory and a recorded exception for anything left unpatched.
subtopics.visual: An advisory inbox hands the learner real-shaped CVEs alongside a fleet inventory of versions, extensions, exposure and roles, and for each one they choose patch now, patch in the window, mitigate and defer, or not applicable — the tool then replays whether the exploit precondition actually held on each instance, which mitigation closed it, and what the chosen path cost in restarts, failovers and application deploys.

subtopics.title: Major-version upgrades: pg_upgrade, logical cutover and blue/green
subtopics.covers: The major-version paths and their one-way doors: pg_upgrade --link hard-linking relfilenodes and rebuilding only catalogs (minutes of downtime, old cluster unusable after, statistics missing until ANALYZE in versions before stats transfer, replicas re-synced via the rsync trick or rebuilt), --clone/copy modes, extension and datatype compatibility checks; logical replication cutover (publication/subscription initial COPY then streaming, replica identity, sequences and DDL not replicated, write-freeze switchover at zero lag, reverse subscription for rollback) and managed blue/green deployments built on it; and MySQL in-place upgrade with the transactional data dictionary and its no-downgrade rule — with the choice framed by downtime budget, rollback window and how many replicas must come along.
subtopics.visual: An upgrade-strategy stepper: the learner picks pg_upgrade --link, logical cutover or blue/green and steps through the phases with downtime, rollback window, replica handling and disk requirement shown per phase, then injects a failure at a chosen phase (a long-running transaction blocking the write freeze, an unsupported extension, lag that never reaches zero) and sees which paths can still roll back and which have already burned the old cluster.

subtopics.title: The collation trap: silent index corruption after an OS upgrade
subtopics.covers: Why changing the sort order underneath a live database corrupts indexes without any error — glibc 2.28 (RHEL 8, Debian 10, Ubuntu 18.10) and later ICU version bumps reorder strings involving punctuation, spaces and case, so a B-tree built under the old comparator is no longer sorted under the new one: equality lookups and range scans skip rows that are present, unique indexes admit duplicates, merge joins and partition routing misplace values, and a replica or restored copy on a different base image silently disagrees with its primary; the detection and repair path — datcollversion/collversion mismatch warnings, amcheck bt_index_check with heapallindexed, comparing sort output across hosts, and REINDEX (CONCURRENTLY) of every text index as the only fix — plus the prevention strategies of pinning an ICU collation version, using C/byte-ordering collations for identifiers and keys, keeping primary, replicas and container base images on one libc, and treating any OS or image bump as an index-rebuild event; MySQL's parallel is the utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci versus utf8mb4_general_ci change across 8.0.
subtopics.visual: A comparator swap over a real index: the learner sees a set of strings sorted under glibc 2.27 with a B-tree drawn over them, flips the host to glibc 2.28 and watches the correct order change while the on-disk tree does not, then runs equality and range lookups that walk the tree and miss rows now on the wrong side of a boundary, inserts a value the unique index wrongly accepts, runs amcheck to get the first failing page, and finally REINDEXes to see the tree re-sorted and every query answer corrected.

subtopics.title: Rolling upgrades and compatibility in clusters
subtopics.covers: How distributed systems survive a mixed-version window: wire-protocol and on-disk format versioning negotiated per node, cluster-version feature gates (CockroachDB's cluster.preserve_downgrade_option and finalization migrations that close the rollback window, MongoDB featureCompatibilityVersion, Kafka's two-phase inter.broker.protocol.version then log.message.format.version bump and KRaft metadata.version, Cassandra SSTable format versions and upgradesstables, Elasticsearch's one-major compatibility rule), draining and lease/leader transfer before restart so Raft groups and Kafka partition leaders do not sit through an election gap, upgrade ordering (followers then leader, controllers last), N−1 client compatibility and schema-registry rules for the data flowing through, and the difference between a rollback window (binary can be reverted) and a point of no return (format finalized).
subtopics.visual: A five-node replicated cluster upgraded one node at a time with per-node binary and protocol version badges and a cluster-version gate: the learner injects a new-format message or SSTable before the gate opens and sees which RPCs are rejected by old nodes, chooses whether to transfer leases before each restart and watches election gaps appear or vanish, and finalizes the cluster version to see the rollback option lock shut.

modules.title: Backups, Restore and Disaster Recovery
modules.why: A backup is only a hypothesis until a restore proves it, and the kind of restore you can actually perform — full, partial, cross-shard, cross-region — decides how much data and how many hours an outage costs.

subtopics.title: Logical backups and their limits
subtopics.covers: pg_dump opens one REPEATABLE READ snapshot (shared across -j workers via pg_export_snapshot) and holds ACCESS SHARE on every table so concurrent DDL blocks, mysqldump --single-transaction / mydumper record a binlog position for later replay, and restore cost is COPY plus full index rebuild plus FK validation plus ANALYZE (hours per TB) — which is why logical dumps suit major-version upgrades, cross-architecture moves, single-table and schema-only restores, but cannot give point-in-time recovery and silently miss sequences, large objects, extension state and roles unless dumped separately.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets database size, index ratio and parallel jobs and watches two elapsed-time bars race — logical (COPY → index build → FK validation → ANALYZE) against physical (file copy → WAL replay) — while a concurrent ALTER TABLE tries to run mid-dump and is shown blocked behind the dump's ACCESS SHARE locks.

subtopics.title: Physical backups and point-in-time recovery
subtopics.covers: A base backup (pg_basebackup or pg_backup_start/stop with backup_label, XtraBackup copying .ibd files plus a redo-log tail) is only restorable together with the continuous WAL/binlog archive that spans it, full_page_writes on so torn pages copied mid-write are repaired by replay; recovery_target_time/lsn/xid/name with restore_command replays to the target and promotion mints a new timeline ID whose .history file the archive must retain or a second PITR forks blind; incremental backups (pgBackRest block-level, WAL-G delta, PG17 pg_basebackup --incremental with the WAL summarizer and pg_combinebackup) shrink full-copy cost; volume snapshots are valid only when atomic across every volume the cluster touches, so the standard layout of data directory, symlinked pg_wal and a tablespace on three separate EBS/LVM volumes yields snapshots taken at different instants whose WAL is older than the pages it must repair — not crash-consistent but silently corrupt, starting cleanly and dying later on a checksum — leaving exactly three safe options (one volume for the whole cluster, a provider consistency group or multi-volume snapshot that is genuinely atomic, or pg_backup_start/stop and pgBackRest/XtraBackup so the backup is valid regardless of snapshot skew) each still requiring the WAL archive that spans the backup; RPO is bounded by archive_timeout and archiver lag, and RDS/Aurora/Cloud SQL hide the same machinery with the same limits.
subtopics.visual: A timeline of full and incremental base backups above a WAL-segment stream; dragging the recovery target highlights exactly which backup chain and segments are needed, plays replay up to the target and branches a new timeline, while injectable faults — deleting one archived segment, dropping a .history file, or snapshotting the WAL volume 30 seconds after the data volume — visibly shrink the reachable window or end recovery in a checksum failure instead of a clean start.

subtopics.title: Restore testing and backup validation
subtopics.covers: A backup is a hypothesis until restored: automated drills restore into scratch and compare row counts and hash aggregates, pg_verifybackup checks the manifest, amcheck and data_checksums catch corruption that copied cleanly, monitoring covers backup age, size trend and pg_stat_archiver failed_count (a missing segment breaks every later recovery point), 3-2-1 with object-lock immutability and off-account copies defends against ransomware and operator error, and true RTO is measured as fetch + restore + WAL replay + index and cache warm-up — GitLab 2017 learned that a pg_dump version mismatch had been producing empty backups for months; because backups and snapshots are encrypted by default the drill must also prove key availability rather than assume it, running as the actual restore principal in the actual target region and account so a missing key-policy grant, a cross-account copy re-encrypted under an unusable key, or a key already destroyed by a crypto-shredding erasure request (compliance-auditing-and-data-governance) fails the drill instead of the incident — the same evidence line the production readiness review in lifecycle-checklists-and-review-gates should demand.
subtopics.visual: A backup pipeline with injectable faults (corrupt WAL segment, archive gap, wrong-version pg_dump emitting an empty file, expired retention tier, missing timeline history, a CMK the restoring role has no grant on, a key crypto-shredded while the backup was still retained); the learner runs a restore drill and watches each verification stage pass or fail with a stopwatch decomposing the measured RTO.

subtopics.title: Partial recovery: restoring one table or one tenant without rolling back the cluster
subtopics.covers: The recovery every team actually performs — restoring the backup to a scratch instance at a timestamp just before the damage and extracting only the affected rows or tenant (pg_restore -t and its dependency limits, COPY out of the scratch instance, a foreign-data-wrapper or dblink pull), then reconciling against everything written since: rows recreated with new ids, sequences that advanced past the restored values, foreign keys pointing at rows that no longer exist, unique collisions on re-insert, and derived stores and caches that must be re-synced too; plus the cost of hydrating a full-size restore to recover a megabyte, delayed standbys and per-table snapshots as the cheaper standing defence, and the decision rule for when a full point-in-time rollback plus replay really is the smaller loss.
subtopics.visual: An incident clock runs while the learner picks a recovery route — full PITR rollback, scratch-instance restore with selective re-import, or a delayed standby — with data-loss, downtime and restore-duration meters per route, then the re-import collides with rows recreated since the incident and an advanced sequence, and resolving each conflict produces a reconciliation report of which rows came back, which were skipped and which were overwritten.

subtopics.title: Disaster recovery: RPO/RTO and multi-region failover drills
subtopics.covers: RPO is bounded by replication mode (async lag or archive interval) and RTO decomposes into detect, decide, promote, cut over traffic and warm caches; standby-region patterns range from backup-only through pilot light and warm standby (async cross-region replica, Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables) to active-active; cutover mechanics are DNS TTLs vs global load balancers vs client-side endpoint lists, the old region must be fenced (failure-detection-leases-fencing) or it keeps accepting writes, failback requires pg_rewind or a fresh base backup, and drills on a fixed cadence with a written runbook are the only way the measured RTO stays honest; the dependency that fails these drills silently is the encryption key — CMKs are region-scoped so a cross-region snapshot copy is re-encrypted under a different key, the key policy must already name the DR-region restore principal (and the target account, since a cross-account copy lands under a key that account can use), KMS itself sits inside the blast radius of the regional event you are restoring from so the restore path must not depend on the dead region's endpoint, and retention collides with governance in both directions — crypto-shredding an erasure request's key can strand a backup you are still required to keep, while legal hold can forbid destroying a key you promised to destroy.
subtopics.visual: A two-region layout with dials for replication mode, DNS TTL and detection timeout, plus a key-topology panel (per-region CMK, copy re-encryption, key policy principals); the learner kills the primary region at a chosen moment and a stopwatch decomposes RTO into phases while a counter tallies acknowledged-but-lost transactions (RPO), and toggling the DR-region grant off — or taking regional KMS down with the region — stalls the restore at 'decrypting' no matter how healthy the storage is, then failback runs and shows the re-seed cost.

subtopics.title: Degrading gracefully: read-only mode when the primary is gone
subtopics.covers: Designing the fallback before the outage — a feature-flagged write freeze enforced server-side (default_transaction_read_only, a provider read-only endpoint) as well as in the application, reads served from a replica with an explicit staleness indication and a bounded lag threshold, shedding non-essential writes first (analytics, search reindex, recommendation updates) so the checkout path survives longest, cached last-known-good responses with deliberately extended TTLs, optional buffering of writes into an idempotent queue with a stated replay contract, the reconciliation on the way back where buffered writes meet whatever happened during the outage, and the discipline that this path is exercised in a game day rather than first run during the incident — the harvest/yield theory behind it lives in consistency-models.
subtopics.visual: A live application whose primary the learner kills before choosing a posture (hard failure, replica reads with staleness banner, cached responses, buffered writes) while user-visible error rate, served staleness and buffer depth respond, then a recovery step replays the buffer against the restored primary and marks which writes reconcile cleanly, which conflict with writes that landed elsewhere and which must be surfaced to a human.

subtopics.title: Consistent backups across shards and replicas
subtopics.covers: Per-shard backups taken at independent moments restore a cluster in which cross-shard transactions are half-applied, so distributed engines back up AS OF one cluster-wide MVCC timestamp — CockroachDB BACKUP with protected timestamps that block GC of the needed versions, TiDB BR pinning the GC safepoint, Spanner's TrueTime snapshots — while MongoDB sharded backups need the balancer paused and per-shard oplog positions and Cassandra nodetool snapshots are per-node and only eventually consistent; single-node clusters take backups from a hot standby to spare the primary and restore every shard to the same recovery target, and incremental backups ride the version history so shrinking the GC/protected window makes older targets unrestorable.
subtopics.visual: An N-shard cluster with per-shard backup clocks and a stream of cross-shard transactions; the learner chooses 'each shard now' or 'AS OF cluster timestamp T', restores, and sees which cross-shard transactions come back half-applied, then drags the GC/protected-timestamp slider and watches old versions pruned until T becomes unrestorable.

modules.title: Incident Response: Classic Failures, Data Repair and Corruption
modules.why: Database incidents are the ones where the cure can destroy more than the failure did, so the senior skill is triage under pressure plus a protocol that keeps the recovery path and the evidence alive.

subtopics.title: Classic incidents: locks, connections and queues
subtopics.covers: The Postgres lock queue is FIFO with no queue-jumping, so an ALTER waiting for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind one long transaction blocks every later SELECT on the table (MySQL: 'Waiting for table metadata lock'), diagnosed with pg_blocking_pids/pg_locks and cured by pg_terminate_backend, lock_timeout with retry, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout and PG17 transaction_timeout; connection exhaustion follows from process-per-connection cost, unbounded app pools, reconnect storms after failover or deploy and 'FATAL: sorry, too many clients already' (superuser_reserved_connections is the operator's lifeline), with the fix at the pooler (PgBouncer pool_size/max_client_conn, ProxySQL) rather than raising max_connections — mechanisms owned by lock-based-concurrency-control and application-access, replayed here as triage when nobody has told you which one it is.
subtopics.visual: The lock module's queue and blocking-tree component embedded inside an incident console with the cause unlabelled and two extra lanes — backend count and pooler wait queue — where the learner picks mitigations in sequence (terminate the head blocker, set lock_timeout, cancel the DDL, raise max_connections, cap the app pool) and is scored on queue depth, backend count and p99 recovered or worsened, with raising max_connections visibly making it worse.

subtopics.title: Classic incidents: capacity, disk full and replication lag
subtopics.covers: pg_wal fills when a stalled replication slot pins segments (max_slot_wal_keep_size, wal_status 'lost'), archive_command fails so nothing is recycled, or temp files and logs share the volume, and a full disk PANICs the server — recovery is drop/advance the slot or fix archiving, never rm files under pg_wal; vacuum falls behind when the xid horizon is pinned by a long transaction, an abandoned slot, a prepared transaction or hot_standby_feedback, so bloat grows and wraparound shutdown approaches (InnoDB: history list length and undo tablespace growth); replica lag comes from single-threaded WAL apply, one huge transaction or DDL, replica I/O saturation and standby query conflicts (MySQL replica_parallel_workers/WRITESET as the cure), and read routing must respect a lag threshold — measurement lives in operating-observability-tuning-capacity.
subtopics.visual: A disk-fill simulation with three faucets (WAL retained by a stuck slot, temp files, dead tuples under throttled vacuum) and a replica-lag curve; the learner toggles drop-slot, fix-archiving, vacuum cost limits and parallel apply and watches free space, wraparound distance and lag respond, while the 'rm -rf pg_wal' button corrupts the instance.

subtopics.title: Ad-hoc production data fixes and undoing a bad one
subtopics.covers: The safe-DML protocol — reproduce the target set with the identical predicate as a SELECT and check its count, snapshot the affected rows' pre-images into a side table in the same transaction, run inside an explicit BEGIN with lock_timeout and a row-count assertion before COMMIT, batch by key range so no single statement locks the table or blows the replica lag budget, and never run it from an autocommitting shell — then the recovery path when it goes wrong: freeze writes, locate the offending commit's LSN or GTID from the log, restore a copy to just before it via PITR or promote a delayed standby, extract the pre-images and merge them back accounting for triggers, cascades and rows changed since, and the honest list of what cannot be undone once the write has been consumed by CDC, derived stores and external side effects.
subtopics.visual: A console where the learner fires an UPDATE whose WHERE clause is accidentally truncated under each safeguard in turn (none, transaction plus row-count check, batched with limits, pre-image snapshot) and watches rows changed, locks held and replica lag respond, then chooses a recovery route (PITR to a clone, delayed-standby promotion, pre-image merge) and sees how many rows each restores while a downstream panel shows the CDC consumers, cascaded deletes and outbound webhooks that already acted on the bad write.

subtopics.title: Running a data incident: roles, severity and the irreversible-action gate
subtopics.covers: Declaring an incident and separating incident commander, comms and scribe from the person at the keyboard, classifying severity by data loss, corruption and exposure rather than latency, capturing evidence before mitigating (volume snapshot, pg_stat_activity and pg_locks dumps, log and metric export) because the fix destroys the diagnostic state, a two-person gate on the irreversible actions (promote, failover, restore over a live cluster, pg_resetwal, force-recovery, DROP) with a written statement of what each one costs if wrong, the explicit write-freeze decision when replicas or shards are diverging, timeboxed escalation to a managed provider when the control plane is the outage, the customer- and regulator-facing duty once data is known lost or exposed, and the blameless postmortem with tracked corrective actions.
subtopics.visual: An incident simulator with a running clock where the learner assigns roles and selects from a mixed list of diagnostic, mitigating and irreversible actions: skipping evidence capture erases the data needed to find the cause, taking an irreversible action without the gate sometimes removes the only recovery path, a status-page and stakeholder timer ticks against the declared severity, and the debrief scores time-to-mitigate, rows lost and how much evidence survived for the postmortem.

subtopics.title: Retry storms, load shedding and backpressure in practice
subtopics.covers: Where a retry storm is actually fought in a database stack and how the on-call engineer gets out of it: the pooler is the choke point (PgBouncer pool_size as the admission gate, query_wait_timeout to fail fast instead of queueing forever), server-side statement_timeout and transaction_timeout must be shorter than the client deadline or work is done for callers that have already given up, reconnect storms after a failover or deploy pay full TCP/TLS/SCRAM establishment cost at the worst moment, and per-tenant priority shedding decides who loses first; the recovery procedure once goodput has collapsed is shed below capacity, drain the queues, discard the retry backlog, ramp traffic back slowly and lift the breaker last — the underlying theory of metastability and the retry-budget, jittered-backoff and deadline-propagation knobs themselves belong to why-distribute, and the cache-restart stampede to application-access.
subtopics.visual: An incident console exposing only operator-visible telemetry — pool wait time, backend count, error rate, p99 and goodput, with the cause hidden and no view of the retry multiplier — where the learner picks interventions in order against a running clock and is scored on time-to-recovery and requests shed, including a run whose only cure is shedding below capacity and ramping back slowly.

subtopics.title: Corruption triage: detect, contain, salvage and forced recovery
subtopics.covers: A decision tree from symptom (page checksum failure, 'could not read block', missing index entries, ERROR reading a toast chunk, wrong results after a glibc/ICU collation change that is really a sort-order break, not damage) to action: confirm with pg_checksums, amcheck bt_index_check/heapallindexed, verify_heapam, innochecksum and dmesg/SMART to separate storage faults from engine bugs; contain first — fence the node, snapshot the volume before touching anything, pull the replica from the read pool, stop autovacuum and any REINDEX from spreading it — knowing the blast-radius rule that a corrupt page still ships as a valid WAL record while a corrupt logical row replicates everywhere; then isolate the damaged relation and blocks via pg_class and ctid probes and climb the salvage ladder in order, restore+PITR to before the damage first, then a logical dump of the healthy remainder with COPY around bad blocks, pg_filedump and pg_waldump to read what is left, REINDEX for index-only corruption (which heap corruption never fixes), and only then the destructive rungs with their cost stated — zero_damaged_pages and ignore_checksum_failure silently discard rows, innodb_force_recovery levels 1-6 each drop more engine machinery and past level 4 writes must never happen, pg_resetwal abandons unreplayed WAL and yields a server that starts and lies until a full dump/restore, single-user VACUUM for xid wraparound, SQLite .recover, RocksDB repair/ldb rebuilding a MANIFEST by scanning files — closing with the duty to rebuild on new hardware and re-verify every replica.
subtopics.visual: A damaged instance the learner triages through the decision tree, choosing actions in sequence (verify, fence and snapshot, isolate, restore+PITR, dump-the-rest, REINDEX, zero_damaged_pages, force-recovery level N, resetwal) while a byte-level page view marks salvageable versus lost tuples, a running tally shows rows recovered against rows destroyed and whether the resulting cluster is trustworthy enough to keep serving, and a replica panel reveals whether the corrupt bytes had already shipped downstream.

subtopics.title: Learning from postmortems: GitHub 2018, GitLab 2017, Cloudflare
subtopics.covers: GitHub October 2018: a 43-second east-west partition let Orchestrator promote a West primary while East kept committing, producing two divergent MySQL histories and a 24-hour reconcile — fencing and topology-aware failover; GitLab January 2017: replication broke under spam load, an engineer ran rm -rf on the primary's data directory and all five backup paths turned out empty or unconfigured — restore drills and least privilege; Cloudflare November 2020: a partial etcd partition acted Byzantine, churned leaders and triggered a Postgres failover to a lagging replica, and November 2025: a ClickHouse permissions change made a metadata query return duplicate rows, doubling a config file past a hard limit and panicking the edge — validate query outputs and cap derived-artifact sizes; each maps to a mechanism taught elsewhere and to a root-cause pattern library for writing blameless retrospectives.
subtopics.visual: A postmortem replay in the cluster simulator: the learner steps through each incident's real timeline with cluster state rendered, and at every turning point may change one decision (turn fencing on, run the restore drill, keep the row limit) and rerun to watch the counterfactual outcome diverge from history.

parts.title: Senior Engineer Judgement
parts.summary: Performance literacy, tradeoff reasoning and misconceptions, then capstone designs, toy-engine builds and the hardware frontier.

modules.title: Performance Literacy: Measurement, Benchmarks and Profiling
modules.why: Seniors reason from percentiles, queues and measured evidence rather than folklore, and can tell a real speedup from noise and a vendor's headline number from the workload it quietly excludes.

subtopics.title: Latency, throughput and percentiles; coordinated omission
subtopics.covers: Latency as a multimodal log-scale distribution (cache-hit, disk and stall modes) where p99/p99.9 govern experience and means or averaged percentiles lie because percentiles do not compose across hosts or time windows (merge HdrHistogram/DDSketch/t-digest histograms with bounded error instead), throughput-vs-latency as two views of one queue, and Gil Tene's coordinated omission: closed-loop load generators (pgbench, default YCSB, JMeter) that wait on a stalled request silently drop exactly the samples that should be recorded, which open-loop constant-arrival tools (wrk2, YCSB -target) or HdrHistogram's expected-interval correction fix by charging latency from the intended send time; fan-out tail amplification and hedging are owned by why-distribute.
subtopics.visual: A simulated server with a tunable periodic stall (e.g. a 2 s checkpoint every 30 s) is driven by a load generator the learner switches between closed-loop and open-loop constant-arrival modes; side-by-side log-scale histograms with live p50/p99/p99.9 readouts show the closed-loop run reporting a clean tail while the open-loop run exposes the stall plateau, and a 'correct for coordinated omission' toggle back-fills the missing samples at their intended send times so the two tails converge.

subtopics.title: Queueing theory, Little's law and the Universal Scalability Law
subtopics.covers: Little's law (L = λW) for sizing connection pools, thread counts and in-flight limits and for inferring hidden concurrency from throughput and latency; M/M/1 and M/M/c hockey-stick behaviour (wait ≈ ρ/(1−ρ), why 70–80% utilization is the practical ceiling and one shared queue beats c private queues); the Kingman variance effect where bursty arrivals and variable service times (checkpoints, compaction, vacuum) raise wait time at equal utilization; and Amdahl's law extended to Gunther's Universal Scalability Law, whose contention (σ) and coherence (κ) coefficients explain retrograde throughput past the peak — Postgres ProcArray/snapshot contention, InnoDB buffer-pool and row-lock mutexes, cache-line ping-pong in 'lock-free' structures — and how to fit σ and κ from a handful of throughput-vs-concurrency measurements.
subtopics.visual: A three-panel queue lab: the learner drags arrival rate toward service capacity on an M/M/c queue and watches queue length and p99 wait climb the hockey stick (a burstiness slider lifts the whole curve at the same utilization), switches to a USL panel where sliding σ and κ bends the throughput-vs-concurrency curve until it turns retrograde, and reads a Little's-law gauge that converts the current throughput and latency into the number of connections actually in flight versus the pool size configured.

subtopics.title: Amortized cost versus tail latency: the potential method and deamortization
subtopics.covers: Aggregate, accounting and potential-method analysis as the reason a B-tree insert, a dynamic array growth, a hash-table rehash and an LSM write are cheap on average, why that average is precisely what a p99.9 SLO does not buy since a doubling rehash, a bottom-level compaction, a full checkpoint and an anti-wraparound vacuum each discharge the whole accumulated debt inside one operation, and the deamortization techniques engines use to spread the payment — Redis incremental rehashing a few buckets per command, RocksDB's rate limiter and subcompactions, checkpoint_completion_target, InnoDB adaptive flushing and page cleaners, Bε-tree flushes bounded per operation, autovacuum cost delays — with the governing rule that deamortization makes the average slightly worse and the tail much better, and the histogram signature that tells you which regime you are in.
subtopics.visual: The learner runs one insert stream against a batched and a deamortized version of the same growing structure while a potential/debt meter accumulates and then discharges in a single spike on the batched side and drains a slice per operation on the other, with both latency histograms and their p50 and p99.9 markers drawn together so the average visibly worsens exactly as the tail improves.

subtopics.title: Benchmarks and what they measure: TPC-C, YCSB, TPC-H
subtopics.covers: What each standard benchmark actually exercises — TPC-C's five transactions with warehouse-scaled contention, think time and 90th-percentile response constraints behind tpmC; TPC-H/TPC-DS's 22/99 analytic queries over scale-factor data stressing join order, scans and aggregation; YCSB's A–F workloads with uniform/Zipfian/latest key distributions and their coordinated-omission defaults; pgbench, sysbench, db_bench and fio — plus the standard cheats (warm caches, fsync/synchronous_commit off, uniform keys, unbounded clients, no think time, cherry-picked scale factors, a write-tuned LSM against a default B-tree, reporting throughput without the latency SLO) and the audit checklist for translating any published number to your hardware, durability settings and data shape.
subtopics.visual: A benchmark configurator where the learner picks a workload family (TPC-C-like, YCSB A–F, TPC-H-like), sets Zipfian theta, read/write mix, working set vs cache size, client count and durability mode against a simulated B-tree and LSM engine, and watches throughput, p99 and read/write/space amplification meters diverge; a 'vendor mode' button applies each cheat one at a time (drop fsync, pre-warm the cache, uniform keys, remove think time) and shows how far each moves the headline number.

subtopics.title: Benchmarks for search, vector, time-series and streaming
subtopics.covers: Applying the previous page's audit checklist to specialized stores whose headline numbers need a second axis: ann-benchmarks' recall@k-versus-QPS Pareto curves and why a single QPS figure is unfalsifiable without its recall, with ef/nprobe sweeps, filtered search and build time and memory as first-class axes; BEIR and MTEB measuring retrieval quality rather than system speed and why relevance and latency must be reported together; ClickBench's cold/hot analytics runs alongside the TPC-DS suite owned above; TSBS for time-series ingest and query with retention, downsampling and compaction actually running; Nexmark for streaming with watermark lateness and state size; and the per-workload cheats (recall tuned per query set, vectors benchmarked without metadata filters, ingest measured before compaction debt comes due, streaming measured with no late events, caches measured warm).
subtopics.visual: The learner sweeps ef and nprobe across two index types to build a recall-versus-QPS Pareto plot, then a 'headline number' mode picks one operating point per index and shows either index winning depending on the point chosen, while toggles that disable metadata filters, background compaction or late events visibly move each reported number.

subtopics.title: Is that speedup real? Variance, confidence intervals and A/B on database changes
subtopics.covers: Where run-to-run variance actually comes from (cache warmth, checkpoint and compaction phase, autovacuum, JIT warmup, page-cache state, cloud noisy neighbours and burst credits), why comparing single runs or means of heavy-tailed latency distributions concludes nothing, bootstrap confidence intervals and rank tests (Mann-Whitney) on paired runs, interleaved or alternating A/B execution to cancel drift, the difference between a statistically detectable difference and one worth acting on, multiple-comparison inflation when a regression scan tests a hundred statements at once, and the discipline of pre-registering the metric (p99 of one named statement class, at fixed arrival rate) before the first run.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets a true underlying difference between two configurations and the tool samples runs with realistic skewed noise, so raising the run count and switching from mean-of-one-run to paired interleaved runs with bootstrap intervals flips the verdict between false positive, false negative and correct, while a regression-scan panel over a hundred statements reports spurious winners until multiple-comparison correction is switched on.

subtopics.title: Misconceptions catalog
subtopics.covers: Database folklore refuted by mechanism: 'indexes are free' (per-index write amplification, bloat, planner ignoring them), 'NoSQL scales, SQL doesn't' (partitioning is the property, not the data model), 'ACID means safe' (isolation defaults, write skew under SI, durability knobs), 'Raft is enough' (stale leader reads without leases/ReadIndex, single-key vs transaction scope), 'a cache fixes everything' (stampedes, invalidation, cold-cache collapse), 'more replicas make writes faster', 'timestamps order events', 'TTL locks are safe' (no fencing token), 'retries are always safe' (idempotency), 'joins are slow' (misestimates and missing indexes are), 'foreign keys are too expensive', 'UUIDs are free' (random-key B-tree locality), 'CAP is a menu and CA exists' — each with the counterexample a reviewer should reach for and a pointer to the module that owns the mechanism.
subtopics.visual: A myth deck that builds no simulation of its own: each card states the folklore as an assertion and deep-links the owning module's existing component — consensus-and-coordination for the stale leader read, failure-detection-leases-fencing for the unfenced TTL lock, b-trees-and-variants for random-UUID leaf fragmentation, application-access for the cache stampede, replication for the replica-count write cost, index-selection-strategy for 'indexes are free' — launched in a serialized preset passed as a single state prop and reflected in the URL (the site-wide rule this page depends on), under a thin falsification overlay whose anomaly counter ticks while the myth's configuration runs and stops only once the learner flips the mechanism that refutes it, returning them to the deck with the card marked.

subtopics.title: Profiling a database: perf, flame graphs and wait analysis
subtopics.covers: On-CPU profiling with perf/eBPF and flame graphs (frame pointers vs DWARF unwinding, JIT and interpreted frames, Postgres process-per-backend vs InnoDB threads), off-CPU and wait-state profiling for lock, latch and I/O blocking (bpftrace offcputime, sampled pg_stat_activity wait_event, performance_schema and InnoDB mutex spin stats, RocksDB perf_context/iostats), classifying a workload as CPU-, I/O-, lock- or memory-bandwidth-bound from per-resource USE metrics, wall-clock attribution of a slow query via tracing plus wait sampling, and canonical signatures (LWLock:BufferMapping on hot pages, WALWriteLock group-commit convoys, ProcArrayLock, lock chains behind a DDL, compaction and checkpoint stalls); routine dashboards are owned by operating-observability-tuning-capacity, this drills beneath them.
subtopics.visual: A simulated database under mixed load whose learner-injected faults (lock storm on a hot row, checkpoint/fsync burst, hot-page latch contention, CPU-bound sort spill) render simultaneously as an on-CPU flame graph, an off-CPU flame graph and a per-backend wait-event timeline, so the learner practices spotting which view lights up for each fault and clicks a frame or wait band to see the wall-clock attribution of a chosen slow query.

modules.title: Tradeoff Reasoning: Bottlenecks, Boundaries and Design Review
modules.why: Seniors can name the next bottleneck before it appears, say where a schema may be cut and what that cut costs, and read a design or a paper for the invariant that breaks rather than the features it lists.

subtopics.title: Service boundaries and data ownership: shared database versus database per service
subtopics.covers: Deciding where a schema may be cut: the ownership rule that exactly one service writes a table while others read through an API or a CDC-fed replica, what is lost at every cut (foreign keys, a single transaction, a join, ORDER BY and pagination across the boundary, cascading deletes) and the replacements that cost something — API composition, a read model, a reference-data copy, a saga or a single-owner claim for cross-service invariants — the shared-database arrangement and the narrow cases where it is still correct (a read-only reporting role, a strangler window, one team), schema-per-service inside one cluster as the cheap middle, the operational multiplication of separate databases (migrations, backups, connection budgets, per-service HA), and the signals that a boundary is wrong: an N+1 of API calls replacing one join, a distributed transaction appearing, or two services racing on the same invariant.
subtopics.visual: An order/inventory/payment schema the learner cuts by dragging boundary lines, with every severed foreign key, join and transaction listed as a debt plus the replacement it now requires, then a scripted checkout runs across the chosen split showing round trips, added latency, which invariant now needs a saga or a single owner, and the anomaly that appears when neither is added.

subtopics.title: Scaling reads and writes: the movable bottleneck
