subtopics.covers: Modelling a deployment as a chain of queues — proxy/connections, CPU, buffer-pool hit rate and IOPS, WAL fsync and group commit, lock/latch hot spots, replication apply and lag, disk space and compaction/vacuum debt — and how each technique (pooling, read replicas with read-your-writes routing, caching and materialized views/CQRS, batching and write-behind, async processing, a bigger box, sharding, switching to an LSM or distributed SQL engine) drains one saturated queue and shifts saturation to the next (replicas cap at the primary's single-threaded apply rate, caches move the wall to invalidation and write throughput, sharding removes cross-shard joins and transactions), with the ordering seniors actually apply and the point where each rung stops helping.
subtopics.visual: A scaling ladder: the learner ramps a simulated app's traffic while gauges for connections, CPU, IOPS, WAL fsync, lock waits and replica lag fill until one saturates and p99 spikes, then drags a technique from a palette (pooler, replica, cache, batching, bigger instance, shard) onto the architecture and watches the saturated gauge drain while a different one climbs, with a cost meter and the currently binding bottleneck named at each rung.

subtopics.title: Choosing and integrating systems
subtopics.covers: A decision procedure from workload shape (point, range, analytic, search, graph), per-operation consistency, write volume and growth, latency budget, team maturity and cost to a candidate architecture — Postgres-first with jsonb, partitioning, pgvector, full-text and logical replication before adding engines — then the integration rules: one system of record with Redis, Elasticsearch and the warehouse as derived stores fed by CDC/outbox rather than dual writes, each with its own staleness window, failure mode and rebuild path, and comparing alternatives by the anomalies they admit under a stated scenario rather than by feature lists; cutover mechanics (dual-write, shadow reads) are owned by the capstones module.
subtopics.visual: Explore mode of the shared architecture simulator: the learner fills a requirements panel (QPS, dataset size, query shapes, per-operation consistency, regions, team size), composes and swaps a topology from one typed component vocabulary — client, pool, primary, replica, cache, queue, derived store, each modelled as a queue with a capacity, a staleness source and a consistency label, with port-legality checks refusing illegal wirings — and replays a fixed scenario of traffic plus a partition plus a component crash while per-hop lag meters, each derived store's staleness window, the observed anomalies (lost update, stale read, duplicate) and an untimed cost panel update.

subtopics.title: Design reviews and reading papers: the invariant hunt
subtopics.covers: Reading a design doc or paper (ARIES, Dynamo, Bigtable, Spanner, Raft, Calvin, Percolator, Aurora, F1, Bw-tree, WiscKey) by extracting its invariants, failure model, consistency claim and what was actually measured, then hunting for where an invariant can break — a lease used after expiry without fencing, quorum intersection across a membership change, GC of versions a live snapshot still needs, a retried commit that is not idempotent, ordering across shards — distinguishing marketing 'strong consistency' from an Adya/Jepsen-named model, the review checklist (per-operation consistency, RPO/RTO, backpressure, rebuild path, hot keys, schema evolution) and the reading order DDIA → Database Internals → CMU 15-445/721 → Red Book → Jepsen reports.
subtopics.visual: A design-review workbench showing a short design (a lease-based lock service, an outbox relay, a range-split protocol) as diagram plus prose; the learner highlights the spots where they believe an invariant can break and picks a fault (clock skew, delayed message, crash after ack, concurrent membership change), a small simulator tries to violate the invariant at that spot and shows either a counterexample trace or that the guard holds, and a tally reveals which seeded weaknesses the learner found or missed.

subtopics.title: System design interview playbook
subtopics.covers: A repeatable 45-minute method — clarify requirements and back-of-envelope numbers (QPS, storage, working set, replication factor, RTT budgets), enumerate access patterns, choose data model and partition key, state consistency per operation, pick the engine with a mechanistic justification (why Postgres vs DynamoDB vs Cassandra vs Spanner for this workload), add indexes, caching and queues, then walk failures (node loss, partition, hot key, replica lag, retry storm) and articulate the tradeoffs accepted — applied to the canonical problems (URL shortener, feed, inventory and ledger, chat, rate limiter, leaderboard) and the single storage decision each turns on.
subtopics.visual: The same architecture simulator in interview mode — identical typed component vocabulary and port-legality checks, nothing bespoke — locked to one of the six pre-authored problems with a countdown clock, where the learner sets the partition key and per-operation consistency and then a scripted probe timeline (10x traffic, region partition, celebrity hot key, replica lag, retry storm) fires on schedule while the canvas animates which requests fail, go stale or overload, ending in a scorecard against the stated requirements and the mechanism a senior answer would cite for each probe.

modules.title: Capstones: Worked System Designs
modules.why: Applying every mechanism to whole product systems — the order, booking, money, metering, in-product analytics, tenancy and authorization designs a senior engineer is actually asked to build, defend and inherit — turns knowledge into judgement, and running them all as presets over one shared simulator makes each design's invariants, bottlenecks and failure modes visible instead of asserted.

subtopics.title: The capstone preset library and assertion format
subtopics.covers: Establishes that every capstone here, in capstones-feeds-messaging-and-delivery and in capstones-data-platforms-and-evolution is a preset over the single shared system-simulator runtime that visual-system-and-preset-contract owns and specifies — the same runtime tradeoff-reasoning-and-design-judgement drives in explore and interview mode — and defines what a capstone preset consists of: a locked topology built only from the runtime's typed component vocabulary (client, service, queue, cache, primary, replica, object store, each with capacity, queueing discipline and staleness), a scripted traffic-and-fault timeline (ramp, skew, node kill, partition, slow disk, clock jump), a declarative invariant assertion list such as 'stock never negative', 'no payment captured twice' and 'no acknowledged write lost' that renders as pass/fail banners, and at most one bespoke panel for that design's signature mechanism, with the visual-system reuse ledger recording every entry point into the runtime so nothing reinvents it or exceeds the one-panel budget.
subtopics.visual: The learner opens one capstone preset and sees its four parts side by side — topology, scenario script, assertion list, bespoke panel — then edits a line of each in turn: swapping a component's capacity, dropping a fault onto the timeline, adding an assertion, and watching a banner flip from green to red before opening the trace of the single request that violated it, so the reading protocol for every later capstone is learned once.

subtopics.title: E-commerce OLTP at scale
subtopics.covers: Designs a Postgres/InnoDB order system end to end: the stock-never-negative invariant enforced via SELECT FOR UPDATE, escrow/commutative decrement rows or SSI with 40001 retries, idempotency-keyed payment capture, orders partitioned by time and customer, outbox-to-Kafka feeding search and the warehouse, replica reads gated by LSN wait, and cache-aside with leases for product pages, then the scaling ladder (replicas, cache, partitioning, customer-keyed sharding on Vitess/Citus) and the classic failure modes of hot-SKU lock pileups, stale order status on lagging replicas and flash-sale stampedes (see application-data-patterns and application-access for the individual patterns).
subtopics.visual: The order topology plus a flash-sale scenario script in the shared runtime, with a bespoke hot-SKU lock-queue panel: the learner raises traffic and Zipf skew over SKUs, watches queue depth, p99, replica lag and cache hit ratio move, then drops in mitigations (escrow counter, idempotency table, LSN-wait routing, lease cache) one at a time while the 'stock ≥ 0' and 'no double capture' assertion banners stay green and the next bottleneck announces itself.

subtopics.title: Booking and availability: holds, overlaps and capacity
subtopics.covers: Reservations as half-open time ranges with the capacity-1 invariant enforced by the engine (tstzrange plus EXCLUDE USING gist with btree_gist, PG 18 temporal PRIMARY KEY ... WITHOUT OVERLAPS) versus capacity-N enforced by an escrow counter per (resource, bucket) or by materialized slot rows claimed with a conditional UPDATE, holds as pending rows with an expiry swept by a due-time partial index (and why a hold that expires on read is not the same as one that expires on a clock), the availability read path — range anti-join against a generated slot spine versus precomputed per-day availability rows — and its index requirements, recurring availability stored as a rule plus an IANA zone so DST does not silently move a 9 a.m. slot, overbooking and waitlists as deliberate policy rather than a bug, idempotent confirm keyed by a hold id so a retried payment callback books once, and the partition-key choice (resource versus time) that decides whether a booking stays single-partition and whether a popular date becomes a hot partition.
subtopics.visual: A resource-calendar topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke seat/slot grid panel: concurrent bookers race for the same slot while the learner switches enforcement between application check-then-insert, SELECT FOR UPDATE, an exclusion constraint and an escrow counter, with 'no double booking' and 'no seat held forever' assertion banners flipping as holds expire, a scripted on-sale surge concentrates every request on one date until the hot-partition meter saturates, and dragging a recurring availability rule across a DST boundary makes a slot vanish or duplicate until the zone is stored with the rule.

subtopics.title: Double-entry ledgers and money movement
subtopics.covers: Money as an append-only double-entry journal: immutable entries of (account, direction, amount, currency) that must sum to zero per transaction, integer minor units or NUMERIC and never floats, balances derived as a running SUM over entries versus periodically checkpointed balance snapshots plus a delta tail, transfers made exactly-once by a client-supplied transfer id under a UNIQUE constraint so a timed-out retry settles once, non-negative balances enforced by conditional UPDATE or escrow rather than read-then-write, authorizations and holds as pending entries closed by compensating entries rather than deletes or updates, ordering and currency conversion recorded as explicit entries, and reconciliation jobs that re-derive balances and diff against the payment processor's statements — as modeled by TigerBeetle's account/transfer primitives and by SERIALIZABLE-plus-retry Postgres ledgers (the escrow and idempotency-key primitives themselves live in application-data-patterns).
subtopics.visual: A ledger topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke journal workbench panel: the learner posts transfers and watches paired debit/credit rows append under a live zero-sum check with balances computed both by full SUM and from the latest snapshot plus delta tail, then the scenario script injects a duplicate request, a timeout-then-retry, a concurrent overdraft race and a crash between external capture and local commit so the assertion banners show which guard (idempotency key, conditional update, outbox) held, and a reconciliation run highlights the one account that drifted.

subtopics.title: Usage metering and billing: exact counts, late events and frozen invoices
subtopics.covers: Raw usage events ingested at-least-once and deduplicated by event id before any aggregation, per-(customer, meter, period) rollups maintained incrementally versus recomputed from raw with a reconciliation job that proves they agree, late and out-of-order events arriving after a period closes handled as an explicit correction or credit rather than by mutating a closed period, invoices frozen against pinned plan and price-list versions so an old invoice re-renders identically years later, quota enforcement reading the same counters on the hot path through an approximate local cache, and the rule that HyperLogLog and sampling — fine for a dashboard — are disqualified the moment the number becomes an amount owed.
subtopics.visual: A metering topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke invoice-diff panel: an event stream carrying duplicates, a burst and an event that lands three days late runs through a pipeline whose dedupe key, rollup strategy and period-close policy the learner chooses, while the panel diffs the computed total against ground truth — the late event producing a silent undercount, a mutated closed period or an explicit correction line — and a price-list change re-renders historical invoices wrongly until version pinning is switched on.

subtopics.title: In-product analytics: per-tenant dashboards on operational data
subtopics.covers: Serving a customer-facing metrics page without letting it run over the transactional primary — declaring a freshness contract per panel (live count versus hourly rollup) and showing it to the user, maintaining per-(tenant, metric, bucket) rollup tables on write or by an incremental job against computing on demand with row, time-range and statement_timeout caps, routing on-demand panels to a replica or a columnar mirror with a per-tenant concurrency cap, the arbitrary date ranges and high-cardinality group-bys that defeat pre-aggregation and force a fallback scan, late and corrected events that must restate a closed bucket, exports and scheduled emails that must never run inline, and the signals that the panel now belongs on a separate store fed by CDC (the serving tiers themselves live in analytical-engines-and-lakehouse-storage and analytics-delivery-semantics-and-activation).
subtopics.visual: A dashboard topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke panel-routing board: the learner assigns each panel to on-demand, rollup or columnar-mirror while tenants of wildly different size load the page simultaneously, watching primary CPU, transactional p99, panel latency and per-panel freshness move together, then a late correction restates a bucket and an added high-cardinality filter makes the pre-aggregation miss and fall back to a scan that trips the row cap and timeout.

subtopics.title: Global multi-tenant SaaS
subtopics.covers: Lays out tenancy as pooled tables with tenant_id leading every index and partition key plus Postgres RLS, schema- or database-per-tenant for large or regulated tenants, and cell-based architecture for blast radius, then adds geo-homing (CockroachDB REGIONAL BY ROW, Spanner placement, Citus/Vitess shard-per-region), residency constraints, noisy-neighbor controls (statement_timeout, connection quotas, per-tenant rate limits), online tenant moves via Vitess MoveTables or Citus shard rebalancer, and running expand/contract migrations across thousands of tenant schemas (isolation mechanics detailed in security-and-tenant-isolation).
subtopics.visual: A multi-region topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke tenant-to-shard map panel: the learner assigns tenants of varying size to pooled, siloed or cell layouts across regions, the scenario script fires queries from clients in each region and makes one tenant abusive so neighbors' p99 rises until quotas are applied, and a drag of one tenant to another shard plays out copy, CDC catch-up and atomic cutover while the residency and 'no write lost' assertions report.

subtopics.title: Authorization data: ACLs, roles and relationship checks
subtopics.covers: Per-object ACL rows versus role tables versus relationship tuples (Google Zanzibar and its descendants SpiceDB, OpenFGA, Ory Keto), the check query as a bounded, memoized graph traversal over nested groups and inherited folders, the far more expensive inverse — list-objects and list-users — that forces either a materialized reverse index (Zanzibar's Leopard), a permission predicate pushed into the SQL query (and its interaction with RLS, sort order and keyset pagination), or a denormalized per-user permission table maintained by fan-out on write, plus the staleness problem where a cached or replica-served check lets a just-revoked user through (Zanzibar zookies and per-request snapshot pinning as the fix for the 'new enemy' case), and the honest threshold at which a joined permissions table in the product database beats a separate authorization service.
subtopics.visual: An authorization topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke relationship-graph panel: the learner builds user→group→folder→document tuples and runs a check, watching the traversal expand with memoization hits and a depth counter, then flips a revocation and sees the check keep passing until the cache TTL or snapshot token is tightened, and finally runs list-objects to watch fan-out explode until a reverse index or a pushed-down SQL predicate is enabled, with rows examined and p99 shown per strategy.

modules.title: Capstones: Feeds, Messaging and Delivery
modules.why: The fan-out family — feeds, recommendations, chat, notifications and outbound webhooks — shares one storage problem the OLTP capstones never hit: per-user or per-destination state that is written far more often than it is read, skewed by celebrities, mega-groups and dead endpoints, and correct only if ordering, dedupe and delivery state are designed deliberately, so each design runs as another preset on the same simulator with its own invariants and its own signature hot spot.

subtopics.title: Social feed and hot keys
subtopics.covers: Contrasts fan-out on write into per-user timelines (Redis sorted sets, Cassandra partitions) with fan-out on read via multi-way merge, the hybrid celebrity threshold used by Twitter, hot-key salting and sharded counters for likes, request coalescing and memcache leases against stampedes, DynamoDB adaptive capacity limits, and the eventual-consistency exposures users actually see (missing own post without read-your-writes, counts moving backwards) plus timeline backfill and cache warming after eviction.
subtopics.visual: A feed topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke follower-graph and fan-out panel over Zipf-distributed follower counts: the learner posts as a normal user and as a celebrity under write, read or hybrid fan-out with an adjustable threshold, watching write amplification, per-partition queue depth and read-merge latency, then hammers a like counter until one shard saturates and salting spreads it, and toggles read-your-writes routing to make the missing-own-post assertion fail and pass.

subtopics.title: Recommendation serving: candidates, already-seen filtering and feedback
subtopics.covers: The retrieval stack whose query is a user — blending candidate sources (ANN over user and item embeddings, item-item co-occurrence lists, recency and popularity pools) then applying eligibility and already-seen filtering at scale with per-user Bloom filters or Roaring bitmaps of impressions whose false positives silently suppress good items, scoped and TTL'd per surface, ranking the survivors from an online feature store inside a strict latency budget, and the write path where impressions and interactions stream back within seconds to update counters, seen-filters and embeddings — plus the storage consequences: per-user state size and churn, cold start with no user vector, post-ranking diversity and business rules, and pagination that must stay stable while the candidate set moves under the reader.
subtopics.visual: A recommendation topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke candidate-funnel panel: the learner requests a feed and watches each candidate source contribute, the already-seen filter remove items with one wrongly suppressed item highlighted as its false-positive rate is dialled, features fetch against a latency budget and the ranker order the survivors, then scrolls to the next page while new interactions stream into the filter and counters — producing duplicated and vanishing items until a stable pagination token is applied.

subtopics.title: Chat and messaging storage
subtopics.covers: Conversation-partitioned message storage where the partition key is the conversation and the clustering key is a per-conversation monotonic sequence (or Snowflake id) so history is one range scan and 'everything after cursor X' is a seek, unread state kept as a per-(user, conversation) last-read cursor instead of per-message flags, multi-device sync driven by a per-user change sequence the client resumes from after being offline, the group fan-out choice between one shared conversation partition with member cursors and per-recipient inbox rows, edits/deletes/reactions as separate rows keyed to the message id, attachments stored by reference, retention by dropping old partitions or buckets, and the mega-group hot partition that forces time-bucketed keys — as built on Cassandra/ScyllaDB (Discord), partitioned Postgres and DynamoDB item collections.
subtopics.visual: A three-device chat topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke partition-and-cursor panel: the learner sends, edits and deletes messages across conversations of different sizes and watches rows land in the conversation partition with their sequence numbers, each device's sync cursor advance and fetch only the delta after a scripted disconnect, unread counts computed from cursors rather than row counts, and a group-size slider grow one partition past its limit until time-bucketing kicks in and the history scan's page count visibly changes.

subtopics.title: Notifications: fan-out, dedupe windows and delivery state
subtopics.covers: Per-user notification rows written by fan-out versus computed on read, preference and mute lookups placed early enough that suppressed notifications are never materialized, coalescing and dedupe keyed by (user, entity, type) within a time window backed by a unique index or a Redis SETNX with TTL, burst digesting with a scheduled flush, a per-channel delivery state machine (queued/sent/delivered/failed/bounced) whose at-least-once sends are made safe by the provider's idempotency key (SES, Twilio, APNs, FCM) plus bounce and unsubscribe feedback loops, unread counts held as a last-read cursor rather than per-row flags, and retention that purges read notifications by dropping partitions.
subtopics.visual: A notification-pipeline topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke stage-funnel panel: a scripted burst of five hundred events for one user runs through while the learner sets the dedupe window, digest interval and where the preference check sits, watching rows collapse or multiply at each stage, a provider timeout retried with and without an idempotency key produce one push or two, and the cursor-based unread count stay correct while the per-row-flag version drifts under concurrent reads.

subtopics.title: Outbound webhooks: per-destination ordering, fairness and poison endpoints
subtopics.covers: A delivery table or per-destination queue keyed by (tenant, endpoint) so ordering is preserved exactly where it was promised and nowhere else, the head-of-line blocking that one timing-out endpoint causes in a single shared queue and the fixes (per-endpoint leases with a concurrency cap, a slow lane, weighted fair scheduling across tenants), exponential backoff with jitter plus a per-endpoint circuit breaker that stops paying for a dead destination, attempt rows recorded for the customer-visible delivery log and their retention cost, signed payloads with a replay window and event ids so receivers can dedupe, dead-letter storage with bounded manual replay, and the capacity arithmetic of attempts per second against retry multipliers.
subtopics.visual: A delivery-tier topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke per-endpoint queue-and-breaker panel: dozens of tenant endpoints with tunable latency and failure rates are served from either one shared queue or per-destination leases with concurrency caps, and the learner kills one endpoint to watch either every tenant's delivery p99 collapse or only the dead one's queue stall, while backoff timers, circuit-breaker state, attempt-table growth and dead-letter counts update live.

modules.title: Capstones: Data Platforms, Boundaries and Migrations
modules.why: The second half of the capstone set moves off the request path and onto the data platform and its lifecycle — ingestion, lakehouse, feature serving, and the two moves a senior is most often handed, splitting a shared database along service boundaries and migrating between engines — where correctness is judged by what survives a backfill, a cutover and a late event rather than by a single request's latency.

subtopics.title: IoT and time-series ingestion
subtopics.covers: Builds the write-heavy path of Kafka partitioned by device into batched writers for TimescaleDB hypertables or ClickHouse MergeTree, with time-chunk/TWCS partitions dropped for retention, Gorilla delta-of-delta and XOR compression, continuous aggregates and downsampling tiers, last-value-per-device via ReplacingMergeTree or covering indexes, label-cardinality explosion (Prometheus head-block memory), consumer-lag backpressure and the raw-vs-rollup storage cost trade (columnar mechanics live in column-stores-analytical-storage).
subtopics.visual: An ingestion topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke Kafka partition-lag and chunk-fill panel: the learner drags device count, label cardinality, batch size and retention window while lag, memtable/chunk fill, compression ratio, active series count and raw-versus-rollup storage growth respond live, the scenario script stalls a writer to show backpressure, and firing a last-value query versus a 30-day range query reveals which tier and how many chunks each touches.

subtopics.title: Analytics platform and lakehouse
subtopics.covers: Traces Debezium CDC from the OLTP primary through Kafka into Iceberg tables with snapshot-based optimistic commits, positional/equality delete files, compaction and snapshot expiry, bronze/silver/gold layers, query engines (Trino, Spark, Snowflake external tables) pruning via manifest min/max stats and hidden partitioning, incremental models (dbt incremental, Materialize) with late-arriving and out-of-order CDC, schema evolution by column id, the small-file problem and freshness-versus-cost of micro-batch commits (table format internals in column-stores-analytical-storage, streaming semantics in logs-streams-derived-data).
subtopics.visual: A CDC-to-lake topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke Iceberg metadata-tree panel: as the learner commits batches the snapshots, manifest lists, manifests, data and delete files grow, a query shows which manifests and files are pruned, compaction and snapshot expiry redraw the tree, time travel returns an earlier snapshot, and the scenario script varies CDC lag against a freshness assertion on an incrementally maintained view.

subtopics.title: Feature store: online/offline parity and point-in-time joins
subtopics.covers: An online store (Redis/DynamoDB) for millisecond feature reads beside an offline store (Parquet/warehouse) for training, materialization jobs and streaming feature updates fed by CDC, point-in-time-correct joins (ASOF against label timestamps) that prevent label leakage, training/serving skew from divergent transformation code, feature versioning and backfills, per-feature freshness SLOs and TTLs, and the Feast/Tecton architecture (CDC and stream semantics in logs-streams-derived-data).
subtopics.visual: A feature-store topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke ASOF-join timeline panel: the learner builds a training set by joining labels to feature history with and without point-in-time correctness and watches leaked future values inflate offline accuracy while the online path returns the as-of values, then triggers a streaming update and a backfill and compares online/offline parity and per-feature freshness against their SLO assertions.

subtopics.title: Splitting a shared database: ownership boundaries, broken joins and staged cutover
subtopics.covers: Decomposing one database that several services write to — building the table-to-writer/reader map from query logs, pg_stat_statements and lineage, enumerating every cross-boundary join, read and transaction a proposed boundary breaks, choosing per case between a synchronous API call, a CDC-fed replicated read model, a denormalized copy or simply moving the table, replacing a cross-boundary foreign key and multi-table transaction with an eventual consistency check plus reconciliation or a saga with compensations, sequencing access removal before data movement (revoke write, then read-only, then move) so the engine enforces the boundary, running the move as a CDC backfill with shadow reads and a reversible cutover, and the anti-goal of a distributed monolith where every request still fans across both stores.
subtopics.visual: A boundary-drawing topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke schema-dependency map annotated with per-table writers and readers: the learner draws a boundary and the tool enumerates every read, join and transaction it severs, applies a remedy to each while staleness, per-request fan-out and coupling meters move, and running the cutover steps in the wrong order shows a service losing write access before its replacement read path exists, with the reversible rollback point marked.

subtopics.title: Migrating between systems
subtopics.covers: Plans a MySQL-to-Postgres or monolith-to-sharded move as CDC-driven snapshot-plus-stream (DBLog/Debezium watermark snapshots) rather than dual writes, whose lost-update and ordering races it demonstrates, then chunked verification with pt-table-checksum-style hashes, row counts and sampling, shadow reads with diffing, cutover via brief write freeze or reverse replication for a rollback window, the strangler pattern for services, and the runbook with explicit abort criteria.
subtopics.visual: A source-and-target topology in the shared runtime with a bespoke chunked-checksum diff panel: with live writes hitting the source the learner picks dual-write or CDC mode, runs the backfill while writes continue and watches the diff flag divergence caused by dual-write races, enables reverse CDC, executes cutover, then the scenario script injects a target-side failure and a rollback while the 'no write lost' assertion reports the verdict.

modules.title: Capstones II: Retrieval, Toy Engines and the Frontier
modules.why: Assembling the search and retrieval stacks nobody hands you a recipe for, then building the storage and consensus engines by hand and looking at where access methods and hardware go next, converts understanding of mechanisms into the ability to build one and to judge what is new.

subtopics.title: Autocomplete and typeahead
subtopics.covers: A design page, not a mechanism page: given a 50 ms keystroke budget, choose among the candidates already built elsewhere — B-tree prefix range scans, pg_trgm fuzzy rescoring, FST completion suggesters, an in-memory trie with per-prefix top-k, Redis ZRANGEBYLEX (mechanics in search-and-vector-retrieval and indexes-beyond-the-b-tree) — on the constraints that actually decide it: per-user permission filtering, which forbids a fully precomputed ranked list and forces over-fetch plus post-filtering with visible recall loss, alongside freshness of new terms, multi-word out-of-order matching, debouncing and edge caching, and the write amplification of re-ranking prefixes from the query stream.
subtopics.visual: The backend bake-off from search-and-vector-retrieval's 'Autocomplete, fuzzy and did-you-mean' embedded read-only at a fixed preset as the given, with the only live controls being ACL shape (public / per-tenant / per-document), over-fetch factor and index-refresh interval, and the meters being recall after filtering, p99 against the stated 50 ms keystroke budget and precomputed-top-k invalidation rate — so the learner discovers that permission filtering, not raw prefix speed, is what rules out the precomputed ranked list.

subtopics.title: Nearby search: geospatial queries at scale
subtopics.covers: A design page for a radius-query service that assumes the index mechanics from geospatial-data: pick GiST bounding-box-plus-refine or a cell covering (geohash, S2, H3) over a sorted KV by reference, then spend the page on what the mechanism page cannot decide — splitting high-churn moving objects in a TTL'd in-memory store from static POIs in the durable store, hot downtown cells that saturate a single partition, ranking that blends distance with relevance and the unstable pagination it creates, and how far over-fetch can be trimmed before results escape the radius or the latency budget.
subtopics.visual: The nearby-search topology in the capstone runtime — moving-object store, POI store, and a read-only embed of the cell-covering panel from geospatial-data — where the learner routes a query across both stores, runs a scripted rush-hour surge that saturates one downtown cell's partition, slides the distance-versus-relevance blend and watches a user's page-two results shuffle under them, and tunes over-fetch down until the 'no result outside the radius' and 'p99 under budget' assertions flip red.

subtopics.title: Retrieval service: keeping indexes true to the source
subtopics.covers: A design page for a retrieval stack whose indexes must stay true to a mutating system of record, assuming hybrid BM25 plus ANN retrieval, chunking and embedding mechanics from search-and-vector-retrieval: the trade is propagation — which updates and deletes must reach both indexes and the caches synchronously (right-to-erasure must reach vectors, query-embedding caches and rerank results) versus the lag you can budget, idempotent re-embedding of only changed documents over the CDC plumbing from logs-streams-derived-data, per-tenant filters from security-and-tenant-isolation, and recall versus latency versus cost at a chosen shard count and quantization.
subtopics.visual: An ingest-and-serve topology in the capstone runtime with a bespoke dual-index propagation panel: the learner ingests a corpus and watches chunks, embeddings and lexical postings populate, then edits and deletes source documents and traces propagation lag into each index (with an erasure assertion that fails while a deleted document is still retrievable), issues tenant-filtered queries against a recall/latency dashboard, and moves shard count and quantization sliders to watch cost and SLO compliance move together.

subtopics.title: Build a toy KV store, B-tree and LSM
subtopics.covers: A guided build in three stages: a Bitcask log with in-memory hash index, hint files and compaction; a B+tree over fixed-size pages with a small buffer pool, redo WAL with LSNs, checkpoints and ARIES-style recovery; and an LSM with memtable, SSTables, Bloom filters and leveled compaction, each subjected to fault injection at every fsync and rename point (torn page, missing fsync, reordered writes) and measured for write, read and space amplification against the simulators from lsm-trees and b-trees-and-variants.
subtopics.visual: A construction bench where the learner assembles each engine from rule cards (what to write first, where to fsync, how to recover, when to compact), runs a workload with crash points placed on a timeline, and sees which key-values survive recovery, which invariant broke (log-before-page, torn commit, lost manifest) and the amplification meters side by side for all three engines.

subtopics.title: Build a toy Raft
subtopics.covers: Implements terms, randomized election timeouts, RequestVote's log up-to-date check, AppendEntries consistency checks with nextIndex backoff, commit only by counting current-term entries (Figure 8), persisting currentTerm, votedFor and log before replying, client session deduplication, read-index and lease reads, snapshotting and joint-consensus membership change, then runs randomized partition, loss and crash schedules and checks the client history with a Porcupine-style linearizability checker (protocol theory in consensus-and-coordination, checkers in verification-jepsen-simulation).
subtopics.visual: An editable Raft engine with rule toggles (disable the current-term commit rule, skip fsync of votedFor, use lease reads without a clock bound): the learner runs thousands of randomized steps under partitions and crashes and watches invariant violations flagged (two leaders in one term, committed entry overwritten) alongside a client history whose linearizability check flips to fail, revealing which rule guards which guarantee.

subtopics.title: Learned indexes and adaptive indexing
subtopics.covers: Treats an index as a model that predicts a key's position: RMI's staged models with a guaranteed error bound plus a local search, ALEX's gapped arrays that absorb inserts, and the PGM-index's piecewise-linear segments, why updates and shifting or adversarial key distributions are the hard part, and database cracking and adaptive merging as the query-driven alternative that builds the index incrementally out of the queries themselves (contrast the B-tree, Bw-tree and ART mechanics in b-trees-and-variants and indexes-beyond-the-b-tree, and the learned *cardinality* estimation in cost-based-optimization).
subtopics.visual: A CDF plot of the key distribution where the learner fits an RMI, a PGM-index and a cracked column to it and sees predicted versus actual position for each lookup, the error-bound window shrinking on smooth data and blowing up as they skew the keys or stream inserts in, and a cost meter comparing probes, cache misses and index bytes against a B-tree over the same keys.

subtopics.title: New hardware and future engines: ZNS, CXL, GPU and DPU
subtopics.covers: Surveys where engines go next: ZNS/FDP SSDs mapping LSM levels to zones so the engine, not the FTL, does garbage collection (RocksDB ZenFS) cutting write amplification; NVMe queue depth with io_uring and SPDK; persistent-memory lessons from Optane (8-byte atomicity, clwb/sfence ordering, and why it died); CXL memory pooling and far-memory buffer-pool tiers; RDMA engines like FaRM; GPU columnar execution (cuDF, HeavyDB) bounded by PCIe bandwidth; DPU and computational-storage offload; and object-store-native engines with ML-tuned knobs.
subtopics.visual: A hardware-tier explorer where the learner swaps block SSD for ZNS, DRAM for CXL-pooled or persistent memory, and CPU for GPU: an LSM's compaction places SSTables into zones versus fighting FTL GC with a live write-amplification counter, the buffer pool tiers pages across local and far memory with latency shown per hit, and a columnar scan's throughput meter pins to PCIe or memory bandwidth as the bottleneck.

parts.title: Reference, Playbooks and Decision Guides
parts.summary: The lookup half of the site: a glossary that disambiguates the field's overloaded words, notation and anchor-number cards, theorem-to-consequence rules, engine and managed-platform comparison matrices, symptom-first on-call playbooks, and an annotated reading map. Nothing here introduces a mechanism — every entry states a fact, a rule or a diagnostic and links to the module that derives it, so the site can be entered sideways from a search engine or mid-incident rather than only read front to back.

modules.title: Reference Cards: Glossary, Notation, Numbers and Laws
modules.why: A learner who lands on the SSI, LSM or ISR page from a search engine needs to decode pageLSN, xmin, q-error, ef or fencing token without reading four prerequisite modules, and a senior in a design review needs the impossibility results as production rules rather than proofs; this module is the site's single authoritative vocabulary, notation, anchor-number and theorem reference.

subtopics.title: Glossary and the ambiguous-term decoder
subtopics.covers: One canonical definition per term the site uses, with explicit disambiguation of the words this field overloads — consistency (ACID's C, CAP's C, replica consistency), partition (network split, table partition, Kafka partition, hash shard), atomic (transaction, sector write, CAS), lock (transaction lock, latch, lease), log (WAL, replication stream, topic, application log), snapshot (MVCC read view, EBS/filesystem snapshot, Raft snapshot, Lucene segment view), commit (client ack, fsync, quorum ack, visible to readers), index (B-tree, inverted, ANN, materialized view) and serializable (ANSI, Adya, strict).
subtopics.visual: A searchable glossary where each overloaded term opens a disambiguation card that places its two to four meanings side by side, every meaning embedding the owning module's own primitive in read-only mode at a named preset — 'partition' showing the network-split, partition-pruning and topic-fanout primitives together — each frozen at one labelled state with a step/scrub control and an 'open in the module' link that hands the preset over intact, with CI failing the card if a preset id stops resolving.

subtopics.title: Notation index and cross-engine synonyms
subtopics.covers: The symbols and field names used across modules — LSN and pageLSN, xmin/xmax and DB_TRX_ID, TID and ctid, N/W/R, f and 2f+1, epsilon for TrueTime, B and M in external-memory cost formulas, k1 and b, M and ef, sigma and kappa in the USL, write/read/space amplification — each with the exact setting or column name it appears as in a real system, plus synonym tables for leader/primary/master, follower/replica/secondary/standby and shard/range/region/tablet/vnode/partition.
subtopics.visual: A term grid where hovering an entry shows its per-engine names side by side and clicking opens a miniature diagram placing the symbol inside the structure it belongs to — pageLSN stamped on a page header, xmax in a tuple header, the high watermark on a partition log — with a jump link to the owning subtopic.

subtopics.title: Probability toolkit: skew, collisions and tail bounds on one card
subtopics.covers: The handful of probability results the rest of the site keeps applying, each as a formula plus the number to round with — Zipf and power-law shapes and the head fraction that sets cache hit rate and hot-key risk, the birthday bound for hash, fingerprint and id collisions at 32, 64 and 128 bits, coupon collector for how long random sampling takes to touch every partition, balls-into-bins max load, Chernoff/Hoeffding tails for sampling error in ANALYZE and for quorum availability, the independence assumption whose failure (shared rack, shared control plane, shared deploy) makes nines arithmetic wrong, and expectation-of-the-maximum for fan-out tail latency.
subtopics.visual: A card deck in which each result carries a live calculator bound to the site's own scenarios — hash width and key count reporting collision probability, replica count with a correlated-failure slider reporting availability nines that visibly stop improving, fan-out plus per-server p99 reporting composite tail — and every card links to the module where that result is actually used.

subtopics.title: Theorem-to-consequence cards: what each result forbids
subtopics.covers: One card per formal result stated informally, then as the production rule it imposes, then with the counterexample that shows what breaks when it is ignored — FLP, Gilbert-Lynch CAP, PACELC, Bailis's HAT availability classes, CALM and I-confluence, Adya's isolation graphs, Fekete's dangerous structures, the external-memory and AGM bounds, the RUM conjecture, Amdahl, the USL and Little's law, Herlihy's consensus numbers, linearizability's composability, quorum intersection and 2f+1 versus 3f+1, and the Bloom-filter space and distinct-count estimation lower bounds.
subtopics.visual: A card deck filterable by symptom ('my acknowledged write vanished', 'two clients both got the username', 'p99 collapsed at 80% utilization') where each card flips from statement to rule to an inline run of the owning module's primitive at the preset that exhibits the violation, steppable in place and openable in the module that proves it.

subtopics.title: Napkin estimation: rows, bytes, QPS and IOPS
subtopics.covers: A repeatable envelope from a product spec to numbers — rows per day from a usage metric, bytes per row from column widths plus tuple header, alignment and null bitmap, index size from key width over fill factor, total storage as data plus indexes plus TOAST plus version overhead times replication times backup retention, working set against RAM, QPS from DAU times actions divided by 86,400 times a peak factor, read IOPS from pages touched discounted by cache hit rate, write IOPS from rows times (1 + secondary indexes) plus WAL bytes per second — with the anchor constants to round against and the discipline of one significant figure and stated assumptions.
subtopics.visual: An estimation drill hands the learner a product spec and they fill each envelope step while rows, bytes, working set, QPS and IOPS recompute live; submitting compares their numbers against the same quantities measured from a simulated system with those parameters and highlights which single assumption caused the largest error.

subtopics.title: Anchor numbers by workload: bytes per document, vector, sample and message
subtopics.covers: The rounding constants that make a specialized store estimable in advance — inverted index size as a multiple of raw text and what stored fields, doc values and positions each add, vector memory as dimension times four bytes plus HNSW's per-node graph overhead and what int8 or binary quantization divides it by, a metrics store's bytes per sample after delta-of-delta and XOR compression against its per-active-series resident overhead, a log line or span's bytes indexed versus bytes stored after compression, Kafka's per-partition throughput ceiling and per-message overhead, typical columnar compression ratios by column kind, and B-tree versus LSM space amplification — each stated with the mechanism that produces it and a link to the module that derives it.
subtopics.visual: A card deck where each constant is a live calculator wired to the site's own simulators — document count and field configuration reporting index size, vector count with dimension, M and quantization reporting resident memory against an instance-size line, series count and scrape interval reporting TSDB memory and daily disk — with a 'check against the mechanism' button that replays the owning module's simulation at those parameters so the estimate is verified rather than trusted.

subtopics.title: Cost and complexity cheat sheet: every operator in the I/O model
subtopics.covers: One table of the asymptotics worth quoting, each stated in the model that makes it true and annotated with the constant that actually decides it — B-tree point lookup and range scan as block transfers in the external-memory model, an LSM read across L levels with and without filters, hash index probes, sequential scan as N/B, external sort and its pass count, nested loop and block nested loop, hash and merge joins, hash versus sort aggregation, top-k with and without early termination, inverted-list intersection, ANN graph search, the distributed additions (broadcast |S|·N against shuffle |R|+|S|, quorum round trips, fan-out tail as the maximum of N draws) and the maintenance side (bulk index build as N log N, compaction and vacuum as bytes rewritten per byte written) — with every row naming the parameter that dominates in practice and linking to the subtopic that derives it.
subtopics.visual: A filterable table where entering N, B, M and a selectivity converts every asymptotic row into a concrete predicted block-transfer count and time estimate under a chosen device profile, and selecting two rows overlays their curves so the crossover the learner actually cares about — index versus scan, hash versus merge, broadcast versus shuffle, ANN versus brute force — is read straight off the chart instead of recalled.

subtopics.title: What breaks at each order of magnitude
subtopics.covers: The scale ladder naming the first practice to fail at each rung — below a million rows almost nothing, at 10^7–10^8 OFFSET pagination, COUNT(*), unbatched backfills, rewriting ALTERs, non-concurrent index builds and nightly logical dumps, at 10^9 with a working set past RAM the cache cliff, bloat and vacuum, index build and restore windows and forced partitioning, past a node's write ceiling sharding or an LSM or columnar engine — run in parallel with the connection-count, replica, region, partition and tenant ladders, each rung naming the symptom, the mechanism and the module that fixes it.
subtopics.visual: A log-scale slider from 10^3 to 10^12 rows drives the previous cards' napkin and cost models rather than a lookup table — bytes per row, secondary index count, cache hit rate and a selectable device profile (NVMe, network SSD, spinning disk) sit editable beside it — redrawing a panel of operations (point lookup, range scan, COUNT(*), deep OFFSET page, ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX, VACUUM, full backup, cross-shard join) whose durations each expand on hover into the pages-touched-over-IOPS arithmetic that produced them, with thresholds lighting up as the slider crosses them so the learner can re-run the whole ladder on their own hardware numbers.

modules.title: Decision Guides: Choosing Stores, Freshness and Placement
modules.why: The question a senior is actually asked is 'what do I use for this, and can the database we already run do it?', and today that answer is spread across forty modules; these guides answer it in one page with concrete thresholds, hard limits and the specific reason each runner-up was ruled out, then link back to the mechanism that explains the limit.

subtopics.title: Which store for which workload
subtopics.covers: A decision tree per workload and data type — OLTP, analytics, time-series and metrics, logs and traces, full-text, vector, graph, geospatial, documents, blobs, queues, caches, ledgers — giving the obvious default first (usually PostgreSQL) with the concrete thresholds at which a specialized store wins (ingest rate, row count, QPS and concurrency, label cardinality, recall target, traversal depth, retention window, item size), what each specialization costs operationally, and which choices are one-way doors.
subtopics.visual: The learner enters their workload parameters and the guide walks the tree node by node, showing at each branch the threshold being tested against their numbers, then lists the runner-up systems with the single limit that ruled each one out and saves the entered parameter set as the shared object every matrix page in comparison-matrices is then filtered and replayed against.

subtopics.title: Choosing freshness: batch, micro-batch, incremental or streaming
subtopics.covers: Deciding per consumer rather than per platform — the freshness the product genuinely needs versus the one it asked for, the ladder from nightly full rebuild through hourly incremental models and minute-scale micro-batch to a continuously maintained view or a streaming job, the engineering burden each rung adds (state, watermarks, late-data policy, restatement, replay) and the operational burden (an on-call for a streaming job versus a rerun for a failed nightly), what each rung does when a late or corrected record arrives, the rebuild and backfill story for each, and the exit rule that when a number becomes an amount owed or a user-visible state transition it leaves this ladder entirely for the transactional path.
subtopics.visual: The learner sets a freshness requirement, event lateness profile and correction rate, and the guide scores every rung with compute cost, code and operational burden and its answer under a late event, then replays a correction landing after a period closed so the rungs that cannot restate visibly disagree with the rungs that can.

subtopics.title: From question to mechanism: the design-question router
subtopics.covers: An index over the canonical design questions (URL shortener, social feed, chat, ledger, inventory checkout, rate limiter, leaderboard, metrics store, audit log, autocomplete, nearby search, notifications, multi-tenant SaaS, usage metering) naming for each only the decisions that actually determine the answer — the partition key and what it makes single-partition, the consistency required per operation rather than per system, the read:write ratio and hot-key shape, and whether any invariant genuinely needs coordination — plus the clarifying questions to ask first, the standard follow-ups every interviewer and reviewer raises (10x traffic, a celebrity key, a region loss, a GDPR deletion, a schema change), and a link to the module that owns each decision.
subtopics.visual: Picking a question card builds an answer skeleton the learner fills in — partition key, per-operation consistency, hot-key mitigation, coordination points — and the router checks the combination for internal contradictions (a global uniqueness invariant under a partition key that scatters it, a strict-freshness read routed to a replica), then reveals which mechanism module each filled slot resolves to and replays one follow-up against the stated design.

subtopics.title: In the database or in the application?
subtopics.covers: A per-concern decision table — uniqueness and referential integrity (a constraint versus a check-then-insert that races), joins and aggregation (one statement versus N+1 round trips or an in-memory join), derived data (trigger versus same-transaction write versus CDC consumer), counters, scheduling and queues, full-text and vector search, encryption and masking, and business rules in stored procedures — scored on the criteria that actually decide it: whether the guarantee survives a concurrent writer, a retry or a second client written by another team, what a replayed statement does, how testable and reviewable the rule is, how tightly it couples deployment and rollback, and how much CPU it pushes onto the tier that is hardest to scale out.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a concern and a placement, then a scripted scenario (two concurrent clients, a timed-out retry, a direct SQL fix from a console, a rollback of one deploy but not the other) replays against that choice showing whether the guarantee holds or is bypassed, with meters for database CPU, round trips per operation and how much of the rule is provable in CI versus only observable in production.

modules.title: Comparison Matrices: Engines, Platforms, Formats and Claims
modules.why: Once the workload has picked a shape, the remaining questions are all lookups a senior must answer precisely — does this engine support what we need, will this managed service take it away, will the version we run allow it, may we legally ship it, and does the vendor's word mean what it sounds like — so all of them share one MatrixExplorer component and one interaction (requirement filter, grey-out with the failing limit named, cell detail, jump link to the mechanism module), and the capability page ends by driving the learner's own numbers into a limit until it breaks.

subtopics.title: Capability and limits matrix by data type
subtopics.covers: A filterable matrix of PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB, ClickHouse, Elasticsearch, Redis, CockroachDB/Spanner, DuckDB and Snowflake across JSON, full-text, vector, geospatial, time-series, graph, queue, blob and ledger workloads, each cell naming the mechanism used, the hard limits (value and document sizes, available index types, transaction scope, secondary-index consistency, cardinality ceilings) and the gotcha that bites in production.
subtopics.visual: This page introduces the shared MatrixExplorer — selecting a required capability set greys out every engine that fails a requirement with the specific failing limit displayed, and clicking a cell expands the mechanism, its limits and a jump link to the module that explains it — then hands the workload parameters carried in from 'Which store for which workload' to the capstone-simulator runtime, which drives real writes and queries through the selected engine's declared ceilings until one actually trips (an oversized item, a partition past its throughput cap, a transaction crossing its scope, one index too many) and shows the error the engine returns rather than the cell text.

subtopics.title: Engine comparison tables: defaults, limits and dialect differences
subtopics.covers: Side-by-side rows for PostgreSQL, MySQL/InnoDB, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle, CockroachDB, Spanner, Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB, ClickHouse and DuckDB covering operational defaults (durability setting and its knob, default isolation level pointing at the engine matrix in transactions-and-isolation, transactional DDL, default replication and failover unit), the capability grid (index types, online DDL, partial and expression indexes, materialized views, upsert form, window and recursive-CTE support, foreign keys), the hard ceilings (row and value size, identifier and index key length, columns and partitions per table, connections, per-partition throughput), and the dialect differences that bite during a migration (upsert syntax, RETURNING, LIMIT versus FETCH FIRST versus TOP, identifier case folding, boolean and timestamp types, NULL sort order, empty-string-versus-NULL, sequences versus auto-increment, collation).
subtopics.visual: The same MatrixExplorer in diff mode: selecting two or more engines and a facet shows only those rows with every differing cell highlighted, clicking a cell opens the one-paragraph consequence and the idiomatic equivalent in the other engine, and a 'migration checklist' button collects every highlighted difference for the chosen source-to-target pair.

subtopics.title: Table format and catalog capability matrix: can your engine read what you just wrote
subtopics.covers: A reference grid of lakehouse format and protocol versions against engine support — Iceberg format v1/v2/v3 (row-level deletes, deletion vectors, row lineage, variant and geometry types), Delta's reader/writer protocol feature negotiation (deletion vectors, column mapping, liquid clustering, type widening), Hudi table versions, and catalog protocol features (Iceberg REST spec versions, credential vending, multi-table transactions) — with each cell stating whether a given engine reads, writes or refuses, and what the failure actually looks like: a writer enabling one feature and silently locking out every older reader, a catalog rejecting the commit, or an engine returning rows that ignore delete files and are simply wrong.
subtopics.visual: The same MatrixExplorer with a feature toggle: selecting the engines in the learner's stack and switching a table feature on flips every engine cell to reads, reads-but-wrong or refuses with the exact error and the minimum version that would fix it, while a 'what breaks first' panel replays the enable as a timeline showing which downstream reader fails, when it fails, and whether it fails loudly or returns wrong rows.

subtopics.title: Version-delta cards: which release unlocked which design
subtopics.covers: A per-engine card deck of the releases that change designs rather than benchmarks — PostgreSQL 14 bottom-up index deletion and Memoize, 15 MERGE and NULLS NOT DISTINCT, 16 logical decoding on standbys and pg_stat_io, 17 incremental base backups, failover slots, streaming reads and TidStore vacuum, 18 asynchronous I/O, UUIDv7, virtual generated columns, OAuth and skip scan; MySQL 8.0's removed change buffer and 8.4's changed defaults; MongoDB 5.0's majority-read default; Kafka's KRaft, KIP-848 rebalancing and share groups; Cassandra 4.0 repair and 5.0 SAI — each card naming the pattern it enables or retires, the minimum version a design now assumes, and the module that explains the mechanism.
subtopics.visual: The learner enters the versions actually running in their fleet and picks a design goal (zero-downtime constraint addition, CDC that survives failover, sub-second follower reads, a high-churn queue table), and each requirement resolves to already available, needs a named upgrade, or impossible on this engine, with the minimum-version path and the upgrade class (minor, major, one-way) shown for each.

subtopics.title: Managed platform matrix: what each service takes away
subtopics.covers: A comparison across RDS/Aurora, Cloud SQL/AlloyDB, Azure Database, Neon, PlanetScale, Supabase, Spanner, DynamoDB, CockroachDB Cloud and managed ClickHouse/Kafka on the facts that change designs — connection ceilings and built-in poolers, superuser substitutes and extension allowlists, logical replication and CDC support, online schema change tooling, backup and PITR windows and cross-region restore, replica and multi-region topologies, per-transaction and per-item limits, autoscaling and scale-to-zero behaviour, encryption and audit options, and maintenance-window and failover semantics — each cell annotated with the internal mechanism that forces the limit.
subtopics.visual: The same MatrixExplorer in requirement mode greys out non-qualifying platforms with the failing limit named and opens the mechanism behind any cell, and the design carried in from the router is then replayed against the chosen platform's connection ceiling, failover window and PITR retention so the learner sees which part of their own design has to change.

subtopics.title: Licenses, forks and the managed-service clause
subtopics.covers: The license shifts a senior must reason about before adopting or upgrading — SSPL and its service-source condition (MongoDB, Elasticsearch pre-2024), BSL with a delayed open-source conversion and its change date (CockroachDB, Redpanda, Terraform, MariaDB MaxScale), the Redis RSAL-then-AGPL turn and Elasticsearch's AGPL addition, the community forks that resulted (Valkey, OpenSearch, OpenTofu, OpenBao) and their growing divergence, set against permissive Apache-2.0 and MIT projects (PostgreSQL's own license, Iceberg, Arrow, DuckDB) — plus what each clause actually restricts (offering the software as a service, not internal use), why a pinned version keeps its original terms, and how all of it interacts with your cloud provider's managed offering.
subtopics.visual: The same MatrixExplorer in scenario mode, where picking a usage scenario (internal service, SaaS product built on it, reselling a managed version, embedding in a shipped binary) resolves each project's cell to permitted, conditional or prohibited with the governing clause quoted, while a year slider replays each project's license history so a version pinned three years ago carries visibly different terms from today's release.

subtopics.title: The vendor-claim decoder
subtopics.covers: Marketing phrases mapped to the formal guarantee they do and do not imply — 'ACID', 'strong consistency', 'serializable', 'exactly-once', 'infinitely scalable', 'zero downtime', 'multi-master', 'no-loss failover', 'sub-millisecond' — naming for each the anomaly still permitted, the configuration or fine print the claim depends on, and the Jepsen report, documentation line or paper that settles it.
subtopics.visual: Hovering a marketing phrase shows the guarantee it maps to beside a ten-second replay of the anomaly it still allows, with a toggle that applies the configuration change the vendor's fine print requires and replays the same history to show the anomaly disappearing or persisting.

modules.title: Playbooks: Symptom-First Triage
modules.why: At 3 a.m. nobody navigates a curriculum by mechanism — they navigate by symptom, and a senior needs the ordered diagnostics, the discriminating signal, the mitigation and its side effects in one place, with every branch linking back to the module that owns the mechanism so the playbook teaches rather than merely instructs.

subtopics.title: The on-call router: symptom to mechanism index
subtopics.covers: A cross-engine lookup from observation to candidate mechanisms — p99 spiked with flat CPU, writes rejected or hanging, connections exhausted, disk filling, WAL or binlog not recycling, replication lag climbing, autovacuum never finishing or wraparound approaching, a plan that flipped overnight, throttling errors on a managed store, a cluster stuck in election, data that looks wrong — each naming the first three queries or commands per engine (pg_stat_activity with wait events and pg_blocking_pids, pg_locks, pg_stat_replication and slot state, pg_stat_statements ranked by the right column, performance_schema and sys views, SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS, nodetool tpstats, RocksDB stall counters), the signal that discriminates between causes, and the boundary between mitigation and root cause.
subtopics.visual: A symptom picker expands into a branching checklist where each step shows the exact diagnostic with realistic simulated output, the learner chooses the branch it implies and is either advanced or told precisely why that reading does not support that branch, with every terminal node linking to the owning module.

subtopics.title: Playbook: you just inherited this database
subtopics.covers: The ordered discovery pass on an undocumented instance — size and growth per relation, the config diff against engine defaults and against the parameter group of record, top statements by total time and by blocks read from pg_stat_statements or the slow log, index hygiene (unused, redundant-prefix, unindexed foreign keys, tables with no primary key), the full replication topology plus every slot, subscriber, CDC consumer and foreign-data wrapper attached to it, backup age and whether a restore has ever been proven, who and what actually connects (activity by application_name, host and role, plus the role and grant graph), jobs running inside the database, and the write-up that converts all of it into a named owner, a ranked risk list and cadence entries.
subtopics.visual: A discovery console over an undocumented instance where each query the learner chooses costs simulated minutes and fills a findings sheet — an inactive slot retaining WAL, a nightly job with no owner, a backup job that exits zero but has never been restored, a primary-key-less table a downstream consumer depends on — then a seeded incident fires on whichever finding they skipped, scored against the time they spent.

subtopics.title: Playbook: the database is at 100% CPU
subtopics.covers: The triage tree that differs from slow-single-query tuning — separate user CPU from system CPU and iowait, rank statements by total time inside the incident window to see whether one class dominates, then discriminate among a plan flip (stale or freshly refreshed statistics, a sniffed generic plan, a crossed cost crossover), a genuine traffic or fan-out increase, a dropped or invalid index, connection churn burning CPU on parse, TLS and auth, internal work (autovacuum, compaction, checkpointer, JIT, an online index build) and spin on a hot latch that presents as CPU rather than a wait — followed by graduated interventions and their side effects.
subtopics.visual: The operations module's diagnostic console is embedded read-only — same panels, same seeded fault library — under an incident wrapper that runs a clock, charges simulated minutes per inspection, makes the learner commit an intervention from an ordered list annotated with its side effects, and then replays the true causal chain against their trace.

subtopics.title: Playbook: will it finish, and what does cancelling cost?
subtopics.covers: Finding the real progress signal per operation class — pg_stat_progress_create_index, _vacuum, _cluster, _copy, _basebackup and _analyze, InnoDB online-DDL row counts and the gh-ost/pt-osc copy cursor, restore and replay measured as LSN or bytes per second, a batched backfill's checkpoint row — and extrapolating a finish time while knowing where the rate is not linear (an index build's sort-then-merge-then-write phases, compaction debt accumulating behind the job, a backfill slowing as replica-lag throttling engages); then the cancel-cost table that decides the call: a rewriting ALTER or a long UPDATE rolls back for roughly the time it already ran and releases nothing until it does, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY leaves an INVALID index that still costs every write until dropped, VACUUM loses only its progress, a checkpointed backfill resumes, a restore or pg_basebackup restarts from zero, and an online-schema-change tool leaves triggers or a ghost table to clean up; plus the collateral question of what is queued behind it and whether killing the blocker or the queue is the faster path to serving traffic.
subtopics.visual: An operation picker (concurrent index build, rewriting ALTER, VACUUM, batched backfill, restore with WAL replay, gh-ost copy) each renders its genuine progress view and a rate curve the learner extrapolates to a predicted finish, with a lock-queue lane showing what is blocked and for how long while they deliberate; pressing cancel then plays the true cost — a rollback bar running as long as the work already done, an INVALID index left behind that a write-amplification meter keeps charging, or a checkpointed job resuming in seconds — and a scoreboard compares the outcome against having simply waited.

subtopics.title: Playbook: the database will not start
subtopics.covers: Triage from the startup log outward when no SQL connection is possible: separating 'recovering, wait' from 'will never start' by watching the redo LSN advance against the checkpoint distance (PostgreSQL recovery messages and pg_controldata, InnoDB crash-recovery phases, a replica applying a huge transaction) and estimating remaining time; the cause ladder — disk or inode exhaustion, permissions and a wrong or moved data directory, a missing or truncated archived WAL segment that a restore_command cannot fetch, an invalid checkpoint record or damaged control file, an extension or collation library missing after an image or OS upgrade, shared-memory, hugepage and ulimit failures, and the xid-wraparound read-only stop that needs single-user VACUUM — each with the log line that identifies it and the non-destructive fix; then the destructive ladder stated with its cost, where restoring the last backup plus PITR is almost always cheaper than pg_resetwal or innodb_force_recovery above level 4, which produce a server that starts, answers and lies; and the containment rules of snapshotting the volume before any attempt and never pointing replicas at an instance recovered destructively.
subtopics.visual: A crash-looping instance where each restart prints a real startup log and the learner may run only host-level diagnostics, choosing at each round to wait (a replay-progress bar advancing at a measured LSN rate with an ETA, or visibly stalled), to apply a non-destructive fix, or to escalate; an incident clock charges every action, taking the volume snapshot first preserves the alternatives, and reaching for pg_resetwal early brings the server up fastest and then returns rows that a consistency check flags as wrong, while the PITR path costs more minutes and passes.

subtopics.title: Playbook: someone deleted the data
subtopics.covers: The first five minutes (revoke the writer or pause the job, do not restart the application, freeze vacuum and any replica that is still behind the statement, and pin the exact time window and transaction id from the statement log, audit table or CDC stream), then the recovery ladder ordered by what still exists and how fast it expires — a delayed standby paused before the statement, PITR restored into a side clone rather than over the live cluster, an unaffected replica or a logical dump, and MVCC leftovers still readable before cleanup (pg_dirtyread, Oracle flashback query, InnoDB undo, MySQL binlog flashback tooling) — extracting only the affected rows and merging them back against everything written since, why DROP, TRUNCATE and a cascaded delete leave nothing to mine, and closing with the permission or guardrail change that makes the retrospective worth writing.
subtopics.visual: An incident clock runs while the learner triages a cluster where an UPDATE with a missing WHERE committed twelve minutes ago: every action costs simulated minutes, background autovacuum visibly erases the in-place recovery option and the delayed standby's lag counts down toward the bad statement, and each chosen path reports rows recovered, minutes elapsed and how many post-incident writes the merge would have overwritten.

modules.title: Playbooks: Wrong Data, Broken Pipelines and After-the-Fact Forensics
modules.why: The second half of on-call is not a database that is slow or down but one that is up and answering wrongly — an error code the client must decide how to retry, an anomaly with a name, rows that vanished somewhere in a five-hop pipeline, a bill and a tail latency governed by object-store request classes — plus the incident that is already over and owes an RCA tomorrow, where the only evidence is whatever telemetry someone configured in advance.

subtopics.title: Error-code triage: SQLSTATE, MySQL and driver errors by response
subtopics.covers: A decision table mapping the errors applications actually see to the correct response — 40001 and 40P01 (restart the whole transaction), 23505 and 23503, 55P03 and 57014 from lock_timeout and statement_timeout, 53300 and 53100, 25P02, 08006/08003 and the in-doubt COMMIT, 57P01 during failover, 42P01/42703 as deploy-ordering bugs, plus the MySQL equivalents (1213, 1205, 1062, 1040, 2006/2013) and driver-level timeouts — each classified as safe to retry, safe only behind an idempotency key, or must fail fast, with the log line and metric that should accompany it.
subtopics.visual: An error router asks which code fired and whether it arrived before or during COMMIT and whether the operation is idempotent, walks to a verdict (retry now, retry with backoff, retry only with an idempotency key, fail and alert), then replays a short animation of the server-side scenario that produced exactly that code.

subtopics.title: Anomaly triage: from symptom to named anomaly
subtopics.covers: A symptom-first index over the whole anomaly space — lost update, write skew, read skew, phantom, long fork, causal reverse, stale read, read-your-writes and monotonic-read violations, resurrected rows, duplicate side effects, torn multi-row reads — each mapped to its Adya class or consistency-model violation, the mechanism that permits it (snapshot isolation's missing predicate check, replica lag, last-write-wins under clock skew, a tombstone past gc_grace, at-least-once delivery without an idempotency key, a non-atomic multi-shard read), the diagnostic that confirms it (an Elle cycle, a version-vector comparison, lag in bytes, a checksum diff) and the fix with its cost.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks the observed symptom and answers three or four questions (one object or many, one shard or several, was there a retry, was the read from a replica) until the playbook names an anomaly, then replays that anomaly's minimal two-client history in a simulator and applies the fix so the same history becomes legal.

subtopics.title: Playbooks for specialized workloads
subtopics.covers: Runbooks for the symptoms the relational playbooks miss — search relevance regressions and slow search queries, ANN recall dropping after a rebuild or model change, vector index bloat and memory exhaustion, metrics cardinality explosion and a hot recent partition, queue-table bloat with stuck leases and tombstone storms, a spatial index the planner refuses to use, a JSON predicate doing a full scan, orphaned blobs — each with the metric to check first, the exact query or command, the probable mechanism, and the fix with its risk.
subtopics.visual: The learner picks a symptom and answers the playbook's diagnostic questions against a simulated system whose metrics actually respond, watching the tree narrow to a root cause and then applying the fix to see the metric recover — or not, which sends them back one branch with the discriminating signal explained.

subtopics.title: Playbook: the incident is over — reconstructing what happened
subtopics.covers: Forensics from what was retained: why cumulative statistics views answer nothing about a past window unless snapshots were taken and differenced (periodic pg_stat_statements/pg_stat_all_tables snapshots in the pgsentinel and AWR style, stats_reset and pg_stat_statements_info tracking so a reset is not mistaken for quiet), sampled Active Session History and Performance Insights windows with their fixed retention, log retention plus which of log_checkpoints, log_lock_waits, log_autovacuum_min_duration, log_temp_files and auto_explain sampling would have recorded the cause, metric resolution and downsampling that flatten a sub-minute stall out of existence, and the artifacts that survive independently (deploy and migration records, cron and batch schedules, checkpoint and autovacuum log lines, replication lag history, provider events); then the reconstruction itself — build one timeline by joining those sources, difference the counter snapshots that bracket the window to rank statements by work done inside it rather than lifetime, and separate correlation from a mechanism you can name — closing with the rule that the deliverable of an unanswerable RCA is the telemetry change that makes the next one answerable.
subtopics.visual: An incident that ended six hours ago where the learner may query only retained artifacts, having chosen the snapshot interval, logging settings and metric resolution before the fact: ranking by lifetime counter totals points at the wrong statement until two bracketing snapshots are differenced, a five-minute metric series hides the stall that a thirty-second series reveals, the offending statement text is present or already rotated away depending on the log settings, and re-running the identical incident after the learner tightens the telemetry shows exactly which decision made the cause recoverable.

subtopics.title: Playbook: the rows are missing downstream
subtopics.covers: Reconciling counts and checksums hop by hop over a bounded time window (source table → outbox or replication slot → topic partitions → consumer-group offsets → sink) to localize the drop before theorizing, then the causes each hop actually produces — an outbox row written but never relayed, a slot advanced or recreated so a snapshot-to-stream handoff left a gap, a schema or filter change silently dropping a field or a record type, a dedupe or upsert key collapsing genuinely distinct rows, an offset committed before processing so a rebalance skipped a batch, retention expiring before a paused consumer caught up, and a sink upsert overwriting on the wrong key — the discriminating signals for each (lag versus end offsets, dead-letter counts, per-window row-count and checksum diffs), and a repair by bounded replay from an offset or timestamp range that is safe to run twice because the sink is idempotent.
