subtopics.visual: A five-hop pipeline with one of six seeded loss causes lets the learner spend simulated minutes running per-hop count and checksum probes until the graph narrows to one hop, after which they choose a replay window and watch counts converge — or watch duplicates appear when the sink turns out not to be idempotent, sending them back a step.

subtopics.title: Playbook: latency and cost in disaggregated and serverless systems
subtopics.covers: The signal set that replaces iostat when the disk is an object store — request counts by class and their per-request cost, cache hit rate at each tier (in-process, local NVMe, regional), first-byte and tail latency on miss, throttling with 503 SlowDown and the retry behaviour that turns it into a metastable storm, prefix hot-spotting and key-layout fixes, compaction and orphan-object GC falling behind ingest, cold starts after scale-to-zero with an empty cache, and cross-AZ and egress bytes as a first-class metric.
subtopics.visual: A live disaggregated stack with injectable faults (throttling, cold cache after resume, a hot prefix, compaction lag) shows request-class counters, cache-hit and first-byte-latency panels and a dollar meter responding; the learner must name the fault from the signals, apply a fix and watch whether latency or cost recovers first.

modules.title: Lifecycle Checklists and Review Gates
modules.why: Part 12 tells you how to choose a system and what to do when one breaks, but nothing covers the gates in between: the evidence a database must produce before it carries real traffic, the recurring work that keeps that evidence true, and the classification that decides how much ceremony a proposed change deserves. Seniors are asked for exactly these artifacts at launch reviews, change-approval meetings and audits, and their absence is the shared root cause of the classic incidents — a backup configured but never restored, a failover never drilled, a certificate nobody re-checked, a routine ALTER that turned out to rewrite a terabyte at peak. Every line here is stated as required evidence or as a predicted failure, and links back to the module that derives it.

subtopics.title: Production readiness review: the go-live checklist
subtopics.covers: The gate a new or newly critical database must pass, each item phrased as evidence rather than a checkbox — a restore performed end to end and timed on production-sized data, stated and drilled RPO/RTO, the short list of pageable conditions wired to linked runbooks, a sized connection budget and pooler, capacity headroom with a days-to-full trend, a rehearsed migration and rollback, the security baseline of no public listener plus enforced TLS, least-privilege roles, rotated secrets and audit, tenancy quotas, working retention and erasure paths, a named owner and rotation, and a cost model.
subtopics.visual: A checklist that scores a described deployment and, for every unmet item, runs the specific failure it predicts against a simulated system — the never-tested restore that returns missing a table, the alert with no runbook stretching time-to-mitigate, the unsized pool exhausting connections at launch traffic, the unrehearsed migration holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for minutes — so each line is justified by the incident it prevents.

subtopics.title: Evidence, not assertion: auditing a readiness claim
subtopics.covers: How to interrogate each checklist answer — distinguishing a backup job that exits zero from a restore whose row counts and checksums were compared, a replica that streams from a promotion that was actually performed, an alert that exists from one that has fired and paged a human — and the freshness rule that evidence older than its drill interval counts as unproven.
subtopics.visual: A claim inspector where the learner submits proof artifacts for each item (a job log, a restore transcript with timings, a failover drill record) and the tool marks each as proven, asserted or expired, then replays the deployment's last quarter to show which expired proofs were silently relied on.

subtopics.title: The operational cadence: what must be re-proved and how often
subtopics.covers: The recurring work that keeps readiness answers honest — restore and failover drills, minor-version and OS patching, certificate and credential expiry, statistics and index maintenance, vacuum and wraparound review, capacity and cost review, access review, extension and dependency audits — each with its interval, its owner, the evidence it produces and the decay that sets the interval.
subtopics.visual: A cadence board that runs a simulated first year forward, firing the event each lapsed task invites — an expired certificate, a never-drilled failover promoting a stale replica, a full disk, a wraparound emergency — while a panel shows which recurring task would have caught it, when it last ran, and how much earlier a tighter interval would have surfaced it.

subtopics.title: Change-risk classification: blast radius, reversibility and one-way doors
subtopics.covers: A taxonomy of database changes — metadata-only DDL, rewriting DDL, concurrent and non-concurrent index builds, throttled backfills, dynamic versus restart-requiring parameter changes, failover and switchover, minor and major upgrades, extension upgrades, and destructive contract steps — mapped to blast radius, reversibility and the rollback story for each: revert, forward-fix only, or a genuine one-way door such as a finalized cluster version, a hard-linked pg_upgrade cluster or a dropped column.
subtopics.visual: A change classifier where the learner describes a proposed change and the tool assigns its class, prints the rollback verdict and the required safeguards, then simulates the rollback attempt so a one-way door visibly leaves the system in a state the rollback button cannot restore.

subtopics.title: Safeguards and timing: lock budgets, throttles, canaries and freeze windows
subtopics.covers: The safeguard each risk class requires and why — lock_timeout with bounded retry, batch size and replication-lag throttling, canary or single-shard-first rollout, a verified backup taken immediately before, a two-person gate on irreversible steps — plus the timing rules that follow from the classification, why freeze windows and peak-hour avoidance exist, and the cases where they are cargo cult that merely delays risk into a worse window.
subtopics.visual: A scheduler that runs the classified change against live traffic at a chosen hour, showing lock wait queues, backfill duration, replication lag and error budget consumed, with each safeguard toggleable so the learner watches an unthrottled backfill starve replicas and a lock_timeout turn a stall into a harmless retry.

subtopics.title: Running the review: the questions that catch the bad changes
subtopics.covers: The review ritual itself — the fixed question list a reviewer puts to a migration diff, a parameter change or a topology change, what the author must attach (plan output, lock analysis, row counts, rollback command), the pre-mortem framing, and how to keep review effort proportional so free changes pass in seconds while one-way doors get a second pair of eyes.
subtopics.visual: A review bench serving real change diffs where the learner approves or blocks each one, then watches it execute in production simulation and sees which questions would have caught the damage, scoring both missed defects and time wasted over-reviewing harmless changes.

subtopics.title: From incident to gate: turning postmortems into checklist lines
subtopics.covers: How a recurring failure becomes a permanent gate — deriving the missing evidence or missing cadence item from a postmortem, writing it as an automated check rather than a human reminder where possible, and pruning checklist lines that no longer predict any failure so the gate stays short enough to be used.
subtopics.visual: A workbench that takes a postmortem timeline, lets the learner propose a gate or cadence item, then replays a library of historical incidents to report how many that gate would have prevented and how much review time it costs per change.

modules.title: The Reading Map: Canon, Modern Sources and What Changed
modules.why: The site is drawn from a specific literature and a senior's growth path is reading it — but only in the right order, for the right takeaway, and knowing which claims have since been superseded; the value a curriculum adds over a bibliography is exactly that annotation, so the site should own it rather than sending people to a stale blog post.

subtopics.title: The annotated canon: papers and practitioner books in reading order
subtopics.covers: A card per foundational work — System R and Selinger, ARIES, Gray and Reuter, Berenson's ANSI critique, Adya's thesis, Fekete/Cahill SSI, Hellerstein's Architecture of a Database System, the Red Book commentaries, C-Store and MonetDB/X100, Dremel, FLP, Gilbert-Lynch, Lamport's Time-Clocks, Chandy-Lamport, Paxos Made Simple and Made Live, Raft, VR Revisited, Chain Replication, Dynamo, Bigtable, Spanner, F1, Calvin, Percolator, CRDTs and dotted version vectors, WiscKey, the Bw-tree, Monkey, The Tail at Scale, Metastable Failures — each with why it was written, the one figure or theorem to take away, what later work superseded it, and the module that implements it — plus a parallel practitioner-books shelf (DDIA and the successors that update it, Petrov's Database Internals, Rogov's PostgreSQL Internals, Winand's SQL Performance Explained, Streaming Systems, and Karwin's SQL Antipatterns) where each book's chapters point into the modules that carry the mechanism, and SQL Antipatterns gets a full per-antipattern index — Jaywalking and Multicolumn Attributes to normalization and functional dependencies, Naive Trees to hierarchies and graphs in relational databases, ID Required to ID generation and to keys in the relational model, Keyless Entry to constraints and server-side execution order, Entity-Attribute-Value to JSONB modeling and to choosing the index for JSONB and arrays, Polymorphic Associations to polymorphic associations and type hierarchies, Metadata Tribbles to declarative partitioning and append-only time-series tables, Rounding Errors to types that bite, Implicit Columns to query anti-patterns and index-only scans, Random Selection to keyset pagination and approximate sampling, and Poor Man's Search Engine to full-text search in SQL — so the refutation of each named antipattern is one click from the shelf.
subtopics.visual: A citation graph whose nodes are sized by a quantity the site can defend — how many curriculum subtopics cite the work, toggleable to how many case-study systems implement it — opening by default on just the computed path of prerequisites for the reader's current module with the full graph behind a toggle, where clicking a node opens its card with the key figure redrawn as a small interactive widget (ARIES's three passes, Dynamo's ring, the RUM triangle) and a second tab shows the books shelf with each SQL Antipattern linking to the subtopic that refutes it.

subtopics.title: The modern reading list, 2020–2026
subtopics.covers: The recent primary sources a senior cannot find in a syllabus — Aurora and Aurora multi-master, the 2022 USENIX DynamoDB paper, FoundationDB 2021, Delos virtual consensus, Photon, Velox and the composable data systems manifesto, BtrBlocks and modern encodings, DBSP and incremental view maintenance, Snowflake, Napa and Procella, the Iceberg and Delta design documents, Protocol-Aware Recovery, Bourbon, tiered and diskless Kafka designs, and the Jepsen reports of this window read as a genre — each with its takeaway, its prerequisites and the module it supports.
subtopics.visual: A filterable dependency graph where the learner picks a topic (consensus, storage engines, analytics, streaming) and the minimal path lights up with an estimated reading time per node, each node opening its takeaway and the site subtopic covering the same ground.

subtopics.title: What changed since DDIA: a 2022–2026 orientation map
subtopics.covers: A claim-by-claim delta between the canonical texts and current practice — object storage as a primary database substrate rather than an archive, compute/storage disaggregation and scale-to-zero, tiered and diskless log brokers versus broker-local disks, DynamoDB revealed as leader-based Multi-Paxos rather than a Dynamo clone, Iceberg and Delta displacing Hive directory listings, vector search arriving inside relational engines, branching and serverless databases changing the dev workflow, durable execution replacing hand-rolled sagas, and single-node vectorized engines reclaiming workloads from clusters — each with the year, the system that changed it and the module carrying the mechanism.
subtopics.visual: A timeline-plus-matrix where selecting an old claim shows the superseding system, the year, a one-paragraph 'what actually changed' explainer and a jump link into the subtopic that carries the new mechanism, with a toggle to regroup the deltas by part of the curriculum.

subtopics.title: Reading a systems paper critically, and where to read source
subtopics.covers: The method — extract the invariants, the failure model, the consistency claim and what was actually measured (on what hardware, against which baseline, with which knobs), separate the contribution from the evaluation, and notice the workload the paper did not run — plus the non-paper sources seniors rely on: engine source trees with a named entry point each (PostgreSQL src/backend/access and storage, InnoDB storage/innobase, RocksDB db/ and table/, SQLite pager.c and btree.c), design documents, release notes and mailing-list threads, and a 'read these five first' path per role.
subtopics.visual: A worked read-through of one paper where the learner is asked to highlight its invariant, failure model and measured claim before the annotated answer is revealed, with a claims-versus-evidence panel showing which figures support which sentence and which sentence has no evidence behind it.

modules.title: The Visual System: Shared Primitives, Presets and Build Order
modules.why: Dozens of interactive visuals across the curriculum are specified in terms of shared components that no module owns — PageView, the TimelineEditor and its precedence/Adya/version-chain graph builders, the space-time message-lane diagram that roughly forty-five distributed subtopics draw, the ring/topology view, the thread-contention animator, ScanLab, the site-wide engine selector that must persist across every comparison page, the toy SQL parser plus instrumented pull executor and planner, and the capstone simulator runtime — while at least seven pages render numbers from data generated offline and committed, and the misconceptions deck already depends on a site-wide rule (a serialized preset passed as a single state prop and reflected in the URL) that is named nowhere. If these are not specified as one contract before module 1 is built, each module reinvents its own lane renderer and its own state shape, every declared reuse silently becomes a rebuild, presets cannot be exchanged between pages, and committed fixtures rot with nobody noticing. This module is the site's engineering appendix and its build order: it reads last and is built first.

subtopics.title: Shared conventions: glyphs, status encoding and the honesty rule
subtopics.covers: The visual vocabulary every simulation must use — the page, record, log record, node and message glyphs, the dual encoding of status by shape and colour rather than colour alone, motion and reduced-motion rules, and the labelling rule promised on the How to use the simulations page: every performance number is a stated model with its assumptions visible, never a measurement.
subtopics.visual: A live legend sheet rendering every glyph and status in one frame, with theme, colour-vision simulation and reduced-motion toggles applied simultaneously so the learner sees which encodings survive each condition and which collapse.

subtopics.title: The preset and fixture contracts: serialized state, versioned data and provenance
subtopics.covers: The two site-wide data rules — all learner-visible state lives in a single serializable preset object passed as one prop, mirrored to the URL, carrying a schema version with a stated upgrade path for old links and a read-only embed mode for use inside prose; and every authored fixture (collation orderings, compression ratios, captured plan texts, recorded candidate SQL, embedding sets, analyzer outputs, GeoJSON) is a committed file whose header records the generator command, tool and library versions and date, regenerated by a script in the repo, versioned like a preset, badged on any page that renders a number from it, and checked in CI so a drifted checksum or schema fails the build.
subtopics.visual: A preset inspector beside a running simulation where hand-editing the JSON drives the simulation and loading a deliberately stale v1 preset shows the upgrade path rewriting it, with a second pane exposing the fixture the page reads — its provenance header, checksum and 'generated offline with X' badge — so tampering with the checksum flips the page's numbers into the stale-fixture state CI would catch.

subtopics.title: PageView: slot map, byte grid, hex decode and fill heat
subtopics.covers: The shared page renderer used by heap files, slotted pages, B-tree nodes, SSTable blocks, WAL pages and column chunks — its props, its four modes (slot map, byte grid, hex plus field decode, fill heat), its selection and annotation model, and the roster of subtopics that consume it.
subtopics.visual: One page rendered simultaneously in all four modes with a linked cursor, so selecting a tuple highlights its slot entry, its bytes, its decoded header fields and its contribution to fill, proving the modes are views of one data structure rather than four drawings.

subtopics.title: TimelineEditor and the graph builders
subtopics.covers: The shared transaction-history editor — operations on a per-transaction timeline, commit points, crash markers and clock skew — together with the graph renderers layered on it for conflict/precedence graphs, Adya dependency cycles and multiversion version chains, plus the history format the isolation, MVCC, SSI and Jepsen subtopics all exchange.
subtopics.visual: A timeline whose edits regenerate the precedence and Adya graphs live, so dragging one read past a commit creates a visible rw-antidependency edge and closes a cycle, with the same history exportable and reloadable into any other page that accepts it.

subtopics.title: MessageTimeline: node lanes, delivery faults and annotation overlays
subtopics.covers: The shared space-time diagram behind roughly forty-five subtopics across why-distribute, time/clocks/ordering, failure detection and leases, replication, every Raft/Paxos/Zab/VR stepper, 2PC/3PC/Percolator, leaderless quorums and Jepsen — node lanes, a message model with per-link delay, drop, duplicate and reorder, injectable node pause, crash and clock skew, an annotation slot for Lamport counters, vector clocks, snapshot markers and consensus term badges, and history export in the same format the verification checkers consume.
subtopics.visual: One lane diagram where delaying, dropping or duplicating a single message re-derives every overlay at once — Lamport and vector-clock stamps, the leader's term badge, the snapshot cut — and the resulting history exports straight into the linearizability and Elle checker pages.

subtopics.title: RingView and ContentionLab: placement and thread contention
subtopics.covers: The two remaining shared renderers with their props, preset shapes and consumer lists — a token ring with virtual nodes, replica placement and ownership recolouring, consumed by partitioning and sharding, leaderless quorums and the Cassandra case study; and the thread-contention animator declared shared in the engine anatomy module and reused for buffer-pool latching, lock queues and deadlock chains.
subtopics.visual: A ring whose vnode count and node membership are editable, recolouring exactly the key ranges that change owner, shown beside a contention lane where raising thread count or critical-section length grows the same lock's wait chain and stalls its holders.

subtopics.title: ScanLab and the site-wide engine selector
subtopics.covers: The shared query/scan bench that access paths, index selection, EXPLAIN and analytical storage subtopics reuse — the table generator, the workload description, the cost model panel — and the engine selector whose choice persists across every page offering a cross-engine comparison, including how a module declares which engines it supports and how an unsupported engine degrades.
subtopics.visual: A scan bench where switching the engine selector re-renders the same query's access path, cost model and plan text in the chosen engine, with a badge showing the selection persisting as the learner navigates to another comparison page.

subtopics.title: The toy engine kit: parser, instrumented executor and planner
subtopics.covers: The shared teaching engine behind the query-processing modules and the build-a-toy-engine capstones — a small SQL parser producing an inspectable AST, a pull-based executor instrumented to emit per-operator tuple counts, timings and spills, and a planner exposing rewrite and cost stages as steppable state.
subtopics.visual: A single query stepped from text through AST, logical plan, rewrite, cost search and physical execution, where each stage is editable and a change at any stage propagates forward so the learner sees an optimization rule change the operator tree and the tuple counters.

subtopics.title: The capstone simulator runtime
subtopics.covers: The one runtime the capstones, the readiness checklist and the change classifier all drive — a described topology, a workload generator, an injectable fault library, clocks and queues, and a scoring panel reporting latency percentiles, error budget and cost — and the interface a module implements to plug a new scenario into it.
subtopics.visual: One topology run under three scenarios from different modules, showing that the same runtime produces the capstone's latency tradeoff, the checklist's failed-restore incident and the classifier's lock-window stall, with the scenario definition shown side by side with its result.

subtopics.title: Build order, ownership and the reuse ledger
subtopics.covers: The dependency order in which primitives must be built before the modules that layer on them — PageView and ContentionLab before Part 2, TimelineEditor before Part 4, MessageTimeline and RingView before Parts 6 through 9 — who owns each primitive and each fixture, the ledger recording every subtopic that consumes them so a change can be assessed, the rule for proposing a new primitive versus extending an existing one, and the accessibility, bundle-size and determinism budgets every component must meet.
subtopics.visual: A dependency graph of primitives, fixtures and consuming subtopics where selecting any node highlights every page a change would break, with a near-duplicate detector flagging proposed components whose props overlap an existing primitive above a threshold.
